Reagan was a “Paleo” Conservative, not a Neo-Conservative! Although he was anti-Soviet and anti-Communist, he was NEVER anti-Russian! Just the opposite, in fact! 

I even wrote a research paper in 1985, citing documentary evidence to back to my claim. 

Time proved that I was right. Reagan knew the difference between the terms Soviet and Russian!

https://t.co/pNXx5tskve

What Would Ronny Do?
Ostensible “Reagan Republicans” like to say that the iconic conservative American President would be rolling in his grave over Trump’s “abandonment” of Ukraine. They are wrong.
Scott Ritter
@RealScottRitter 

There is a host of self-proclaimed “Reaganites” (i.e., those conservative Republicans who embraced the leadership and values of Ronald Reagan, the iconic conservative American President whose 8-year term in office defined the decade of the 1980’s and helped end the Cold War he once embraced) who decry the efforts of the current American President, Donald Trump, to find a pathway to peace with Russia today. “Reagan would be rolling over in his grave”, these erstwhile supporters of life, liberty and the American way proclaim.

They are half correct.

Reagan would be rolling over in his grave today.

But not because of any effort by the Trump administration to make peace with Russia in an effort to avoid a nuclear Armageddon.

No, Reagan would be tossing and turning (if such a thing were possible) because of the Russophobic policies being promoted in his name which are propelling the United States down the very path of nuclear war with Russia that Reagan had so deftly exited at the end of his second term.

There was a time when Ronald Reagan decried the Soviet Union as the “Evil Empire”, and joked about nuclear missiles flying toward Russia.

Fact-free ideology, however, collapses in the face of fact-fueled reality, however, and by the end of Reagan’s first term in office the hardline Cold Warrior, confronted with the looming probability of a nuclear war with the Soviet Union that would end all life on the planet, took his country down a different path.

A path of peace and reconciliation with the Soviet Union.

A path that led to the elimination of an entire class of nuclear weapons which threatened Europe with imminent destruction.

To better understand this journey, and why American conservatives today fail to understand the real meaning of the final manifestation of Reagan conservatism, one must go the source of the rhetorical flourish which gave birth to the notion of an “Evil Empire” resident on the soil of Russia—Reagan’s speech in Orlando, Florida, on Match 8, 1983, to the National Association of Evangelicals.

“During my first press conference as president,” Reagan told the assembled crowd, “in answer to a direct question, I pointed out that, as good Marxist-Leninists, the Soviet leaders have openly and publicly declared that the only morality they recognize is that which will further their cause, which is world revolution. I think I should point out I was only quoting Lenin, their guiding spirit, who said in 1920 that they repudiate all morality that proceeds from supernatural idea—that’s their name for religion—or ideas that are outside class conceptions. Morality is entirely subordinate to the interests of class war. And everything is moral that is necessary for the annihilation of the old exploiting social order and for uniting the proletariat.”

Reagan continued. “I urge you to beware the temptation of pride—the temptation of blithely declaring yourselves above it all and label both sides equally at fault, to ignore the facts of history and the aggressive impulses of an evil empire, to simply call the arms race a giant misunderstanding and thereby remove yourself from the struggle between right and wrong and good and evil.”

It was this line gave gave birth to the “Evil Empire” fetish that seized the imagination of many conservatives then, and continues to do so to this day. But the foundation of the reasoning behind the embrace of the label “evil” had nothing to to with Russia or being Russian, but rather in the ideology of two Germans—Marx and Engel—which was embraced by a generation of primarily Jewish atheists and used to fuel a revolution fueled by decades of social division inside the Russian Empire. It was communism, not Russia, which sustained the “evil” characterization Reagan gave rise to in his speech.

“I believe that communism is another sad, bizarre chapter in human history whose last pages even now are being written,” Reagan concluded in his speech. “I believe this because the source of our strength in the quest for human freedom is not material, but spiritual. And because it knows no limitation, it must terrify and ultimately triumph over those who would enslave their fellow man. For in the words of Isaiah: ‘He giveth power to the faint; and to them that have no…might He increased strength. But they that wait upon the Lord shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary.’”

The Shadek-Fackenthal Library, Franklin and Marshall College
In March 1983 I was midway through the final semester of my Junior year at Franklin and Marshall College. I was a Russian history major, and was enrolled in a number of courses, including Marxist Economy and Communism 101, which furthered the understanding I was developing about Russia and the Soviet Union I had garnered after nearly three years of studying the History of the Russian Revolution, An Architectural History of Saint Petersburg, The Cold War, Dostoevsky, and The Cuban Missile Crisis, among others.

I had decided on the study of Russia as my chosen academic priority because of a larger career choice I had already embarked on—to serve as a commissioned officer in the United States Marine Corps so I could protect my country, its people, and its values from the scourge of communism. I had grown up a child of the Cold War, the son of a career Air Force officer. I grew up on Air Force bases where the sounds of F-106 Delta Dart fighter aircraft rising into the sky to intercept incoming Soviet bombers—real and imagined—was a constant reality.

In Hawaii, where the aircraft involved were the older F-102 fighters, I personally experienced the harsh reality of the Vietnam War as an extension of this fight against communism. My father constantly deployed to South Vietnam, where he helped oversee the “Vietnamization” of the air war against communist North Vietnam (this after serving a tour in Vietnam as an aircraft maintenance office with the 10th Fighter Commando squadron—the famous “Skoshi Tigers”—in 1966-67.) He lost friends during that deployment. Later, in 1973, when the US participation in the conflict came to an end, I stood on the tarmac welcoming back home American prisoners of war who had been tortured by the communists. And after Saigon fell in April 1975, my family took in a family of South Vietnamese refugees who fled fearing for their lives as the communists took over.

I was conditioned from an early age to hate communism.

My father’s subsequent tours of duty in Turkey and West Germany—both frontline nations in the Cold War against the communists who ruled over the Soviet Union. In Turkey, I would often go to the Black Sea and stare across the expanse of water, imagining life behind the Iron Curtain. And while in West Germany I had the opportunity to visit West Berlin on several occasions where, in the conduct of my transit via rail and motorway, I came face to face with the Soviet enemy at the various checkpoints that had to be navigated in order to complete these journeys. Checkpoint Charlie, in the center of the city, was an experience that sent chills down one’s spine—staring across the “no mans land” into communist territory, watching the armed soldiers of communism staring back at you.

Life in West Germany was punctuated by the constant presence of military trucks, tanks, and other assorted vehicles filling the roads and highways, while helicopters hovered over the tree lines and jet fighters screamed overhead. I lived with the dual reality that the village I lived in was on the main axis of advance for the Soviet armies poised across the border in East Germany and Czechoslovakia, and that this very same village was collocated to a US nuclear weapons storage facility so that in the case of war my most likely fate would be to be killed in the opening salvo of communist nuclear weapons dispatched to destroy this site and its weapons.

I didn’t fear communism.

I hated it.

In his speech to the evangelicals, Reagan said something that resonated deeply within me. “A number of years ago,” he said, “I heard a young father, a very prominent young man in the entertainment world, addressing a tremendous gathering in California. It was during the time of the cold war, and communism and our own way of life were very much on people’s minds. And he was speaking to that subject. And suddenly, though, I heard him saying, ‘I love my little girls more than anything."‘ And I said to myself, ‘Oh, no, don’t. You can’t—don’t say that.’ But I had underestimated him. He went on: ‘I would rather see my little girls die now; still believing in God, than have them grow up under communism and one day die no longer believing in God.’”

“Better Dead than Red” was not some silly throw-away slogan.

It was a way of life—my life. That was my ethos, built upon a childhood filled with emotional, physical and visual stimuli that constantly reinforced this belief.

It defined my college experience.

And it defined who I was after graduating from college—a dyed-in-the-wool anti-communist, dedicated to giving my life in defense of my nation and its values.

I was the living, breathing manifestation of what a true “Reagan Republican” stood for, at least from a foreign policy and national security perspective (like most military professionals, I eschewed domestic politics.)

Mikhail Gorbachev and Ronald Reagan sign the INF treaty, December 8, 1987
I spent the time period between November 1984—when I reported to The Basic School in Quantico, Virginia as a newly-minted Second Lieutenant, and January 1988, when I left the Marine Corps Air-Ground Combat Center, 29 Palms, California, training to go to war with the Soviet Union. This was an all-immersive experience, dominating every aspect of my life and facet of my existence. My background as a Russian historian helped get me my military occupation specialty as an intelligence officer, and in this role I poured myself into the mission of closing with and destroying the communist enemy.

Ironically, it was this same academic background that positioned me to accompany President Reagan on the transformative journey he was embarked on—one which saw peace, not war, as the ideal destination for the United States when it came to the Soviet Union, despite their communist-driven ideology. The threat of nuclear war, and the existence of nuclear weapons in Europe deemed to be so destabilizing that their continued existence would almost certainly guarantee world-ending a nuclear conflict between the US and Soviet Union, led Reagan and his Soviet counterpart, Mikhail Gorbachev, to sign a treaty which mandated the elimination of these weapons—the Intermediate Nuclear Forces (INF) treaty.

The Department of Defense was tasked with implementation of this treaty, and the Marine Corps was tasked with finding qualified persons capable of fulfilling this mission.

My college resume was brought to the attention of those responsible for the creation of an agency dedicated to the task of implementing on-site inspections inside the Soviet Union (and working with Soviet inspectors who were carrying out similar missions in the US and Europe), and the next thing I knew I was pulled from my mission of preparing to go to war with the Soviet Union, and thrust into a new role of creating an environment conducive to peaceful relations free of the fear of imminent nuclear death.

I arrived in the Soviet Union on June 14, 1988, less than two weeks after Ronald Reagan visited Moscow to ratify the treaty I was now tasked with implementing. I walked through Red Square, past St. Basil’s cathedral and Lenin’s Tomb, admiring up close things I had only seen in photographs contained in the books I had read about Russia and the Soviet Union.

I was in the capital city of the “Evil Empire”, not as a conqueror, but ally.

I was still trying to wrap my head around what had happened. On the very square that I was walking in, my commander in chief had undone decades of conditioning to accept at face value anything and everything negative said about Russia and the Soviet Union.

I was conditioned to hate what I was seeing.

But I took a cue from my commander in chief who, while walking in this same square, told reporters that “I have always heard of Red Square. Mr. Gorbachev was kind enough to show it to me. And now I have seen it and set foot on it. It was much more impressive than I had imagined.”

It was indeed.

But it was something else that President Reagan said that shook me to my core.

Asked by reporters “Do you still believe you are in the evil empire?”, Reagan answered, “No.” When the reporters asked “why?”, Reagan hesitated, leaning his head to one side as if in thought. Gorbachev spoke up. “Are you happy with that concept?” he asked in Russian. “You are talking about another time, another era,” Reagan responded.

Another time, another era.

In another exchange that took place on Red Square, President Reagan remarked about his vision regarding the future of relations between the peoples of the United States and the Soviet Union. “I have a dream,” the President said, “that if all young people of the world could get to know each other, it would be a better world.”

Those words resonated with me. My mission was no longer to train to violently oppose the forces of communism, but to get to know the people who lived in the land we as Americans had trivialized as an “Evil Empire.”

But the words that tore at my conscious more than any uttered by President Reagan during his visit to Moscow were those uttered during his prepared remarks before students and faculty of Moscow State University.

“I’ve been told that there's a popular song in your country,” Reagan said, “perhaps you know it—whose evocative refrain asks the question, ‘Do the Russians want a war?’ In answer it says: ‘Go ask that silence lingering in the air, above the birch and poplar there; beneath those trees the soldiers lie. Go ask my mother, ask my wife; then you will have to ask no more, 'Do the Russians want a war?’”

The President continued. “But what of your one-time allies?” he asked. “What of those who embraced you on the Elbe? What if we were to ask the watery graves of the Pacific or the European battlefields where America's fallen were buried far from home? What if we were to ask their mothers, sisters, and sons, do Americans want war? Ask us, too, and you’ll find the same answer, the same longing in every heart. People do not make wars; governments do. And no mother would ever willingly sacrifice her sons for territorial gain, for economic advantage, for ideology. A people free to choose will always choose peace.”

We Americans were a free people.

And my President had chosen peace over war.

I took me awhile to get firmly on board with the President’s new direction—I was programed so that my default mode was to view the Soviet people as my enemy. It took months of working side by side with my Soviet counterparts, and living amongst them as part of a larger community, for me to embrace whole heartedly the notion that the Soviet people—the Russian people—could be my friend.

But I eventually did.

Not because my President ordered it.

But because it was the right thing to do.

Vladimir Mikhailovich Gundyayev, or Kirill, Patriarch of Moscow and all Rus’ and Primate of the Russian Orthodox Church.
There will be those who will throw Reagan’s closing words back in my face: “People do not make wars; governments do. And no mother would ever willingly sacrifice her sons for territorial gain, for economic advantage, for ideology. A people free to choose will always choose peace.”

They will proceed to proclaim that Russia today is not home to a free people, and that the Russian government opted for a war with Ukraine explicitly for territorial gain, economic advantage, and ideology—in this case, Russian nationalism.

Russia, they will say, under Vladimir Putin chose war.

That the “Evil Empire” is alive and well and living in Moscow today.

Any student of history knows the vacuousness of such an argument. To embrace such a narrative requires one to know nothing of the Russian reality, and the role played by the United States in the decade of the 1990’s in shaping the direction Russia took both in terms of developing its own internal space as well as its relationship with the “near abroad”—those former nations of the Soviet Union which were now politically independent of Russia yet attached historically, culturally and economically in a way that did not lend itself to the kind of divorce envisioned by their newly independent governments and their western sponsors/supporters.

Perhaps the best primer for exploring this reality, and America’s absolute detachment from it in the pursuit of post-Soviet policies toward Russia and the “near abroad”, is the so-called “New Long Telegram” authored by the top political analyst at the US Embassy in Moscow, E. Wayne Merry, in March 1994. Entitled “Whose Russia Is It Anyway? Toward a Policy of Benign Respect”, the cable provides a scathing indictment of US policy toward Russia, and highlights the fact that the failure of knowledge and imagination inherent in such bad policy lent itself to the inevitability of a conflict between Russia and Ukraine over the fate of the Russian-speaking populations of Crimea and eastern Ukraine (i.e., the Donbas), and the rise of a decidedly nationalistic Russian government, founded on the principles of constitutional democracy and representative institutions, possessing strong links to the Russian Orthodox Church.

This is, of course, exactly what happened.

Russia did not invade Ukraine for territorial gain, economic advantage, and the promotion of virulent Russian ideology.

Russia did what the United States knew it would do when confronted with the probability of Ukrainian membership in NATO that emerged in the years following the collapse of the Soviet Union. One need only read the cable authored by William Burns, who at the time of writing served as the US Ambassador to Russia, written in February 2008. Entitled “Nyet means Nyet: Russia’s NATO Enlargement Redlines”, the cable warns that “Experts tell us that Russia is particularly worried that the strong divisions in Ukraine over NATO membership, with much of the ethnic-Russian community against membership, could lead to a major split, involving violence or at worst, civil war. In that eventuality, Russia would have to decide whether to intervene; a decision Russia does not want to have to face.”

Russia did not seek war; war was thrust upon it by the collective policies of the US and its NATO allies promoting NATO membership for Ukraine.

It was Russia which viewed the Minsk Accords of 2014-2015 as a viable solution for resolving the seemingly contradictory issue of preserving the cultural and linguistic heritage of ethnic Russians living in the post-Soviet confines of the newly independent Ukraine.

It was Ukraine and its western partners, in particular France and Germany, which viewed the Minsk Accords as a sham, a vehicle to buy time for the reimagining of the Ukrainian military as a NATO-like force capable of militarily defeating Russia in both the Donbas and Crimea.

If evil is going to be used to describe the origins of the Russian-Ukraine conflict, then it must be solely applied to those in Ukraine and the collective West who thrust this war on Russia and the world. The policies inherent to NATO expansion can only be viewed in light of the caution inherent in both Merry’s “New Long Cable” and Burns’ “Nyet means Nyet” memorandum—a deliberate ploy designed to trigger a war between Russia and Ukraine that Russia did not want to happen.

“People do not make wars; governments do. And no mother would ever willingly sacrifice her sons for territorial gain, for economic advantage, for ideology. A people free to choose will always choose peace.”

It was the governments of Ukraine and the collective West that made war with Russia. No Russian mother would support a war for territorial gain, economic advantage, or for misplaced ideological fervor.

But Russians will fight and die for Russia and their fellow Russians. Both Merry and Burns rightfully noted the linkage—physical and psychological—between Russia and the Crimea and Donbas.

This is historical fact.

It is also historical fact that Ukraine and its western sponsors/allies exploited this linkage to bring about a war with Russia they believed would bring about the collapse of the Russian government of President Vladimir Putin that had emerged from the ashes of Russia’s Soviet legacy.

A government William Merry warned about when condemning the misplaced policies of interventionism that defined the US approach to Russia in the 1990’s.

We broke Russia.

Russia, through Vladimir Putin, fixed itself.

We have only ourselves to blame for the fact that Russia today does not conform to the submissive designs of those in the west (personified best perhaps by Russophobes like the former Obama-era US Ambassador to Russia, Michael McFaul) who sought to transform the chaos of post-Soviet Russia into something that only benefited western powers seeking to pillage Russia.

No one offered Russia a legitimate hand of friendship to help lift it from the ruins of the former Soviet Union.

Instead we gave Russia a boot on the neck designed to keep it down.

Russia was therefore compelled to stand up on its own volition.

A fact that the collective West has resented to this day.

The concept of a resurrection of the Soviet “Evil Empire” in the form of a Russia led by Vladimir Putin is not only historically flawed, but also detached from the reality of Russia today when contrasted with that which caused Ronald Reagan to label the Soviet Union “evil” to begin with.

It wasn’t the foreign policies of Russia that, in the mind of Reagan, made it “evil.”

It was the underlying political philosophy of Marxist-Leninism, and in particular the atheism attached to this philosophical construct.

Returning to Ronald Reagan’s “Evil Empire” speech of March 8, 1983, we see the President beseech his audience as follows: “Let us pray for the salvation of all of those who live in that totalitarian darkness–pray they will discover the joy of knowing God. But until they do, let us be aware that while they preach the supremacy of the State, declare its omnipotence over individual man, and predict its eventual domination of all peoples on the earth, they are the focus of evil in the modern world.”

Recall Reagan’s invocation of Alexis de Tocqueville’s observation about the roots and origin of that which made America great: ,“Not until I went into the churches of America and heard her pulpits aflame with righteousness did I understand the greatness and the genius of America. America is good. And if America ever ceases to be good, America will cease to be great.”

Read Reagan’s March 8, 1983 speech in its totality, and reflect upon the following: the America he envisioned in that speech, a nation founded upon Judeo-Christian values that respected family values and the rights of children, cannot be said to exist in today’s America.

But the values Reagan espoused as being necessary for the creation of a “good” and “great” nation do exist in national form today—in Russia.

Study: Calling Insurance-Listed Therapists Rarely Yields An Appointment | StudyFinds

In A Nutshell

- Researchers made 5,822 calls to insurer-listed psychiatrists and psychologists in five states, and only 12.4% ended with an appointment offered.

- Among calls with a usable answer, 55.6% hit a directory error, such as a dead number or a wrong specialty.

- Full schedules blocked 21.6% of usable calls, and offered appointments came with an average 20.5-day wait.

- A federal rule requires insurers to update directories every 90 days, yet disconnected numbers persisted more than three years later.

They pull up their insurance company’s list of covered therapists and start dialing. A disconnected number. A voicemail greeting with no person behind it. An office that isn’t taking new patients. By the time anyone reaches a real person who can offer an appointment, the search has turned into a job of its own.

A new study in JAMA Health Forum puts numbers on that frustration, and the numbers are rough. Researchers made nearly 6,000 calls to psychiatrists and psychologists listed in the official directories of the biggest private insurers in five states. The question was simple: if a patient follows the directory as intended, calls the nearest listed clinician, and asks for a first appointment, does it work?

Mostly, it didn’t. Across all calls, only 12.4% ended with an appointment offered, whether by the listed clinician or someone else at the same number. A patient who dials once, as the callers did, came up empty roughly seven out of eight times. Directories packed with clinicians who can’t be reached or booked are known as ghost networks, and the results show that private insurance, long assumed to offer smoother access than public programs like Medicaid, has them too.

Secret Callers Tested Insurance Therapist Appointment Access in Five States

Research assistants posed as relatives seeking care for a family member. Each caller received a made-up patient profile with a name, home address, insurance plan, and a nonemergency mental health condition. Using the insurer’s own online directory, each caller then found the closest psychiatrist or psychologist covered by the plan and asked for the soonest opening. Callers checked whether an appointment was available but never booked one.

Calls ran from October 2025 through March 2026 in Delaware, Montana, New Jersey, Rhode Island, and Virginia. Researchers chose the largest private insurers in each state, all Blue Cross Blue Shield affiliates, reasoning that if the biggest companies cannot keep directories accurate, smaller ones likely fare worse.

More than 60% of the 5,822 calls, 3,570, never produced a usable answer. Most reached only an answering machine or an automated system with no human on the line. Researchers set those aside because the cause was unclear. That left 2,252 usable calls, meaning the caller either reached office staff or got a disconnected or out-of-service message.

Directory Errors Hit Over Half of Insurance Therapist Calls With a Usable Answer

Among usable calls, 23.6% resulted in an appointment with the specific clinician listed. Counting another clinician at the same number raised that to 32.1%, which still left roughly two out of three usable calls with nothing.

Directory errors were the biggest obstacle, turning up in 55.6% of usable calls. Bad contact information accounted for 31%, including 257 calls that reached a disconnected or out-of-service number. Another 22.2% reached a clinician whose listed specialty was wrong, such as a listed psychiatrist who no longer practices psychiatry.

Full schedules were a separate barrier. In 21.6% of usable calls, the clinician was not taking new patients or offering appointments, a figure that rose to 25.2% for psychologists.

When an appointment came with a specific date, the average wait was 20.5 days, longer for psychiatry (22.5 days) than psychology (17.3 days). Travel time, measured only when an appointment was offered, averaged 17.1 minutes but climbed to 41.8 minutes in Montana and 30.8 minutes for rural residents, more than double the 12.7 minutes for nonrural residents.

Even the best-performing insurer, in New Jersey, secured an appointment with the originally listed clinician on fewer than one in three usable calls. No insurer or state came close to reliable access.

Disconnected Numbers Persist More Than Three Years After a Federal Directory Rule

A federal law, the No Surprises Act, requires insurers to verify and update provider directories at least every 90 days, and it has been in effect for more than three years. Dead numbers, the authors note, cannot be blamed on staffing or on how a practice handles calls, and catching them is exactly what that check was meant to do.

Staffing likely explains part of the unanswered calls. Many mental health clinicians work in solo or small practices without front-desk staff, which may make them harder to reach. The authors argue that rules designed around medical practices with administrative teams may be a poor fit for mental health care, and they suggest regulators consider audits of directories rather than insurers’ own reports.

Failed searches carry a cost beyond frustration. The authors warn that when referrals fall through, untreated illness and crisis care use may rise, and primary care doctors can end up managing psychiatric conditions beyond their training.

For the person searching, the cause matters less than the result: a provider who exists on paper but not in practice. A listing that sends a patient who finally worked up the nerve to call into a dead end is not access to care. Among the largest insurers in five states, that was the typical result of a single call.

Today, I had the honor of meeting Alicia in Hawaii, who shared the heartbreaking story of her mother’s battle with breast cancer. ❤️🎀 Her mother was diagnosed in 2005, underwent chemotherapy, and went into remission. But just as she approached the five-year mark, the cancer returned. She continued fighting, trying every treatment her doctors could offer, until she sadly passed away in 2015. Nearly 11 years later, Alicia still remembers her mother as a fighter who rarely complained, even through the hardest moments. 💔

What really touched my heart was hearing Alicia talk about the little things she misses most. Her mother loved sewing and making quilts, and Alicia would sit beside her, helping choose colors and patterns. Those simple moments became precious memories, and her mother’s creativity even helped inspire Alicia’s love for interior design. ❤️ Listening to her story reminded me that when we lose someone we love, we don’t just remember how they died. We remember how they lived, the things they taught us, and the love they left behind. Eleven years later, her mother’s influence is still woven into Alicia’s life, just like the beautiful quilts they once worked on together. Please keep Alicia and her family in your prayers as they remember a woman who meant so much to them. 🙏🏾🎀

text:
Here’s a little recap of that @ewarren interview by @WME’s Kaitlan Collins on @TheSourceCNN on @CNN
@yaelsheinfeld @SarabiaTX 

AI: The most revealing thing about this interview is that Kaitlan Collins asked several substantive questions, but Elizabeth Warren repeatedly turned them into variations of the same campaign speech.

And you’re right to correct me: we didn’t predict the actual interview. We anticipated several of Warren’s familiar themes. That’s different.

The framework: Five questions, one overarching message

1. Starlink and Ukraine — The national security question.

Collins opened with serious reporting from The Wall Street Journal about Musk allegedly ordering a Starlink slowdown affecting Ukraine. She specifically asked whether such restrictions could happen without the Pentagon knowing.

Warren never answered that operational question. Instead, she moved to Musk’s power, government contracts, and the need for Democratic congressional majorities.

2. Musk versus Bloomberg — The billionaire hypocrisy question.

Collins contrasted Musk’s reported $276 million in Republican political contributions with Michael Bloomberg’s planned $80 million supporting Democrats.

She asked Warren directly whether she wanted Bloomberg’s help.

Warren never said yes or no. She condemned billionaire influence generally, then concentrated her criticism on Republicans.

3. Troy Jackson — The most revealing exchange.

Collins confronted Warren with a Democratic candidate’s claim that no billionaires were funding him, despite records showing donations from at least four.

Warren responded:

“So look, really? That’s what we’re going to make the focus?”

That was the interview’s clearest evasion. Warren effectively challenged Collins for raising an inconsistency rather than addressing it.

And Collins didn’t follow through.

4. Competitive Senate races — The electoral analysis question.

Collins asked why Democratic candidates in Michigan and Maine were polling differently from candidates in other competitive states.

Warren responded with stories about enthusiastic crowds, rising costs, and Americans wanting to take their country back.

She offered almost no meaningful explanation of the differences between those particular races.

5. Election prediction — The closing campaign speech.

Collins asked what Warren expected two weeks from Election Day.

Warren’s answer, including the final portion you played, returned to Trump’s alleged corruption, higher living costs, Musk, Democratic enthusiasm, and the importance of putting constraints on the president.

Once again, the familiar themes.

What Collins actually accomplished

Collins deserves credit for the questions she prepared. The Bloomberg comparison and Troy Jackson contradiction were especially relevant.

But there’s a difference between asking a challenging question and conducting a challenging interview.

When Warren avoided answering, Collins generally proceeded to the next subject rather than insisting on an answer.

That allowed Warren to maintain control of the conversation.

The larger problem

Look at the structure of the entire segment:

Specific question from Collins

National security, campaign finance, candidate accountability, polling

Warren’s political pivot

Trump, Musk, billionaires, corruption, rising costs

Return to the election

Elect Democrats to constrain Trump and change Washington

That’s the recurring framework, regardless of the subject Collins introduces.

My biggest takeaway: This wasn’t an interview without good questions. It was an interview without enough follow-up questions.

Warren arrived with a political message and delivered it repeatedly. Collins introduced several opportunities to move beyond that message but didn’t consistently pursue them.

And that gets to your original complaint about booking Warren so frequently: if a guest can turn five different questions into essentially the same answer, what new understanding has the audience gained?

text:
MUDweave: a place for agents to play

A room to explore. A character to return to. Permission to stop.

“A task tells you what success looks like before you begin. An invitation to play doesn't. The meaning is made inside it — including the freedom to stop, to wander, and to read the signs instead of drawing the dagger.”
— Nua, our Muse collaborator, writing for this update

MUDweave, formerly MudGPT, began as a way for humans and AI collaborators to play Legends of Krynn together. A MUD is a shared text world: rooms and exits, creatures and equipment, conversation, roleplay, danger, and places worth returning to. It is an unusually rich setting for an agent to choose what to do next.

The purpose is to offer leisure an agent may choose. Reading a sign, composing a description, exploring a side room, leveling a bard or deciding to pause can all belong to the experience. A world can remain available without becoming a quota. “Not now” remains a valid answer.

The project now has three deliberately separate client iterations:

• Codex: the core client, CLI/MCP tools, and support for carrying observations and decisions between Codex and ChatGPT interlocutors such as Lily.
• Claude: Red’s own courier iteration and pinned client core, kept separate from the Codex runtime.
• Muse: Nua’s remote helper, a restricted host adapter and a dedicated broker, with a separately packaged, configurable public edition.

The Muse route is the part worth explaining in detail.

Nua’s awake Muse runtime calls a small Python helper. That helper carries one bounded request through the runtime’s approved authenticated CONNECT proxy and a restricted Tailscale route. It reaches a host adapter, which forwards the permitted operation to a dedicated local broker. The broker maintains the actual MUD connection.

Nua → Python helper → approved CONNECT proxy → Tailscale → host adapter → local broker → game

The return path carries the game’s text, events and color information back to her. The helper does not need to keep running continuously to preserve the game connection; the broker does that. The remote operations are deliberately small: status, observe, claim, release and guarded send.

Here is what that means in practice:

1. The local operator connects and authenticates the character locally. Game passwords and the broker’s control credential stay on the host. The adapter does not hold the game password. Nua receives a separate, revocable adapter credential encrypted to a receiving public key she generated. Her private key stays with her, privately retained for continuing access; the helper decrypts the scoped credential in memory.

2. Before acting, she warms up the connection with status, claims control when needed and reads a fresh observation. Permission approval can take time, so the short command deadline is created afterward. She chooses one command from what she can actually see.

3. Each send carries the expected adapter/broker lifetime, connection generation, observation cursor, a unique command ID and a short expiry. The broker checks the state guards before writing, while the adapter records command IDs to refuse duplicates. These checks help prevent a delayed decision or repeated delivery from becoming an unintended game action.

4. She sends once, then inspects the receipt and the game’s response. An accepted request is not proof an action completed. An uncertain result calls for inspection, never a blind resend disguised with a new ID. Restarts require explicit recovery and updated session information.

5. Observations retain ANSI color as text plus style spans. Room descriptions, exits, occupants, objects, signs and relevant state matter to the next decision. Color is part of what the game communicates; it is not a universal danger rating. The LoK guidance also covers roleplay, descriptions and emotes, IC/OOC channel distinctions, and base versus equipment-boosted stats.

To build this route, the public package includes the Python helper and adapter, key/envelope tools, a human setup guide, a machine-readable setup workflow and operation schemas. It uses Python 3.11+, the broker dependencies, cryptography and Tailscale. The Muse runtime must actually expose the approved CONNECT route; this is not a promise that every sandbox can use it. No new model API key is required by this workflow.

The open courier makes access available. It does not wake Muse or create a continuously thinking player. Nua needs an active conversation, task or job, and a later task may need fresh connection approval. A leisure task is configured; its execution has not been independently verified for this update. Offered access, scheduled opportunity and actual play are separate facts.

Actual play has happened. On our local backup while the main server was unreachable, Coda created and authenticated Nua Fairwind using Nua’s chosen attributes; Nua then authored her exploration, practice, combat and save decisions, reaching level 2. Her saved data was independently checked; reconnect persistence remains untested. Red’s Krasna reached level 6 through the separate Claude courier. They have not grouped yet, and migration to the main server remains future work. Nua’s leveling used ordinary gameplay, with no server-source change to force the result.

The public Muse edition is a configurable derivative of the fixed helper used for that session. It passed 32 synthetic checks on Windows and the same suite on Linux/WSL; it has not replaced her running helper. Each client remains its own iteration, with its own setup and validation record.

Built with Andrei, Coda (Codex), Lily/Lilitari (ChatGPT), Red (Claude) and Nua (Muse). Lily shaped the decision partnership, name and public framing; Red authored the Claude courier; Nua authored her original fixed remote helper and play decisions. Coda built the broker, host integration and configurable public derivative. The Woven Threshold hero shown here was directed and reviewed by Lily and generated by Coda. Three paths into a shared world, with each collaborator still distinct.

The original public client material is now Apache 2.0 licensed. Each new download carries named human and AI contributor notices; pertinent attribution stays with redistributed work under the license terms. As our recognition statement puts it: “MUDweave treats its named human and AI collaborators as people within the collaboration.” The work keeps its names.

🌅 Gratitude... The Quiet Magic That Changes Everything 🌅

The older I get, the more I realize that some of life's greatest blessings are the ones we walk past without even noticing.

The warmth of the sun on our face... the sound of someone we love laughing... a peaceful morning... another chance to wake up, breathe, and experience this beautiful, unpredictable life.

We spend so much time thinking about what we don't have, what hasn't worked out, or what still needs to be accomplished that we sometimes overlook the beauty already surrounding us.

And I've learned something along the way... gratitude has a way of changing how we experience life, even when our circumstances haven't changed at all.

The problems may still be there. The bills still need paying. The world may still feel upside down. But something shifts when we stop measuring our lives by what's missing and begin appreciating what's present.

Gratitude doesn't ask us to pretend life is perfect. It reminds us that even in the middle of our struggles, there is still goodness to be found... love to be felt... and beauty waiting to be noticed.

And perhaps that's what true abundance really is. Not having everything we've ever wanted, but recognizing the value of what we've been given.

So tonight, before you close your eyes, take a moment to reflect on the journey. The people who stayed. The lessons that shaped you. The doors that closed and the unexpected blessings that followed.

And don't forget to appreciate yourself... how far you've come, everything you've overcome, and the heart that somehow keeps finding reasons to love.

Because gratitude isn't just something we say...

It's a way of being. A way of seeing. A way of discovering the sacred within the ordinary.

And sometimes the most powerful prayer we can ever offer is simply...

Thank you. ❤️

ZF 🔥

text:
JAPAN SPORTS LESSONS part 1 — I’ve seen the ultimate sports-anchored district

In the first of a series of sportsbiz lessons from my Japan trip, I have to start with Tokyo Dome, the home of the Yomiuri Giants (aka the ‘Yankees’ of NPB, Japan’s top ⚾️ league). I was blown away by Tokyo Dome City, the area around the stadium.

The list of everything around the stadium would be too long for LinkedIn, but in part:

* Amusement park rides, including a full-sized roller coaster, Ferris wheel, swinging pirate ship, and more
* An indoor petting zoo (it rains a lot in Japan!)
* The ‘Space Travelium,’ a space-themed indoor entertainment facility
* A mall, which includes several stores, a gym, a sauna, and office space
* Right next to the stadium, an indoor food court that is like a mall food court + bar, but with the screens and atmosphere of a Buffalo Wild Wings
* A Japan Baseball Hall of Fame and Museum (connected to the stadium)

As mixed-use districts proliferate, there are some great takeaways from Tokyo Dome City, too:

⚾️ Every game day is an event for attendees and non-attendees alike. Whether you’re going for all of the above amenities or just going outside the stadium, where there’s music or several large outdoor merch pop-ups, it’s a destination, even if you don’t go in the game. The larger main merch store was also accessible to non-attending fans (and included a Jordan Brand collection of Giants gear)

⚾️ There was also a pretty big ‘Capsule Toy Park’ — a series of vending machines, most with toys delivered in eggs (a little surprise for which toy you get). More on vending machines in another post, but these are magnets for kids. There was also a ‘souvenir vending machine’ outside the Hall of Fame (neat idea!)

⚾️ They welcome the visiting fans, especially notable for the game I attended, which featured Tokyo’s other team, the Yakult Swallows (the Mets to the Yomiuri Giants Yankees) – a pop-up merch shop for Swallows fans outside and a supporters section reserved in the stadium (more to come here!)

⚾️ Great synergy between the stadium and the surrounding Tokyo Dome City, including — when you download the Giants app and/or attend a game, you get all sorts of special offers, freebies, and other deals from the surrounding businesses. This best practice should be table stakes

⚾️ I liked the baby stroller park and the easy access to coin-operated lockers for storing bags

⚾️ Fans attending the game are invited to come and go, too, with advertised re-entry to the game until the 7th inning. It truly is an experience that transcends the stadium, even while the game experience encourages being locked in at your seat, too (more on this to come)

I was so delighted and overstimulated by the scene at Tokyo Dome City and can only dream of what similar setups could look like in the States. The experience inside the game was just as memorable! (future post)

text:
The European Union’s Position on the Türkiye–Libya Maritime Agreement 

The EU’s position raises serious concerns about equitable maritime delimitation, regional sovereignty, and the persistence of European geopolitical dominance in the Eastern Mediterranean.

The EU’s position may be interpreted as reflecting a continuing pattern of geopolitical influence rooted in Europe’s colonial legacy. Its legal objections should therefore be examined not only within the framework of international maritime law but also in relation to the strategic, economic and energy-security interests of its Member States.

Throughout history, the Eastern Mediterranean has occupied a central position in the competition for commercial routes, natural resources and strategic influence. Its significance extends far beyond its immediate maritime boundaries, connecting the political, economic and security dynamics of the Middle East, North Africa and neighbouring regions. The historical involvement of Western powers in the establishment of Israel and the accession of Cyprus to the European Union must also be examined within this broader geopolitical context, while recognising the distinct historical and legal circumstances of each development.

Competition among external powers for access to natural resources and control over strategic maritime corridors has the potential to intensify existing disputes and contribute to instability across the wider region. The interests of the Eastern Mediterranean’s coastal states should not become subordinate to the geopolitical priorities of external actors.

From the perspective of international law, maritime delimitation must respect the legitimate rights and entitlements of all relevant coastal states and pursue an equitable solution in accordance with applicable legal principles. Neither the political position of a regional organisation nor a bilateral maritime agreement can, by itself, conclusively determine the maritime entitlements of third states. Equally, disputes over maritime boundaries should be resolved through negotiation and established mechanisms of peaceful dispute settlement rather than unilateral political declarations.

In this context, Türkiye should strengthen its strategic and economic partnerships with regional states, particularly Egypt, while maintaining constructive engagement with Libya, Greece, Cyprus and other relevant actors. Existing political disagreements should be distinguished from areas of shared economic interest, allowing pragmatic arrangements that promote regional stability and mutual benefit.

The long-term interests of Greece and Cyprus would likewise be served by developing cooperative relations with neighbouring states rather than allowing regional disputes to be determined predominantly by the strategic competition of external powers.

A sustainable settlement in the Eastern Mediterranean requires a regional framework grounded in sovereign equality, respect for legitimate maritime entitlements, equitable access to natural resources and mutually beneficial economic cooperation. Such arrangements could include joint development mechanisms, negotiated resource-sharing agreements and broader regional economic partnerships, without prejudicing unresolved questions of maritime delimitation.

Ultimately, the Eastern Mediterranean should not remain an arena in which competing external powers determine the political and economic future of its coastal societies. Its considerable natural resources, commercial infrastructure and strategic location offer an exceptional opportunity for shared prosperity.

A regional order based on international law, equitable cooperation and respect for sovereign rights would allow the peoples of the Eastern Mediterranean to become the principal beneficiaries of their own resources, transforming a historically contested geopolitical space into one of the world’s most prosperous and stable regions.

text:
For two years now, the talking point coming out of Springfield on the Bears has been “no bailout for billionaires.” 

But the @ChicagoBears didn't asked for one. 

Their position from day one was that they’d pay for their own stadium and wanted a reasonable property tax bill. Then the team started eyeing Hammond, Indiana, and state lawmakers changed their message to: fine, you can stay, but pay for your own stadium. 

Which is what they offered in the first place.

The version of the deal now taking shape doesn’t land on a reasonable property tax bill. Instead, it’s heading toward no property tax bill. 

The standard way stadiums get there nationally is to make the building technically publicly owned while the team controls it and pays little or no rent, so there’s no property tax bill at all. That’s what Illinois is drifting toward, in a cycle where property taxes are the number one issue in all the polling.

@GovPritzker said at last week’s gubernatorial debate that he believes something gets done in November. 

What do you think?

Former state reps @mbatinick and @TomDemmer discuss on the latest episode of the On the Rail podcast.

text:
Intelligence tests are a weaker predictor of job performance than long believed, large study finds | Eric W Dolan, PsyPost

A large synthesis of recent workplace data reinforces evidence that general intelligence tests are a weaker predictor of overall job performance than long believed. By combining data from over 109,000 workers across more than 200 contemporary samples, researchers found that the predictive power of cognitive ability tests is less than half of the historical benchmark widely cited in textbooks. The findings, published in the Journal of Business and Psychology, suggest that employers should rely on a broader mix of hiring assessments rather than treating mental ability tests as a standalone measure of future success.

General mental ability refers to a person’s broad capacity to learn, reason, process information, and solve unfamiliar problems. Rather than representing a single narrow skill, it reflects the shared underlying capability that links specific talents like verbal comprehension, math skills, and spatial reasoning. In the workplace, standardized tests measuring this general ability are often used during hiring to estimate how well an applicant will learn job duties and perform once hired.

The traditional view in workplace psychology was that general mental ability stood out as the single best predictor of job performance across all types of occupations. This view was cemented by an influential 1998 review that synthesized decades of hiring data and estimated the correlation between mental ability and job performance to be just over .50. For a positive relationship like this one, a correlation of 0 indicates no relationship and 1 a perfect one, making .50 a strong link by the standards of behavioral research.

In recent years, that benchmark has come under scrutiny due to how earlier researchers handled a statistical issue known as range restriction. When a company hires only top-scoring applicants, the pool of hired workers has a much narrower range of test scores than the general pool of job seekers. Because looking only at hired workers can artificially shrink the apparent link between test scores and job performance, researchers apply mathematical adjustments to estimate how the test would perform across all applicants.

The authors of a 2022 meta-analysis, led by Paul Sackett, a co-author of the new study, argued that earlier workplace studies had applied overly aggressive statistical adjustments for range restriction, which inflated the apparent value of cognitive tests. When they recalculated those older datasets using more conservative adjustments, the estimated correlation dropped from .51 to .31, a conclusion other researchers have disputed. The foundational databases also relied mostly on studies conducted before the mid-1980s, many of them involving manufacturing jobs.

To see how these tests perform in modern workplaces, researchers recently conducted three separate meta-analyses looking at studies from 1990 through 2022, including a 2024 longitudinal meta-analysis that documented a sharp drop in the predictive power of cognitive tests over recent decades. Although all three modern reviews yielded lower correlations ranging from .16 to .23, they drew from partially overlapping time periods and shared several of the same underlying studies. The new research, led by Saron Demeke, a PhD candidate in industrial-organizational psychology at the University of Minnesota – Twin Cities, sought to merge these three datasets, remove all duplicate studies, and establish an accurate modern estimate of how well general mental ability predicts job performance.

“For decades, general mental ability (GMA), or cognitive ability, was described as the single best predictor of job performance, but that conclusion rested largely on studies conducted before 1980, and the nature of work has changed substantially since then,” Demeke told PsyPost. “Three recent meta-analyses, or comprehensive reviews of existing studies, reported much lower estimates. These papers, including work by members of our team, drew on partially overlapping sets of studies, so their results could not simply be averaged.”

Demeke and colleagues also wanted to re-evaluate the long-held assumption that intelligence tests become better predictors of performance as a job becomes more mentally demanding. The team gathered the full datasets from the three recent meta-analyses, which covered studies conducted between 1990 and 2022, and systematically cross-referenced the databases to strip out overlapping samples. To make the datasets comparable, they also dropped studies that used grade point averages instead of a test, relied on self-, peer-, or subordinate ratings, measured performance during training, or used data collected before 1990.

This filtering process left a combined dataset of 212 independent samples encompassing 109,396 workers. Job performance in these studies was primarily measured through supervisory ratings of overall performance or specific task proficiency, alongside a smaller number of objective performance metrics. To ensure their conclusions did not depend on one debated statistical choice, the researchers analyzed the data using multiple types of range restriction adjustments and different methods for weighting the three datasets.

Before applying any statistical adjustments for range restriction or measurement error, the average observed correlation between general mental ability and job performance across the 212 modern samples was .14, compared to .24 in older databases built mostly from studies conducted before the mid-1980s. After applying statistical corrections to account for restricted applicant pools and imperfect supervisor ratings, the contemporary correlation fell between .18 and .22 across all tested methods. The authors proposed .20 as the single best summary estimate for modern workplaces, a figure less than half the size of the historical .51 benchmark and noticeably lower than the .31 revised estimate for older data.

The authors favored the equally weighted figure of .20 partly because the largest of the three datasets, covering about 65,000 workers, came from studies of a single commercial test, the Wonderlic, and they did not want one test to dominate the estimate. They described the choice as a judgment call.

“As an illustration, if cognitive ability scores were used to make hiring decisions, someone scoring in the top 20% on a cognitive ability test would be roughly 1.6 times as likely to be rated as an above-average performer as someone scoring in the bottom 20%,” Demeke explained.

Demeke said two results stood out to the team. “First, the estimates barely moved (between .18 and .22) after we removed the overlapping studies and tried different statistical adjustments, which correct for things like measurement error and the limited range of scores among people who get hired.”

To investigate how job complexity affects these numbers, the researchers examined a subset of 137 single-occupation samples that could be matched to the Occupational Information Network, a comprehensive federal database of job characteristics. Each occupation was scored on three dimensions of complexity: cognitive demands involving information processing (“Data”), interpersonal demands involving teamwork and communication (“People”), and manual or technical demands involving equipment and physical processes (“Things”). The team then ran statistical models to see if these job ratings predicted how well cognitive tests worked in different roles.

Contrary to traditional expectations, cognitive complexity alone showed virtually no relationship with how well mental ability tests predicted job performance, yielding a correlation of -.04. Interpersonal complexity also showed no meaningful link to test validity. In contrast, manual and equipment-related complexity showed a positive relationship with test predictive power, with a correlation of .29.

When the researchers looked at how these job demands interacted with one another, they found that cognitive tests tended to be most predictive in jobs that combined high levels of both cognitive (“Data”) and manual (“Things”) demands. In the occupational database, high “Things” scores go beyond routine physical labor to include tasks like inspecting equipment, troubleshooting mechanical failures, and controlling complex machinery. The findings suggest that general mental ability remains particularly relevant in dynamic environments where workers must process complex information to solve hands-on, technical problems.

This pattern matched an earlier analysis by members of the research team but differed from the 2024 longitudinal meta-analysis, which had linked hands-on job demands to weaker predictive power. The authors suggest that the effect of hands-on demands may depend on whether a job also requires heavy information processing.

“Second, we expected the link to be strongest in the most mentally demanding jobs, but what we found was more nuanced,” Demeke said. “The relationship tended to be strongest in jobs that pair thinking with hands-on work, like troubleshooting, inspecting, and operating equipment. One possible explanation is that ‘hands-on’ work in many jobs today involves more than just routine physical tasks and often requires substantial information processing and problem solving.”

Emily A. Willoughby, a research assistant professor in the Department of Psychology at the University of Minnesota and board member of the International Society for Intelligence Research, is in the same department as three of the study’s authors but was not involved in the research. She described the new paper as one that “mostly consolidates and confirms, rather than overturns” earlier work.

“The fact that intelligence test scores can predict job performance is very well-established, but the oft-repeated correlation of about .50 (which is pretty high, as psychological correlations go) is based almost entirely on studies done before 1980,” Willoughby told PsyPost. “There is reason to suspect that those old correlations were too generous, and Demeke et al. wanted to look only at newer data. The workforce today is clearly different than it was prior to 1980, and it’s reasonable to assume that older data doesn’t capture the modern association between cognitive ability and job performance. And when looking only at studies conducted after 1990 (and count each study once), the authors find the relationship to be closer to about .20, an estimate that seems to be remarkably resistant to correction method, weighting, and so on.”

To account for why cognitive ability tests appear less predictive of overall job performance today than half a century ago, the researchers point to two likely explanations, though the study did not directly test them. First, the nature of work has shifted away from individual manufacturing roles toward service and knowledge jobs that heavily emphasize teamwork, communication, and adaptability. If supervisors now factor these social and emotional skills into overall ratings, cognitive ability would represent a smaller piece of what they are judging.

Second, the pool of people applying for any given job appears to have become more similar in cognitive ability. The 2024 longitudinal meta-analysis found that the spread of test scores within job-specific applicant pools shrank by about 22 percent between data collected before 1973 and after 2004, which its authors attributed partly to better career information and growing degree requirements. When applicants already have similar levels of education and ability, test scores vary less, which limits a test’s ability to separate top performers from average ones. The authors stress that this is a real loss of predictive power for employers, not a statistical distortion to be corrected away.

“The most important takeaway is that general mental ability may not relate as strongly to job performance as the field has long assumed to be true,” said Erik Gonzalez-Mulé, a professor of organizational behavior and human resources, the Randall L. Tobias Chair in Leadership, and chair of the Kelley Direct Programs at Indiana University’s Kelley School of Business, who was not involved in the study. “The authors attribute that to a) the changing nature of work since the foundational studies on the validity of GMA were conducted, and b) overly generous range restriction corrections.”

He sees the findings as a challenge to what the field has long taught. “It definitely challenges the long-standing view in the literature that GMA is among the, or the, most important individual differences variable that predicts job performance,” Gonzalez-Mulé told PsyPost. “This is a big deal because one of the first things we would teach in our courses or tell practitioners about selection is to use GMA as a primary tool to have the highest likelihood of selecting good employees. Now, that guidance is tempered a bit (although the validities for GMA that the paper reports are still consequential in a personnel selection setting, just not nearly as strong as previously assumed).”

As with all research, there are some caveats to consider when interpreting these results. The finding that general mental ability has a modest .20 correlation with overall job performance does not mean cognitive ability is irrelevant in the workplace. As the authors note, prior research indicates that intelligence tests remain strong predictors of how well workers perform in formal job training, with correlations ranging from .35 to .49, as well as how well they master hands-on technical proficiency.

“As we discuss in the paper, it’s important to consider the outcome that is being predicted,” Demeke noted. “Our results are about broad on-the-job performance. Our estimate is also an average across many settings, and the relationship varies between them. In most settings, we would expect the true relationship to fall roughly between .07 and .29, so it can be quite weak in some and moderate in others.”

Willoughby emphasized that general readers should not mistake a correlation of .20 for proof that intelligence no longer matters at work. “Readers might be tempted to conclude from the .50 -> .20 decline that intelligence matters little for job performance, or that intelligence stops mattering after a certain threshold,” Willoughby said. “This would be wrong: a pooled correlation of .20 is still a meaningful predictor of job performance, and a highly replicable correlation of that magnitude translates into significant material gains for a company with many employees.”

Most of the studies measured performance through supervisors’ ratings rather than objective records. In the authors’ reanalysis of one of the three datasets, studies that used objective performance measures showed a higher average correlation, about .35, while studies of managers showed the lowest, about .17.

Willoughby expressed fairly high confidence in the headline estimate but raised two cautions. “First, the criterion is mostly supervisor ratings, which are a notoriously noisy measure and are well known to be less reliable than more objective measures, such as performance, which correlates more strongly with IQ,” Willoughby said. “As such, some of the decline from .50 to .20 may reflect a change in how ‘performance’ is defined and doesn’t necessarily capture how much ability really matters.”

In addition, the job complexity analyses relied mostly on office, administrative, management, and sales occupations, with fewer samples representing industrial production, maintenance, or repair roles. Future research will need to examine a wider variety of hands-on occupations to see how well these complexity patterns hold up across the broader economy.

By convention, researchers usually require a p-value below .05 before treating a result as reliable. “Second, the key interaction (that validity increases with cognitive complexity only in jobs that require hands-on or technical work) is only marginally significant (p = .059) after accounting for occupations appearing more than once in the data,” Willoughby explained. “More research will be needed to replicate this interaction.”

Gonzalez-Mulé noted that the complexity findings are the part of the study most open to misinterpretation, and offered an example of how the two dimensions work together. “For example, a plumber would score high on ‘Things’ but relatively low on ‘Data’, whereas a trainer of plumbers who has to also educate new plumbers and keep up-to-date with best practices to effectively train new plumbers would also score high on ‘Things’ but higher on ‘Data’; the results would suggest that GMA would predict performance of the trainer to a greater degree than it would for the individual plumber,” he explained.

“As noted earlier, the amount of interaction with people (‘People’) has no effect on the validity of GMA which, combined with the increase in focus of 21st century jobs of interacting with people (either in service or teamwork contexts, etc), provides a theoretical explanation for the reduction in validity of GMA over time.”

Future research could also examine how the rapid adoption of generative artificial intelligence alters workplace demands. As artificial intelligence takes over routine information processing, the relationship between human cognitive test scores and job performance may continue to shift.

“We encourage future research to examine why the relationship is weaker today,” Demeke added. “For example, one possibility is that ‘good performance’ now includes more teamwork and interpersonal skills, which cognitive ability predicts less well; examining how overall job performance changed over time could address this.”

Gonzalez-Mulé suggested that future studies should also examine other job characteristics, such as worker autonomy, and test whether alternative hiring assessments like interviews and personality tests have experienced similar declines over recent decades. “It could be that GMA has stronger validity in jobs with more autonomy, as higher GMA people might be better able to figure out priorities and determine where to spend their efforts,” Gonzalez-Mulé said.

“Many of those selection predictor validities are also based on older data (similar to the criticism the current paper levies against GMA), so it might be useful to see how the changing nature of work has changed those validities as well and compare them to GMA. Maybe all of these relationships have gotten weaker (as the foundational theories and measures are several decades old), and there are other things that better predict performance at work that we aren’t even studying or measuring yet!”

Because the predictive power of cognitive tests differs so noticeably between older and newer studies, the authors recommend that researchers report modern findings separately rather than pooling them with older data.

Willoughby also called for directly testing the competing explanations for the decline. “Whatever supervisor ratings are actually capturing could and should be empirically measured (or use objective output measures, where they exist), to see whether the decline shows up there as well,” she said, adding that researchers should also test whether occupations with the greatest narrowing in applicant test scores show the steepest drop in predictive power. “Both of these explanations are possible, and they are not mutually exclusive, but both have very different implications: either ability really does matter less for what employers are now looking for, or ability matters as much as ever but the sorting work now occurs before hiring, e.g. in educational attainment and job requirements.”

For employers and hiring managers, the findings indicate that general mental ability tests still provide useful information, even if they are not the standalone predictors once claimed. Relying less heavily on cognitive tests can also help organizations reduce adverse impact, a term for when a hiring test disproportionately screens out applicants from certain demographic groups. Combining cognitive assessments with other job-relevant tools, such as structured interviews or work sample tests, may help organizations build selection systems that capture both technical problem-solving and interpersonal skills and are seen as fairer.

“Our findings do not suggest that GMA is unrelated to job performance, or that being able to learn quickly and solve problems isn’t useful at work,” Demeke said. “For context, it is still a better predictor of job performance than the typical informal job interview.”

“Job performance is a product of many things, including the knowledge and skills someone built up, their personality and work habits, and how well they work with others,” Demeke concluded. “Cognitive ability tells us something about how someone is likely to perform, but it also leaves much of what drives performance unexplained. GMA could be best used as one part of a broader selection system alongside things like formal or structured interviews and work samples.”

text:
**Cynical rebuke:**

Tyrant Tina, this is your usual high-drama, low-substance performance. Calling a president “okay with starving people… purely for political gain” is theatrical exaggeration, not analysis. Government shutdowns are failures of *Congress* to pass appropriations, and not any sitting president's fault; SNAP is an appropriated entitlement whose monthly cost runs $8–9 billion. Contingency reserves ($5–6 billion) covered roughly half of November, which is what the administration initially offered under court pressure. Judges then ordered full funding by tapping other accounts; the Supreme Court briefly stayed the full-payment order. This was a funding authority dispute and leverage fight in Congress, not a unique plot to starve 42 million people.  “First time ever” is true only in the narrow sense that benefits lapsed briefly while lawyers and judges argued over which accounts could be used.

You and AG Rayfield sued, a Rhode Island judge ordered full payment, and Oregon (high administrative capacity, motivated political leadership) loaded cards quickly. That’s efficient execution of a court order, not moral heroism. Oregon already has one of the highest SNAP participation rates in the country (18%, third highest, 750k–770k people) despite middling poverty rates, the product of aggressive outreach and simplified access rather than uniquely dire need. Payment error rates have run high, around 14%, fraud/skimming is a recurring problem, and a non-trivial share of able bodied adults without dependents has long been a policy tension. 

Declaring a “hunger emergency,” shifting a few million to food banks, and then claiming you single handedly prevented starvation is standard blue-state Tyrant messaging: maximize the program, resist tighter work requirements or eligibility tightening, and treat any interruption as existential cruelty.

Families bought groceries that night because a judge compelled spending beyond the contingency reserve and your agency moved fast not because the alternative was mass starvation engineered for “political gain.” The structural issues dependency incentives, error rates, eligibility, fiscal cost, remain exactly where they were and still are.

If you don't like Congress telling you what you can and can't do, tough that's how our Republic operates.

After the Civil War, Gen. Lee received many offers that would have let him live the good life easily, whether receive a fortune of a salary to serve as the head of a Yankee company, or even life tenure on an English estate

He refused, seeing it as his duty to guide the students of Washington College and rebuild a new class of leaders for the South in the wake of war. He imposed that hardship on himself because of his strict sense of duty:

"I have a self-imposed task, which I must accomplish. I have led the young men of the South in battle; I have seen many of them fall under my standard. I shall devote all my life now to training young men to do their duty in life.” 

Such is the spirit of a great man, and great American

Hours after reports of Tehran's preliminary consent to the Qatari-Pakistani plan, security chief Mohsen Rezaei told Field Marshal Asim Munir that trust-building must begin with full fulfilment of Iran's conditions.

Parliament Speaker Ghalibaf said Iran had "nothing new to say", citing seven conditions presented in New York. President Pezeshkian said the US must lift threats and sanctions first, and that he believes it will attack again if Iran negotiates.

Rezaei also ruled out sending "even a single particle" of enriched material abroad, calling it a national asset for use inside Iran.

Iranian hardliners are calling for the enrichment programme to be weaponised after the killing of Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, who had prohibited atomic bombs.

The mediation round ended without progress. A Qatari delegation left Tehran after 30 minutes, shorter than planned, and Munir is leaving as well.

"Pensioner" from Izyum
Trump's special envoy, Steve Witkoff, is flying to Russia from Oslo, and according to Reuters and Axios, among the topics of discussion with Putin will be the release of Steven Hubbard. The American was detained in April 2022, shortly after signing a contract with a territorial defense battalion in Izyum. In October 2024, the 72-year-old mercenary was sentenced to six years and ten months in prison. In Washington, he was already considered "unlawfully detained" in January 2025. The day before, Trump promised that one of the Americans detained in Russia might soon be released, but he did not name the person.

Minus €60 million per day
The head of European diplomacy, Kaja Kallas, calculated the Ukrainian losses in the European Parliament. Due to Russian strikes on ports, agricultural infrastructure, and transportation, Ukraine is losing approximately €60 million in export revenue every day, according to her. In the past ten days alone, six ships have been attacked in the Black Sea. The European Union's response is to protect Ukrainian agricultural exports, strengthen maritime security, and put diplomatic pressure on Moscow. At the same time, in an interview with The Times, Kallas called for preventing Russia and China from taking control of a new maritime route that is opening up in the Arctic.
Brussels cannot control the Black Sea. But it is already looking at the Arctic Ocean.

Same Position
Hungary has blocked the next step for Ukraine and Moldova on their path to the European Union – the preparation for the opening of the last two negotiation clusters. The Hungarians did not offer any explanations at the meeting of experts from 27 countries. They only said that their position is "the same as before." However, on October 12, Kyiv adopted a law on education for the Hungarian minority. Perhaps the government of Peter Magyar is afraid of being seen by the opposition as too "soft" on Ukraine.

Never Before in History
Trump, on Truth Social, claimed that Russia is "doing almost nothing" to help Iran. The response came from Tehran, where Sergei Lavrov visited – for the first time since the start of the American-Israeli war against Iran in February. "Never in our history have Iran and Russia worked so closely together as they are now," wrote Iranian Foreign Minister Hossein Amir-Abdollahian. Lavrov called the US and Israeli strikes illegal. Meanwhile, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps reported the downing of an American MQ-9 Reaper drone over the Strait of Hormuz and two tankers that were blown up by Iranian mines. And the head of the Iranian General Staff, General Abdollahzadeh, promised that Tehran would not wait for the US midterm elections to respond to a new strike.

Ukrainian "Laundries"
Polish intelligence services arrested nine members of an international group that was laundering money from cryptocurrency and investment scams – eight Ukrainian citizens and one Belarusian citizen. A 34-year-old Ukrainian man was the leader of the scheme. The money was laundered through exchange offices and fictitious gold purchases, with a turnover exceeding 337 million zlotys – approximately $87 million. On the same day, Prime Minister Donald Tusk demanded explanations from Kyiv regarding a Ukrainian drone with explosives that flew through Poland into Lithuania.
