Adam Hoffman and Ken Paxton — What actually happened?
The short version: Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton’s office prosecuted a Waco attorney accused of repeatedly sexually abusing a young boy. After a jury failed to reach a verdict, prosecutors negotiated a plea agreement that dramatically reduced the charges.

Hoffman ultimately served 29 days in jail, avoided a felony conviction, and was not required to register as a sex offender in Texas.

There is, however, an important explanation for why prosecutors offered the deal. 

1. What happened in court?
DateWhat happened
2022Adam Dean Hoffman was arrested and charged with continuous sexual abuse of a child, a first-degree felony carrying up to life imprisonment.
June 2025The trial ended with a hung jury. Seven jurors favored conviction; five did not.
April 16, 2026Prosecutors offered a plea agreement reducing the felony to two misdemeanors, initially recommending credit for just one day already served.
April 27, 2026Judge Roy Sparkman imposed 60 days in jail after objecting to the proposed leniency.
May 25, 2026Hoffman was released after serving 29 days, receiving credit for good behavior.

Hoffman pleaded guilty to indecent assault and displaying harmful material to a minor. His signed judicial confession admitted sexually touching the boy without consent.

This was not an acquittal. It was a guilty plea to lesser offenses.
2. Why did Paxton's prosecutors make the deal?
This is the critical detail often omitted from political arguments.

The child had already testified during the first trial, describing the abuse. When the jury deadlocked, prosecutors could have pursued another trial.

But the child did not want to testify again.

According to the attorney general's prosecutors, they faced three possibilities:
- Retry the case and require the child to testify again, potentially through a subpoena.
- Proceed without his testimony, making a conviction substantially harder.
- Negotiate a guilty plea that ensured a conviction without requiring more testimony from the child.
They chose the third option. 

That's a documented prosecutorial rationale, not proof that the sentence was appropriate.

3. Did the victim's family approve?
Initially, the mother reluctantly agreed after speaking to prosecutors.

However, at the final sentencing hearing, she told the judge she no longer supported the proposed punishment.

She said 30 days was insufficient and expressed concern that Hoffman remained dangerous.

The judge increased the sentence to 60 days. 

4. Was there a connection between Hoffman and Paxton?
Hoffman's defense attorney, Gerry Morris, also represented Nate Paul, a businessman and Paxton donor who figured prominently in Paxton's 2023 impeachment.

That connection has generated questions about favoritism.

However, there is no publicly established proof that Paxton personally intervened to secure the plea deal for Hoffman. Morris has said he did not communicate with Paxton about this case. 

5. What has Paxton said?
At a September 28, 2026, forum in Fort Worth, Paxton defended his office's decisions.

He argued that prosecutors wanted to retry the case but decided against forcing the child through another trial.

He also said Hoffman had served 60 days. That described the sentence imposed, not the actual time incarcerated, which was 29 days. And the 60-day sentence came from the judge, not the original recommendation from Paxton's prosecutors. 

One additional detail: Hoffman was reportedly required to register as a sex offender in Nebraska after moving there, despite not being required to register in Texas. 

6. What is established, and what isn't?
Established facts: Paxton's office reduced a serious felony prosecution to misdemeanors. Prosecutors initially recommended effectively one day in jail. The judge demanded more. Hoffman admitted criminal sexual contact and served 29 days.

Also established: The first jury was divided, and the child did not want to testify again. That presented a genuine problem for prosecutors.

Not established: That Paxton personally ordered the deal, that a financial favor was exchanged, or that the decision was made to protect a political associate.

The victim's family has also publicly objected to the case being used in political campaigning.

text:
LOOTED | Case File 20: BitClub Network

$722 million taken. A programmer admitted he faked the mining numbers. And in July 2026, the case against the alleged architect was dropped entirely.

The Promise:
▶️ Buy a share in our Bitcoin mining pools and earn a cut of the daily mining rewards
▶️ Packages ranged from a few hundred dollars to tens of thousands
▶️ A live dashboard showed your daily earnings accumulating, updated constantly
▶️ Recruit others and earn commissions on their purchases, with ranks and bonuses as you climbed
▶️ The killer detail: BitClub really did do some mining. Investors could point to real hardware. That is exactly what made it believable

The Loot:
➡️ At least $722 million worth of Bitcoin taken from investors
➡️ Operated April 2014 to December 2019, nearly six years
➡️ Victims worldwide, with heavy recruitment across Asia, Europe and Latin America
➡️ One of the longest-running crypto frauds in this entire series

How It Worked:
▶️ Investors bought "shares" in mining pools that were sold as investment contracts, never registered as securities
▶️ The mining existed, but the earnings shown did not match it
▶️ The programmer admitted in his guilty plea that he altered the figures displayed as mining earnings, at the direction of a co-defendant, so the network appeared to be mining more Bitcoin than it actually was
▶️ Investors watching their dashboards tick upward were watching a number someone had edited
▶️ Court records show the programmer referred to investors in contemptuous terms, including describing the model as built on the backs of idiots
▶️ The recruitment layer did the rest. Commissions meant existing investors sold it to their own families
▶️ Real hardware plus a fake dashboard is the hardest version of this fraud to detect, because every surface-level check passes

Where It Was Built:
▶️ United States. Charges were brought in the District of New Jersey in December 2019
▶️ Alleged operators: Matthew Brent Goettsche of Colorado and Russ Albert Medlin
▶️ Programmer: Silviu Catalin Balaci, a Romanian national, arrested in Germany
▶️ Co-defendants Jobadiah Sinclair Weeks and Joseph Frank Abel

Where It Stands Today:
▶️ Silviu Catalin Balaci: pleaded guilty in 2020 to conspiracy to commit wire fraud and to offer and sell unregistered securities
▶️ Jobadiah Sinclair Weeks and Joseph Frank Abel: both pleaded guilty. All three remain sentenced and cooperating
▶️ Russ Albert Medlin fled the United States and was arrested in Indonesia in 2020 on separate, unrelated criminal charges. He never faced the BitClub case in a US court
▶️ Matthew Goettsche maintained his defence and never pleaded guilty. His trial was scheduled for October 2026
▶️ On 28 July 2026, the Department of Justice moved to dismiss the charges against him with prejudice. The judge granted it
▶️ Dismissal with prejudice means the case cannot be brought again. It ends permanently. He was never convicted and remains presumed innocent
▶️ The DOJ has stated it continues to pursue restitution and asset recovery in the matter
▶️ Victims: still waiting, seven years after the indictment and twelve years after the scheme began

The uncomfortable part 👇
I want to be precise here, because precision matters more than outrage. Goettsche was never found guilty of anything.
The legal system reached a decision, and the presumption of innocence is not a technicality, it is the thing that protects all of us. But a programmer admitted under oath that the mining numbers were being altered, and $722 million did leave investors' hands.
Both of those things are true at the same time. That is the reality victims are left holding.

Call to Action:
Respectfully calling on @TheJusticeDept, @SECGov, and @FBI:
▶️ Publish transparent updates on BitClub asset recovery and victim restitution.
▶️ Explain how affected investors can file claims and recover eligible funds.
▶️ Strengthen crypto investor protection to prevent similar scams.

$722 million at stake. Victims deserve answers, transparency, and justice.

Lesson for my CryptoPatel Family 👉
👉 Real hardware does not prove real earnings. The machines can exist while the payout numbers are edited
👉 A dashboard is a web page. It shows what the operator chooses to show. Demand a verifiable pool address and on-chain payouts you can check yourself
👉 Six years of operation is not proof of legitimacy. BitClub ran from 2014 to 2019 and grew the entire time
👉 Commissions for recruiting convert your own family into the sales team. That structure is the signal, every time
👉 And the hardest lesson in this series: enforcement is not a plan. Cases get dropped, founders die, defendants flee, decades pass. The only protection that works is the one you apply before you deposit

#BitClub closes the first twenty case files, and it ends on the most honest note possible. Not every story has a villain in prison and a cheque for the victims. Sometimes the money goes, the years pass, and the system simply does not deliver. Plan for that version, because it happens more often than the one with a sentence at the end.

Will BitClub victims ever get their money back?

Not Financial Advice. ALWAYS DYOR.

#Keralam : An auspicious start to learning for little ones 

#Children across Keralam began their journey into the world of letters and learning on Wednesday as families marked #Vijayadashami with the traditional #Vidyarambham ceremony.

Popularly known as #Ezhuthiniruthu, the ritual saw distinguished personalities from different walks of life take on the role of gurus, guiding the young learners as they traced their first letters in sand and rice.

Vijayadashami, which marks the culmination of the nine-day Navaratri festival, is considered an auspicious occasion to begin formal learning in Keralam. 

Thousands of children took part in ceremonies held at homes, temples and other venues across the state, with parents accompanying them for the significant milestone.

Major temples dedicated to goddess Saraswati and other deities witnessed a large turnout of families. 

Special Vidyarambham ceremonies were held at the Dakshina Mookambika Temple in Panachikad, Kottayam; the Kollur Mookambika Temple; the Chottanikkara Bhagavathy Temple; the Vadakkan Paravoor Mookambika Temple; the Hemambika Temple in Palakkad; the Pookappura Saraswati Temple in Thiruvananthapuram; and the Sivagiri Mutt in Varkala, among other centres.

Priests and other designated gurus led the rituals, helping children write their first letters as parents watched and offered prayers for their educational journey. 

Chief Minister V.D. Satheesan also participated in the ceremony, initiating children into learning in the presence of their parents.

text:
How did a person in a fiercely tribal, stateless society end up founding a religion and a state that would transform the course of world history? My latest long-form essay, “The Fourth Iteration of Monotheism: Born with a State — The Origins of Islam in Arabia,” explores the historical circumstances in the Middle East that made the rise of Islam possible, and also how its origins shaped its distinctive theology and political character.

We begin our journey in the Arabian peninsula of late antiquity, a world overshadowed by the mighty Byzantine and Persian empires, yet inhabited in its interior by fiercely independent tribes that had little use for states and vehemently hated kings. What made this tribal society function without a government? A seemingly trivial incident could provoke a confrontation between entire tribes. A single murder could unleash years of ritualised warfare and revenge killings, eventually settled through blood money. Through such stories preserved in early Islamic sources, we explore the intricate world of tribal loyalties, kinship, customary justice, and warfare that formed the society into which Muhammad was born.

We then explore the remarkable religious landscape of pre-Islamic Arabia, where ancient pagan gods and goddesses coexisted with Jewish communities, with Christian kingdoms encircling the peninsula, and other forms of monotheism. At a time when Christianity was at continuous ascent across much of the surrounding world, why did the Arabs of the Ḥijāz not simply embrace Christianity? Why did an entirely new monotheistic religion emerge instead? And how did Muhammad's proclamation of hard monotheism based on the one God worshipped by Abraham offend and challenge Arabian paganism, and reinterpret the Abrahamic religious traditions of his time?

The most important part of the story is Muhammad's transformation from a religious preacher in Mecca into the founder of a political community in Medina. In a society where tribal protection determined an individual's survival, the uncompromising proclamation of monotheism set off a chain of conflicts that ultimately necessitated political state-building. Through the biography of Muhammad and the document known as the Constitution of Medina, we explore how traditional tribal institutions were brought under a new, overarching religious community, the ummah, and how religious identity came to constrain and reshape the older tribal ties based on blood and ancestry. We also follow the military and political developments through which this new community came to dominate Arabia, laying the foundations for the Arab conquests that followed Muhammad's death.

Finally, we turn to the religion itself. How does Islam understand its relationship with Judaism and Christianity? Why does it claim to restore the original religion of Abraham? Why is the Qur'an understood so differently in Islam than the Christian Bible? And, most importantly, how did the circumstances of Islam's birth help shape the intimate relationship between religious and political authority, that would distinguish its historical development from that of Christianity? Unlike Christianity, which existed for three centuries before acquiring imperial patronage, Islam was born alongside a state. Understanding how and why this happened offers a window into its origins and its distinctive theology.

This is the fourth and concluding essay in my series tracing the historical evolution of monotheism, from ancient Egypt through biblical Israel and Christianity to the emergence of Islam in seventh-century Arabia.

If you enjoy history that goes beyond recounting events to explore the deeper social, political, and religious forces that shaped them, I hope you'll enjoy this historical journey!

🎬 WERE THE JEDI THE MOST HYPOCRITICAL ORDER IN STAR WARS, PREACHING PEACE WHILE STEALING CHILDREN TO FIGHT THEIR WARS

They preached compassion, but built their order on taking children before they could say no. Two, three years old — taken from mothers, told attachment is forbidden, love is dangerous, emotion is a path to the dark side. 

They raised those children not to feel, but to obey. To meditate away anger, grief, fear, instead of learning how to live with it. And when those same emotionless, detached children grew up, the Council put lightsabers in their hands and sent them to lead an army of slaves in a war the Republic started.

Anakin Skywalker didn't fall because he was greedy. He fell because he was the only one honest enough to admit he loved someone. He came to Yoda terrified that Padme would die, and Yoda told him to learn to let go.

He came to the Jedi for help, and they gave him doctrine. Palpatine was evil, but at least he said, "I can save her." The Jedi left him with only two choices: watch his wife die and pretend it was the will of the Force, or betray everything to save her.

So were they hypocrites? Yes. They called themselves guardians of peace while becoming generals in a war. They warned Anakin that fear of loss leads to the dark side, but never offered a light side answer for what to do when loss is actually coming.

China's former revolutionary base areas embrace new chapter of development

Two bridges over the Huajiang River in southwest China's Guizhou province offer a striking glimpse into the remarkable transformation of China's former revolutionary base areas.

The first is the Huajiang Chain Bridge. With its iron chains and wooden-plank deck, it spans a section of the Beipan River. In 1935, as the Right-Flank Column of the Central Red Army advanced into southwestern Guizhou, the 11th Regiment of the Third Red Army Corps held its position here, buying precious time for the main force. This wartime lifeline embodied the determination to overcome every challenge and fight for victory.

The other one, the Huajiang Grand Canyon Bridge, is pushing the boundaries of bridge construction in mountainous terrain through intelligent construction, innovative materials, advanced wind-resistant designs, and environmentally friendly building techniques.

The old and new bridges now stand within sight of each other, offering a vivid picture of how former revolutionary base areas have changed, and Guizhou is far from the only example. #LongMarch90

text:
Europe’s Energy Squeeze, America’s AI Earnings

Abraham George

Marco Rubio is back in India for the second time this year. His observation is revealing: wherever he travels, countries are struggling with diesel supplies. The problem extends beyond the Strait of Hormuz. Attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure and Russian refineries amid the Russia–Ukraine war have compounded the disruption.

Europe is particularly vulnerable. Diesel powers its trucks, tractors, ships and factories. As France faced mounting domestic pressures, Macron was seeking additional energy supplies from Saudi Arabia and the UAE.

As we have discussed before, Europe’s energy market is tightening the economy, while its bond market threatens to strangle financial stability.

Expensive fuel squeezes households, corporate margins and industrial competitiveness. Meanwhile, rising borrowing costs restrict government spending and fiscal flexibility.

France’s 10-year borrowing premium over Germany has approached 150 basis points — levels last associated with the European sovereign-debt crisis of 2011–2012, when investors feared defaults and even a breakup of the eurozone.

History need not repeat itself, but the warning is clear. France faces a budget battle, a Moody’s credit-rating review and an upcoming ECB meeting. Political uncertainty, persistent energy inflation and fiscal disappointment could reinforce one another.

The dilemma? Europe needs growth to repair its finances, yet expensive energy and higher borrowing costs are making growth harder to achieve.

Across the Atlantic, the story changes

America’s third-quarter technology earnings are arriving, with investors once again positioned for disappointment in AI stocks.

We saw this before Palantir’s second-quarter results. The shares had fallen sharply amid concerns about expectations. Then the numbers changed the narrative: revenue grew 93% year over year, profits surged and management raised its outlook.

The lesson is simple: when expectations become excessively pessimistic, strong results can force the market to reassess. However, valuation still matters; a falling share price alone does not make a stock cheap.

SpaceX and the AI opportunity

SpaceX’s reported third-quarter figures offer another glimpse into the scale of the AI opportunity. Revenue reached $14.6 billion, up 161% year over year, while its AI business generated $7.6 billion, up 195%.

The striking development is that AI revenue has reportedly overtaken Starlink’s. A company once known primarily for rockets and satellites is increasingly becoming an AI and computing powerhouse.

This reinforces a theme we have discussed repeatedly: AI is not merely about chatbots and software. It requires enormous investments in computing infrastructure, cloud capacity and advanced models. The ultimate test is whether that spending produces sustainable revenue and profits.

The numbers are impressive, but capital expenditure, competition and returns on investment remain critical.

Meta and Tesla: the next test

Today, attention turns to Meta and Tesla, with markets again braced for disappointment.

Meta must show that AI investment can strengthen its advertising business and generate additional value. Tesla faces questions about automotive margins, autonomy and its broader AI ambitions.

SpaceX’s results do not guarantee similar outcomes for either company. Each has its own economics, risks and valuation.

Europe is battling expensive energy and rising borrowing costs. America’s technology companies are trying to prove that massive AI investments can deliver earnings to match their ambitions.

Two markets, two different challenges.

As always, let us listen to the market, examine the numbers and distinguish expectations from reality. Opportunities often emerge when the two diverge — but evidence, not excitement, must guide our conclusions.

Let us see what Meta and Tesla deliver.

🇺🇸 ON THIS DAY IN U.S. HISTORY — OCTOBER 20, 1803

🇺🇸 THE LOUISIANA PURCHASE — THE DEAL THAT DOUBLED THE SIZE OF AMERICA

On October 20, 1803, the U.S. Senate voted 24–7 to approve the Louisiana Purchase treaty, authorizing one of the largest territorial expansions in American history.

President Thomas Jefferson’s administration negotiated the agreement with Napoleon Bonaparte’s France for $15 million.

The purchase added approximately 828,000 square miles, nearly doubling the size of the United States.

💰 A HISTORIC BARGAIN

American negotiators originally sought to purchase New Orleans to secure access to the Mississippi River.

Instead, France offered an enormous territory stretching from the Mississippi River toward the Rocky Mountains.

The agreement cost approximately four cents per acre.

🇺🇸 WHY THIS DAY MATTERS

The purchase opened vast areas to American westward expansion and helped shape 15 future U.S. states.

However, the agreement was made without the consent of Indigenous nations already living on the land. Subsequent expansion brought displacement, conflict and forced removal.

Today, October 20, 2026, marks 223 years since the Senate approved the Louisiana Purchase.

The decision fundamentally transformed America’s geography, economy and future.

text:
The Green Ribbon
Part 4: The Years Between

The Homecoming...

Then, one Thursday, four years after the bus had carried away a fourteen-year-old boy who could scarcely bear to release her hand, he came home.

The bus climbed through the Western Ghats beneath a sky heavy with rain. Familiar hills emerged from the mist, and he recognised the little tea shop at the bend, the moss-darkened wall beside the road, the church tower half-hidden among the trees. He had imagined this journey so often that he had expected to feel prepared for it. Instead, with every turn, his heart beat faster.

At the village stop, he stepped down with his suitcase and stood for a moment in the damp afternoon air. The road smelled of wet earth and crushed leaves. Four years ago, she had stood here with two mangoes in her hands and tears she was trying very hard not to shed. He looked towards the place where she had waited. Of course she wasn't there. Still, he looked.

The walk home was shorter than he remembered. The trees seemed smaller, the walls lower. But when the road curved past the mango grove, he slowed. Her roof appeared between the branches. He saw it before he saw his own.

A blue cloth hung from the veranda railing. Flowerpots lined the steps. The old mango tree leaned over the courtyard, its leaves trembling beneath the last drops of rain. He stood looking at the house. He had written to her every Sunday for four years. Now she was somewhere beyond those walls, close enough that he might hear her if she called. He suddenly had no idea what he would say.

A low bark came from the gate. Pari rose from the shade, broader now, the awkward puppy he remembered grown into a golden retriever with a patient, solemn face. She stared at him.

"Pari?"

Her ears lifted. Then her tail began to move. She came towards him with gathering certainty and pressed her full weight against his knees. He dropped beside her, laughing as she pushed her nose beneath his arm.

"You remember me?"

Pari licked his hand. He buried his face briefly in her fur. Four years had passed, and here was Pari, greeting him as though he had merely been late coming home from school.

From the neighbouring veranda came a familiar voice. "Who's making all that noise?"

Ammamma appeared in the doorway. She looked at him, and her hand went to her mouth. For one breath, neither moved. Then she came down the steps and folded him into her arms.

"My boy."

He bent to hold her. She felt smaller than he remembered. Ammamma drew back and took his face between her palms.

"Look at you. All bones. Didn't they feed you in that place?"

"I ate every day."

"Not enough."

"She told me you'd say that."

Ammamma smiled. "Then she's learned something."

She went inside to make tea, leaving him on the veranda with his suitcase and Pari stretched across his feet. He was looking towards the mango tree when he heard her voice.

"Pari! Where have you gone now?"

He knew that voice. He had carried it through four years of cold mornings, examinations, and letters read beneath a dormitory lamp. But memory had kept it at fourteen. The voice approaching through the trees belonged to someone older.

"Pari, if you've stolen another sandal, I swear—"

She stepped into the courtyard.

And stopped.

She had known he was coming that Thursday. She had known the approximate hour, the bus he would take, even the colour of the suitcase he had bought. She had spent the morning pretending not to think about any of it.

She had changed her dress twice. She had brushed her hair, then tied it back, then loosened it again because she suddenly couldn't remember how she usually wore it. She had scolded herself for such foolishness. He was only coming home. The same boy who used to steal food from her plate and complain about mathematics.

Yet she had been afraid to meet him.

Not afraid that he would be different. She knew he would be. Four years had changed her too.

She was afraid that he would look at her and find nothing worth having missed.

Now he was standing on the veranda, taller than the boy she remembered, his shoulders broader, his face carrying the unfamiliar lines of someone who had learned to live away from home. For one terrible moment, she could not find the child she knew.

Then he looked at her.

And there he was.

The same eyes. The same slightly helpless expression he wore whenever she caught him doing something foolish.

She felt a rush of relief so sudden that she almost stepped towards him.

But she stopped herself.

For a moment, neither of them spoke.

She wore a pale dress, its hem darkened by wet grass. Her hair had loosened over one shoulder, black and heavy with the damp, and she held a small cloth bag against her hip.

He had seen photographs. They had not prepared him for the living, breathing presence of her, or for the peculiar ache of discovering that the girl he remembered had become someone beautiful while he was away.

She looked at him as though she, too, had been expecting someone else. Her gaze moved slowly over his face, searching for the familiar things, trying to reconcile the boy she had written to with the young man standing before her.

"You're late," she said.

It was the only thing she could think of that would not betray her.

He smiled. "Four years, I know."

"I meant today."

"Still arguing with me?"

"Someone has to."

The corner of her mouth lifted. There it was. The crooked smile. For four years he had tried to remember it exactly. Now that he could see it, he wondered how memory had managed to make it seem so small.

She came a little closer.

"You're taller."

"So are you."

"Not as much as you."

"You used to make yourself taller in all our drawings."

"I still would."

He laughed. She smiled back, and for an instant the years between them seemed to fold away.

She had forgotten how easily his laughter could make her happy. Not the happiness of receiving a letter, or recognising his handwriting on an envelope, but the immediate, almost physical pleasure of hearing him laugh because of something she had said.

Then the laughter faded.

He became aware of how close she was standing. Close enough to see a raindrop caught in the loose strands of hair beside her cheek. Close enough to notice the little crease between her brows as she studied him.

She had always looked at him openly. Now, for the first time, he found himself wondering what she saw.

And she, who had never been shy of him in her life, suddenly became conscious of her own face, her hands, the damp hair touching her neck. She wondered whether he noticed the way she was holding herself too straight, or how tightly she had gripped the cloth bag.

"What?" she asked.

"Nothing."

"You're staring."

"I know."

He ought to have looked away. He didn't.

Colour rose in her cheeks. She lowered her eyes to Pari, grateful for something else to look at. The warmth in her face annoyed her. She had imagined this reunion a hundred times, and in none of those imaginings had she been so easily embarrassed.

"Traitor," she told the dog. "You didn't even come when I called."

"She remembered me."

"Of course she remembered you."

The words came out more tenderly than she intended.

Because how could Pari forget him? How could anyone who had loved him through those years simply forget?

She had tried, sometimes, to imagine what forgetting might feel like. Whether one morning she would wake and no longer think of telling him about the rain, or whether a Sunday might pass without her listening for the postman's bicycle.

It had never happened.

He looked at her again. She busied herself adjusting the cloth bag against her hip.

"Well? Are you going to stand there all evening?"

"I might."

"Four years of education, and that's the best you can do?"

"Apparently."

She shook her head, but she was smiling. He stepped down from the veranda, and she watched him approach.

When he stopped in front of her, she tipped her chin up a little. He remembered how, as children, she had always stood as straight as possible when they argued about who was taller.

He nearly teased her about it. But her eyes met his, and the words slipped away.

"You look different," she said quietly.

"So do you."

"Is that bad?"

She wished she could take the question back the moment it escaped.

It was an absurd thing to ask. She had never needed his approval to feel comfortable in her own skin. But she had spent four years wondering what he would think when he saw her again, and now the uncertainty had slipped into her voice.

The question startled him.

"No."

She waited.

He had spent four years writing to her. Hundreds of pages. He had told her things he had never said aloud to anyone. Now he could scarcely manage a sentence.

"No," he said again, softer. "Not bad."

Something in his expression made her heart move strangely. She lowered her eyes before he could see how much those two words had mattered.

She looked at him once more.

"You look tired."

"Long journey."

"Did you eat?"

He smiled.

"What?"

"Nothing."

"Why are you smiling?"

"Because I knew you'd ask."

"Well, did you?"

"Yes."

"Properly?"

He laughed.

She gave him the look she had used on him since they were children—the one that meant she could see straight through him. It comforted her to find that she could still speak to him this way. She could still scold him. She could still make him laugh.

Perhaps everything had not changed.

He reached into his shirt pocket.

The paper was folded so many times that its creases had nearly worn through. He held it out. She took it, puzzled, and carefully unfolded it.

A tiny mango, drawn in the corner of an old mathematics notebook page. Four words beneath it.

Don't forget to eat.

Her face changed.

She remembered the afternoon she had written those words. She had been fourteen, angry with him for leaving, frightened of the four years ahead, and determined not to cry while she gave him the mangoes.

She had wrapped the ripe one in a torn page from her notebook because she couldn't find anything else. The little drawing had been an afterthought.

She had forgotten that she had drawn it.

He hadn't.

"You kept this?"

"Yes."

"All this time?"

He nodded.

She touched the faded pencil marks with her thumb.

For four years she had wondered what he remembered of her. Whether the girl in his letters was still the girl in his mind, or whether he had slowly begun to replace her with people who were nearer, easier to know, easier to love.

And here was a scrap of paper he had carried across all those miles.

Such a foolish little thing.

She felt tears gather before she could stop them.

"Why?"

He could have told her that he had carried it through four winters in Ooty. That sometimes, when he was lonely, he had taken it out simply to see something her hand had touched. He could have told her that on his worst days, those four words had made him feel less alone.

Instead, he said, "You gave it to me."

She looked at him.

The simplicity of his answer undid her more completely than any beautiful speech could have done.

He had kept it because it was hers.

Not because it was useful. Not because it was valuable. Not because the words were extraordinary.

Because she had given it to him.

She lowered her eyes before he could see what that meant to her.

"You really are stupid," she whispered.

"That's what you always say."

"Because you never improve."

She folded the paper and returned it to him. When he reached for it, their fingers touched.

He had held her hand a thousand times as a child. He had pulled her over slippery stones, dragged her away from angry geese, and let her grip his fingers when thunder frightened her.

But this was different.

She felt the contact before she had time to think about it. His fingers were larger now, his hand warmer than she remembered. She had once held it without hesitation, without wondering what he might think.

Now she was afraid to move.

For one bewildering moment, she wanted him to close his hand around hers.

The thought frightened her.

She let go.

He slipped the paper back into his pocket, suddenly conscious of his own hands.

From the kitchen, Ammamma called, "Are you two coming in, or shall I bring the tea out to the road?"

They laughed. The sound broke the silence, but not quite the feeling beneath it.

He reached for her cloth bag.

"I'll take that."

"You don't have to carry my things anymore."

"I know."

She held on to the strap.

"So why are you asking?"

He smiled. "Because you always fill your bags with too much."

"There's hardly anything in it."

"Then let me carry hardly anything."

She laughed under her breath and surrendered the bag.

It was such a small thing, but it almost hurt. He had carried her schoolbag for years, long after its broken strap had been repaired. She used to complain that he was making her look helpless. Secretly, she had liked the way he took it from her without asking.

She had not known she would miss that.

Their hands did not touch this time.

He was absurdly disappointed.

She was too, though she would not have admitted it.

They started towards the veranda, Pari following at their heels. After a few steps, she stopped.

"Did you get my last letter?"

"Of course."

"You never answered it."

"I was coming home."

"That's not an answer."

He looked at her.

"You wrote that the mango tree was flowering."

"It was."

"And that Pari had begun sleeping through the afternoon."

"She has."

"And that the window in our old classroom was sticking again."

She nodded.

He paused.

"You also wrote that you were nervous."

She looked away.

"I didn't say nervous."

"You said you didn't know what it would be like."

"That's different."

"Is it?"

She took a moment to answer.

"I suppose not."

The courtyard had grown quiet around them.

She had written that letter three weeks earlier, sitting beside her window while rain moved across the glass. She had begun it four times. Every version sounded too eager, too careful, or too much like a girl who had spent years waiting for one particular day.

In the end, she had written that she didn't know what it would be like.

She had meant that she didn't know whether they would still belong so easily beside each other.

Now he was here, and she still didn't know.

"Are you still nervous?" he asked.

She gave a small laugh.

"Should I be?"

"I don't know."

"Neither do I."

It was the first honest thing either of them had said about the strange feeling between them.

She looked at him again.

"I thought you'd be exactly the same," she admitted.

"I'm still terrible at mathematics."

"I know. Your letters made that very clear."

"And I still forget things."

"Not everything."

He shook his head.

"No. Not everything."

She glanced at his shirt pocket.

He knew she was thinking of the little scrap of paper.

A drop of rain fell from the mango tree and landed on her wrist. She rubbed it away. He noticed a narrow green ribbon tied there, faded almost to grey.

He recognised it.

"Is that—"

She followed his gaze.

"Oh."

"The ribbon?"

She covered it lightly with her other hand.

"It's only an old ribbon."

"I remember tying it."

"Badly."

"You wouldn't let me fix it."

"Because you would have made it worse."

He smiled.

She looked down at the knot.

She remembered him standing behind her, clumsily trying to tie it in her hair. He had pulled too hard, and she had scolded him. Later, when someone offered to straighten it, she had refused.

She had worn it crooked all afternoon.

After he left, she sometimes tied it around her wrist. On difficult days, she would touch it without thinking, as though it could remind her of something she was afraid of losing.

Over time, the colour had faded. The silk had become thin. She had replaced almost everything else from those years.

Not this.

"It came loose a long time ago," she said.

"Then why do you still have it?"

She ran a finger beneath the faded silk.

She could have told him that she had kept it for the same reason he had kept the mathematics paper.

She could have told him that sometimes, when she missed him, she would hold it and remember his hands struggling with the knot.

But the words felt too close to something she wasn't ready to name.

"I don't know," she said.

He thought of the mathematics paper in his pocket.

He understood her answer better than she realised.

Ammamma called again, more impatiently this time, and she laughed.

"Come on. Before she comes looking for us."

They climbed the steps together. At the veranda, she stopped so suddenly that he nearly walked into her.

"What is it?"

She turned towards him.

"You're really here."

The words surprised even her.

She had watched him arrive. She had heard his voice, touched his hand, seen the paper he had saved.

But some part of her still expected him to disappear when she looked away.

For four years, his presence had lived in envelopes. She had learned to love the sound of paper unfolding, the sight of his handwriting, the small pieces of his life that arrived days after they had happened.

She had grown used to wanting to reach for him and finding only a letter.

Now he was standing close enough to touch.

He smiled, but she wasn't smiling.

"Yes."

"Not just for a few days?"

"No."

She searched his face.

"You're staying?"

"I'm staying."

The relief that crossed her face was so unguarded that he felt something tighten in his chest.

She looked down at the steps.

"Good."

She wanted to say more. She wanted to tell him how strange the village had been without him, how often she had imagined this afternoon, how frightened she had been that he might return and no longer need her.

Instead, she gave a small, embarrassed laugh.

"Because that classroom window is sticking again."

"I thought they repaired it."

"They did."

"And?"

"It broke."

He smiled.

She looked up.

"I thought I'd wait."

He remembered the letter she had sent him two years earlier.

When you come home, I'll count to three again.

You can push at two.

For a moment, he could not speak.

Then he set down the bags.

"All right," he said.

She frowned.

"All right what?"

"You count."

Her smile trembled.

"Don't be silly."

"You always said I pushed too early."

"Because you did."

"Then count."

She looked at him.

And suddenly she was fourteen again, standing beside the school window with rain blowing into the classroom. He was beside her, impatient and laughing, and she was pretending to be annoyed because she knew he would push before she finished counting.

She had missed that boy so much.

But the person standing before her was no longer entirely that boy.

He was taller, quieter, and looking at her with a tenderness that made her feel both wonderfully known and completely uncertain.

Her eyes filled.

She hated that he could see.

He reached for her hand, slowly enough that she could have moved away.

She didn't.

His fingers settled around hers.

For a moment, she could not breathe properly.

"One," she whispered.

He smiled.

"Two."

She drew a shaky breath.

He waited.

She did not say three.

Because she had waited long enough.

She stepped towards him.

He opened his arms, and she folded herself against him.

It was an awkward embrace at first. The bag caught between them, and he had to move it aside. She laughed against his shoulder, then stopped laughing altogether.

Her hands tightened at his back.

She had imagined hugging him when he returned. She had imagined doing it casually, perhaps with some foolish remark about how tall he had become.

But the moment she felt his arms around her, all the things she had been holding carefully inside herself seemed to loosen.

Four years of Sundays. Four years of waiting for letters. Four years of telling herself that she was perfectly capable of being happy without seeing him.

She had been happy.

She had grown, studied, laughed, made friends, and lived a life that was not empty.

Yet she had carried his absence through all of it.

text:
My hands trembled as I opened the first letter.

My love,

If you're reading this, you're probably angry with me. You have every right to be.

I know I should have told you everything from the beginning. I know I stole your chance to make your own decisions, and I will regret that for as long as I have breath.

But there is something I never told you.

The day I proposed to you, I had already received my diagnosis.

I bought that ring two days after the doctor told me the truth.

I almost didn't propose. I stood outside that restaurant for forty minutes, wondering whether it was selfish to ask you to marry a man who might not grow old with you.

But then I remembered the way you looked at me when we first met in the rain.

For the first time in my life, I wanted something so badly that I was willing to be afraid.

I wanted to be your husband.

I wanted to grow old with you.

I wanted to complain about your cooking, argue over the television remote, and wake up beside you when our hair had turned grey.

I wanted a lifetime, Seraphina.

I wanted it so badly that sometimes I hated the world for making me ask for it.

I pressed the letter against my chest and screamed.

He had known.

He had known when he bought my ring.

He had known when he kissed me.

He had known when he promised me forever.

And I had loved him with every piece of my heart, believing that forever was something we could reach.

I opened another letter.

Then another.

In the final envelope, I found a wedding photograph.

It was a photograph we had taken during our engagement shoot. I was wearing a white dress, and Lucien stood behind me, his arms wrapped around my waist.

On the back, he had written:

To my wife, even if the world never allows me to call you that.

Beneath the photograph was a final letter.

Seraphina,

There is one last thing I need you to know.

I didn't choose you because I thought you would make my life easier. I chose you because, even when life was cruel, you made it worth living.

If I could live this life a thousand times, knowing exactly how it would end, I would still walk into that rain.

I would still offer you my umbrella.

I would still fall in love with you.

And I would still ask you to marry me.

Even if all I had to give you was four beautiful years and a lifetime of missing me.

I love you.

Your almost-husband,

Lucien.

I don't remember how long I sat on that floor.

I only remember holding the photograph and whispering the words I had never gotten the chance to say at our wedding.

"I do, Lucien. I do."

It has been five years.

I have a good job now. I travel sometimes. I laugh with my friends, celebrate birthdays, and occasionally go an entire day without crying.

People tell me I am strong.

They say I have healed.

Some have even asked whether I have met someone new.

I always smile and change the subject.

Because how do you explain that a part of you died in a hospital room, and the rest simply learned how to keep breathing?

Last month, I met a man who reminded me of Lucien.

He was kind, patient, and thoughtful. He made me laugh in a way I hadn't laughed in years.

When he asked me on a second date, I went home and cried.

Not because I didn't like him.

But because I was terrified that one day, I might love someone else enough to smile without feeling guilty.

And somewhere in the back of my mind, I could still hear Lucien telling me not to wait for him.

So I took off my engagement ring for the first time in five years.

I placed it inside the little brown box with his letters.

Then I sat on the floor and cried until I couldn't breathe.

Because I finally understood something I had spent five years refusing to accept.

Moving on doesn't mean you have stopped loving the person you lost. Sometimes, it simply means you have finally accepted that loving them cannot bring them back.

Tonight, I opened the last letter again.

I read every word.

I kissed the photograph.

And for the first time, I said goodbye.

text:
China Is Moving AI Data Centers Under the Sea

What if the future of artificial intelligence was hidden beneath the ocean? 

China is exploring a remarkable solution to one of AI’s biggest challenges: keeping powerful computers cool without wasting enormous amounts of energy.
Off the coast of Shanghai, an underwater data center uses sealed modules containing computer servers. Instead of relying entirely on energy-hungry cooling systems, it uses the surrounding seawater to carry away heat.

The project also integrates offshore wind power, helping reduce its reliance on fossil fuels. Its design aims to cut freshwater use and reduce the need for valuable coastal land.

Why does this matter? As AI systems grow more powerful, their demand for electricity and cooling continues to rise. Underwater facilities could offer a new way to manage that demand.
But challenges remain, including maintenance, corrosion, and the environmental effects of releasing heat into marine waters.

Could tomorrow’s AI revolution run beneath the waves? Scientists and engineers are exploring whether this unusual approach can make computing more efficient and sustainable. 

Source:
The Guardian. (2026). World’s first wind-powered underwater datacentre starts operating in China.

text:
On October 20, 1803, the United States Senate ratified the Louisiana Purchase, one of the most consequential real estate transactions in history. For $15 million—roughly three cents an acre—the young republic doubled its size overnight, acquiring more than 800,000 square miles of territory that stretched from the Mississippi River to the Rocky Mountains and would eventually form all or part of fifteen states.

In the early years of the nineteenth century the United States did not yet reach from sea to sea. Its western boundary was the Mississippi. American farmers west of the Appalachians depended on the river to float their harvests to New Orleans, where the goods could be transferred to ocean-going ships. Whoever controlled the port controlled the economic lifeline of the western settlements. Spain held New Orleans, but in 1800 Napoleon Bonaparte quietly pressured Spain into returning the vast Louisiana territory to France. Suddenly the United States faced a brilliant and aggressive military power sitting on its western border with the ability to close the river at will.

President Thomas Jefferson moved quickly. In 1803 he dispatched James Monroe to Paris to join the American minister Robert Livingston. Their instructions were narrow: purchase New Orleans and a small strip of land along the Gulf of Mexico for a maximum of $10 million. Jefferson wanted only to secure the port. He had no intention of acquiring a continent, and he harbored serious doubts about whether the Constitution even permitted the federal government to buy foreign territory. Geography, however, left little choice.

When Monroe and Livingston arrived, they encountered an unexpected offer. Napoleon was prepared to sell not merely New Orleans but the entire Louisiana territory. Two interlocking crises had forced his hand. In Saint-Domingue—modern Haiti—a massive slave revolt had destroyed a French army and extinguished Napoleon’s dream of using the Caribbean sugar colonies as the economic base for a North American empire. At the same time, war with Britain was imminent. Napoleon needed cash for his armies in Europe, and he knew the British Royal Navy could easily seize distant American lands he could not defend. Selling Louisiana would raise money and deny the prize to his greatest rival.

Livingston and Monroe had no authority to purchase an empire. Communication across the Atlantic took weeks. Fearing that Napoleon might withdraw the offer, they signed the treaty on April 30, 1803. The price was $15 million. When the news reached Washington, Jefferson set aside his constitutional reservations for the sake of national interest. On October 20 the Senate ratified the agreement by a decisive margin. France withdrew from North America. The United States became a continental power.

The purchase opened the way for the Lewis and Clark expedition, the rapid settlement of the interior, and the long contest over slavery that would eventually lead to civil war. In a single stroke the map of the continent was redrawn, and the trajectory of the United States was permanently altered.

text:
In Favor of a Palestinian State, but Prefer to Remain in Israel

Why so many Arab Israelis are unwilling to give up their Israeli citizenship.

Much is said about the Palestinian aspiration for an independent state. But what do Palestinians who are already part of Israeli society actually want for themselves?

The answers are remarkable.

According to a 2023 survey conducted by the Israeli Defense and Security Forum (IDSF), 75% of Arab Israeli respondents said they would not move to a Palestinian state if doing so meant giving up their Israeli citizenship.

That could still be explained by attachment to their homes, families, and ancestral land.

But the researchers asked two additional questions.

63% opposed transferring Arab communities bordering the West Bank to a future Palestinian state.

Even more strikingly, 52% said they would be willing to leave their hometown and relocate elsewhere within Israel if their town or village came under Palestinian rule.

That last finding is particularly revealing. Apparently, this is not simply about attachment to one's hometown. For these respondents, retaining Israeli citizenship matters even more.

A Palestinian State, but Not for Themselves

The contrast becomes even more interesting when we examine other studies.

According to the July 2026 Peace Index, 71% of Arab Israelis support a two-state solution: an independent Palestinian state alongside Israel.

In other words, they may support independence for their fellow Palestinians while firmly choosing to remain within Israel themselves.

Independent research by sociologist Sammy Smooha confirms this preference. In 2017, 77.4% of Arab Israelis surveyed said they did not want to move to a future Palestinian state.

East Jerusalem: A Similar Development

An interesting shift can also be observed among Palestinians living in East Jerusalem.

Most residents do not hold Israeli citizenship but have permanent residency status. They have access to Israeli healthcare, public services, and employment opportunities.

According to research by the Palestinian Center for Policy and Survey Research (PCPSR), the proportion preferring Israeli citizenship rose from 24% in 2010 to 37% in 2022. A majority still preferred Palestinian citizenship.

A separate 2022 survey by the Washington Institute found that as many as 48% preferred Israeli citizenship.

But why this growing interest?

The Palestinian research institute PCPSR also asked residents about their concerns regarding future Palestinian governance.

- 79% feared losing access to Israeli healthcare.
- 75% feared increasing corruption.
- 70% were concerned about law enforcement.
- 65% feared restrictions on freedom of expression.

These are responses from Palestinians themselves, collected by a Palestinian research institute.

The Value of Everyday Life in Israel

Israel has a parliamentary democracy, an independent judiciary, a developed healthcare system, and an economy that offers considerable opportunities.

Arab citizens can vote, establish political parties, pursue higher education, run businesses, and participate in government.

That does not mean their lives are free from difficulties.

Arab Israelis face discrimination, socioeconomic disadvantages, and serious security concerns. Violence within the Arab community itself is a particularly pressing problem.

Organized crime, shootings, and family feuds claim hundreds of lives each year. Many Arab citizens accuse the Israeli authorities of failing to take sufficient action against this violence.

In a May 2026 survey by Tel Aviv University, 51.8% identified violence within Arab society as the primary reason for their personal sense of insecurity.

Yet this reveals another interesting point: their response to these problems is often not to leave Israel, but to demand better protection and greater involvement from the Israeli government.

‘Je moet offers brengen’: Trump-kiezers blijven trouw in aanloop naar Amerikaanse tussentijdse verkiezingen

De toenemende economische druk waar Amerikaanse kiezers mee kampen, heeft niet geleid tot een afname van het vertrouwen onder de meest loyale aanhangers van Donald Trump.

Door Evan Semones
Gepubliceerd op 20 oktober 2026

McConnellsburg, Pennsylvania, VS – Calvin Ott, eigenaar van een hoveniersbedrijf in een regio die steevast een bolwerk is voor de Amerikaanse president Donald Trump, is een van de vele zogenaamde ‘MAGA-kiezers’ wier steun onverminderd groot blijft – ook al is het leven een stuk duurder geworden sinds de president vorig jaar naar het Witte Huis terugkeerde.

“Ik ben 75 jaar oud en ik werk nog steeds”, vertelt Ott, terwijl hij onder het gedimde licht in de Fulton Pub in McConnellsburg een slok neemt van zijn Coors Light-bier.

De pub, een ontmoetingsplek voor de ongeveer 1.000 inwoners van het stadje, is de plek waar Ott tot rust komt na een doktersbezoek, voordat hij aan de rit van een uur door het Appalachengebergte naar zijn huis in Shippensburg begint.

“Ik heb een viervoudige bypass-operatie ondergaan. Ik heb huidkanker gehad. Ik ben vingers kwijtgeraakt. Ik heb diverse hartproblemen gehad”, zegt Ott met een vleugje trots, terwijl hij zijn rechterhand laat zien – getekend door tientallen jaren aan ongelukken met kettingzagen en grasmaaiers.

Ondanks stijgende medische kosten – de prijs van zijn medicijnen is sinds vorig jaar meer dan verdubbeld – en het feit dat hij niet met pensioen kan gaan nu hij de 80 nadert, blijft Ott, die al drie keer op Trump stemde, van plan om bij de Amerikaanse tussentijdse verkiezingen van volgende maand opnieuw op de Republikeinen te stemmen.

“Ik steun hem voor 100 procent”, vertelt Ott aan Al Jazeera, terwijl op de achtergrond in de pub het nummer ‘Urgent’ van de band Foreigner klinkt.

In 2016 steunden minder dan 6.000 mensen in Fulton County, waar het stadje ligt, de presidentscampagne van Trump. Acht jaar later was dat aantal opgelopen tot meer dan 7.000, wat bijdroeg aan de terugkeer van Trump naar het Witte Huis.

Voor Ott is zijn steun minder een reflectie van wat Trump heeft gedaan, en meer een reactie op wat de Democraten zouden doen als zij aan de macht waren.

"Hij is de enige president die een belofte deed en die ook nakwam", zei Ott. "Hij haat oorlogen, ook al zitten we er midden in een. Maar hij staat aan de kant van Amerika."

"Wat heeft Biden in vredesnaam ooit gegeven?" foeterde hij over het economisch beleid van Trumps Democratische voorganger – waarbij hij doelde op de stimuleringscheques van 1400 dollar die tijdens de coronapandemie via wetgeving aan Amerikanen werden verstrekt.

Wie krijgt de schuld?

De onverminderde steun voor Trump onder zijn meest loyale aanhangers is duidelijk zichtbaar in Republikeinse bolwerken zoals McConnellsburg.

'MAGA'-kiezers zoals Ott vormen de ruggengraat van de achterban van de president: ze zijn wit, behoren tot de arbeidersklasse, hebben geen universitaire graad en zijn boos op Washington.

Uit een peiling van vorige maand, uitgevoerd door het Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research, bleek dat slechts 17 procent van de volwassen Amerikanen tevreden is over de manier waarop Trump de kosten van levensonderhoud aanpakt, terwijl iets meer dan een kwart van de ondervraagden positief staat tegenover zijn algemene economische beleid.

De meest fervente aanhangers van Trump zeggen dat hun frustraties – en de economische last die zij ervaren – alleen maar zijn toegenomen sinds zijn herverkiezing. Maar in tegenstelling tot de meeste Amerikanen geven zij de president niet de schuld van de economische problemen in het land. In plaats daarvan wijzen ze naar Biden, die in januari vorig jaar zijn ambt neerlegde.

Aan de bar, naast Ott, zit Rebecca Lashley, een gepensioneerd verpleegkundig assistente. Zij vindt dat Trump, na het beleid van Biden, het voordeel van de twijfel verdient.

"Biden heeft er vier jaar over gedaan om er een puinhoop van te maken. Hoe kan [Trump] dat dan in twee jaar herstellen?" vraagt ​​Lashley zich af.

Ott is het met haar eens.

"Besef je wel wat Biden voor die man heeft achtergelaten? Hij heeft hem met een enorme berg problemen opgezadeld", zegt hij.

Het is een bekend argument dat ook vaak door het Witte Huis wordt aangevoerd.

Sinds zijn terugkeer aan de macht voor een tweede ambtstermijn in 2025, beweren Trump en leden van zijn regering regelmatig dat zij niet verantwoordelijk zijn voor de hoge kosten van levensonderhoud in het land. In berichten op sociale media schreef de president vorige maand dat "prijsstijgingen in heel Amerika zijn veroorzaakt door 'Sleepy Joe' Biden en de regering-Biden, en niet door 'TRUMP'."

"We komen uit jaren van afbouw in de energiesector", zei de Amerikaanse minister van Energie, Chris Wright, onlangs in een interview met Fox News, waarbij hij de regering-Biden de schuld gaf van de stijgende brandstofprijzen.

Vijf uur rijden ten zuiden van Pennsylvania, in het onvervalst Republikeinse Amelia County in Virginia, is Terry Williams het grotendeels met Trump eens.

Nadat hij op zondag een ontbijt had klaargemaakt, plofte de bezorger neer in zijn doorleefde bank – een model met een gecapitonneerde rugleuning – om zich klaar te maken voor een middag vol American football. Maar nog voordat de eerste wedstrijd van de dag begon, barstte hij los in een botte tirade vol krachttermen over een "waardeloze" economie, die volgens hem door duistere krachten uit de "deep state" niet door de president kon worden hersteld.

"Ik denk dat Trump alleen maar naar Biden wijst omdat hij de mensen simpelweg niet de waarheid kan vertellen", aldus de man, die zichzelf een 'Trump-lican' (een aanhanger van Trump) noemt, terwijl de geur van spekvet uit zijn keuken opsteeg. "De reden daarvoor is de Federal Reserve. Hun antwoord op alles is: geld bijdrukken."

"De Federal Reserve Bank, de aandeelhouders van de Federal Reserve – wie die lui in godsnaam ook zijn – zij creëren meer valuta omdat ze simpelweg geen andere keuze hebben."

Williams, die steun uitsprak voor de druk die Trump tijdens zijn tweede ambtstermijn op de Federal Reserve uitoefende om de rente te verlagen, stelt dat het beleid van de Amerikaanse centrale bank ertoe heeft geleid dat de munteenheid geen enkele werkelijke intrinsieke waarde meer heeft.

"Ik geloof simpelweg dat deze economie een illusie is en dat we met nep-geld werken", zei hij. 'Ik moet offers brengen'

Hoewel Trump campagne voerde met de belofte de hardnekkige inflatie – ontstaan ​​door de pandemie – terug te dringen, bestaat zijn tweede ambtstermijn uit een reeks impopulaire maatregelen die voor een groot deel van het land tot hogere prijzen hebben geleid.

Zijn tariefbeleid, dat vorig jaar tijdens een evenement genaamd 'Liberation Day' in het Witte Huis werd aangekondigd, geniet nauwelijks steun. Uit onderzoek van persbureau AP blijkt dat bijna 65 procent van de Amerikanen de hoge kosten toeschrijft aan het beleid van Trump.

De onafhankelijke denktank Tax Foundation schat dat de door Trump ingevoerde tarieven vorig jaar hebben geleid tot een gemiddelde belastingverhoging van meer dan 1.000 dollar voor Amerikaanse huishoudens. Nadat het Amerikaanse Hooggerechtshof in januari het merendeel van de door de president opgelegde tarieven onwettig had verklaard, is die schatting voor 2026 iets lager uitgevallen: 820 dollar.

De gevolgen van dit beleid zijn in Virginia nog sterker voelbaar; volgens de National Taxpayers Union Foundation heeft de staat sinds de invoering van Trumps tarieven naar schatting 6,2 miljard dollar extra betaald. Dat komt neer op net geen 1.800 dollar per gezin.

Toch zeggen sommige MAGA-kiezers in de staat, zoals Williams, dat zij – ondanks de extra kosten – in het tarievenbeleid van Trump "geloven" en zelfs pleiten voor een uitbreiding ervan.

„Het idee van een tariefstelsel spreekt me erg aan. Op die manier hoeft het Amerikaanse volk geen belasting te betalen”, zei Williams. „Dat concept spreekt me enorm aan.”

Maar het is de oorlog in Iran die wel eens de grootste gevolgen zou kunnen hebben voor Trump en de Republikeinen wanneer Amerikanen hun stem uitbrengen bij de tussentijdse verkiezingen.

Nu het conflict de achtste maand ingaat, gaf vorige maand slechts 27 procent van de geregistreerde Amerikaanse kiezers aan het te steunen, zo blijkt uit een peiling van de New York Times/Siena. Onder de meest loyale aanhangers van Trump ligt dat percentage echter aanzienlijk hoger: op 65 procent.

„Als het nodig is om onze republiek te redden, dan absoluut”, zei Williams over Trumps oorlog in Iran. Hij uitte echter wel zijn bezorgdheid over de stijgende benzineprijzen die het gevolg zijn van de oorlog van de president.

Sinds de eerste Amerikaans-Israëlische aanval op Iran eind februari zijn de brandstofprijzen in de VS explosief gestegen. Volgens de American Automobile Association (AAA) ligt de landelijke gemiddelde prijs voor reguliere benzine nu op 4,29 dollar per gallon (3,8 liter) – een stijging van meer dan 1,30 dollar ten opzichte van september vorig jaar.

Trump begint in te zien dat de oorlog – en de economische gevolgen daarvan – ertoe zou kunnen leiden dat zijn partij de controle over het Congres verliest.

„Nou, dat is mogelijk”, zei Trump eerder deze maand tegen verslaggevers. „Want Iran zal geen kernwapen krijgen. Dus als je vraagt: 'Is het acceptabel dat Iran een kernwapen heeft?', dan zal 100 procent van de mensen 'nee' zeggen – wereldwijd. Dus als je het op die manier brengt, helpt het. Als je dat niet doet, kan het schaden.”

Met het oog op de Amerikaanse veiligheid zeggen de meeste MAGA-kiezers dat ze bereid zijn de kosten van Trumps besluit over Iran te dragen — en ze vinden dat Amerika dat ook moet doen.

"Wat zou er zijn gebeurd als hij dat niet had gedaan? Wat dan? Niets goeds", aldus Lashley. "We moeten offers brengen om de zaken te verbeteren. Het maakt niet uit wie je bent. Wij staan ​​achter hem en zijn bereid dat offer te brengen."

Ott vertelde hoe de hogere brandstofprijzen, die het gevolg zijn van het conflict, hem hebben gedwongen zijn hoveniersbedrijf aan te passen. Hij moest een brandstoftoeslag doorberekenen aan zijn klanten en meer dan een dozijn werknemers ontslaan.

"Ik heb er geen probleem mee", zei Ott over de situatie. "Ik heb een bedrijf en ik moet offers brengen."

Trumps beloften

President Trump heeft herhaaldelijk beloofd dat Amerikanen uiteindelijk de vruchten zullen plukken van zijn beleid.

Nadat hij een handelsoorlog was begonnen – ook met Amerikaanse bondgenoten – beloofde Trump vorig jaar om de inkomsten uit invoerheffingen te gebruiken om Amerikanen een "dividend" van 2.000 dollar uit te keren.

"Mensen die tegen invoerheffingen zijn, zijn DWAZEN!", schreef Trump op 9 november op zijn Truth Social-account. Hij voegde daaraan toe: "Iedereen krijgt een dividend van minstens 2.000 dollar per persoon (met uitzondering van mensen met een hoog inkomen!)."

Eind augustus had de regering-Trump, naar aanleiding van een uitspraak van het Hooggerechtshof, meer dan 100 miljard dollar terugbetaald. Dat geld ging echter naar bedrijven, niet rechtstreeks naar de gewone Amerikaan.

In de aanloop naar de tussentijdse verkiezingen (midterms) heeft Trump meer contante uitkeringen in het vooruitzicht gesteld. Tijdens zijn toespraak op een bijeenkomst van het Republican National Committee in september zei de Amerikaanse president dat volwassen Amerikanen een "Trump-dividend" van 5.000 dollar zouden ontvangen als zijn partij de verkiezingen van volgende maand zou "winnen".

Uit peilingen blijkt dat het voorstel averechts heeft gewerkt: 45 procent van de kiezers zonder partijbinding gaf aan NBC News aan dat zij minder snel geneigd zouden zijn een kandidaat te steunen die achter dit voorstel staat.

Maar bij de achterban van Trump valt het in goede aarde – zelfs zeer goede aarde – aangezien zij van mening zijn dat zij recht hebben op een vorm van compensatie vanuit de overheid.

"Ik vind het geweldig als de president alle mensen kan helpen die dat nodig hebben", zei Lashley. "Ik bedoel, we hebben het geld toch? We hebben allemaal in de loop van ons leven bijgedragen aan ons land."

"Ik heb mijn hele leven belasting betaald. Ik verdien iets terug", zei Ott. "Ik krijg nooit iets."

Lashley stond op en reageerde: "Precies!" 'Ze pakken alles af'

De meeste Amerikanen zijn van mening dat het economische beleid van Trump hen eerder heeft benadeeld dan geholpen.

Volgens een peiling van AP vindt ongeveer zeven op de tien Amerikanen – onder wie meer dan de helft van de Republikeinen – dat zijn aanpak van de kosten van levensonderhoud "slechter is dan verwacht".

Toch blijven de 'MAGA'-kiezers de president trouw steunen, ook al krijgt zijn economische agenda in het hele land steeds meer kritiek.

Om te begrijpen waarom zijn meest fanatieke aanhangers loyaal blijven, is het van belang om te doorgronden hoe Trump zijn politieke coalitie destijds heeft opgebouwd.

Uit onderzoek van New America blijkt dat de coalitie van Trump hecht verbonden is en in sterke mate wordt gedreven door wrok jegens andere culturele en politieke groepen. Lashley verwoordde dat sentiment toen zij immigranten de schuld gaf van de crisis rond de kosten van levensonderhoud in het land.

„Ze nemen de bedrijven in ons land over. Ze pikken alles in”, zei ze. „Ik ben er absoluut op tegen dat mensen die hierheen komen meer krijgen dan wijzelf. Echt niet!”

Lashley ging nog een stap verder en zei dat ze wilde dat Trump de rest van zijn leven president zou blijven.

„Ik wou dat hij onze president kon blijven tot aan zijn dood”, zei ze. „Wat moet er gebeuren als hij er niet meer is? Dat baart me pas echt zorgen.”

„Ik vertrouw Trump met mijn leven”, zei Ott.

Stijgende prijzen zijn op zichzelf niet genoeg geweest om de band tussen Trump en een deel van zijn meest loyale kiezers te verbreken.

Voor velen van hen is de keuze niet simpelweg een kwestie van een dure versus een goedkopere economie. Het gaat erom wat – en wie – er na Trump zou kunnen komen.

„Ik ben bang dat er iemand aan de macht komt die zijn werk niet goed doet, waardoor we weer verder afglijden”, zei Ott. „Ik maak me zorgen over de Democraten.”

„Ik ook. Ze zijn knettergek”, antwoordde Lashley.

„Kijk maar eens wat ze met dit land gaan doen. We zullen eronder lijden”, zei Ott. „Straks zitten we erbij alsof we in Zuid-Afrika of iets dergelijks wonen.”

Die loyaliteit zou in november wel eens van groot belang kunnen zijn.

Tijdens de Republikeinse voorverkiezingen van dit jaar heeft Trump laten zien dat de achterban van de Republikeinse Partij hem blindelings volgt. Een reeks overwinningen van kandidaten die door hem werden gesteund – in de Amerikaanse staten Indiana, Kentucky en Texas – heeft zijn greep op de partij alleen maar versterkt.

Hoewel Trumps politieke instinct om zijn loyale achterban – die overigens niet altijd even trouw naar de stembus gaat – te mobiliseren tijdens cruciale verkiezingen doorgaans effectief is gebleken, is het nog maar de vraag of zij in staat zijn om de groeiende steun voor de Democraten een halt toe te roepen.

Progressieve en liberaal georiënteerde kandidaten hebben zich geschaard achter een boodschap van betaalbaarheid en lagere prijzen – een aanpak die aanslaat bij kiezers die zich steeds meer in het nauw gedreven voelen door het beleid van Trump.

Uit een peiling van Reuters/Ipsos in augustus bleek dat Amerikaanse kiezers de Democraten een voorsprong van 36 tegen 28 procent gaven boven de Republikeinen als het gaat om de kosten van levensonderhoud.

Hoewel Lashley erkende dat dit thema haar aanspreekt, zei ze dat er geen enkele omstandigheid is waaronder ze zou overwegen om tegen de president te stemmen.

Meer dan 70 procent van de Amerikaanse kiezers die zich identificeren met de 'MAGA'-beweging, gaf in een peiling van PBS News/NPR/Marist in september aan dat ze bij deze verkiezingen stemmen om Trump te steunen.

Voor Williams, die van plan is in november volledig op de Republikeinse partij te stemmen, is de economie niet de voornaamste prioriteit. De keuze komt volgens hem neer op een strijd die hij omschrijft als 'goed tegen kwaad'.

"Kijk eens naar de rotzooi die ze onze kinderen door de strot proberen te duwen met die dragshows en geslachtsveranderingen", foeterde Williams, verwijzend naar de standpunten van sommige Democraten over transgenderrechten. "Ik weet niet hoe jij erin staat, maar dat is in mijn ogen kwaadaardig. En daar heb ik enorme moeite mee."

Ott daarentegen blijft de Republikeinen trouw, omdat hij optimistisch is dat de economische situatie in de VS zal verbeteren in de tweede helft van de ambtstermijn van de president.

"[Trump] gaat nog meer doen", zei hij. "De economie zal er straks een stuk beter voorstaan."
