text:
🇿🇦💼 Sjoe! The Sovereignty Bill Is Coming Due — Who's Picking Up the Tab? 🧾🔥 ~ 🚗 AGOA, DIRCO and the Great Political Balancing Act: Who Gets the Bill? 🧾⚖️ ~ 🧾 The Coalition's Fine Print: More Bargaining Power, No Constitutional Magic 🪄📜
21 October 2026, South Africa’s governing party is ranking the prestige of speaking to the world higher than the unglamorous work of keeping factories running, services reliable and rural communities secure. 

That ranking is about to meet three simultaneous tests: local election arithmetic, a possible American trade decision, and the delivery scorecards voters can already compare.

The African National Congress has treated the Department of International Relations and Cooperation as near-sacrosanct since the 2024 Government of National Unity was formed.

Secondary ministries, by contrast, appear tradable. 

The weeks ahead will reveal whether protecting the foreign-policy high ground still looks like strategic wisdom once jobs, municipal results and comparative performance records enter the same ledger.

1. When Local Ballots Cannot Touch the Union Buildings

Section 86 of the 1996 Constitution is clinical. The National Assembly elects the President. Municipal elections decide only who sits in local councils. The 4 November 2026 local polls will rearrange ward and proportional seats across cities and towns. They will not touch the President, the Deputy President or any national minister.

Any later movement of Cabinet posts can occur solely through negotiation inside the existing coalition or through a deliberate reshuffle ordered by the President. Expectations of an automatic “new president” or overnight Cabinet reset after the local results collide with constitutional architecture, not merely with political preference. 

South Africa deliberately separated the spheres of government to prevent precisely this kind of instantaneous national upheaval. The firewall is structural. What remains is the slower craft of bargaining.

This design has consequences. Parties that perform strongly in municipalities gain leverage at the national negotiating table without gaining the power to rewrite the executive by automatic operation of law. 

The distinction is not technical pedantry; it is the difference between constitutional order and political theatre.

Sjoe!
The Constitution, it turns out, is the ultimate party-pooper. It refuses to let local drama rewrite the national script overnight. Some will find this disappointing. Others will find it the only thing standing between competitive politics and permanent instability.

Questions Stirring:
If local results cannot rewrite the national executive, what precise form of leverage do stronger opposition showings actually create? 
Why does public conversation so often treat municipal outcomes as national regime change? 
And if real power resides in negotiation rather than automatic translation, who ultimately sets the price of each ministry?

What these questions together matter:
Taken as a set, they redirect attention from theatrical expectations to the actual arena in which power is redistributed: the bargaining table. 

Understanding that arena is the precondition for any realistic assessment of what 4 November can and cannot deliver.

2. The Portfolio Hierarchy That Will Not Bend

Inside the post-2024 coalition the ANC has consistently ranked DIRCO among its highest strategic assets. Control of the foreign-policy narrative—relations with Washington, the BRICS partners, and proceedings at the International Court of Justice—is treated as central to national sovereignty and to the party’s own long-term identity. 

Ronald Lamola remains in place. Speculation about change has settled instead on secondary posts: Sport, Arts and Culture, or other mid-tier delivery portfolios.

The underlying logic is classic coalition behaviour observed in multi-party systems elsewhere. Parties protect the portfolios that define their ideological self-image and international posture, even when doing so requires offering domestic delivery posts as bargaining chips. 

Symbolic sovereignty ranks higher than operational leverage. 

That ranking now functions as the quiet organising principle of any future reconfiguration.Political scientists have long noted that liberation movements in power often prioritise the outward projection of sovereignty because it validates the historical narrative that brought them to office. 

The cost of that prioritisation is paid in reduced control over the very departments that shape daily experience for citizens. The trade-off is rational within the party’s own preference ordering; whether it remains rational for the broader electorate is a separate question.

Sjoe!
In the hierarchy of political desire, the ability to address the United Nations appears to outrank the ability to make the Home Affairs queue shorter. One of these tasks photographs better. The other is noticed every time a citizen needs a document.

Questions Stirring:
How many secondary ministries can the ANC surrender before the cost to its own organisational coherence becomes prohibitive? 
What does it signal when a governing party values the capacity to speak to foreign capitals more than the capacity to run the departments citizens encounter daily? 
And if DIRCO is truly untouchable, what does that imply for the relative standing of every other portfolio?

What these questions together matter:
Collectively they make visible the internal price list the ANC is using. Once that price list is public, both voters and coalition partners can judge whether the ranking still serves the country’s practical needs or primarily the party’s self-conception.

3. The External Shock Already Announced

On 19 October 2026 President Cyril Ramaphosa told the country it must prepare for possible exclusion from the African Growth and Opportunity Act. He described the potential job impact as “devastating.” 

Congress has extended the programme, yet the final eligibility decision rests with the United States executive. The annual review process remains active. Announcements typically arrive in late October or early November to satisfy the statutory 60-day notice period before a 1 January effective date.

Automotive manufacturing supports tens of thousands of direct and indirect jobs dependent on duty-free access. Broader estimates that incorporate agriculture and linked supply chains run higher. Official messaging continues to attribute external pressure to “fringe groups” and to frame policy adjustment as a sovereignty concession. 

The distance between preparedness rhetoric and the political reality of concentrated job losses is now the central tension.

Preference programmes like AGOA create both opportunity and vulnerability. They concentrate export success in specific sectors and regions; when preferences are withdrawn, the pain is correspondingly concentrated. 

Alternative markets exist, yet they rarely absorb volume, price or standards with perfect substitutability. The economic literature on preference erosion is unambiguous on this point: adjustment is possible, but it is neither automatic nor painless.

Sjoe!
Nothing focuses the mind like the phrase “devastating” uttered by a sitting president about an employment outcome that still lies within his government’s partial control. Preparedness is wise. It is also an admission that the preferred ranking of priorities is about to meet an external bill.

Questions Stirring:
If the job losses materialise, will the sovereignty-first narrative retain its persuasive power among those most directly affected? 
How rapidly can alternative markets absorb the volume currently moving under AGOA preferences? 
And what becomes of the political capital of a government that prepares the public for pain it then struggles to mitigate?

What these questions together matter:
They convert an abstract foreign-policy stance into concrete employment numbers that will be experienced in specific provinces and industrial nodes long before the 2029 national election. Abstract principle meets payroll reality.

4. The Scorecard Voters Can Already See

If the Democratic Alliance continues to register measurable improvements in the national portfolios it holds, while the ANC fails to close corresponding gaps in its own departments, and if that differential coincides with AGOA-related job losses and further ministerial concessions, the ANC will approach the 2029 election from a defensive posture. 

It will retain organisational depth, rural and township networks, and the largest single-party base. It will also confront a clearer comparative record of competence versus historical loyalty.

Proportional representation continues to reward the largest plurality. Sustained relative under-performance nevertheless raises the probability of further vote-share erosion and another multi-party outcome. 

Delivery differentials inside a coalition do not remain internal. They become campaign material that independent voters can weigh.

Comparative politics offers repeated examples of senior coalition partners who protected symbolic portfolios at the expense of delivery capacity and later discovered that voters had begun to treat competence as a separable currency from historical loyalty. 

The pattern is not unique to South Africa; it is a recurring feature of prolonged multi-party government.

Sjoe!
Historical loyalty is a powerful political asset until the day competence becomes a competing currency. At that point the exchange rate starts to matter.

Questions Stirring:
How large must the delivery gap become before it outweighs organisational loyalty for undecided voters? 
Can the ANC close that gap in the three years remaining, or has the ranking of portfolios already locked in a structural disadvantage? 
And if competence becomes decisive, what does that do to the traditional liberation narrative?

What these questions together matter:
They project the short-term trade-offs of 2026 forward into the electoral arithmetic of 2029. The scorecard is already being compiled, whether or not the parties choose to read it.

5. The Domestic Mirror

Agriculture Minister Willie Aucamp has repeatedly requested that farm attacks and related rural violence be formally designated priority crimes. Such status would unlock dedicated resources, improve coordination and strengthen prevention. 

The designation has not been granted under South African Police Service or Directorate for Priority Crime Investigation frameworks.The decision occupies the intersection of resource allocation, political signalling and narrative control. 

Declining to elevate the category allows the government to reject certain external characterisations while leaving the issue available for domestic contestation. The same preference for narrative control over operational prioritisation that appears in foreign-policy and trade decisions reappears here in purely domestic form.

Priority-crime designation is not costless. It redirects finite police and prosecutorial capacity. The choice not to designate is therefore a genuine prioritisation decision, not a technical oversight. 

It reveals, once more, the ranking of concerns that has structured the other trade-offs examined above.

Sjoe!
Some problems are treated as emergencies requiring specialised machinery. Others are treated as ordinary crime requiring ordinary responses. The classification itself is never neutral; it is a statement of what the state considers urgent.

Questions Stirring:
If the criteria for priority-crime status are technical, why has the technical decision not been taken? 
What political cost is being avoided by keeping the category ordinary? 
And does the same ranking that protects DIRCO also explain the reluctance to elevate rural safety?

What these questions together matter:
They complete the pattern. The preference for symbolic and narrative control over operational delivery is not confined to one portfolio or one international dispute. It is a governing habit visible across domains.

Synthesis: The Bill That Will Come Due

The five strands form mutually reinforcing evidence. 
Local elections cannot rewrite the national executive; only negotiation can. 
Inside that negotiation the ANC has ranked DIRCO above secondary delivery posts. 
An imminent AGOA decision will convert that ranking into employment numbers. 
Comparative service records will convert those numbers into voter perceptions. 
The continued non-designation of farm attacks as priority crime shows the same ranking operating on domestic terrain.

The argument is testable. 
If alternative markets rapidly absorb lost AGOA volume, if ANC-held departments close the delivery gap, and if rural safety improves without priority status, the ranking will have been vindicated by results. 
If job losses mount, delivery differentials widen and rural insecurity persists, the ranking will stand exposed as costly. 

Constitutional text, public presidential statements, observed portfolio behaviour, trade-process rules and the absence of priority-crime designation already point in one direction.

Objections and Replies

Some will insist that sovereignty is non-negotiable and that external pressure must be resisted on principle. The reply is not that sovereignty is unimportant. It is that sovereignty without delivery capacity eventually erodes the domestic consent required to sustain it.

Others will argue that local elections remain decisive because they shift bargaining power. Correct—they shift bargaining power. They do not, however, rewrite the Constitution or the existing Cabinet by automatic legal operation.

A third objection holds that AGOA exclusion is not yet certain. True. The risk is live, the presidential language is already public, and the employment exposure is documented. Preparedness language does not cancel the exposure; it acknowledges it.

Closing

The ANC’s post-2024 formula has systematically ranked the protection of sovereignty assets above the retention of domestic delivery leverage. Local elections cannot change that ranking. Only internal negotiation can. An AGOA decision will turn the ranking into jobs. Comparative records will turn those jobs into votes. The same ranking appears again in the treatment of rural violence.

When the bill for these trade-offs comes due in 2029, will the party that chose symbolism over leverage still command the arithmetic of power, or will the arithmetic have chosen differently?

The converging evidence of constitutional text, presidential statements, portfolio behaviour, trade-process rules and the continued absence of priority-crime status for farm attacks sustains the claim with cumulative force: the governing ranking privileges sovereignty over delivery, and that ranking is now under simultaneous stress from every direction that matters to the country’s next electoral chapter.

Mr Wahid,

Thank you for responding. 

You're right that @dailywaadaa didn’t contact you before the piece was published. Kindly note it was published as a profile rather than an investigation — it’s structured on court records, company filings and prior reporting. 

You're also correct  about two things I missed. Your January 2014 Foreign Policy piece on the Hasina affairs. And the decree number for your Order of Merit. Both will be corrected.

Where we differ is on the word "defamatory". The piece makes no allegation of wrongdoing against you. Every contested fact is attributed to its source: the Swiss investigation to the Swiss Attorney General's office; the Kazakh contract terms to the Neue Zürcher Zeitung and the FT; the Litco agreement to a federal magistrate's written decision; Felix Sater's claims to Felix Sater, with the court's refusal to entertain them noted in the same paragraph. Your denials are printed beside each. If a specific sentence is wrong, name it and I will look at it.

Two things in your tweet reply I need to put back to you.

First, you stated Kazakhstan earned Arcanum "several hundred million dollars" yet amounted to less than 5 per cent of the group's business. Taken together, those two figures put your group's revenues somewhere above several billion dollars. That is a far larger business than anything previously reported, and larger than the FT's $3.7 million or the NZZ's $250,000 a month suggested. If that's the number, I'd like to publish it with your confirmation.

Second, you present the Kazakh relationship as something that ended years ago, and note you haven't visited since 2015. But the Department of Justice’s own FARA file tells a longer story. 

RJI Capital Corporation, of which you are listed as a director and 70 per cent owner, registered in December 2019 as a foreign agent of Kazakhstan's Ministry of Justice. In the second half of 2020 it paid a Washington lobbying venture $220,000 to work the Senate Foreign Relations Committee and Senator Menendez's office on Astana's behalf. In February 2021 it signed a $3 million contract to represent the Ministry before Congress, the State Department and international tribunals. Those are your filings, not any tabloid's. Is that engagement still live, and if not, when did it end?

You ask what evidence supports the piece's scepticism about your early career. The honest answer is that there is none either way, which is the point. In twenty years no senator, committee or employer has been named for the Senate post, the arms-control work or the transition role, and no one outside your own company has ever confirmed them. You say the record exists. I'd welcome it. 

I would like to offer this. Send me the retractions and corrections you refer to, the facility clearance, and whatever documents the Senate and transition roles, and I will publish your response in full, unedited, alongside the piece.

My email is in my bio.

text: Calling single-payer "the solution" skips the obvious question: who pays, and who decides? A government-run system does not abolish rationing; it just moves it from insurers to bureaucrats. When one payer controls every bill, it controls every treatment — what gets approved, what gets delayed, and what doctors are allowed to offer. "Free" care is never free: it is paid for through higher taxes on working people, and once Washington owns the payment, patients lose the one power that matters, the power to walk away. Markets are not perfect, but competition, price transparency, and letting people keep plans they actually like do something a monopoly cannot: they reward providers who serve patients well and punish those who do not. A single payer does the opposite — it rewards political loyalty, punishes dissent, and concentrates life-and-death decisions in the hands of the state. That is not compassion; it is control dressed up as care.

🇦🇿🇹🇷🇮🇱 Commentary: Aliyev Is Increasingly Aligning Himself with Israel Rather Than Turkey

Azerbaijan’s President Ilham Aliyev is increasingly adopting a pro-Israel stance. Most recently, a dispute arose between Erdoğan’s advisor Oktay Saral and Azerbaijan’s ruling party over the headscarf ban in schools. In this regard, Aliyev is demonstrating the typical instinct of a successful Middle Eastern politician: to side with the winner at the right time. And that winner is likely to be Israel at present, which could play a central role in shaping a new Middle East order—with Gulf capital, Israeli technology, and military strength. Turkey, on the other hand, is struggling with economic problems and, despite its large armed forces, does not possess Israel’s level of technology.

🇦🇿 Why Aliyev Is Reorienting Himself

Aliyev knows to whom Azerbaijan owes part of its victory over Armenia: Turkish support, Armenia’s regional isolation, Russian passivity, and the training of Azerbaijani troops to NATO standards. Nevertheless, he does not want to remain Erdoğan’s junior partner indefinitely. For Baku, Israel offers access to Western military technology, closer ties to Washington, and strategic cooperation with an influential partner. Added to this are contacts in the U.S. and intelligence cooperation with the Mossad, which can provide authoritarian rulers with significant advantages.

🇮🇱🇹🇷 Israel as a Partner, Turkey as a Potential Rival

Israel, on the other hand, has no interest in turning Azerbaijan into a satellite state. Baku is important to Jerusalem as a strategic location between Iran, Russia, and Turkey, as well as an example of cooperation with a predominantly Muslim country.

Erdoğan, on the other hand, views Azerbaijan more as a junior partner within the context of broader Turkish integration. Aliyev, who has eliminated his domestic political rivals, is likely to have little interest in sharing his power with another authoritarian leader. This is precisely where a fundamental contradiction of authoritarian regimes lies: they promote integration as long as it does not challenge their own power.

☀️ There is also a historical complicating factor: Aliyev’s father, Heydar, was head of the Azerbaijani KGB. In the 1980s, he is said to have supported the supply and arming of the PKK, which at the time was fighting for a Kurdish state in southeastern Turkey. Ankara has likely not forgotten this past. It is therefore entirely conceivable that there are opponents of Azerbaijan’s current president even within Erdoğan’s power apparatus.

text:
Washington State 

Washington Appellate Project (WAP)

Non-profit that helped end Washington’s death penalty could soon shut down

By Eric Wilkinson
Oct. 20, 2026

A non-profit law group that has had a major impact on defendants' rights in Washington could soon be forced to close, leaving the appeals of hundreds of people in limbo.

The Washington Appellate Project is the only non-profit in the state that handles appeals for people who otherwise couldn't afford an attorney. It was responsible for landmark cases, including the 2018 ruling that overturned Washington's death penalty and 2021's Blake Decision that essentially legalized possession of small amounts of drugs.

Another case, one that got far less publicity, involved Stephen Dowdney.

Prisons across Washington are required to actively rehabilitate inmates through drug treatment, job training and education. But at the Washington State Penitentiary in Walla Walla, Stephen Dowdney said his rehabilitation amounted to little more than being locked in his cell most of the time.

"I mean, that place, top to bottom, is contrary to anything that the Washington State Legislature outlined," Dowdney said.

The convicted bank robber challenged what lawyers say was an unwritten rule at the prison: that languishing in a cell counted as a "rehabilitation program." He reached out to the Washington Appellate Project and won, ending the problematic practice.

"The Washington Appellate Project is basically the guardians of the galaxy," Dowdney said.

But a contract dispute between the project and the state Office of Public Defense is now putting those "guardians" on guard themselves.

The non-profit handles about half of all of the indigent appeals in Washington.

Now, the Office of Public Defense is changing how attorneys are paid to include "requirements on accountability" and to ensure that firms are "paid proportionately" to the amount of work they do.

"Under the resulting new contracts, attorneys are now being paid at higher rates and their caseloads are at historical lows consistent with WA Supreme Court rules. However, the new contracts also include requirements on accountability and ensure that firms are paid proportionately to the number of case credits they accept," wrote Katrin Johnson, deputy director for operations for the Washington State Office of Public Defense.

Richard Lechich, an attorney with the project, said the change encourages attorneys to cut corners for its more than 400 clients who need help.

"It incentivizes sort of a race to get your case done," Lechich said. "It doesn't incentivize doing the necessary work to provide effective representation."

Johnson countered, "WAP chose not to conform to the (new) requirements and refused to accept the terms offered by OPD. They don't have a contract for the new 2027 fiscal year because they didn't want one."

The two sides are now facing off in court. WAP is asking the court to allow it to continue working on the 400 to 500 cases it is currently servicing. If WAP loses, Lechich said it will likely be forced to disband at the end of the year.

Dowdney hopes his support will call attention to the organization's plight.

"You don't always have to stand tall, but sometimes you have to stand up," he said.

text:
Elon Musk offered $97.4 billion for OpenAI. Sam Altman answered in one line:

"no thank you but we will buy twitter for $9.74 billion if you want"

Exactly one tenth of the offer. Musk replied with one word. "Swindler."

The two started OpenAI together in 2015 as a nonprofit. Musk left the board in 2018 and has been fighting Altman ever since, including in court.

The bid landed in February 2025, right when OpenAI was trying to turn itself into a for-profit company. A few days later OpenAI's board rejected it unanimously. Altman's own guess was that Musk was "probably just trying to slow us down."

I don't think either of them expected a sale. Musk's offer made OpenAI's restructuring harder and more expensive. Altman's reply turned a serious legal move into a meme the whole internet shared.

Still, it's wild to watch two of the richest men in tech fight like this over a company they started together.

Who won this round, Musk or Altman?

Holding $TSLA is the higher-EV path if you assign any meaningful probability to a deal. Both companies have now formed special committees of independent directors to explore a combination, and Musk has publicly called a merger “a good idea” given the overlap in AI, robotics, chip design (Terafab), and orbital infrastructure.

Typical large-cap tech control premiums run 20–35%. At current valuations (~$1.48T TSLA / ~$2.0T SPCX), an all-stock offer even at a modest 25% premium would imply a meaningful step-up for TSLA shares on announcement—before any synergy or multiple re-rating in the combined ~$3.5T entity. Selling now locks in the pre-premium price, crystallizes a large tax bill, and transfers the upside to the acquirer side. The asymmetric payoff sits with the target.

text:
Today in 1975, a quiet cul-de-sac in Monasterevin County Kildare, became the centre of the world’s attention. Members of the Gardaí and the Irish Defence Forces surrounded a modest suburban house where Dutch industrialist Tiede Herrema was being held hostage by members of the Provisional IRA. 

Herrema was no ordinary businessman. Born in the Netherlands, he had fought with the Dutch Resistance during the Second World War and survived imprisonment by the Nazis in Poland. In later life he became an industrialist, managing Ferenka, a steel cord manufacturing plant in Limerick that employed 1,400 people. In an Ireland still struggling with unemployment and instability, Ferenka was a rare success story.

That fragile optimism was shattered on the 3rd of October 1975. As Herrema left his home on the outskirts of Limerick for work, his car was intercepted by a gang led by Eddie Gallagher and Marian Coyle, both members of the Provisional IRA. Their operation was crude but effective. Herrema was forced into another vehicle and spirited away. 

The motive was not political. Gallagher was the lover of Rose Dugdale, an English heiress turned revolutionary who was then imprisoned in Limerick for the 1974 Russborough House art theft, a heist that netted paintings worth £8 million. Dugdale had given birth to Gallagher’s child in prison, and it was his desperate wish to secure her release that drove the kidnapping.

The IRA demanded the release of Dugdale, along with Kevin Mallon and J. B. O’Hagan, two senior republicans held in Portlaoise Prison. The Irish government, led by Liam Cosgrave, refused to negotiate. Instead, a nationwide manhunt was launched. More than 9,000 soldiers and Gardaí were mobilised in one of the largest search operations in the history of the State.

The breakthrough came when one of the kidnappers, Brian McGowan, was captured and interrogated. Under questioning, he revealed the hideout’s location in Monasterevin. The Gardaí quickly surrounded the house, cutting off power and communications. Inside, Gallagher and Coyle barricaded themselves in an upstairs bedroom with their hostage.

The siege dragged on. Journalists camped outside the cordon, politicians urged patience. Herrema’s wife, Elisabeth, watched and waited in anguish. The kidnappers sent out increasingly desperate messages, alternating between defiance and exhaustion. Garda Commissioner Edmund Garvey refused their demands for prisoner releases but offered leniency, four years for Gallagher, two for Coyle, if they surrendered peacefully.

On the 7th of November, after seventeen tense days, the standoff ended. Gallagher and Coyle emerged, gaunt and exhausted, and surrendered. Herrema, remarkably, was in good condition though suffering from neck pains after weeks of confinement. In an almost surreal gesture, he handed Gardaí a .38 bullet the same one Gallagher had kept in his gun throughout the ordeal. Given to him, he said, as a souvenir.

Herrema later returned to the Netherlands but maintained warm ties with Ireland, even becoming an Irish citizen. The man who had survived the Nazis, and then the IRA, remained remarkably without bitterness. “They were misguided,” he once said of his captors, “but they were human.”

Five Palestinian students who won places at University College London (UCL) could miss out on their studies and remain stuck in Gaza because their scholarships don’t cover the cost of their fees. 

The students have been offered Global Masters Scholarships from UCL worth £15,000 but still can’t afford the remainder as they are being charged international fees, which can be over £40,000.

The UK government has agreed to help Gazan students offered places at UK universities leave the territory and get visas. But this support is limited to those with fully funded scholarships covering both fees and living costs.

That means students with offers who lack full scholarships will have to get out of the territory without UK government help. 

As Gaza has no airport and its coastline is blockaded by the Israeli military, anyone looking to leave the territory has to do so via a third country, creating administrative hurdles for the students. 

Last year, advocacy groups who assisted Gazan students coming to the UK with the immigration process described the process as “chaos”. Some students ended up not arriving until December, months into their course. 

The campaign group UCL Action for Palestine has set up a fundraiser for the students that has so far raised £50,000. 

They are calling on UCL to waive international fees for Gazan students and charge them home fees instead. Typically, home fees are reserved for UK residents and Irish citizens but there are exemptions. Students from Ukraine, for example, are eligible. 

“This is not a radical ask,” UCL Action for Palestine told Novara Media. “If UCL cared about Palestinian students, they would be trying to remove the barriers that stand in the way of them having a real opportunity to study at our university, not kicking the can down the road and promising to do better next year.”

A spokesperson for UCL said the university does not comment on individual student circumstances, but noted that over the last two years, it “has worked extensively to support students from Gaza through a combination of scholarships, philanthropic funding, accommodation, immigration support and specialist wellbeing services.” 

They added: “We continue to work closely with offer holders to understand their circumstances and explore what support may be available to them.

"We are currently reviewing our humanitarian scholarship provision to consider whether, and how, support could be expanded in future years. As part of that work, we are carefully considering how best to support students affected by conflict and humanitarian crises.” 

The five students are Mais, Reem, Amjad, Reham and Farah. They are due to start masters in public health nutrition, civil engineering, sustainable education, urban planning and project management, respectively.

text:
(3/4) So the critique of Islamism from the left is constrained these days; Islamophobia, however, seems to be growing, and not only on the populist or nationalist right. Why is this happening? The new Islamophobia Studies Journal (a bi-annual publication sponsored by Berkeley’s Center for Race and Gender), in an editorial in its second issue, identifies the source of the trouble:

For some, rising anti-Muslim sentiments are immediately explained away as a “natural” outcome of the many violent events in the Muslim world and “terrorism” in general. However, we maintain that the rising negative sentiments may have to do with the presence of a well-organized and well-funded Islamophobic industry that has managed to invade and capture civil society and public discourses without serious contestation. Up to this point, anti-racist and progressive voices have not been effective in challenging this industry, nor have they been able to provide the needed resources to mount regional and national responses.

This is nicely self-serving: more resources for the Journal would certainly be a big help in combating the Islamophobic industry. But notice the reluctance to engage with “the many violent events in the Muslim world.”

One can find a similar reluctance in a series of otherwise excellent articles published in a special issue of the Nation in July 2012. Jack Shaheen’s “How the Media Created the Muslim Monster Myth” is an example of an argument very much like that of the editors of the Islamophobia Studies Journal. The novelist Laila Lalami in “Islamophobia and its Discontents” recognizes that “retrograde blasphemy laws” and “unfair divorce laws” may have something to do with hostility to Islam but rightly refuses to treat these as excuses for the harassment she has lived with here in the United States. Nor would “violent events in the Muslim world” provide any such excuse. Islamist zealotry should never be used to justify or “explain” European and American prejudice. But the entirely legitimate desire to avoid prejudice isn’t a reason to avoid those “violent events.” I don’t mean to single out the Nation here, whose editors organized that useful special issue; so far as I can tell, no leftist magazine or website has attempted a serious engagement with Islamist zealotry.

Most leftists, whatever problems they have understanding religion, have no difficulty fearing and opposing Hindu nationalists, zealous Buddhist monks, and the messianic Zionists of the settler movement (the phrase “no difficulty” is a gross understatement in this last case). And, of course, no one on the left makes common cause with Islamist militants who kidnap schoolgirls, or murder heretics, or tear down the ancient monuments of rival civilizations. Acts like these, insofar as they are noticed, are routinely condemned. Well, not quite routinely: Nikolas Kozloff, in an excellent article, “A Tale of Boko Haram, Political Correctness, Feminism, and the Left,” has documented the strange unwillingness of a number of leftist writers to blame Muslim zealots for the kidnapping of the Nigerian schoolgirls.8 Less outrageous, but bad enough, is the unwillingness of many more leftists who do recognize such crimes to attempt a generalizing analysis and an encompassing critique of Islamist zealotry. What stands in the way of analysis and critique?

Deepa Kumar’s book, Islamophobia and the Politics of Empire,9 suggests one possible answer to this question: what stands in the way is the fact that Islamists today are opponents of “the West,” that is, of Western, really American, “imperialism”—bases in Saudi Arabia, the two Iraq wars, the Libyan intervention, support for Israel, drone strikes in Somalia, and so on. I would argue that this list requires a selective response: opposition in some cases, certainly, but also agreement in others. I dare say that the overthrow by Islamist zealots of the regimes the United States has supported in the Middle East, bad as some of them are, would not be terribly helpful to the people of the region. But leftist opponents of imperialism don’t usually make selective judgments, and neither do the Islamists. So “the enemy of my enemy is my friend.” We watched this maxim being acted out in last August’s demonstration in London, sponsored by the UK Stop the War Coalition, which was attended by vocal supporters of Hamas including secular leftists and religious Muslims (some of them fundamentalist, some not). The secular leftists were fierce opponents of Islamophobia, though they were not entirely free of other phobias.

But there is another reason for the reluctance to condemn Islamist crimes, and that is the great eagerness to condemn the crimes of the West. The root cause of religious zealotry is not religion, many leftist writers insist, but Western imperialism and the oppression and poverty it has bred. So, for example, David Swanson, first on the War Is A Crime website and then on the Tikkun website (with a nervous but only partial disclaimer from the editor), asks “What to do about ISIS?” and answers: “Start by recognizing where ISIS came from. The U.S. and its junior partners destroyed Iraq . . .”10 That’s right; there would be no ISIS in Iraq without the U.S. invasion of 2003, although if Saddam had been overthrown from within, the same religious wars might well have started. For ISIS doesn’t “come from” the U.S. invasion; it is a product of the worldwide religious revival, and there are many other examples of revivalist militancy. Swanson might offer a similar explanation for all of them, but the explanation loses plausibility as the instances multiply.

The left has always had difficulty recognizing the power of religion. Aren’t all religions the ideological tools of the ruling class? And aren’t all millenialist and messianic uprisings the ideologically distorted response of subaltern groups to material oppression? Religious zealotry is a superstructural phenomenon and can only be explained by reference to the economic base. These ancient convictions are particularly obfuscating today. Parvez Ahmed, a Florida professor who is fully cognizant of the “scourge” of Boko Haram, provides a typical example in a recent blog. He argues that “much of the violence [committed] in the name of Islam is less motivated by faith and more so by poverty and desperation.”11 Similarly, Kathleen Cavanaugh from the National University of Ireland, writing on the Dissent website, insists that “the violent and oppressive actions [of ISIS] have little to do with religion per se,” but rather are “underpinned” by material interests.12 But is this right? Why don’t poverty, desperation, and material interests produce a leftist rather than an Islamist mobilization? In fact, the religious revival, not only among Muslims but around the world, among Jews and Christians, Hindus and Buddhists, has enlisted supporters from all social classes, and the driving motive of revivalist activity seems, incredibly, to be religious faith (Fawaz Gerges’s Journey of the Jihadist: Inside Muslim Militancy provides ample evidence of religion’s power).13

There are also people on the left who believe that Islamist zealotry is not only produced by Western imperialism but is a form of resistance to it. Whatever groups it actually attracts, it is fundamentally an ideology of the oppressed—a version, though a little strange, of left politics. Think of the leftist writers who described the Sunni and Shi’ite militias fighting against the U.S. occupation of Iraq as “the resistance”—deliberately invoking the French Resistance to the Nazis in the Second World War. But nothing about the Islamist militias was leftist except for the fact that they were fighting against Americans. This example was featured by Fred Halliday in a 2007 article in Dissent called “The Jihadism of Fools.”14 That’s a good tag, but it didn’t stick, as we can see from Slavoj Žižek’s claim the following year that Islamic radicalism is “the rage of the victims of capitalist globalization.” I have to acknowledge that Žižek is not afraid to be called Islamophobic; he advocates a “respectful, but for that reason no less ruthless” critique of Islam and of all other religions.15 But he won’t get the critique right so long as he thinks that the object of Islamist rage is the same as the object of his own rage.

Judith Butler makes a similar mistake when she insists that “understanding Hamas [and] Hezbollah as social movements that are progressive, that are on the left, that are part of a global left, is extremely important.”16 She said that in 2006 and then repeated it with interesting amendments in 2012: Hamas and Hezbollah belong to the global left because they are “anti-imperialist,” but she doesn’t support every organization on the global left, and she specifically doesn’t endorse the use of violence by those two. I am grateful for that last amendment, but the left identification was as wrong in 2012 as it was in 2006—usefully wrong, perhaps, since it helps explain why so many leftists support or won’t actively oppose groups like Hamas and Hezbollah. The only thing that makes these organizations “leftist” is that they are fighting against Israel, which stands in here for imperial America.

The postmodernists haven’t done any better than the anti-imperialists with regard to Islamist zealotry. Remember Michel Foucault’s apology for the brutality of the Iranian revolution: Iran doesn’t “have the same regime of truth as ours.”17 This version of cultural relativism has become a commonplace, as we can see in the case of Azar Nafisi, the author of Reading Lolita in Tehran, a lovely account of cultural subversion in an Islamist state. In exile in the United States, Nafisi told an interviewer in Boston: “I very much resent it in the West when people from—maybe with all the good intentions or from a progressive point of view—keep telling me, ‘It’s their culture.’ . . . It’s like saying, the culture of Massachusetts is burning witches. . . . There are aspects of culture which are really reprehensible. . . . We shouldn’t accept them.”18 Those well-intentioned and progressive people were probably advocates of a radical multiculturalism, which might well allow the burning of witches so long as it didn’t happen in Massachusetts.

The strongest postmodern defense of Islamic radicalism comes from Michael Hardt and Antonio Negri, who argue that Islamism is itself a postmodern project: “The postmodernity of fundamentalism has to be recognized primarily in its refusal of modernity as a weapon of Euro-American hegemony—and in this regard Islamic fundamentalism is indeed the paradigmatic case.” And again: “Insofar as the Iranian revolution was a powerful rejection of the world market, we might think of it as the first postmodern revolution.”19 Is it cruel of me to point out how eager the Iranians are these days to rejoin the world market?

All these left responses to Islamist zealots—identification, support, sympathy, apology, tolerance, and avoidance—look very strange if we consider the actual content of their ideology. Jihadi opposition to “the West” should provoke serious worry on the left before any other response. Boko Haram began with an attack on “Western-style” schools, and other Islamist groups have undertaken similar attacks, especially on schools for girls. Values that the zealots denounce as “Western” are very much in contention here: individual liberty, democracy, gender equality, and religious pluralism. No doubt, Westerners don’t always live in accordance with these values and often fail to defend them when they need defense, but these are values to which Western hypocrisy pays tribute—and which some of us Westerners struggle to uphold. In recent years, Russia and China have sometimes claimed to oppose both Western imperialism and Western values, but these two countries look more like rival imperial powers than opponents of imperialism. While their leaders occasionally resort to value arguments (as when Chinese rulers endorse the Confucian ideal of “harmony”), they don’t seem strongly committed to the values they proclaim. But the Islamists are definitely committed. They have their own large ambitions, but these are highly idealistic ambitions, which leave little room for material interests. Their zealotry is a value zealotry, theologically driven, and it is a real challenge to “Western” values.

But individual liberty, democracy, gender equality, and religious pluralism aren’t really Western values; they are universal values that first appeared in strong, modern versions in Western Europe and the Americas. These are the values that pretty much define the left, which also first appeared in its strong, modern version in Western Europe and the Americas. The left is an eighteenth-century invention, an invention of the secular Enlightenment. There were, of course, people who held potentially leftist positions in all the major religious traditions—pacifists, communitarians, proto-environmentalists, advocates for the poor, even people who believed in equality or, better, who believed in the equal standing before God of all believers (I should probably say, of all male believers). But nothing like the classic left ever existed among Hindus, Jews, Buddhists, Muslims, or Christians. And the values of the left are those “Western” values, taken very seriously. So the opposition to those values is really something that the left should confront—and the strongest opposition right now comes from Islamist radicals. And this is the very reason that many leftists are reluctant to confront the Islamist radicals.

Kaduna gets its name from the Hausa word "kada," meaning crocodile, because the Kaduna River once had a large crocodile population. It was founded in 1900 by the British as the Northern administration center.

Permit me to say that Kaduna is the Northern Agriculture Powerhouse in Nigeria. When you have Bank of Agriculture having its headquarters in Kaduna you should know it's not play.

First, let’s establish the fact that Kaduna is Big!

The state covers approximately 46,053 square kilometres and has 23 Local Government Areas.

Kaduna is Nigeria's leading ginger-producing state. The crop is particularly important in Southern Kaduna, where communities have built livelihoods around growing, harvesting, drying, processing and selling ginger.

But ginger farming has also faced serious challenges. In 2023, a fungal disease outbreak devastated farms across parts of Southern Kaduna, causing significant losses. 

Maize is another major agricultural strength. Kaduna is the highest Maize producing state in Nigeria... No other state match their Maize power.

The popular GMO Maize (TELA maize) was developed through the Institute for Agricultural Research (IAR) at Ahmadu Bello University in Kaduna state.

You see Kaduna is a strong contender for Tomatoes production in Nigeria. If you're driving from Katsina to Zaria some communities there sundry their tomatoes along road side.. everywhere go just red!

Groundnuts, sorghum, Soyabean, millet, cowpeas and rice also contribute to the state's agricultural diversity. These crops support household food supplies, local markets and businesses that process and trade grains.

 Kaduna's agricultural strength is not built around a single crop; it comes from the combination of cereals, legumes, root crops, vegetables and industrial crops.

Kaduna also has a substantial livestock economy, Cattle rearing is an important activity in the state's livestock sector, supported by pastoral and other livestock-keeping communities. Goats and sheep are raised for meat, household income and commercial trade.

Dairy production offers opportunities to collect, process and market milk, while livestock feed creates demand for maize, soybean meal and other agricultural crops.

If you visit Kaduna and you didn't eat Tuqo Chinkafa and Miyan Kuka - your visit is not complete.

Kaduna's agricultural story is not just about what grows in its soil. It is about the people who turn those resources into food, businesses, jobs and opportunities.

Kaduna State carries the slogan "Centre of Learning" because it houses major educational and military institutions, including the Nigerian Defence Academy and Ahmadu Bello University in nnZaria.

Shout out to every food value chain players in Kaduna, we see you and we celebrate you for the amazing work you do to feed every Nigeria.

May you never sow in vain.

text:
A simple Odia meal of Dahi Pakhala and Saga Bhaja or Tarakari holds a special place in Maha Dashami rituals at several Durga Puja pandals in Cuttack. The offering reflects a belief in welcoming the Goddess with the flavours of the land and the food traditionally eaten by its people.

Dahi pakhala, made with fermented rice and curd, is valued for its cooling properties, while saga bhaja or tarkari, a preparation of leafy greens with vegetables and pulses, represents the simplicity of a traditional Odia meal. Together, they symbolise nourishment, humility and gratitude for nature’s bounty.

The practice is also associated with the belief that Maa Durga, worshipped as a daughter returning to her parental home during the festival, should be offered familiar, home-style food. 

While specific explanations may vary across puja committees and local traditions, the offering reflects Odisha’s distinctive food culture and the intimate bond devotees share with the Goddess.

text:
In 1998, Warren Buffett gave a 1-hour masterclass on how to never lose money investing.

Here are the 22 most valuable lessons from his lecture:

1. You only have to get rich once. If you have $100 million and can make 10% unleveraged or 20% leveraged, the difference between $110 million and $120 million at year-end means nothing to your life, your family, or anything. But the downside, especially with other people's money, is disgrace, humiliation, and facing the friends whose money you lost. The equation never makes sense.

2. To make money they did not need, they risked money they did have and needed. That is just plain foolish, Buffett says, regardless of your IQ. If you hand him a gun with a million chambers and one bullet and offer him any sum to put it to his temple and pull once, he will not do it. There is nothing on the upside that justifies the downside. People do this financially all the time without thinking.

3. The smartest people in finance went broke, and that is the most fascinating story Buffett knows. Long-term Capital Management had 16 people with possibly the highest average IQ of any business in the country, 350 to 400 combined years of experience, and most of their own net worth in the firm. They still went bankrupt. Buffett says if he ever wrote a book, it would be called why smart people do dumb things.

4. Beta and sigmas tell you nothing about the real risk of going broke. The LTCM team relied heavily on mathematics and believed a six- or seven-sigma event could not touch them. They were wrong. History does not tell you the probabilities of future financial events. The real risk is not volatility. It is a permanent, irreversible blind spot in something crucial, often caused by knowing a great deal about something else.

5. Invest only in businesses you can understand. That one rule narrows the field by about 90%, and that is fine. Buffett can understand Coca-Cola. he cannot value an internet company, and he says if a student handed him a valuation of one on a final exam, he would flunk them. People thought Enron was incredible because it had a good track record, but almost nobody understood how it made money. That was the signal to avoid it.

6. You want a business that is a castle with a wide moat around it. Inside the castle, you want an honest, able, hard-working duke. The moat can be low cost, like Geico in auto insurance, or brand, or patents, or location. But a wonderful castle will always be attacked, so the job of every manager Buffett owns is one thing: widen the moat. Throw crocodiles and sharks into it to keep competitors out.

7. Moats change slowly and invisibly, but they change. Thirty years ago, Kodak's moat was as wide as Coca-Cola's. They had share of mind; the little yellow box meant best in everyone's head. Then they let Fuji into the Olympics and narrowed their own moat. Coca-Cola's moat, by contrast, is wider now than 30 years ago. Every time infrastructure gets built in a country that is not yet profitable, the moat widens a little. You cannot see it day by day, but in 10 years, the difference is enormous.

8. Share of mind beats share of market. When you say Disney, every person in the room has something in their head. Say Universal Pictures or 20th Century Fox, and you have nothing. A mother with two kids will pick the $17.95 Disney video over the $16.95 alternative because she knows it will be fine and does not want to preview ten videos to decide. That little bit of certainty in the customer's mind is worth a fortune.

9. The best businesses have pricing power and require little capital. see's candy sold 16 million pounds at $1.95 when Buffett bought it for $25 million. The entire thesis was whether the price could go to $2.25 without hurting sales. It could, because nobody wants to hand their valentine a box of candy and say, "This year I took the low bid." Today, See's makes $60 million on the same formulas and still takes almost no capital. Compare that to GM, which had to reinvest every dollar into better factories and whose stock barely moved over 50 years.

10. The best businesses earn a royalty on other people's capital. Coca-Cola sells a formula and collects a royalty on every drink. American Express takes a few percent of every dollar you spend. You put up the capital, they take a cut. Low capital intensity is one of the most underrated qualities in a business and one of the surest paths to durable wealth.

11. Define your circle of competence and stay inside it. The size of the circle does not matter. Staying inside, it does. If you know which 30 companies out of thousands you actually understand, you are fine. Buffett understood H.H. brown shoes and Frank Rooney, so he closed that deal in five minutes. If you do not know enough to understand a business instantly, you will not understand it in a month either.

12. Ignore the macro entirely. Buffett has never bought or skipped a business because of a feeling about interest rates, the economy, or any macro forecast. If Alan Greenspan and Bob Rubin both whispered exactly what they would do for the next 12 months, it would not change what he pays for anything. You want to focus on what is important and knowable. The macro is important but not knowable, so you ignore it.

13. Inactivity is the strategy, not a flaw. Wall Street makes money on activity. You make money on inactivity. A broker is like a doctor paid by how often he changes your pills. If everyone in a room trades their portfolio with everyone else every day, they all end up broke, and the intermediary keeps the money. Buffett looks for one good idea a year and rides it to its full potential. He measures Berkshire by how little turnover there is, like a church where the same people fill the seats every Sunday.

14. If you understand businesses, diversification is a mistake. For the 99% who will not evaluate businesses, Buffett recommends a low-cost index fund and extreme diversification. But if you bring real intensity to evaluating companies, owning more than six is a terrible idea. Very few people got rich on their seventh best idea. A lot of people got rich on their best one. Buffett keeps about half his money in what he likes best.

15. Buffett's biggest mistakes are mistakes of omission, not commission. The times he understood a business well enough to act and instead sat there sucking his thumb. He passed on healthcare stocks during the Clinton plan and on Fannie Mae in the mid-eighties, each a multi-billion-dollar miss. Accounting never captures these. The $2,000 he put into a Sinclair service station as a young man, money he lost, has an opportunity cost of about $6 billion today.

16. Focus on what will happen, not when. Coca-Cola went public in 1919 at $40 a share and dropped to $19 within a year. There was always a reason not to buy: the great depression, world war, sugar rationing, thermonuclear weapons. But one share bought then and reinvested would be worth about $5 million. If you are right about the business, you will make a lot of money. The timing is the tricky part, so do not focus on it.

17. When hiring, look for integrity, intelligence, and energy. But if the person lacks the first one, you actually want them dumb and lazy. Because a person with intelligence and energy but no integrity will destroy you. Buffett borrowed this from Pete Kiewit. The trait everyone screens for last is the one that matters most.

18. Here is a thought experiment Buffett gives students. Imagine you could own 10% of one classmate for the rest of their life. You would not pick the highest IQ or the best grades. You would pick the person you respond to best, the one who is generous, honest, gives credit to others, and has leadership qualities. Now imagine you also had to short one classmate. You would pick the egotistical, greedy, slightly dishonest one. The qualities that decide both are not talent. They are character.

19. Every quality on the admirable side is achievable, and every quality on the repellent side is removable. The things that make you want to own 10% of someone are not the ability to throw a football or run fast; they are behavior, temperament, and character, all of which anyone can choose. Buffett's point: you already own 100% of yourself, so you might as well become the person worth betting on.

20. The chains of habit are too light to be felt until they are too heavy to be broken. Buffett sees people in their forties and fifties trapped by self-destructive patterns they can no longer change. At a young age, you can choose any habits you want. Ben Franklin and Ben Graham both did exactly this, looking at people they admired and simply deciding to behave like them. There was nothing impossible about it.

21. Take a job you would take if you were already independently wealthy. Buffett told a 28-year-old at Harvard who wanted a consulting job "to look good on his resume" that it was like saving up sex for your old age. There comes a time to just start doing what you love. Buffett offered to work for Ben Graham for free, was told he was overpriced, and kept pestering him for years. Take the job you would jump out of bed for. You cannot miss.

22. You won the ovarian lottery, and that should shape how you think. Buffett imagines a genie 24 hours before your birth letting you design the world's rules, with one catch: you do not know which of 5.8 billion balls you will draw. Born here or in Afghanistan, with an IQ of 130 or 70, male or female, able-bodied or not. If you could put your ball back and draw one of 100 random others, most people would not, because they are already in the luckiest 1%. Buffett knows he is perfectly wired for a market economy that pays him like crazy, while an equally good citizen leading scout troops and teaching Sunday school is not, purely by luck.

RT @velitesgear | Full Text Article: https://t.co/Vmx9s26zPk | Author: @militarnyi Australia’s Ghost Shark Underwater Drone to Carry Asteria Smart Mines and ALTIUS Kamikaze Drones 
Australia has revealed the weapons systems of its new Ghost Shark underwater drone, developed by Anduril, for the first time.

The War Zone reported on this.

The weapons were demonstrated during a visit by Pat Conroy, Australia’s Minister for Defence Industry, to Anduril Australia’s facility in Sydney. Although government officials provided only a general description of the weapons, released photographs offer a clearer view of the systems carried by the underwater drone.

The Ghost Shark was designed as a modular platform that allows its payload to be quickly changed to suit different missions. Its design features separate bow and stern sections, along with a central section whose length can be adjusted to accommodate different types of equipment.

Photographs show several cylindrical components of unknown purpose. These may be ballast tanks or containers for specialized equipment, including reconnaissance systems.

 ALTIUS-family drones alongside the Ghost Shark vehicle. Photo credits: Australian Department of Defence

ALTIUS-family drones, which can carry out strike and reconnaissance missions, were also displayed alongside the underwater vehicle. This suggests that Ghost Shark could be used to covertly deploy these drones. However, the method of launching them from the underwater vehicle and the number that could be carried onboard remain unknown.

Photographs also suggest that Australian Ghost Shark vehicles may be equipped with Rheinmetall’s Asteria “smart” 533 mm naval mines. The same diameter is used by standard Western-made torpedoes, including the Mark 48.

This suggests that the vehicle could potentially also employ torpedo armament, although this capability has not yet been officially confirmed.

The development of Ghost Shark is a strategic project for the Royal Australian Navy, being carried out under the Advanced Strategic Capabilities Accelerator program. In May 2022, an order for three prototypes was announced,and the first vehicle was launched in April 2024.

In late October 2025, Militarnyi reported the opening of an Anduril facility in Australia dedicated to manufacturing these underwater drones.

 Ghost Shark autonomous submarine. Photo credits: Anduril Industries

The total contract value is estimated at approximately $1 billion. The Australian government had previously invested around $140 million in developing the platform, its mission modules, and the associated manufacturing infrastructure.

The facility is expected to produce “dozens” of these vehicles, although the exact number has not been disclosed. The technical specifications of Ghost Shark also remain classified.

𝗥𝗛𝗔𝗣𝗦𝗢𝗗𝗬 𝗢𝗙 𝗥𝗘𝗔𝗟𝗜𝗧𝗜𝗘𝗦  

CHRIST JESUS—THE ULTIMATE REDEEMER

TUESDAY  21ST  OCTOBER  2026

PASTOR CHRIS OYAKHILOME

In whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of his grace (Ephesians 1:7).

Redemption is one of the beautiful truths in the Gospel because it reveals not only what Christ accomplished, but also who He is. The Scriptures present the picture of a redeemer as one who has both the legal right and the ability to secure another's freedom. In the Lord Jesus Christ, we find the perfect and ultimate fulfilment ofthat picture. He is the Redeemer who paid the full price for our salvation and brought us into everlasting freedom. 

In the law of Moses, a kinsman-redeemer could redeem a relative who had fallen into debt or bondage. The redeemer had a legal right to act on behalf of the one in need, but he also had to pay the required price. Freedom wasn't obtained by mere desire or good intentions; a price had to be paid. 

This helps us understandthe significance of Christ'ssacrifice.Humanity'sgreatest problem was not merely the devil's oppression; it was the issue of sin. Sin had brought separation from God and placed mankind under judgment. The righteousdemandsofjusticehad to be satisfied.A price had to be paid. 

What a blessing to know that the Lord Jesus took our place and paid the full price required for our redemption. The payment wasn't silver or gold; it was His precious blood. The Bible says, “Forasmuch as ye know that ye were not redeemed with corruptible things, as silver and gold…But with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot” (1 Peter 1:18-19). 

When He shed His blood, He obtained eternal redemption for us. The debt was settled. The claims against us were satisfied.The penaltyofsinwasfullyaddressed. The Lord Jesus paid the price you could never pay. He accomplished what you could never accomplish for yourself.

UK students are being taught that Britain must forge closer links with China in a textbook accused of peddling “propaganda”. The A-level book, widely used in schools by British teenagers studying Mandarin, says the UK should “deepen cooperation” with Beijing in the wake of Brexit.

Using language associated with China, it also promotes: China’s Belt and Road Initiative; the “positive impact” of Chinese students coming to the UK; the “crucial role” of Confucius Institutes.

Pearson, the UK’s largest education and assessment company, which endorses the textbook for students taking its Edexcel A-level Chinese qualification, launched a review on Oct 19.

The book titled “Chinese for A-Level” is published by Cypress Books, which describes itself as the largest distributor for Chinese publications in the UK.

The London-based company is under the overall control of 🇨🇳 China International Communications Group (CICG / 中国国际传播集团), the CCP’s public relations and publishing arm, which is owned and operated by the Publicity Department of the Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party 👉🏻 the CCP’s Central Propaganda Department.

CICG promotes the 🇨🇳 government’s message internationally through books, magazines, and journals.

The textbook was written by Frank Fan (范学群), a Mandarin teacher at Melbourne Village College in Cambridgeshire at the time of publication in 2025, but who has since left the school.

In one section of the textbook, students are asked to translate into Mandarin a 124-word passage written in English that describes how Brexit has weakened the UK’s financial standing.

The passage states that the growth of trade between the UK and China has “stalled” in recent years as “the market uncertainty created by the UK’s exit from the EU has weakened its influence in the global financial system, causing China to be more cautious about investing in the UK”.

It says that “in light of these circumstances”, the two countries “must enhance communication, seek win-win cooperation opportunities, and find mutually beneficial solutions”.

The phrase “win-win cooperation” is a favorite of the CCP. It was first used by Xi Jinping during a state visit to Russia in 2013, where he reportedly proposed a “new type of international relations featuring win-win cooperation”. Chinese officials use it frequently in official statements about foreign policy and international relations.

The phrase is used again in another passage — this one written in Mandarin that students are asked to translate into English — which states that the UK and China should “deepen their cooperation”.

The textbook also repeatedly states that the UK and China should seek cooperation and trade outcomes that are “mutually beneficial”, which is another commonly used phrase by the CCP.

Cameron and Janice Hooker seemed harmless, but roughly 30 minutes later, Cameron pulled onto a dirt road, threatened Colleen with a knife, and kidnapped her. Incredibly, Colleen was eventually permitted to leave the house, work a job, and even visit her parents. Her family had no idea she was being held captive.

In August 1984, Janice finally admitted to Colleen that “The Company” was completely fictional, helping her break free from Cameron’s control. Colleen escaped after more than seven years of captivity. Cameron Hooker was convicted of kidnapping and assault in 1985 and sentenced to 104 years in prison. According to the 2025 Israeli Democracy Index, 90% of Arab respondents supported integration into Israeli society. And in May 2026, more than 77% supported the participation of Arab parties in the Israeli government.

They do not merely want to stay. They also want a say in how the country is governed.

What Does This Preference Tell Us?

Naturally, these figures must be interpreted carefully.  Moreover, preferring Israeli citizenship does not mean abandoning one's Palestinian identity or refraining from criticizing Israel.

Nevertheless, several studies point to an important reality.

Many Arab Israelis see their future within Israel. And among Palestinians in East Jerusalem, the quality of public services, legal protections, and concerns about Palestinian governance appear to be important factors in their citizenship preferences.

Perhaps this offers an important part of the explanation.

People who experience the opportunities provided by a democratic system governed by the rule of law, accessible healthcare, and economic development may become so attached to these benefits that they are unwilling to give them up for the national ideal of a state of their own.

Israel is not without its problems. But many Arab residents appear to value opportunities that are far less readily available in significant parts of the Middle East.

And that brings us back to one particularly striking finding:

Supporting the establishment of a Palestinian state is one thing. Being willing to leave your own home in order to remain in Israel tells a different story.

text:
Before a state government spends millions on skills training, it should be able to answer one question:

Where are the jobs this training is supposed to lead to?

Before approving a programme, decision-makers should investigate:

Which occupations offer realistic opportunities in the state?

What skills are employers seeking?

How many relevant opportunities are available, and how reliable is that evidence?

What barriers could prevent trained participants from getting hired?

Vacancy data can help identify advertised demand. 

Employer interviews, labour-market statistics, and local economic analysis can provide additional context.

No single source tells the whole story.

But together, these sources can help governments make better-informed decisions about which training pathways to prioritise.

Training people is an investment.

The question is whether that investment is connected to credible employment opportunities.

Before deciding how many people to train, investigate where the opportunities are.

text:
A juice carton, tree bark and a hidden camera: How Russia recruited an 18-year-old Ukrainian to help target cities and prepare a terrorist attack in Kyiv.

Oct. 21, Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU) had arrested an 18-year-old man from Odesa suspected of helping Russian intelligence identify targets for drone strikes and prepare an attack in the Ukrainian capital.

The case reveals how Russian intelligence services allegedly recruit young Ukrainians through online job offers and use them for reconnaissance, targeting and covert surveillance.

According to investigators, the teenager was recruited after losing his job at a postal facility in Odesa. Looking for quick money, he turned to Telegram channels, where he allegedly came into contact with Russian handlers.

His first reported assignment was to help Russia identify targets for aerial attacks.

In August, the suspect allegedly provided Russian intelligence with the coordinates of a postal logistics terminal in Odesa. The facility was subsequently attacked by Russian jet-powered drones.

Investigators said he also collected information about Ukrainian air defense positions and defense industry facilities in the Odesa region.

He later traveled to Dnipro, where he was instructed to verify coordinates supplied by his Russian handlers and gather additional intelligence.

The next assignment was different: preparing surveillance for a planned terrorist attack in Kyiv. According to the SBU, the suspect installed a concealed camera opposite the home of a potential target.

He hid the device and its power bank inside an empty juice carton, then covered it with tree bark to disguise it as discarded material near a tree.

Russian intelligence allegedly intended to use the recordings to establish the target’s daily routine and movements. The suspect retrieved the camera to download the footage and send it to his handlers. SBU officers arrested him before he could transmit the report.

Investigators seized the camera and a smartphone allegedly containing evidence of his cooperation with Russian intelligence.

The significance of this case goes beyond one teenager and one improvised surveillance device. It illustrates how Russia can use locally recruited operatives to support several stages of hostile operations: identifying infrastructure, verifying strike coordinates, collecting intelligence on air defenses and conducting surveillance of individuals.

Such activities allow Russian intelligence to gather information inside Ukrainian cities without deploying its own personnel across the border.

The recruitment method is also significant. According to investigators, the suspect was approached through Telegram channels offering opportunities to earn money — a means of exploiting financial vulnerability to recruit potential agents.

The teenager has been charged with high treason under martial law. He remains in custody without bail and faces life imprisonment if convicted. The allegations have not yet been tested in court.

Russia’s attacks on Ukrainian cities do not always begin with a missile launch or a drone taking off. Some allegedly begin with a Telegram conversation, a set of coordinates or a camera hidden in a juice carton.

Source: Security Service of Ukraine, Oct. 21, 2026.

text:
Wait, what?! Oh my God! 😱

Now Türkiye must be absolutely terrified!

The mighty Ursula von der Leyen might even threaten to kick Türkiye out of the European Union!

Oh, wait… 😂

We're not even in the EU, are we?

How terribly embarrassing!

Of course, we did want to join. We knocked on your door for decades. But apparently, we weren't quite European enough.

Never mind. We still thought we should be helpful.

Millions of refugees to accommodate? Certainly! Why trouble Europe's delicate social equilibrium when Türkiye can shoulder the burden with a little financial assistance and a great deal of European gratitude?

European defence needs military capabilities? Naturally! From Estonia to Spain, Turkish military capabilities have contributed to Europe's security. Membership, of course, is an entirely different matter. Let's not get carried away!

A Customs Union that works rather more comfortably for European industry than for Türkiye? But of course! We wouldn't dream of disturbing such a beautifully arranged relationship.

European companies and banks want access to the Turkish market? Be our guests! Our largest private bank is even under Spanish control. How much more welcoming could we possibly be?

And now, after all these years of hospitality, strategic cooperation and economic accommodation, we are apparently expected to ask Brussels for permission to exercise our sovereign rights in the Eastern Mediterranean?

Oh, Madam President, how wonderfully imperial of you!

And how exactly do you propose to stop us?

With a stern warning from Brussels? A disapproving finger? Perhaps a French fleet? Or shall we expect a British military expedition to teach NATO's second-largest army a lesson in obedience?

How fascinating!

The very military capabilities Europe relies upon are apparently supposed to tremble at the sound of a Brussels press statement.

A raised finger is not a fleet. A declaration of disapproval is not an instrument of coercion. And diplomatic indignation, however theatrically delivered, is no substitute for actual power.

But surely there has been a misunderstanding.

We offered partnership, not guardianship.

We offered cooperation, not submission.

And we certainly never offered Brussels a seat at the head of Türkiye's sovereign decision-making table.

Our sovereignty is not a privilege granted by Brussels, nor is its exercise subject to European approval.

There is, after all, a limit to modesty. Even Turkish modesty.

Perhaps it is time Europe learned the difference between partnership and permission, between diplomatic rhetoric and geopolitical reality.

And Madam President, do forgive us if we fail to tremble.

You might wish to get used to it,afterall.😎
