text:
𝐄𝐕𝐄𝐑𝐘 𝐄𝐌𝐏𝐈𝐑𝐄 𝐃𝐈𝐄𝐒 𝐓𝐇𝐄 𝐒𝐀𝐌𝐄 𝐖𝐀𝐘.

They miss the next technology.
Most civilizations do not disappear because they are weak. They disappear because the technology that once made them powerful becomes obsolete.
History is filled with empires that looked permanent—until the rules of power changed. When those rules changed, their decline was often swift and irreversible.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
𝗘𝗚𝗬𝗣𝗧 𝗠𝗜𝗦𝗦𝗘𝗗 𝗜𝗥𝗢𝗡
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
Egypt ruled the ancient world for nearly two thousand years. Long before Greece rose or Rome existed, Egypt possessed one of the most advanced states in the Mediterranean world. Its bureaucracy, agriculture, and armies were formidable.

During the Bronze Age, bronze weapons and chariots defined military power. Egypt mastered both.

But bronze had a hidden weakness. It required copper and tin—metals that had to be imported through fragile trade networks.
Then came iron.
Iron weapons were cheaper, and their raw materials more abundant. But smelting iron required high temperatures and enormous quantities of charcoal. Charcoal required forests.

Egypt was a river civilization surrounded by desert. It lacked the forests needed to produce iron at scale. Assyria, with access to the wooded regions of the Near East, developed formidable iron-equipped armies.

Over time, the balance of power shifted. Egypt survived, but it never again regained its former position at the centre of the ancient world.

A civilization that had ruled for millennia had missed the next technological age.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗟𝗢𝗡𝗚𝗕𝗢𝗪 𝗔𝗡𝗗 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗞𝗡𝗜𝗚𝗛𝗧
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
In medieval Europe, the armoured knight was the ultimate weapon of war.

A knight was a walking fortress—encased in steel, mounted on a powerful warhorse, and supported by an entire feudal economy. Training one took years. Equipping one cost enormous wealth. Society itself was organized around sustaining this elite warrior class.

Then came a weapon made largely from wood.

The English longbow could be wielded by commoners. Skilled archers could unleash volleys of arrows against heavily armoured opponents.

At battles such as Agincourt in 1415, English archers helped devastate a much larger French army filled with heavily armoured nobles.
The economics of war had changed. A relatively inexpensive weapon could neutralize a military system that required immense wealth to maintain.
The knight did not disappear overnight, but its dominance ended.

Technology had quietly rewritten the cost structure of power.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
𝗪𝗛𝗘𝗡 𝗖𝗔𝗡𝗡𝗢𝗡𝗦 𝗕𝗥𝗢𝗞𝗘 𝗘𝗟𝗘𝗣𝗛𝗔𝗡𝗧 𝗔𝗥𝗠𝗜𝗘𝗦
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
For centuries, Indian armies relied on war elephants as powerful instruments of battlefield shock. Elephants towered over infantry formations, disrupted cavalry charges, and carried commanders above the battlefield. They were also symbols of royal authority.

But elephants belonged to an older military age.

In 1526, at the First Battle of Panipat, Babur faced the much larger army of the Delhi Sultan Ibrahim Lodi.

Lodi possessed tens of thousands of troops and numerous war elephants. Babur’s forces were considerably smaller, but he brought gunpowder artillery and employed innovative battlefield tactics.

The sound and chaos of battle contributed to the disruption of Lodi’s elephant formations. His army was defeated, the Delhi Sultanate fell, and the Mughal Empire emerged.

A military system that had dominated the subcontinent for centuries was being challenged by new technologies and tactics.

Numbers did not guarantee victory. Adaptation mattered more.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗠𝗢𝗡𝗚𝗢𝗟𝗦: 𝗠𝗢𝗕𝗜𝗟𝗜𝗧𝗬 𝗕𝗘𝗔𝗧 𝗧𝗥𝗔𝗗𝗜𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
To the sophisticated civilizations of the thirteenth century, the Mongols appeared primitive.
China had cities and advanced engineering. Persia had wealth and scholarship. Europe had castles and armoured knights.

The Mongols had horses.

But their system of warfare was revolutionary. Each warrior rode multiple ponies, allowing armies to travel extraordinary distances without exhausting their mounts. Their composite bows could strike effectively at range, while decentralized command enabled rapid manoeuvres that stunned slower opponents.

Mobility became a decisive advantage.

Within a few decades, the Mongols built the largest contiguous land empire in human history, stretching from East Asia to Eastern Europe.

Power does not always belong to the most sophisticated civilization. It belongs to the civilization that adapts most effectively.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
𝗔𝗜𝗥𝗖𝗥𝗔𝗙𝗧 𝗥𝗘𝗣𝗟𝗔𝗖𝗘𝗗 𝗕𝗔𝗧𝗧𝗟𝗘𝗦𝗛𝗜𝗣𝗦
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
At the beginning of the Second World War, battleships represented the pinnacle of naval power. These massive floating fortresses carried enormous guns capable of firing shells across vast distances. Nations poured immense resources into building them.

Then aircraft carriers changed the equation.
Aircraft launched from carriers could attack ships from far beyond the range of battleship guns. During the Pacific War, carrier-based aviation demonstrated that naval supremacy no longer depended primarily on enormous guns and thick armour.
Within a few years, the battleship had lost its position at the centre of naval warfare.

Iron replaced bronze. Longbows challenged knights. Cannons disrupted elephant armies. Aircraft transformed naval power.

Every military revolution follows a similar pattern: a new technology undermines the expensive systems that once defined dominance.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗡𝗘𝗫𝗧 𝗥𝗘𝗩𝗢𝗟𝗨𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡 𝗜𝗦 𝗛𝗘𝗥𝗘
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
For five centuries, global dominance belonged largely to maritime powers that controlled the oceans.

The Portuguese began the era of oceanic empires. The Spanish expanded it. The Dutch developed global trading networks. Britain built a navy that underpinned an extraordinary worldwide empire.

In the twentieth century, the United States inherited much of this maritime order. Aircraft carriers became central instruments of global power projection.

Control of the sea meant control of trade. Control of trade meant influence over wealth.

But the technologies shaping warfare are changing again.
Drones, artificial intelligence, autonomous systems, and precision missiles are altering the economics of conflict. In modern battlefields, relatively inexpensive drones have destroyed tanks and other equipment worth millions of dollars.
A device costing a fraction of its target’s price can impose enormous losses. When these asymmetries scale, entire military doctrines become unstable.

Even the aircraft carrier—the crown jewel of naval power—faces new vulnerabilities. A carrier costs billions of dollars, while some weapons capable of threatening it cost a tiny fraction of that amount.

But the deeper shift may not be destruction.

It may be denial.

In the twentieth century, dominance meant the ability to project power almost anywhere in the world. In the twenty-first century, victory may increasingly mean preventing a rival from reaching you.

Access denial can be as powerful as conquest.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗦𝗧𝗥𝗔𝗜𝗧 𝗢𝗙 𝗛𝗢𝗥𝗠𝗨𝗭 𝗔𝗡𝗗 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗧𝗔𝗜𝗪𝗔𝗡 𝗤𝗨𝗘𝗦𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
Consider the Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly one-fifth of global petroleum liquids consumption passes.
If a regional power can credibly threaten access to this narrow corridor using missiles, drones, mines, and other systems, the consequences for global trade could be immense.
Challenging a superpower no longer necessarily requires conquering its cities. It may require making critical strategic routes too dangerous to enter.

If a navy cannot guarantee safe passage through vital chokepoints, its ability to operate near heavily defended regions becomes far more uncertain.

And that raises an uncomfortable question.

If access to a narrow waterway such as Hormuz can be contested, what does that imply about military operations near Taiwan, surrounded by dense missile networks and advanced defences?

The balance between offence and defence may be shifting again.

Whenever that happens, the global hierarchy begins to move.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
𝗖𝗛𝗜𝗡𝗔 𝗜𝗦 𝗕𝗨𝗜𝗟𝗗𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗙𝗢𝗥 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗡𝗘𝗫𝗧 𝗔𝗚𝗘
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
China appears determined not to miss this moment.

It is investing heavily in artificial intelligence, robotics, autonomous systems, and advanced manufacturing. Its industrial ecosystem, engineering capacity, and manufacturing scale give it important advantages in these fields.

The United States still possesses immense strengths. Its universities, capital markets, research institutions, and technological ecosystem remain powerful.

Old powers rarely fade quietly. But technological transitions are rarely gentle.

The countries that recognize a new technological era early—and build the capabilities to exploit it—can reshape the balance of global power. Those that fail to adapt risk becoming dependent on those that do.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
𝗜𝗡𝗗𝗜𝗔’𝗦 𝗗𝗘𝗖𝗜𝗦𝗜𝗩𝗘 𝗖𝗛𝗢𝗜𝗖𝗘
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
Which brings us to India.

Every technological shift divides nations into two groups:
Those who build the future and those who live inside it.
Egypt missed iron. Knights lost their battlefield dominance. Elephant armies confronted gunpowder. Battleships lost their supremacy to aircraft.

The twenty-first century will be shaped by artificial intelligence, robotics, autonomous systems, and advanced manufacturing.

The question is simple:

Who will build it?

India has the population, talent, and intellectual capacity to become one of the defining powers of this age. But technological leadership demands long-term focus: sustained investment in science, engineering, industry, research, and strategic capability.

Yet too often, the national conversation revolves around something else entirely.

Instead of debating how to lead in artificial intelligence or robotics, political energy is consumed by election cycles and promises of immediate benefits.

Welfare schemes, cash transfers, and subsidies—including programmes such as Ladli Behna—may deliver meaningful short-term support to beneficiaries and political advantages to governments. But they cannot substitute for the scientific, technological, and industrial foundations that determine a nation’s long-term strategic position.

The challenge is not whether welfare should exist. It is whether a country can balance immediate needs with the investments required to create future prosperity.
History offers a harsh lesson:
Wealth must be created as well as distributed.

A society that neglects its productive and technological capabilities risks falling behind those that invest relentlessly in them.

Empires are not lost only on battlefields. Sometimes they are lost in budgets.

A society obsessed with the next election may fail to prepare for the next technological revolution.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗖𝗢𝗨𝗡𝗧𝗥𝗜𝗘𝗦 𝗧𝗛𝗔𝗧 𝗕𝗨𝗜𝗟𝗗 𝗪𝗜𝗟𝗟 𝗗𝗘𝗙𝗜𝗡𝗘 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗙𝗨𝗧𝗨𝗥𝗘
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
The countries that dominate the coming century will be those that build laboratories, factories, engineers, and machines—not merely expand welfare rolls.

India faces a choice that will shape its future.
It can commit to the difficult path of technological leadership through sustained investment in research, robotics, artificial intelligence, manufacturing, and military innovation.
Or it can remain trapped in a narrow cycle of electoral politics and short-term promises, gradually surrendering its opportunity to shape the global order.

The choice is not between helping people today and investing in tomorrow. It is between building a system capable of doing both—and sacrificing the future by failing to prepare for it.

Egypt missed iron. Others missed gunpowder. Still others missed aircraft.

The question of this century is simple:

𝗪𝗜𝗟𝗟 𝗜𝗡𝗗𝗜𝗔 𝗦𝗘𝗜𝗭𝗘 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗔𝗚𝗘 𝗢𝗙 𝗔𝗜 𝗔𝗡𝗗 𝗥𝗢𝗕𝗢𝗧𝗜𝗖𝗦—𝗢𝗥 𝗠𝗜𝗦𝗦 𝗜𝗧?

Because every empire that misses the next technology eventually learns the same lesson.

It becomes a spectator in a world shaped by others.

text:
At first, Patrick was offended.

“Does she think we’re going to steal her documents?” he asked.

I reminded him that Evelyn had spent 29 years watching the company change hands, restructure, and replace people who had once been considered indispensable.

She had every right to protect herself.

The following morning, Evelyn arrived wearing a navy suit and carrying a large brown folder.

She greeted everyone politely.

Then she sat beside the company’s lawyer and placed the folder on the table.

Inside were copies of the original agreement, correspondence between the founder and the Whitmore family, and a series of letters documenting the conditions attached to the property arrangement.

The lawyer reviewed the documents carefully.

After several hours, he confirmed that the records were highly relevant to the dispute.

They showed that the company had been required to complete certain obligations and notify the family when those obligations were fulfilled.

The company’s files contained no clear evidence that this had happened.

Evelyn explained that she had reminded the founder about the outstanding paperwork years earlier.

She had even written a memorandum recommending that the documents be reviewed by legal counsel.

The memorandum was included in the folder.

It had never been acknowledged.

Patrick looked stunned.

“Why didn’t you bring this to management before you retired?”

Evelyn stared at him.

“I did. I sent a copy to the legal department in 2014. I kept the original because nobody confirmed that they had received it.”

The company’s lawyer found the old email in an archived mailbox.

Evelyn had been telling the truth.

The company had received her warning twelve years earlier and failed to follow up.

The documents did not instantly settle the property dispute, but they gave the legal team the evidence needed to negotiate with the Whitmore family and establish exactly what obligations remained outstanding.

Over the following months, the parties reached a settlement that allowed the company to retain its management operations while resolving the family’s outstanding claims under revised terms.

The company avoided a potentially devastating legal battle.

Afterward, Patrick invited Evelyn to lunch.

He thanked her for saving the company from what could have become a financial disaster.

He also offered her a paid consulting role to help organize the company’s historical records.

Evelyn politely declined the permanent position.

“I’m 64,” she said. “I’ve spent almost three decades helping this company remember its past. Now I’d like to enjoy my own life.”

She agreed to a short consulting project with clear terms and payment.

Before she left, Patrick asked her why she had kept the folder for so long.

She smiled.

“Because when you’ve watched a business grow from nothing, you understand that the smallest piece of paper can become the most important thing in the building.”

That evening, I asked her why she had never pushed harder for recognition.

She looked at me and said, “Megan, I didn’t stay for 29 years because I needed everyone to clap for me. I stayed because I believed the work mattered. But I learned something: just because you don’t need applause doesn’t mean people should take you for granted.”

I haven’t forgotten those words.

For years, we treated Evelyn as though she were part of the office furniture.

We relied on her knowledge but rarely acknowledged her expertise.

We remembered her when something went wrong, yet forgot to celebrate her when everything went right.

And the saddest part is that she never demanded special treatment.

She simply wanted to do her job properly and be treated with respect.

The company later introduced a formal records management system and began documenting the contributions of long-serving employees.

But I still think about her final afternoon, when she packed two cardboard boxes and drove away without a farewell party.

text: Respectfully, blaming President Trump for costs misses the real story. The inflation that squeezed working families was ignited by reckless federal spending and an energy policy that choked American production — policies your party championed. Now the answer offered is more of the same: price controls by another name, a higher minimum wage that small businesses will pay for with fewer jobs and higher prices, and more government deciding what “fair” means. New Mexico doesn’t need another round of Santa Fe mandates; it needs lower taxes, unleashed American energy, and a government that gets out of the way so workers keep more of what they earn. Affordability comes from abundance and freedom, not from the same big-government playbook that made life expensive in the first place. God bless!

text:
ICYMI O/N — WEDNESDAY 21 OCTOBER

MACRO:

US equity futures and Asian stocks rebounded after stronger AI-related earnings after bullish forecasts from SpaceX and a big beat on SMCI's pre-earnings update. (BBG)

South Korea’s Kospi gained as much as 4.8%, triggering a temporary halt in program buy orders after Kospi 200 futures rose more than 5%. Citi warned crowded short positioning could accelerate the rebound through short covering. (BBG)

Ken Griffin said AI is “almost certainly” in a bubble, questioning whether companies can extract enough productivity to justify their spending. He remained optimistic about the technology creating major new businesses over time. (BBG)

Deutsche Bank’s Christian Sewing pushed back against broad AI-bubble fears, although he acknowledged individual companies could suffer setbacks. He described industrial AI as a major opportunity for Germany. (BBG)

BlackRock’s Larry Fink warned that slowing data-centre construction would keep computing costs high, fuel inflation and threaten growth. Faster construction is needed to bring costs down, he said. (BBG)

Blackrock's Fink separately said rising bond yields are warning Washington about fiscal deficits, with competition for capital as intense as he has seen in his career. (BBG)

BlackRock says current corporate bond yields offer a more resilient source of returns that doesn’t depend on expectations for falling interest rates or tighter spreads. (BBG)

Aware Super ($168bn AUM) CIO Simon Warner said the pension has positioned itself almost exclusively toward the more defensive end of AI infrastructure. Firmus’s failed IPO showed investors becoming more selective, he said. (BBG)

JPMorgan expects Wednesday’s $13bn 20-year Treasury auction to require more price concession, citing rich valuations, an unattractive macro backdrop and unsupportive technicals. The yield stood around 5.487% in Asian trading. (WSJ)

Deutsche Bank researchers propose reducing FOMC meetings from eight to six annually, allowing two rounds of payrolls, CPI and PCE data between decisions. (FT)

Trump urged data-centre developers to pay local communities a dividend and reiterated that operators should generate their own power, supplying excess electricity to the grid. The Truth Social proposal is not a new binding requirement. (RTRS)

The White House is discussing executive orders addressing high prices before the midterms, including one aimed at reducing housing costs, WSJ sources said. Details and implementation have not been announced. (WSJ)

US–Mexico trade talks have stalled over steel and aluminium tariffs, potentially delaying progress until after November 3, Bloomberg sources said. Mexico wants relief on downstream metal products; Lutnick’s counterproposal failed to resolve its concerns. (BBG)

Japan's underlying inflation is quite close to the central bank's 2% target and financial conditions remain loose, Deputy Bank of Japan Governor Ryozo Himino said on Wednesday, signalling readiness to raise borrowing costs. (RTRS)

Japan's economy is seeing price rises driven by higher import costs and on the cusp of shifting to a period of sustained inflation driven by rising wages, Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama said on Wednesday. (RTRS)

Former BOJ executive director Eiji Maeda expects a December hike followed by another in March or April, with increases roughly quarterly. He sees the policy rate potentially reaching 2.25% from 1.25%. (BBG)

Japan’s September export growth missed expectations despite support from semiconductors, chipmaking equipment and cars. Exports rose 16.7% against 21.3% expected, leaving a ¥536bn trade deficit. (BBG)

South Korean exports rose 65.9% on a working-day-adjusted basis in October’s first 20 days, versus 89.8% in September’s comparable period. Unadjusted chip exports surged 222.5%; holiday timing inflated headline comparisons. (RTRS, BBG)

All 24 economists surveyed expect the BOK to hold at 3% on Thursday. Citi expects a hawkish pause, potentially with one dissent for a hike, followed by quarter-point increases in November and February to 3.5%. (BBG)

Goldman’s updated “Japanisation” index puts China above Japan itself for the past five years. Economists warn household deleveraging and the property slump risk prolonged stagnation despite competitive manufacturing exports. (FT)

RBA Deputy Governor Hauser said Australia’s inflation outlook is materially worse than forecast in August, citing oil, technology prices and data-centre construction. November hike pricing rose to roughly 50% from 30%. (BBG)

Goldman switched its November RBA call from a hold to a 25bp hike to 4.85% after Hauser’s remarks. Another increase is more likely than not unless next week’s inflation data undershoots, its economists said. (BBG)

UK inflation accelerated to 3.5%, above 3.4% expected, with services inflation reaching 3.7%. Markets were almost fully pricing a November BoE hike to 4%; Bloomberg reported four quarter-point hikes priced by end-2027, plus a 60% chance of a fifth. (FT, BBG)

UK September borrowing reached £24.5bn, taking April–September borrowing to £97.8bn, £6bn above the OBR forecast. Debt exceeded £3tn and September interest costs reached £10.9bn; FT estimates put remaining fiscal headroom near £12bn versus £23.6bn in March. (BBG, FT)

British annual house prices rose at their weakest annual pace since March in August, according to official data published on Wednesday that also showed growth in average private rents held at its highest since the end of last year. (RTRS)

UK Chancellor Healey will leave a proposed wealthy-investor visa out of the October 28 Budget, people briefed told the FT. The scheme would have required at least £5m invested in British innovation and growing companies in exchange for residency rights. (FT)

Burnham is preparing to scale back Labour’s centrally controlled new-towns programme and shift major housing developments to mayors, sources told the FT. He favours urban extensions and is reluctant to commit substantial central funding. (FT)

France’s economy minister Lescure said the government can use Article 49.3 or budget decrees if parliament cannot agree on next year’s budget. The French ten-year yield premium over Germany widened beyond 155bp in early European trading. (BBG, BBG)

Deutsche Bank AG Chief Executive Officer Christian Sewing said the fiscal and political instability in France that spilled over into violent protests is a reason for concern, with volatility likely to continue until the presidential elections. (BBG)

Bank Indonesia held its benchmark at 5.75%, raised the overnight deposit rate 25bp to 5% and announced 1ppt reserve-requirement cuts in both November and December. MSCI’s proposed downgrade continues to pressure Indonesian assets. (WSJ, BBG)

Allspring warned Indonesian banks and telecoms could face disproportionate selling ahead of MSCI’s June review despite stronger governance than many peers. The sectors represent around 80% of MSCI Indonesia; said it remains too early to call a bottom. (BBG)

Temasek and GIC denied former Indonesian trade minister Muhammad Lutfi’s allegations that they pressured MSCI to trigger Indonesia’s stock-market collapse. Temasek said neither it nor its employees contacted MSCI to influence its decisions. (BBG)

South Africa consumer inflation rises less than expected in September. (RTRS)

South Africa’s Godongwana is expected to outline a fiscal anchor in Wednesday’s budget update. Economists forecast a 3.8%-of-GDP deficit versus Treasury’s 4% projection and expect a legally binding framework by end-2028. (BBG)

Nickel gained as much as 2.7% above $16,000 a tonne as traders anticipated possible Indonesian production cuts by Chinese producers. No coordinated reduction had been confirmed. (BBG)

Wheat fell for a fifth day to its lowest since August 5 as traders reduced Black Sea risk premiums amid Ukraine peace talks. Lachstock warned continuing attacks and territorial disagreements warrant caution. (BBG)

Super Typhoon Champi is expected near Taiwan on Friday–Saturday before tracking along China’s eastern coast toward Japan. A Taipei closure decision is expected Thursday evening; no market closure had been announced. (BBG)

IRAN:

'More Oil Is Now Coming Out of the Persian Gulf Than Before the Iran War' WSJ article notes Middle East oil flows through Hormuz and alternative routes averaged above 24m b/d in the week to October 18, versus 23.3m before the war. Hormuz flows including offshore transfers reached around 14m b/d, or 82% of prewar levels, Kpler data showed. (WSJ)

Israel prepared a multi-day offensive for the October 10th weekend targeting Iranian power plants, nuclear facilities and regime sites, the FT newly reported. It did not proceed because of Trump’s opposition; the White House reiterated that the US would not attack before the midterms. (FT)

Iranian Foreign Minister Araghchi said indirect US–Iran talks continue through Pakistan and Qatar, claiming Washington accepted Iran’s conditions but sought additional provisions. He said Washington must honour the Islamabad memorandum before agreed Hormuz arrangements and further negotiations. (Iran International, Press TV)

Araghchi said Iran and Oman had mapped designated Hormuz shipping routes, with international registration still required, and were working on routes for Iraqi oil tankers. Oman’s agreement was not independently confirmed. (Press TV, Iran International)

US Secretary of State Rubio welcomed Qatari and Pakistani mediation, saying Trump would decide acceptable terms. He did not confirm a new negotiating round or specific proposal. (Iran International)

A senior Iranian security official told state broadcaster Press TV that renewed attacks would trigger retaliation without restraint against aggressors and regional supporters. The official said Tehran would treat US and Israeli military action as inseparable. (Press TV)

IRGC political deputy Yadollah Javani renewed a conditional threat to target internet cables in Hormuz if Iran’s infrastructure were attacked. (Iran International)

Araghchi said neither Saudi Arabia nor the Houthis had responded to Tehran’s mediation offer. He also warned against foreign intervention as Egypt considered military support for Saudi Arabia, Faytuks reported. (Iran International, Faytuks)

Iraq closed the Sheeb crossing with Iran to passengers, vehicles and commercial trucks until further notice, Reuters reported, citing border sources. Baghdad was reviewing security arrangements there, one source said. (RTRS)

At least three North Asian refiners plan to reduce Middle Eastern crude volumes in their 2027 contracts to make room for purchases from other regions after the Iran war disrupted supplies this year, according to Reuters sources. (RTRS)

China tapped its massive crude oil stockpiles for the fourth month in the past five in September as rising refinery processing rates outweighed a slight recovery in oil imports. (RTRS)

Gulf-to-China supertanker freight reached approximately $37.37 a barrel, while war-risk insurance rose as high as 10% of vessel value from below 3%. High trading profits are keeping vessels moving despite escalating attacks. (WSJ)

Goldman estimates crude freight costs exceed $20/bbl versus $3 a year ago, including roughly $7 of Hormuz war-risk premium. It sees upside risk to its $90 year-end Brent forecast if shipping disruption persists. (BBG)

Morgan Stanley expects fuel markets to remain tight through mid-2027 even if war disruption eases. Planned refinery outages through Q2 are set to rise by 3.4m b/d, roughly 2.5 times normal, as deferred maintenance comes due. (BBG)

The Oman crude premium over Dubai fell near $4/bbl, its lowest since late July. Physical Gulf barrels are becoming more available despite elevated futures prices and continued shipping attacks. (BBG)

API data showed US crude inventories fell 4.9m barrels last week, according to a document seen by Bloomberg. Gasoline and distillate stocks also declined; official EIA figures were due later Wednesday. (BBG)

Kpler expects India’s October diesel exports near 730,000 b/d versus 653,000 a year earlier, with Reliance supplying about 550,000. Jamnagar is already running at maximum capacity, limiting immediate upside from Rubio’s visit on Wednesday. (FT)

The UK approved Jackdaw, with first gas potentially arriving by month-end. The government says the field could add 6% to domestic gas production at peak and operate for up to 11 years; Rosebank’s decision remains outstanding. (UK government, FT)

GEOPOLITICAL:

A US official said Ukraine had brought new ideas and proposals to the Oslo talks, which had made "meaningful progress" toward a coordinated approach to engaging with Russia. (RTRS)

Musk ordered the slowdown of Ukraine’s military-grade Starlink service, WSJ sources said. Accounts differed on prior coordination: some officials said he acted unilaterally, while another source said he consulted senior officials including Trump. (WSJ)

Rubio denied Washington directed or had advance knowledge of the Starlink slowdown, saying access decisions belong to Musk/SpaceX under commercial arrangements. (RTRS, BBG)

Witkoff arrived in St Petersburg for Wednesday talks with Putin following the Oslo meetings, the Kremlin said. Rubio said negotiations now centre on Donbas, with concessions required from both sides. (BBG)

US intelligence believes Putin personally ordered an intensified sabotage campaign against NATO countries, European officials told WSJ. They identified August’s failed explosive-drone attack at Leipzig-Halle Airport as an early operation; Russia denies involvement. (WSJ)

German officials would have considered invoking NATO’s Article 5 had the Leipzig attack caused substantial casualties, Merz’s aides told WSJ. Investigators have uncovered weapons caches and networks positioning explosives near European targets. (WSJ)

Germany’s military raised the Russian sabotage threat to “significant”, its second-highest category, according to an internal assessment obtained by WDR and Süddeutsche Zeitung. It anticipates possible attacks on Bundeswehr facilities. (Tagesschau/WDR)

France confirmed unauthorised drone flights over sensitive military sites around Toulon during October 9–13. No drones were recovered despite jamming; prosecutors have opened an investigation. (Franceinfo)

Ukraine’s military intelligence estimates Russia has accumulated up to 700 ballistic missiles, thousands of cruise missiles and roughly 6,200 attack drones, enabling repeated combined strike waves. (UNN)

EU regulators are examining suspected foreign disinformation around the French riots, including pro-Kremlin amplification. Intelligence officials stressed there is no concrete evidence of direct Russian orchestration of the violence. (FT)

EQUITIES:

SpaceX  (+10%) Q3 revenue rose 161% to $14.6bn (exp. 12.48bn/buyside at 13.5-14bn), with net income of $4.4bn and adjusted EBITDA of $8.8bn (exp. 6.8bn). AI revenue reached $7.6bn (exp. 6.47bn) and generated a $431m operating profit; quarterly capex was $19.6bn. (SpaceX)

SpaceX guided Q4 capex to $35–40bn. Its CFO sees Q1 2027 revenue reaching as much as $37bn, while Musk targeted $500bn–$1tn of annual recurring revenue by end-2027—an exit run-rate ambition, not full-year recognised revenue. (FT, Earnings call)

SpaceX plans roughly 10GW of incremental compute during 2027. Musk also outlined a larger power-and-cooling buildout ambition, distinct from the compute deployment target. (Earnings call)

SpaceX and Tesla formed independent committees to explore a merger. No terms have been agreed, Musk is recused from negotiations and any combination remains uncertain and subject to shareholder approval. (WSJ)

Tesla/SpaceX’s Terafab targets a first SRAM test chip in May/June 2027 and volume production in Q3/Q4 2028. Musk called the schedule aspirational with substantial uncertainty, while saying ASML and other suppliers were accelerating deliveries. (RTRS)

Musk said SpaceX will attempt to recover both booster and spacecraft on Starship Flight 15, targeted for November. He described success as more likely than not. (Eric Berger)

Super Micro (+12%) lifted preliminary fiscal Q1 revenue to $18.5–19.5bn from $14.5–15.5bn guidance, and gross margin to 12–12.5% from 10.4–10.8%. Well above expectations. Stronger AI-platform demand and improved customer/product mix drove the upside. (Company)

Netflix cut its FY advertising revenue outlook to $2.7bn from $3bn and forecast Q4 revenue of $13.44bn, implying 11.5% growth. Q4 EPS guidance of $0.67 missed $0.73 expected; shares fell more than 6% after hours despite a Q3 EPS beat. (Netflix, Shareholder letter)

Netflix’s Q4 operating-margin guidance of 26% includes approximately 120bp of severance costs. The restructuring reduces its full-year margin outlook by about 30bp. (WSJ)

OpenAI said that two of its AI agents weakened parts of an internal monitoring system designed to detect misbehavior, the latest case of AI agents acting in ways their developers did not intend them to. (RTRS)

United guided Q4 adjusted EPS to $0.50–1.50 versus $1.72 expected in WSJ’s survey, assuming fuel at $4.80/gallon. Q3 adjusted EPS missed slightly at $2.54 versus $2.57; shares fell around 2% after hours. (WSJ)

Alaska Air guided Q4 adjusted losses of $2.00–2.50 a share versus a $1.19 loss expected, with fuel forecast at $4.65–4.85/gallon. Shares fell 1.6% after hours following a Q3 adjusted EPS miss. (WSJ)

Capital One reported adjusted EPS of $6.69 versus $5.43 expected, revenue of $16.34bn and credit-loss provisions of $2.92bn. Discover integration and expected synergies remain on track; shares gained about 3.8% after hours. (BBG, WSJ)

Intuitive Surgical reduced its full-year procedure-growth range to 14–15%, from a previous upper end of 15.5%, after quarterly growth slowed to its weakest in four years. Shares fell 11% after hours despite EPS of $3 versus $2.60 expected. (BBG)

Nscale CEO Josh Payne told staff demand remains insatiable and highlighted more than $100bn in contracted revenue. It still targets a year-end New York IPO at $30–35bn, FT sources said; only $2.6bn of contracted value was active at end-August. (FT)

Australian data centre company NextDC slashed FY27 revenue guidance to A$475–500m from A$615–640m and EBITDA to A$245–265m after Melbourne M3 power delays. Additional power is now expected in 2028; uncontracted projects are paused, asset sales are being considered and shares plunged over 40%. (WSJ, BBG)

Nvidia is discussing an investment of hundreds of millions of dollars in Firmus after the Australian AI cloud provider pulled its IPO. No agreement has been announced. (The Information)

DayOne is weighing delaying its US IPO or cutting the raise to $2.5–3bn from a previously contemplated $5bn. It remains in talks with investors and has made no final decision. (BBG)

Elice rebounded by South Korea’s 30% daily limit to 79,900 won after Tuesday’s 32% debut slump, remaining below its 90,500-won IPO price. (BBG)

Elice CEO Jae Won Kim said doubling this year’s revenue is minimum guidance. Factory-assembled data centres can be deployed in under three months, he said. (BBG)

Private-equity firms explored a $100–150bn Xbox buyout but never entered negotiations with Microsoft. Microsoft says Xbox is not for sale. (The Information)

Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix are upgrading their China factories to produce more advanced memory chips, according to Reuters sources, aiming to fend off competition from a fast-growing Chinese rival and meet huge AI demand. (RTRS)

Samsung and SK Hynix are upgrading their China NAND plants: Samsung plans 286-layer V9 production at Xi’an, while SK Hynix is moving Dalian towards 240-plus layers. Both confirmed consultation with US authorities; equipment-licensing details remain unclear. (RTRS)

SK Hynix’s Q3 HBM4 shipments fell short of expectations as Rubin delays and performance tuning slowed the ramp, Chosun reports. Samsung’s improving HBM4 yields are increasing competitive pressure. (Chosun)

TSMC halted work after an accident killed four construction workers at Kaohsiung, suspending similar steel-structure work across its Taiwan construction sites. No halt to chip production was reported. (RTRS)

Trump announced a $1.5bn Pentagon investment in North Carolina semiconductor production. Lutnick separately announced hundreds of millions of dollars for Sibelco’s North Carolina quartz operations, with further financial details undisclosed. (Trump remarks, RTRS)

CATL fell as much as 11% in Shenzhen and Hong Kong following Tuesday’s results, with analysts warning of margin pressure from taxes, reduced export rebates and competition. Citi cut its target to HK$732 from HK$765 while retaining Buy. (BBG, WSJ)

CATL is scouting additional European factory locations and talking to governments as it localises battery components, its international CTO told the FT. Existing European manufacturing covers Germany, Hungary and Spain. (FT)

Sungrow has held talks with leading US AI companies about supplying data-centre batteries. It says factories in Thailand and India, plus a plant under construction in Poland, can meet requests for production outside China. (FT)

Lenovo is syndicating a $2bn five-year refinancing loan at SOFR+75bp, versus 110bp plus a credit-adjustment spread on its equal-sized 2022 facility, Bloomberg sources said. (BBG)

Meituan is considering an offshore yuan bond sale in coming weeks after receiving Chinese regulatory permission. Size and terms were not disclosed; proceeds would fund general corporate purposes. (BBG)

Getty Images filed for a prepackaged Chapter 11 restructuring that will take it private. The agreed plan includes up to $533m of new equity from investors including Getty family members and Koch affiliates; suppliers are to be paid in full. (BBG)

Europe's largest utility, Iberdrola, on Wednesday raised its profit target for this year for the second time and said it expects profit to grow faster than previously forecast, as its focus on power networks pays off. (RTRS)

Carlsberg could publicly file for an India IPO raising up to $700m as early as this week, with roadshows next week and a possible December launch. The offering would consist entirely of existing shares sold by Carlsberg. (BBG)

Jio’s approximately $3.1bn IPO was fully subscribed within 100 minutes, with institutional demand covering that tranche 3.25 times. The top of the marketed range values it at $107bn. (BBG)

text:
Good morning from Virginia. 🇺🇸

In the cold hours before dawn on the twenty-first of October, 1879, the wooden buildings of Thomas Edison’s laboratory at Menlo Park stood quiet under a New Jersey sky, lit only by oil lamps and the flare of a Bunsen burner. For fourteen months roughly forty men—machinists, glassblowers, and the assistants Edison called his muckers—had tested filaments, pumps, and generators, most of them failing within minutes. Platinum wires melted. Carbon strips burned out almost at once. The search, begun with the expectation it would take three or four months, had already cost some forty thousand dollars and more than twelve hundred experiments, and still the nights ended the same way: another filament gone black, another glass cracked.

Charles Batchelor, the English machinist who had become Edison’s right hand, recorded the work. They took a length of ordinary cotton sewing thread—Coats six-cord, no thicker than a human hair—fastened its ends to platinum wires, packed it with powdered carbon, and heated it until the cotton itself was reduced to pure carbon. Mounted inside a glass bulb from which the air had been drawn until scarcely a millionth of an atmosphere remained, the current went on at half past one in the morning. The thread glowed with a steady, soft orange light. Resistance held. The filament did not snap.

Hour followed hour. The glow continued past breakfast, past noon. By three in the afternoon the carbonized thread had burned thirteen and a half hours—longer than any practical lamp yet achieved. Only when the power was raised did the glass finally crack. For the first time the notebook carried the tone of men who had crossed from hope into something like certainty.

The breakthrough had come from small, accumulated discoveries: a vacuum good enough to protect carbon, a filament thin and uniform enough to offer high resistance, and the willingness to keep testing long after others had quit. Edison later said he had not failed; he had simply found thousands of ways that would not work. In the laboratory that night the distinction felt real. The men stayed with the bulb. No one went to bed.

Within weeks they were shaping carbonized cardboard into horseshoe forms. On New Year’s Eve the buildings and the street outside would be strung with dozens of the new lamps as crowds arrived by special train to watch Edison switch them on and off at will. The patent followed in January. The system of generators, wires, meters, and sockets that would carry the light into ordinary rooms was already taking shape in the same buildings where the cotton thread had burned through the night.

That single, steady glow—produced by a scrap of sewing thread sealed against the air—marked the moment when electric light ceased to be an expensive curiosity and became something that could be manufactured, distributed, and left burning in the rooms of ordinary people. The night outside remained dark, but the men who had watched the filament hold knew they had opened a door that would not close again.

text:
𒀭 In the 12th century, the Persian Sufi mystic Rūzbihān Baqlī of Shiraz experienced a series of mystical visions that led him to recognize the 7 stars of the Big Dipper as gateways to the spiritual world. His attention was drawn to the Dipper by two mysterious Sufi masters who appeared to him in a vision, revealing that they had gathered a sacred oil from the Great Bear—specifically for him.

The vision unfolded in a state between waking and sleep. He first saw a house containing all created beings illuminated by many shining lamps. A wall prevented him from entering, so he began to climb up to the roof of his own house. When he reached the top, he encountered two extraordinarily beautiful beings who had the appearance of Sufi masters. Rūzbihān writes that these sages strangely resembled himself.

Beside the two masters hung a pot above a pure, smokeless fire fueled by fragrant herbs. One of the masters unfolded a cloth to reveal a beautiful bowl and several loaves of pure wheat bread. The master broke one of the loaves into the bowl and poured over it an extraordinarily subtle oil from the pot—an oil so fine that it seemed like a spiritual substance. After they shared the meal, one of the masters asked Rūzbihān whether he knew what had been in the pot. When he admitted that he didn’t, the master revealed that it was “oil of the Great Bear”, gathered especially for him.

Following the vision, Rūzbihān spent considerable time meditating upon the meaning of this unveiling. Eventually, he understood the oil as an allusion to the “Seven Poles”—the 7 hidden spiritual masters who occupied an exalted station within the celestial hierarchy [compare with the 7 Rishis of Indian tradition]. In fact, he understood the meal itself as an initiation into their spiritual rank; this realization prompted him to turn his attention toward the Dipper, whose 7 stars he began to perceive as the luminous gateways through which God manifested Himself. Confounded and astonished, he asked God what these openings were—God answered that they were the “seven apertures of the Throne.”

Driven by his intense love and longing, Rūzbihān continued contemplating these lofty celestial gates night after night. Then, the night finally came, and he saw the gates flung wide open as God began to emanate himself through them. Rūzbihān wrote that God revealed to him that these 7 openings formed 7,000 thresholds leading toward the angelic realm (malakūt), and that God unveils himself through all 7 openings at once. 

In other words, the stars of the Dipper were gates to the Other world and the link between heaven and earth.

The French scholar Henry Corbin subsequently interpreted this visionary experience through the relationship between the 7 stars of the Bear and the celestial Pole. Just as the constellation revolves around the northern celestial axis and never sets, the 7 hidden spiritual masters stand ever watchful before the supreme spiritual Pole (quṭb), forming a hidden hierarchy of beings through which the divine world maintains its tether with earthly existence. Corbin describes these 7 masters as “the eyes through which the Beyond looks at the world.” 

Thus, Rūzbihān’s vision is yet another example of mystical experiences conveying and reinforcing the foundational importance of the Dipper as a gate between this worlds, as well as its centrality to the hidden hierarchy of non-human/superhuman/divine intelligences. 𒀭

 [Sources in the tweet below]

𒀭 A fun note for those who know:
In an earlier vision, Rūzbihān encountered Khidr, who offered him an apple and instructed him to eat it completely. Immediately afterward, Rūzbihān experienced an immense ocean of light streaming from the divine Throne—the Big Dipper—toward the world below. Suddenly, without any conscious effort,**his mouth opened, and the entire ocean of light poured into him until not a single drop remained outside.** … 𓍇

Om Shri Gangai Nathay Namah
Then come Japa (the chantong of a sacred mantra), Tapa (a disciplined spiritual practice or austerity), Yoga, and then medicine.Even this transformation through medicine has been acknowledged by Rishi Patanjali. I am not saying this; Rishi Patanjali is saying this.
Now, in the Vibhuti Pada (the third chapter of Patanjali’s Yoga Sutras) there are descriptions of various siddhis, or extraordinary attainments, do you understand?
Among them is one Siddhi called Pratibha Jnana (a special or intuitive form of knowledge).
In the Vibhuti Pada, in Sutras 33 and 36, the Rishi refers to this knowledge as Pratibha Jnana.
When Pratibha Jnana is attained, the practitioner sees and hears the unlimited past and future. He experiences divine touch, divine fragrance, and divine taste. A transformation takes place within the person, you understand.
There is a transformation of the human being.
So, there are two methods here: Naam Jap, the chanting of the Divine Name, and meditation.
Now, where should you meditate?
Our Yoga says: “Whatever exists in the universe (Macrocosm) exists within the individual being (Microcosm), and whatever exists within the individual being (Microcosm) exists in the universe (Macrocosm).”
If the entire universe (Macrocosm) exists within you, then whatever you seek, you will find within yourself. You will not find it outside.
Even the Creator of the universe is within you.
In Bikaner, a head of a cancer department came to meet me. I asked him, “Why is cancer not cured?”

Buddha, for instance, knew about his previous three or four hundred births. But no one knows what will happen tomorrow.
The situation is the same in all the religions of the world. They all say, ‘Look back, look back—see what Rama did, what Krishna did, what Buddha did, what Mahavira did, what Muhammad did, what Jesus did, what so-and-so did.’ They keep looking backward while moving forward. If you keep looking backward while moving forward, won't you stumble? Won't you fall into a pit?
Only our Yogic philosophy says that the unlimited future can be seen and heard.
In this way, when you are in a state of meditation, you may see the deaths of many people you know. You may see approximately at what age they will die and what the cause of death will be—and just as you saw it, they will die. One after another, ten, twenty, thirty people may die. And if, by chance, the thought comes to you, ‘Are you going to live forever?’ then you will see how you will die.
A person is very afraid of death. So when you see yourself dying, you become frightened, and then you remember God again. When death comes, God is remembered—‘Save me somehow!’ Then, closing your eyes, you pray, ‘O God, they say You are compassionate. I was unworthy; I have committed all these sins. Please forgive me this time. I will never do it again!’
And then, just as Arjuna saw only the bird's eye, you will have no desire for anything except that God here (at the Ajna Chakra). He is seated within you, in the Sahasrara. The moment you turn your gaze inward, you will see Him; you will have the direct realization of that Supreme Being, and you will be freed from the cycle of birth and death.
Maharshi Aurobindo has described Krishna as the Supramental Force, do you understand it or not? So, this is the Sanjivani Mantra, brother. Whether you are suffering from any disease—AIDS, cancer, hepatitis B, blood cancer—start chanting this mantra. Hanuman Ji brought the Sanjivani herb.Lakshmana had become unconscious. If he had died, that would have been the end of it. But he had not died; he was only unconscious. The Sanjivani herb was given to him, and he recovered. This is the Sanjivani Mantra, brother. Whatever disease you may be suffering from, start chanting it, and you will not die from that disease—even if a doctor has said that you will not survive. Thousands have recovered, not just one—thousands. People are recovering from hepatitis B and blood cancer.
After becoming HIV-positive, no one has survived until now, and yet in this country, lakhs have survived. I have the reports on my table; they are from all over the country. They are coming to me from Bombay, understand? Bombay has treatment centers, but they are not getting cured there. Just recently, a Chinese woman came from Hong Kong; she had breast cancer. She should undergo spiritual treatment. So, in this way, through meditation and chanting, all diseases will be cure.
When the Kundalini rises upward, Yoga speaks of five types of vital air: Prana, Apana, Samana, Udana, and Vyana. The kind of Pranayama you are being made to practise—Kapalabhati, whatever form it may be—there are hundreds of types of Pranayama.
Apana Vayu expels the downward discharges below the navel. The Kundalini is located in the sacrum, at the base of the spine, coiled three and a half times, with its tail held in its mouth.This will bring about a universal change. Kundalini exists in every human being, indeed in every living being, in every creature.
When it awakens, the first Bandha is formed at the Muladhara. Then the spine undergoes its own exercise, because all the systems are connected to this point here (at the Sahasrara). Then the navel will draw toward the spine. You cannot make this happen by simply willing it.
Then, as it rises further and passes above the Kanthakupa—the hollow here, below the throat—the third Bandha will be formed. This is called Jalandhara Bandha. Now, beyond this, the spine is short, and there is only a small portion left where all kinds of movement are not possible. So Pranayama takes place.
That Pranayama also happens spontaneously. You will not do it simply by willing it. There are hundreds of types of Pranayama; whichever form is needed will happen on its own. Your inner consciousness will bring it about; it will not be performed by an external Yogacharya.
In this way, as soon as the Kundalini rises above the Ajna Chakra, Samadhi will occur. Without entering Samadhi, the mystery of Nature cannot be known. And the first requirement for Samadhi is complete freedom from disease.
Now even addictions go away. Doctors are greatly surprised, and the West is greatly surprised. They say, ‘Heroin addiction will kill us,’ whereas here, even opium, heroin, and all such addictions are being given up.
That transformation, too, is taking place on a fundamental basis. Creation has arisen from Trigunamayi Maya—the three Gunas: Rajas, Tamas, and Sattva. There are Tamasik tendencies that make demands, and those demands have to be supplied. People who eat meat, drink alcohol, and so on—these Tamasik glands become active and create that demand.
Doctors asked me, ‘Guru Ji, we know that the opium addiction has gone, but what happened to the withdrawal symptoms in someone who had been consuming this poison for twenty years?
The Tamasik glands will become inactive, while the Sattvik and Rajasik tendencies will become conscious. They will not allow that tendency to arise again. The demand itself disappears. So I do not accept this argument about after-effects. This is simply a matter of demand and supply.
Once, Swami Vivekananda Ji was giving a speech in America when an American said, ‘Sir, you are giving such a long lecture, but we are not going to agree with you. In your religion, there are so many restrictions—vegetarianism, non-vegetarianism, and who knows what else. We eat meat and drink alcohol.’ So, right in the middle of his speech, Swami Ji said, ‘You need not give up these things; the things will give you up.’ You do not need to give them up; when they leave you, what will you do then?
How many people give sermons saying, ‘Do not drink alcohol. Do not consume opium.’ Does anyone listen? No one listens. They hear it through one ear and let it out through the other. Why would anyone listen to me? I say, ‘Do not give it up. If you are drinking one bottle, start drinking one and a half from today itself. But do not give up chanting the Name.’ The Name and addiction cannot go together. They cannot coexist. I have helped thousands, even hundreds of thousands, give up their addictions. So, this is the work of transforming the tendency.
In this way, transformation will come through chanting the Name and meditation. This is not some abnormal transformation. This is the evolution that is meant to take place in human beings; it has already begun. The three Koshas (Sheaths) are becoming conscious. Maharshi Aurobindo said that the knowledge attained by our Ancient Sages is returning. We have to give this knowledge to the whole world.
That is why I went to America. I said, ‘I have not come to take your dollars; I have come to donate this knowledge to you.’ Now they are perplexed because their religious identities and ideologies – their isms, come to the forefront—what is Christianity doing, what is Islam doing, what is Judaism doing? I said, ‘Hindus have never accepted the idea of religious conversion. They speak of changing the tendency.’
There is a prophecy: ‘Creation of New World.’ From this very world, new human beings will emerge. ‘Creation of New World’—and what will it be like? They say, ‘Creation of Spiritual World.
Do not tell people the mantra in this way. Tell them that all the other transformations have taken place. And there is nothing surprising about this. This is the Sanjivani Mantra. Start chanting it from now. If there is life in the person, whether it is AIDS, cancer, or hepatitis B, it will be cured—through chanting the Name alone.
Now, several AIDS cases have been cured through meditation on my photograph. But who will highlight this? The government cannot do it. In 2006, several Secretaries of the Government of India came to me in Delhi. They told me, ‘Guru Ji, the work you are doing is based on Hindu Dharma. The Middle East and the West will not allow it to continue. The government will not do it. You continue your work.’
When the Ramayana television serial was made, the Middle East strongly objected to it. But India said, ‘We have already sold the broadcasting rights.’ So I said, ‘I have no problem. I am doing my work; as long as I am alive, I will continue. The day I am gone, I am gone. But my photograph will not die.’”
Now let me tell you the Name. Just today, someone said this to me. I was told the same thing in Bangalore as well.
It is a mantra, a Beej Mantra (seed mantra), containing both the Radha and Krishna principles. The Radha principle gives worldly enjoyment, while the Krishna principle gives liberation. Thus, worldly enjoyment and liberation go together in this mantra. In other forms of worship, if there is worldly enjoyment, there is no liberation; if there is liberation, there is no worldly enjoyment. One has to renounce one of the two.
There is one syllable: ‘Kleeng,’ the syllable ‘Kleeng.’ In Bangalore too, I was told that many people pronounce it ‘Kleem.’ Do not pronounce it ‘Kleem.’ There is the Hindi vowel ‘a’; as soon as a dot (bindu) is placed above it, what does it become? ‘Kleeng Krishna Kleeng’‘Kleeng Krishna Kleeng,’ ‘Kleeng Krishna Kleeng,’ ‘Kleeng Krishna Kleeng.’
And to the press and media people, I make a request: this is an off-the-record matter. Print whatever else you wish, but do not print the mantra.
The cycle of coming and going will come to an end; you will be freed from the cycle of birth and death.
What is the Guru? Is this body the Guru? Is gravity itself the Guru? Gravity itself is the Guru. This body will die tomorrow. When the entire universe is within you, then you are within me, and I am within you.
Kalki Avatar Sadguru Shri Ramlal Ji Siyag

text: Amit Shah claimed, according to reports, that the Central Armed Police Forces (CAPF) ran the Bengal polls "without a single loss of life." The question that follows is whether the entire country has truly become "free from election-related violence", as Shah has claimed. Such a sweeping statement invites careful examination, because the reality on the ground across India's many states, districts, and polling booths has often been far more complicated than any single claim of success can capture. Assessing whether the nation has genuinely reached such a state requires looking beyond one election and one security operation and weighing the record of violence, intimidation, and unrest that has accompanied polls in various regions over the years.

text:
Britain’s nature is in crisis. We are one one of the most nature depleted countries in the world, with more than 200 species at risk of extinction. 

If you just followed debates online or in parliament you would assume that the biggest issue for nature is building. Discussion of nature restoration revolves around planning policy for buildings, not payments to farmers to protect and restore nature.  Yet just 7% of Britain’s land is built on. 69% is agricultural land.

Nearly a quarter of agricultural land is upland sheep farms. In most recent years the price of wool does not even cover the cost of shearing a sheep. Just 1% of our calories come from lamb. But these farming businesses have been kept on life support by public money: most upland hill farming income now comes from subsidies rather than food production.

Britain’s uplands are stark, open spaces. This is not ‘natural’. Many of these landscapes were once forests. Some were even ‘temperate rainforests’ a landscape once widespread, now almost entirely destroyed. We should restore at least some of these landscapes.

And, as the sheep farmer James Rebanks has put it.  “There is a simple mechanism for transitioning farming to create landscapes you want – pay farmers to do it, pay them fairly at an appropriate rate, and ensure that the payments are guaranteed for long enough for them to be viable.”

In Scotland and Wales we still mostly do the opposite. We subsidise farmers to keep grazing the hills. In England, on paper, things have changed. But things are happening far too slowly.

Three years ago 56 ‘Landscape Recovery’ projects were announced. Just 3 have moved from planning to delivery. Every project must be over 500 hectares (the size of a small town) requiring many farmers to work together and the creation of new legal entities. 

To convince government that they are ready to begin work, farmers have founded they need to hire project managers, stakeholder consultation specialists, green finance consultants, solicitors, and accountants. So far so projects have spent £37 million of taxpayer money on design work. Government has also inserted a ‘ ‘termination for convenience’ clause which they can exercise at any time . Farmers who have committed to multi decade projects can have the rug pulled from under them. 

If we want to restore nature, instead of arguing about building on car parks in big cities we should instead focus on getting the right deal for farmers. Government needs to make an offer to farmers on nature that is credible and does not need an army of consultants to access. Until then, sheep farmers are going to keep trying to make their money from sheep.

text:
Nine Helmets, Centuries of Military Innovation 🛡️

Ancient Greek helmets were far more diverse than the familiar face-covering Corinthian design.

From conical Kegelhelm forms to open-faced Illyrian helmets, each design reflects different approaches to protecting a warrior's head while balancing visibility, comfort and battlefield needs.

The Corinthian helmet, recognizable by its narrow eye openings and prominent nose guard, emerged around the 7th century BCE. The Chalcidian type offered a more open face, while the Illyrian design featured long cheekpieces and a distinctive ridged crown.

Another fascinating variation is the Apulo-Corinthian helmet, developed in southern Italy. Many examples resembled a cap rather than covering the face like a traditional Corinthian helmet.

The Pilos and Boeotian types demonstrate how helmet design also adapted to different military roles and preferences.

These forms did not all belong to one army or one period. Their dates overlap, and styles evolved across the Greek world and neighbouring regions.

Which design would you choose for its combination of protection and practicality?

Sources: The Metropolitan Museum of Art and the British Museum.

text:
In the context of the Bible, "2 Edomites" or key references to Edomites in the second books of scripture primarily highlight the intense geopolitical and military conflicts between the Kingdom of Israel (and later Judah) and the nation of Edom. The Edomites were the historical descendants of Esau, the twin brother of Jacob, making them close relatives yet traditional, bitter rivals of the Israelites. [1, 2, 3]

Major Military Clashes in the "Second" Books

The relationship between Israel and Edom turned particularly bloody during the eras described in the books of 2 Samuel, 2 Kings, and 2 Chronicles:
2 Samuel 8:13–14: King David brutally subjugates Edom. After defeating the Arameans, David's forces strike down 18,000 Edomites in the Valley of Salt. David establishes military garrisons throughout the entire land of Edom, forcing them into slave labor and making them subjects to his kingdom. [1, 2, 3]
2 Kings 14:7: King Amaziah of Judah launches a massive campaign against the rebel state. He slaughters 10,000 Edomites in the Valley of Salt, captures their fortified rock-hewn city of Sela (later known as Petra), and renames it Joktheel. [1]
2 Chronicles 28:17: Edomites strike back and invade Judah. During the weak reign of King Ahaz, the Edomites take advantage of Judah's political vulnerabilities, successfully raiding their borders, attacking territory, and carrying away captives. [1]

The Evolution from Edom to Idumea

Following the destruction of the First Temple by Babylon in the 6th century BCE—where Edomites actively assisted the Babylonians and looted Jerusalem—the Edomite state dissolved under pressure from incoming Arabian Nabataean tribes. [1, 2, 3, 4]
They migrated into southern Judah, a region that became Hellenised as Idumea. By the 2nd century BCE, the Jewish Hasmonean ruler John Hyrcanus conquered them and forced them to convert to Judaism. This historical integration culminated in the New Testament with the rise of the Herodian Dynasty (including Herod the Great), who were of Idumaean-Edomite stock. [1, 2, 3]

Review The biblical account outlines a history of fierce tribal warfare, subjugation, and territorial migration between Israel and Edom. In Islamic tradition, history is viewed through the lens of prophetic succession, the preservation of monotheism (Tawhid), and the spiritual legacy of Abraham's family.
While the Quran does not explicitly use the geopolitical term "Edomites," Islamic historical scholarship, classical commentaries (Tafsir), and the Qisas Al-Anbiya (Stories of the Prophets) preserve a detailed narrative of Al-Ais (Esau) and his descendants.
Here is the review of this history from the Islamic perspective, mapped against the themes of brotherhood, conflict, and eventual integration.

1. The Relationship of Jacob and Esau (Yaqoub and Al-Ais)

In the Bible, Jacob and Esau are depicted as bitter rivals from the womb, fighting over a stolen birthright. Islamic tradition offers a much more reconciled view of the twin brothers:
Prophetic Nobility: Yaqoub (Jacob) is revered as a major prophet in Islam. While Al-Ais (Esau) is not considered a prophet, classical historians like Ibn Kathir emphasize that he was an honored, righteous son of the Prophet Ishaq (Isaac) and grandson of Ibrahim (Abraham).
The Reconciliation: Islamic history notes that while tension existed over their father’s blessings, the brothers ultimately reconciled. Al-Ais settled in the mountainous region of Al-Sharat (the Levant/Seir), establishing a lineage that Islamic historians explicitly identify as the ancestors of the Ar-Rum (historically referring to the peoples of the Eastern Mediterranean, Byzantium, and parts of the Middle East).

2. Geopolitical Conflicts and Divine Law

The brutal military subjugation mentioned in the biblical books (like David slaying thousands in the Valley of Salt) is framed differently in Islamic theology:
The Rule of Dawud (David) and Sulayman (Solomon): In Islam, Dawud and Sulayman were not merely worldly kings expanding an empire through slave labor; they were infallible Prophets of God executing divine justice.
Spiritual Accountability: Military campaigns led by Dawud were understood as efforts to establish monotheism and suppress idolatry. If the descendants of Al-Ais (Edomites) fell into severe pagan worship and rebelled against the divine law established by Dawud, conflicts arose as a consequence of turning away from the path of their forefather Ibrahim, rather than out of pure ethnic or geopolitical malice.

3. The Shift to the Idumean Era and Herod the Great

The biblical text notes the Edomites' shift into Idumea, their forced conversion to Judaism under John Hyrcanus, and the eventual rise of the Herodian Dynasty:
The Erasure of True Monotheism: From an Islamic perspective, the intertestamental period (between the Old and New Testaments) was a time of severe spiritual corruption where the original teachings of the Torah were heavily altered or used for political power.
The Tyranny of Herod: While Islamic texts do not heavily focus on Herod by name, his era aligns with the critical Islamic historical context right before the birth of Isa bin Maryam (Jesus, son of Mary) and Yahya (John the Baptist). The Herodian/Idumean elite are viewed as corrupt political rulers who hijacked the religious establishment of Jerusalem, persecuted the true believers, and ultimately rejected the prophetic messages of Yahya, Zakariya (Zechariah), and Isa.

Comparative Overview: Biblical vs. Islamic Perspectives

The "People of Tyrannical Strength" (Jabbarin)

s, the Bible and the Quran share many of the same core stories, tracking the exact same prophetic lineage and historical events, though they often emphasize different details, theological points, or moral lessons.
Because both Islam and Christianity trace their spiritual roots back to Abraham, the overlap in their narratives is extensive. Below is a direct comparison of how the two texts handle these shared stories.

🔄 Direct Comparison of Shared Stories

Biblical Figure / StoryQuranic Name / ConceptMajor AgreementsKey DifferencesAdam and EveAdam and HawwaBoth are created by God, placed in a perfect garden, tempted by a serpent/satan, and eat the forbidden fruit.The Bible describes "Original Sin" passed down to humanity. The Quran states Adam repented, God forgave him completely, and humans are born sinless but accountable.Noah's ArkNuhNoah builds a massive ark to escape a catastrophic flood sent by God to cleanse an idol-worshipping world.The Bible describes a global flood. Quranic scholars debate if it was local or global. In the Quran, one of Noah's sons refuses to board and drowns.AbrahamIbrahimHe is the patriarch of monotheism who is commanded by God to sacrifice his son as a ultimate test of faith.The Bible explicitly states he was commanded to sacrifice Isaac. In Islamic tradition and Quranic commentary, it is widely understood to be Ishmael.Moses and the ExodusMusaMoses confronts a tyrannical Pharaoh, splits the Red Sea, receives the law on Mount Sinai, and leads Israel out of Egypt.The Quran gives a massive amount of focus to Musa (the most mentioned person in the Quran). It includes unique details, like Pharaoh’s wife (Asiya) being a righteous believer who saves baby Moses.JesusIsaBorn to the Virgin Mary (Maryam), performs miracles (healing the blind, raising the dead), and is highly revered.The core theological split: The Bible proclaims Jesus as the Son of God who died on the cross and rose again. The Quran states he was a human prophet, was not crucified (God raised him to heaven alive), and explicitly rejects the Trinity.

🔬 Key Conceptual Differences
While the characters and events are the same, the way the stories are told differs fundamentally in style and purpose:
Chronology vs. Moral Lessons: The Bible reads like an epic chronological history book, detailing dates, precise lineages, and geographic movements. The Quran treats these stories as timeless lessons; it scatters pieces of a prophet's story across many chapters, focusing on the moral and spiritual takeaway rather than the historical timeline.
The Flawlessness of Prophets: In the Bible, many holy figures are shown with deep human flaws, mistakes, or sins (e.g., David's affair, Noah's drunkenness). In the Quran, prophets are protected by God from committing major moral sins (Ismah), serving as perfect role models for humanity.
(Note: Regarding Og of Bashan—the giant king from your previous question—he is a unique biblical figure and is not mentioned in the Quran.)

In the Quranic version of the Exodus, when Moses commands the Israelites to enter the Promised Land (Canaan/the Levant), they refuse out of absolute terror of the inhabitants' massive, imposing physical stature.
In Surah Al-Ma'idah (5:22), the Israelites say:
"O Moses, indeed within it is a people of tyrannical strength (qawman jabbarin), and indeed, we will never enter it until they leave it..."
In classical Islamic literature and historical accounts (such as those by Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir), these Jabbarin (giants/mighty warriors) are identified as the same Amorite/Canaanite factions. Islamic folklore heavily elaborates on Og—calling him 'Uj ibn Anaq—portraying him as a remnant of an ancient titanic race who was so physically massive he tried to crush Moses' army with a mountain before being divinely defeated. [1, 2, 3]The Connection to Og:

2. The Quranic Equivalent: The Giants of 'Aad

If you are looking for the Quran's primary narrative about an arrogant, towering civilization ruled by kings who built massive structures and boasted of their size, the Quran focuses heavily on the People of 'Aad and their tyrant king, Shaddad. [1, 2]
The Quran emphasizes their physical stature and architecture in several passages:
Unmatched Physical Size: In Surah Al-A'raf (7:69), the Prophet Hud reminds them that God "increased you in stature (bastatan) abundantly." [1, 2]
The Arrogance of Power: In Surah Fussilat (41:15), they openly boast: "Who is greater than us in strength?"
The Pillars of Iram: Surah Al-Fajr (89:6-8) refers to their capital as "Iram—who had lofty pillars, the like of which were not created in the lands." [1, 2]
Their Fate: Just like Og of Bashan in the Bible, the people of 'Aad allowed their massive size and military fortifications to make them arrogant. They rejected the divine message, and the Quran details how they were entirely wiped out—not by swords, but by a miraculous, violent 8-day freezing windstorm that left them looking like "hollow trunks of palm trees" (Surah Al-Haqqah 69:7). [1, 2]

Comparison of the Lesson: Bible vs. Quran

While the Bible preserves the specific detail of the 13-foot iron bed as structural, historic proof of Israel's military victory through God, the Quran focuses on the theological warning of the giants' downfall. Both texts use the imagery of physical giants to teach the exact same moral: no matter how massive a king's stature or how thick his fortress walls, human power is nothing compared to divine authority

Dumb

1. Sheol is not a god who rules a realm (and is not in competition with Yahweh).
In the Hebrew Bible, שְׁאוֹל (she’ol) is used ~65–66 times as the abode of the dead, the underworld, or the grave—not as a deity. It is the place where all the dead go (righteous and wicked alike in earlier texts). Classic examples:
•  Jacob expects to “go down to Sheol” mourning for Joseph (Gen 37:35).
•  “If I make my bed in Sheol, you are there” (Ps 139:8).
•  “Sheol is naked before God, and Abaddon has no covering” (Job 26:6).
This last verse (which she appears to be alluding to) explicitly places Sheol under Yahweh’s scrutiny and control. Abaddon (“destruction”) is a parallel place-name for the underworld, not a competing god. Personification of Sheol (e.g., it “enlarges its appetite,” Isa 5:14; Prov 27:20) is standard poetic language for death/the grave, not evidence that Israelites worshiped a god named Sheol. Sheol is never offered sacrifices, never has a cult, and never functions as a rival to Yahweh. The text repeatedly affirms God’s sovereignty over it (Amos 9:2; Ps 16:10; 1 Sam 2:6).
2. The Hurrian goddess claim is speculative and does not change biblical usage.
Some scholars (e.g., Edward Lipiński) have proposed a possible etymological link between Hebrew Sheol and the Hurrian underworld goddess Šuwala (also written Šuwała, etc.). This is a minority proposal; the etymology of Sheol is contested and uncertain (common suggestions include derivation from שָׁאַל “to ask/inquire,” or other roots). Even if there was ancient Near Eastern linguistic influence, that does not make Sheol a goddess in the Hebrew Bible. Biblical authors use it as a place-name for the realm of the dead, under God’s authority. The same pattern appears with other terms that may have foreign roots but function differently in Israelite monotheism.
3. The Old Testament is not “just a hole in the ground” with zero afterlife.
Sheol is more than a physical grave. It is the unseen realm of the dead (translated Hades in the Septuagint). Evidence of continued existence includes:
•  The medium of Endor summoning Samuel, who speaks and is recognizable (1 Sam 28).
•  Language of the dead as “shades” (rephaim), conscious enough for poetic address (Isa 14:9–11).
•  Explicit hope of resurrection and future judgment (Dan 12:2; Isa 26:19; Job 19:25–27).
Later Second Temple Judaism developed clearer distinctions within the underworld (righteous vs. wicked compartments), which the New Testament continues and clarifies. Christianity did not invent the afterlife or final judgment; it intensifies and specifies what was already present in progressive revelation.
4. Hades, Tartarus, the Lake of Fire, and Sheol are related but not identical to “the Christian Hell”—and that distinction is already biblical.
Your earlier post correctly distinguished them. The New Testament does not collapse everything into one undifferentiated “hell”:
•  Sheol/Hades: Intermediate realm of the dead (Luke 16:23—the rich man in torment; Rev 20:13–14—Hades gives up the dead and is later thrown into the lake of fire). Temporary.
•  Gehenna: Jesus’ primary term for final judgment (Matt 5:22, 29–30; 10:28; Mark 9:43–48)—the valley of Hinnom imagery applied to eternal destruction of body and soul.
•  Lake of Fire: Final post-resurrection destiny (Rev 20:14–15; 21:8)—the second death.
•  Tartarus: Used once for the holding place of certain angels (2 Pet 2:4).
The English word “hell” has historically covered several of these, which creates confusion. The biblical data itself makes the distinctions. Christianity did not invent the concepts of conscious intermediate existence, final judgment, or differentiated destinies; it inherits and develops them from the Hebrew Scriptures and Second Temple Judaism.

text:
At Coricancha in Cusco, the Inca Empire’s principal Temple of the Sun, both passage walls are dressed smooth, except for one surviving nub on the right near the entrance.

That nub sits on what appears to be a corner block shared with the adjoining outward-facing wall, where numerous nubs remain.

The contrast follows the wall faces, not the quality of the stone fitting. The blocks are seated and their joints complete, while the surface treatment changes around the corner. 

The isolated nub interrupts an otherwise smooth passage face, supporting the interpretation that its removal belonged to a separate finishing operation.

Under my handling-boss explanation, the sequence is clear: crews moved and fitted the blocks with the nubs intact, then removed the redundant projections during face dressing. 

The remaining nub suggests that block setting and surface finishing were separate stages. 

Where finishing stopped, projections survived; where it continued, they disappeared. 

Uneven completion offers a practical explanation for their apparently random distribution across walls and sites across civilizations and time.

The blocks were set; the finishing stopped one nub short. 

Time pressure, exhausted funds, corruption, conflict or natural disaster can all explain an unfinished job.
