This was such a fun read for my dark romantasy loving heart! With its gothic atmosphere, dangerous magic, and the angsty tension between the fae princess and former knight. Morally complicated heroine, forbidden romance, and dark fantasy elements, it was a perfect fall vibes read! Get this one on your TBR if those elements call to you!

Thank you to @thenerdfam for the gifted book!

She is becoming the end of the world. He is sworn to stop her—no matter the cost.

In Hollowmire, fae magic can unfurl the petals of a rose, spark a flame, or summon a spring breeze—unless you’re Vireth, who can only leave rot-hungry mushrooms, poisonous slime molds, and soft clouds of bone-white spores in her wake.

Shunned for her decay magic and overshadowed by her perfect sisters, she has spent her life staying small, quiet, contained. But something is changing. Her rot is spreading. And when a fortune teller names her the Blight Mother—harbinger of the world’s end—Vireth can no longer pretend she is merely unwanted.

She is something far worse.

Beyond Hollowmire, the Kingdom of Valehar is dying. Its crops grow beautifully, yet they feed no one. Its people starve with full bellies. Desperate, the regent summons the only man who might end the blight: Renard, a war-hardened knight turned farmer exiled to the edge of a forest that whispers of ancient things. To restore balance, the Blight Mother’s blood must be spilled.

When his path crosses Vireth’s, he finds not a monster—but a woman fierce, bitter, and heartbreakingly alone. A woman who could save the world… or unmake it entirely.

As famine spreads and ancient forces stir, they are drawn together by fate and a dangerous, impossible desire. But love offers no sanctuary here.

Because if she becomes the Blight Mother, he will have to kill her.

And if he hesitates, the world will not survive.

text:
Somewhere over Ohio, a 3rd-year learned that accepting my window seat was a tactical error.

I’d offered it before takeoff.

He thanked me and settled in.

Then I asked whether he planned to work.

He said yes.

I asked what would happen if he needed the bathroom and I fell asleep in the aisle.

He said he’d wake me.

I asked if waking a partner was really his preferred travel protocol.

He reconsidered.

We switched.

I took the window.

Then I slept for 90 minutes.

When I woke up, he said he’d been waiting to use the bathroom.

I asked why he hadn’t gone before boarding.

He had.

I asked why that plan had failed.

He didn’t have an answer.

On the return flight, he booked himself an aisle seat.

I boarded, pointed at it, and said, “Perfect.”

He moved without a word.

Travel builds judgment quickly.

text:
CME INDIA – Clinical Pearls

FDA Novel Drug Approvals | July–September 2026 | Nature Reviews Drug Discovery

22 New FDA Drug Approvals in Q3 2026: From Weekly Insulin to Precision Oncology

The third quarter of 2026 witnessed 22 selected novel FDA drug approvals, highlighting a remarkable shift towards precision medicine, targeted molecular therapies, innovative biologics and more convenient treatment strategies.

The most clinically relevant advances include a once-weekly basal insulin for type 2 diabetes, a PCSK9 inhibitor for LDL cholesterol reduction, an orexin receptor agonist for narcolepsy and molecularly targeted treatments for pancreatic cancer.

12 CME INDIA Clinical Pearls

1\. Once-weekly insulin enters a new era of diabetes management.

Insulin efsitora alfa (Onswi​​k; Eli Lilly), approved on September 23, represents an important advance in basal insulin delivery for type 2 diabetes. Once-weekly administration may reduce injection burden and improve treatment acceptability. However, dose titration, hypoglycaemia risk and the consequences of dosing errors require particular attention.

2\. LDL cholesterol lowering continues to evolve beyond statins.

Enlicitide decanoate (Lipfendra; Merck), a PCSK9 inhibitor, represents an additional approach to LDL cholesterol reduction. Its clinical significance lies in the potential for convenient, potent lipid lowering, particularly among patients who remain above LDL-C goals despite standard therapy. Cardiovascular outcome benefits must be distinguished from LDL-C reduction alone.

3\. Narcolepsy treatment moves towards correcting orexin deficiency.

Oveporexton (Orzeyfult; Takeda), an orexin-2 receptor agonist, targets the underlying neurobiology of narcolepsy type 1. Unlike conventional wake-promoting agents, this approach directly stimulates a pathway affected by orexin deficiency.

4\. Pancreatic cancer therapy increasingly targets oncogenic signalling.

Daraxonrasib (Rasonque; Revolution Medicines), a RAS inhibitor, highlights progress in targeting pathways historically considered difficult to treat. Its clinical application must be interpreted according to the approved patient population, molecular eligibility and supporting trial evidence.

5\. Breast cancer treatment becomes increasingly mutation-directed.

Camizestrant, an oral selective oestrogen receptor degrader (SERD), targets ER signalling in hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer with ESR1 mutations. Molecular testing is becoming central to selecting endocrine treatment.

6\. PI3K/mTOR inhibition offers another precision-oncology strategy.

Gedatolisib targets PI3K/mTOR signalling in HR-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer without a PIK3CA mutation. The approval illustrates that treatment decisions depend on pathway biology rather than receptor status alone.

7\. IgA nephropathy enters the era of targeted immunomodulation.

Atacicept (Trutakna), a BAFF/APRIL-targeted fusion protein, addresses B-cell survival and immunoglobulin production pathways in IgA nephropathy. This represents a shift from predominantly supportive renal protection towards disease-specific immune modulation.

8\. Hepcidin replacement opens a new therapeutic pathway in polycythaemia vera.

Rusfertide (Mimrylo), a hepcidin mimetic, regulates iron availability for erythropoiesis. This mechanism offers an alternative strategy for controlling erythrocytosis and potentially reducing the need for repeated phlebotomy.

9\. Rare genetic diseases are increasingly becoming treatable at the molecular level.

Zilganersen, a GFAP-targeted antisense oligonucleotide, represents a targeted therapeutic approach to Alexander disease. This illustrates how understanding disease-causing protein expression can lead to treatments for previously difficult-to-treat neurological disorders.

🇮🇷| Izadi’s Arithmetic: The House Could Change Hands, and War Funding Could Dry Up

Iranian scholar Fouad Izadi offers an assessment: the likelihood of the U.S. House of Representatives slipping from Republican control is rising, and funding for a war with Iran could face serious challenges.

This is not a "prediction." It is a diagnosis of the financial structure of the war.

💥 Who Holds the Purse Strings

Article I of the U.S. Constitution grants the power of the purse the authority to appropriate funds to the House of Representatives. War requires money, and money requires a vote in the House.

The war against Iran has been ongoing for eight months. C-5M transport aircraft are landing at Al Udeid Air Base; a third carrier strike group is steaming toward the Middle East. $8.6 billion in emergency arms sales have bypassed congressional review, and another $5 billion in arms sales to Saudi Arabia was approved in September. Meanwhile, stockpiles of Patriot interceptor missiles have fallen to just 25% of the required levels.

These expenditures do not simply fall from the sky; they require supplemental appropriations bills, which in turn demand a majority in the House.

If the Republicans lose the House, the Democrats will take control of the Appropriations Committee. They could attach conditions, delay funding, slash budgets, or reject requests entirely.

A war does not continue simply because a president wants to fight; it continues because Congress provides the money.

🎯 The Administration Is Already Aware of This Risk

Rubio has invoked emergency authority three times to bypass congressional review and push through arms sales to Gulf allies. Meanwhile, allies of Trump are openly discussing the implementation of martial law should the midterm elections be "rigged."

Both developments point to the same conclusion: they know they might lose and they know that if they do, the purse strings will be pulled from their grasp. Consequently, they are seeking workarounds in advance and preparing to contest the election results.

An administration that believes it will win has no need to discuss martial law. A president who believes his party will retain the House has no need to use emergency provisions to circumvent Congress.

📜 Iran’s Strategic Logic: Making the War Politically Unsustainable

Izadi’s assessment is not an isolated analysis; it aligns with a strategy Iran has pursued over the past eight months: the imposition of costs.  Rezaei states: The costs of the war have left the enemy in a state of confusion. Within the United States, 70% of the population opposes the war, and Trump’s approval rating has seen an unprecedented decline.

Hajizadeh notes: Missile stockpiles have increased by 150%.

Araqchi asserts: The U.S. has failed to achieve any of its war objectives, a strategic defeat for the United States.

Taken together, these points form a coherent logical chain: no prospect of a swift military victory → economic costs that are unsustainable → a political situation that cannot be maintained → the eventual necessity of accepting Iran’s terms.

The seven conditions are not merely a "negotiating position"; they are a countdown timer.

⚔️ Washington’s Dilemma

To continue the war, the U.S. needs funding which requires the approval of the House of Representatives. Yet, control of the House may soon shift.

To stop the war, the U.S. would have to face the political fallout of having failed to win a devastating blow to Trump, whose entire political brand is built on the concept of "winning."

To escalate the war, the U.S. would need more money, more troops, and greater domestic support. Instead, domestic support is waning, the military is exhausted, and financial resources are dwindling.

This is the arithmetic Washington faces and Iran is simply waiting for the final tally.

🔻 The Real Stakes

Tehran is betting that the American political system will fracture before Iran’s will to resist breaks.

Izadi’s assessment serves as a data point for this wager: the House could change hands, funding could dry up, and the war might be forced into de-escalation due to a lack of capital.

Meanwhile, Iran’s missile production lines will not halt because of a vote in the U.S. Congress; the rules governing the Strait of Hormuz will not change because an appropriations bill is rejected; and Iran’s enriched uranium will not vanish simply because the Democratic Party might take control of the House.

**The Seal, the Acropolis, and the Demand to Restore Order**

Behind Vice President JD Vance, as he chairs the White House Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, stands the Great Seal of the United States. *E Pluribus Unum*—out of many, one. The motto is not decorative. It is the founding claim that a single political community can be formed only under law that restrains the strong from preying on the weak. Without that restraint, the many do not become one; they become prey.

The Department of Justice announcement that began this conversation—$42 million in SNAP fraud, benefits diverted, food taken from children—was not merely a budget story. It was an illustration of a deeper problem. When systems designed to protect the vulnerable are captured by fraudsters, traffickers, or gangs, the state itself becomes an instrument of predation. Under the Trump administration, Homeland Security and related agencies have treated this as a core security problem rather than a mere accounting issue. The fraud task force under Vance, mass suspensions of fraudulent accounts, aggressive prosecutions, and the broader enforcement posture against gang networks and benefit trafficking are practical expressions of the same duty: remove those who take from the needy so that aid reaches those for whom it was intended.

That duty has ancient roots. The biblical texts already cited treat the exploitation of the poor, the widow, and the fatherless as an offense requiring judgment, not management. “Do not rob the poor, because he is poor, or crush the afflicted at the gate, for the Lord will plead their cause and rob of life those who rob them” (Proverbs 22:22-23). Exodus promises that the cry of the mistreated widow and orphan will bring the sword. The prophets describe the houses of the powerful filled with the spoil of the needy. God draws near as a swift witness against those who oppress the hired worker, the widow, and the fatherless (Malachi 3:5). Classical sources add the figure of the philosopher-king: Plato’s ruler who prioritizes the true good of the city over popularity or procedure when the city is being consumed.

Nayib Bukele has claimed the title outright. After the collapse of El Salvador’s once-world-leading homicide rate under a state of exception, mass arrests, and CECOT, he has presented concentrated authority as the means of restoring ordinary life. The results are measurable; the risks of permanent emergency power are real. The alternative—continued gang predation—was worse for the people living under it.

Donald Trump’s partnership with Bukele makes the same logic operational for American homeland security. The CECOT arrangement places certain deportees alleged to belong to transnational gangs into a facility built to neutralize them. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has described the offer as an unprecedented act of friendship and proof of alignment. The distinction between foreign and domestic security collapses when the same networks divert resources meant for children or turn neighborhoods into hunting grounds. The administration’s continued reliance on the partnership treats neutralization of organized predators as a homeland priority.

Rubio’s speech at the Acropolis in Athens placed this posture in a longer civilizational frame. Standing before the Parthenon, he traced the West’s inheritance from ancient Greece through Rome and Christendom to the American founding. Athens, he said, gave democracy, philosophy, and the ideas of law, virtue, and citizenship. The founders of the United States were fascinated by that heritage; Greek architecture and vocabulary remain carved into the republic. Yet Rubio warned that the West now stands at an inflection point. Nations that open borders, outsource industry, allow militaries to decay, and prioritize the “global community” over their own people risk atrophy and decline. The Trump administration, he argued, chooses the unapologetic pursuit of national power and the revitalization of an old friendship rather than the polite management of decline. text:
WODEMAN
A Romaunce in Three Actes

CARNAL DESYRES III

When mornyng came, he took the axe and carried it some distaunce from the wall. He left it among the stones, where it could no longer be reached without effort. Then he retourned to the body.

Robert lay upon his back, his face tourned towards the pale skie.

Brando looked at him for a long time.

"May God judge thee," he whispered.

Then he tourned westward.

Brando had no idea how far he must travel.

The track continued beyond the broken wall, wynding between fields that had long since retourned to scrub. At intervals he found traces of cultivatioun: a collapsed terrace, a dry irrigatioun channel, the stump of an orchard, a stone trough overtourned beside a spring. These signs gave him courage, though they offered no food.

He walked until his legs failed him.

Then he crawled.

He drank from streams when he found them, taking only enough to keep himself from becoming syck. He chewed a little grass, then spat it out. Once he found a hondful of shrivelled berries beneath a thornbush and ate them slowly, one by one. Their bitternesse remained in his mouth for hours, but they gave him a little strength.

He slept beneath trees, beneath rocks, and once in the hollow of a ruined wall. He woke shivering, with his teeth knocking together and his stump brennyng beneath the filthy linen. His feuver retourned in waves, and he began to lose track of the days.

He no longer thought of Robert.

He no longer thought of Andronikos.

He thought only of the next stream, the next patch of shade, the next place where he might lie without being discovered by men who would take his last possessiouns.

Sometimes he spoke aloud.

He recited prayers, fragments of Latin, and lines from a song he had learned in his youth. He spoke to his father, to his mother, and to Salomone. He begged the physicien to forgive him for having fled the chamber, though he knew that the old man could not hear him.

On the third day alone, he found a dead goat beside a fence.

The animal had been dead for some time, and the smell drove him away. He searched the surrounding ground, hoping to find a shepherd's hut, but there was nothyng. The fence continued for perhaps a hundred paces before collapsing into the brush.

He followed it until sunset.

On the fifth day, he found a road.

It was little more than a track between fields, but it bore the marks of wheels. Brando knelt beside the ruts, touching the earth with his ryght hond. He could scarcelie believe that the signs were real.

He followed the road.

It led through a valley where the trees had been cut back, then climbed a low ridge. Beyond the ridge lay another valley, and beyond that a distaunt line of hills.

He saw no houses.

He saw no people.

Yet he continued.

The sixth day brought rain. Brando sheltered beneath an overhanging rock, curled upon the earth, and tried to keep his wound dry. The water ran down the stone above him and collected in a shallow hollow. He drank from it, then slept fitfully until the cold woke him.

On the seventh day, he found a little flour in a ruined hut.

It had been stored in a woden chest, and most of it had been spoiled by damp. Brando scraped together what remained, mixed it with water, and ate the paste from his fyngers. It tasted of mould and earth. He swallowed it slowly, afraid that his stomach would reject it.

For once, it remained down.

He lay back agaynst the wall and began to cry.

He had eaten flour.

A little flour, filthy and spoiled, scarcelie enough to fill his mouth.

Yet he had eaten somethyng that had not belonged to a dead man.

The knowledge was so overwhelming that he could scarcelie endure it.

On the ninth day, he saw smoke.

It rose beyond a ridge, thin and grey agaynst the afternoon sky. Brando stared at it for a long time, fearing that it might be mist or dust. Then the wynd shifted, and he smelled wodesmoke.

He began to walk more quickly.

He fell twyce. The second time he could not rise without crawling to a tree and pulling himself upryght by its branches. His legs shook so badly that he had to stop everie few paces. He felt as though his body had become a sack of bones, looselie bound together by skin and sinew.

Still he continued.

On the eleventh day, he reached a stream crossed by a narrow woden bridge. The bridge was old but sound. He crossed it on his honds and knees, then lay upon the opposite bank, drynking until he could drynk no more.

Beyond the stream, the road widened.

There were wheel ruts, hoofprints, and the marks of many feet. Brando followed them through a stand of trees and into open country.

He saw a field.

Then a wall.

Then a roof.

He stopped.

At fyrst he thought he had found another ruin. The buildings stood low agaynst the earth, their walls pale beneath the sun. A church tower rose above them, crooked and weather-beaten. Smoke drifted from several chimneys.

Then a door opened.

A man came out carrying a bucket.

Brando stared at him.

The man lifted the bucket, walked a few paces, and set it beside a trough. He tourned to call somethyng towards the house, and a woman appeared in the doorway.

A dog ran across the yard.

Brando began to tremble.

He had seen people.

Lyving people.

The sight of them was almost unbearable.

He tried to call out, but his voyce was gone. He tried agayn, forcing air through his dry throat.

"Help."

The word emerged as a whisper.

The man did not hear him.

Brando stumbled forward.

He crossed the field, falling once upon the rough earth. He rose, then fell agayn. His honds were torn, his knees bruised, and his head swam so violently that the buildings seemed to move before him.

He reached the road.

The man with the bucket tourned.

For a moment he stared at Brando without recognitioun. He saw a gaunt figure in filthy rags, with hollow cheeks, sunken eyes, and a left sleeve hanging empty. The pilgrim's skin was yellow-grey, his lips cracked, and his beard matted into dyrk clumps. His body had been reduced to such a state that the clothes seemed to hang upon a skeleton.

The man dropped the bucket.

"Jesú Christ!"

The woman appeared behind him.

Brando tried to speak.

"I am..."

His voyce failed.

The man approached cautiously, then stopped a few paces away.

"Who art thou?"

Brando looked at him.

He tried to remember the answer.

His name was Brando. He was a man of Lombardie. He had crossed the zee, survived the loss of his hond, and escaped from Caffa when the pestilence and the siege had made the cité a place of death. He had travelled through the wyldernesse with seven companiouns, and one by one they had perished. He had eaten human flesh. He had killed Robert Guiscard in the dyrknesse. He had walked alone for fourteen days.

He tried to say all these thyngs.

Only one word came.

"Christian."

The man crossed himself.

The woman began to weep.

They approached him, slowly now, and took him by the arms. Brando felt their honds upon him, warm and living. He tried to stand upryght, but his legs gave way, and they caught him before he struck the ground.

"Water," he whispered.

"Yes, son," the woman said. "Water."

They carried him towards the house.

As they passed through the doorway, Brando saw a hearth, a table, a loaf of bread, and a woden bowl. The fyre burned steadily, and the room smelled of smoke, wool, and ordinary human lyfe.

He began to weep.

The woman laid him upon a bed. The man brought water, and the woman held the cup to his lips, allowing him to drynk slowly. Brando swallowed, then closed his eyes.

Outside, the settlement continued its ordinary businesse. A cart creaked along the road. Someone called to a child. A hammer struck iron in a distaunt wyrkshop. The church bell rang, its sound carrying across the fields and into the hills.

Brando heard it.

He had not heard a bell in many weeks.

He lay verie still, listening to the sound fade into the distaunce.

He had reached civilizatioun at last.

He was not triumphaunt. He was not restored. He was scarcelie recognizable as the man who had left Caffa, and the wyldernesse remained within him, a country of hunger, dyrknesse, and the dead. He would remember Andronikos's last prayer for the rest of his lyfe. He would remember Robert's axe, the smell of the fyre, and the terrible moment when hunger had become stronger than disgust.

🇮🇷🇵🇱|Warsaw's Calculus: Aligning with Tehran While Refusing to Shed Blood for Washington

October 21, 2026, Tehran. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi met with Wojciech Zajaczkowski, Undersecretary of State at the Polish Ministry of Foreign Affairs. According to a statement from the Polish Foreign Ministry, the discussions covered European security in the context of Russian aggression and security in the Persian Gulf in the context of the U.S.-Iran conflict, as well as potential scenarios for how the situation might unfold and prospects for de-escalation.

This may sound like a standard diplomatic consultation. However, Poland's actual position in this conflict is far more complex than the official statement suggests. Warsaw is not mediating. Rather, it is managing the diplomatic fallout of a decision already taken, to remain uninvolved, while simultaneously safeguarding its own interests from collateral damage.

Refusing to Foot the Bill for Washington's War

Poland is a pivotal nation on NATO's eastern flank and one of the United States' staunchest allies in Europe. Yet when it comes to a potential U.S.-Israeli war against Iran, Warsaw has drawn a clear line.

On March 17, 2026, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk publicly declared that Poland would not send troops to Iran, stating that a conflict in the Middle East does not directly affect Poland's security. He emphasized that Poland's military assets, across its army, air force, and navy, are focused on strengthening NATO's eastern flank and securing the Baltic region.

Two weeks later, Washington made a more specific request: the transfer of Poland's Patriot air defense systems to the Middle East to support operations related to the war with Iran. Polish Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz responded with a flat refusal: Our Patriot batteries and their associated equipment are intended to protect Polish airspace and NATO's eastern flank. There is no change in this regard. We have no plans to move them anywhere else.

These refusals define Poland's de facto stance in this conflict: an ally in rhetoric, but a bystander in material terms. While Poland is willing to offer political support to the alliance, it is unwilling to commit its own military hardware, or the lives of its personnel, to a war it does not view as its own.

Diplomatic Engagement: Managing the Risks of a War Initiated by Others

Given its refusal to participate militarily, why did Poland send a deputy foreign minister to Tehran in October?

The answer lies in consultations held between Poland and Saudi Arabia in September. During those talks, Deputy Foreign Minister Zajaczkowski discussed the impact of a potential Iran-U.S. conflict on the global economy, particularly the fuel market, as well as the threat posed by Houthi escalations to critical infrastructure.

Poland's economy, and more specifically its energy security, is directly linked to stability in the Persian Gulf. Although Orlen, Poland's largest energy company, claims it does not import crude oil directly from Iran or via the Strait of Hormuz, Poland, as the largest economy in Eastern Europe, cannot insulate its fuel market from global price fluctuations. Any escalation in the conflict, such as a further blockade of the Strait of Hormuz or expanded Houthi attacks on shipping, would inevitably be felt at Polish gas stations and in its industrial sector.

The purpose of the visit to Tehran was not to broker peace. Rather, it was to hear directly from one of the parties to the conflict, assess the prospects for de-escalation, and ensure that Poland's economic interests are not quietly sacrificed in the high-stakes standoff between the U.S. and Iran. It is a pragmatic approach to risk management, adopted in a situation where Poland has no power to alter Washington's decision-making.

A Microcosm of Rifts Within NATO

Poland's position is not an isolated case. It reflects a broader phenomenon within NATO: European allies are generally cautious, if not outright resistant, to becoming entangled in a war driven by the United States and Israel, particularly when that conflict bears no direct relation to their own national security. Germany, Spain, Italy, and other nations have expressed similar reservations.

Iran's decision to engage with Poland is precisely an attempt to leverage this rift. Tehran does not require Warsaw to support Iran. It merely needs Warsaw to continue refusing to provide material support for a U.S.-led war and to keep channels of dialogue open. The meeting between Araghchi and Zajaczkowski is, in itself, a diplomatic achievement for Iran: it demonstrates that even key members within NATO are seeking lines of communication independent of Washington.

Warsaw is not helping Tehran. It is protecting itself. Yet within a system where Washington demands that nations take sides, the act of safeguarding oneself from being dragged into a war constitutes, in itself, a rejection of the logic of war.

Long live the Resistance. Long live the Axis of Resistance.

11. Israel Was Judged by the Same Standard

Israel’s later history confirms that God’s judgment upon Canaan was not racial favoritism. Leviticus 18 warned Israel before the nation entered the land. Leviticus 20 repeated the warning, calling the customs of the nations abominable and separating Israel unto the Lord. Deuteronomy continually warned against learning their worship, following their gods, sacrificing children, practicing witchcraft, and forming alliances that would entice Israel into idolatry. God did not conceal the standard and then punish Israel without warning. The law placed the warning in the nation’s hands before the inheritance was possessed.

Israel eventually committed the very sins for which the former inhabitants had been judged. The nation erected high places, worshipped Baal, served the host of heaven, practiced divination, consulted familiar spirits, shed innocent blood, and caused children to pass through the fire. Second Kings 17 explains the fall of the northern kingdom by recounting these abominations. Judah later followed the same road until Jerusalem and the temple were destroyed by Babylon. The land that had vomited out the Canaanites vomited out disobedient Israelites. The instrument changed; the moral government of God did not.

Yet Israel’s exile did not erase the Abrahamic covenant or convert the Church into a replacement Israel. God disciplined the nation while preserving His sworn purposes concerning the seed, land, throne, and future restoration. That distinction is indispensable. Conditional enjoyment of covenant blessings does not mean the unconditional covenant has been cancelled. Israel could be removed from present possession without God surrendering His future promise. The same God who judged Israel more severely because of greater light will also restore the nation according to His word. Discipline proves the seriousness of the covenant relationship; it does not prove its extinction.

12. How to Read National Judgment Responsibly

Genesis 15 concerns a specific covenant, a specified land, a chosen seed, identified nations, a foretold period, and a later divinely authorized conquest. Every one of those details matters. A modern government cannot quote “the iniquity of the Amorites” over its enemy and thereby inherit Joshua’s commission. A church cannot claim Canaan’s borders, replace Abraham’s physical seed, and transform political ambition into holy war. The fact that God once commanded a particular judgment does not authorize every ruler with an army and a Bible to imitate it.

We must also distinguish divine judgment from personal vengeance. Israel’s conquest under Joshua occurred within a unique covenantal and revelatory setting. It was not a model authorizing Christians to conquer unbelievers, confiscate their land, or compel conversion by force. The Church is commanded to preach the gospel, suffer wrong, love enemies, and wield spiritual weapons. The body of Christ does not possess a territorial commission to eliminate Canaanites. Mixing Israel’s national instructions with the Church’s present ministry produces exactly the kind of religious violence that comes from refusing to rightly divide the word of truth.

The responsible lesson is not that believers may declare war upon anyone they consider wicked. The lesson is that God rules nations, moral rebellion accumulates consequences, patience has a boundary, covenant promises will be fulfilled, and final judgment belongs to the Lord. We should proclaim what Scripture reveals and refuse to use Scripture as camouflage for what human ambition desires. The Bible is sharp enough without taping a politician’s knife to it. When God wants a man to know that a particular judgment has been appointed, He is perfectly capable of saying so. Until then, our duty is to preach His word, warn against sin, offer mercy through Christ, and leave the throne occupied by its rightful King.

text:
Amazing true story: 

His name was Sergeant Major, a nine-year-old Belgian Malinois who spent seven years deployed overseas with the U.S. Army, clearing paths and sniffing out danger to protect American lives.

When his handler, an Army veteran named Marcus, fell on unimaginably hard times after returning home to civilian life—battling severe invisible wounds and finding himself living out of his car—he refused to surrender his military partner to a crowded shelter.

For months, Marcus shared his last piece of bread and his only blanket with Sergeant Major on the cold streets, keeping his loyal companion warm while going hungry himself.

One freezing evening, local authorities forced Marcus off a public bench, telling him he couldn't stay there. Heartbroken and exhausted, Marcus made the agonizing decision to walk to a local fire station. Leaving Sergeant Major tied safely to the post with a handwritten note tucked into the dog's collar, Marcus wept in the dark.

The note read: "Please take care of my brother. He served his country faithfully. I have nothing left to give him, but he deserves a warm bed and a full bowl. Thank you, and God bless America."

When the firefighters walked out and found the shivering dog alongside that raw, tear-stained letter, every single man stood in silence. They didn't just take Sergeant Major in; they read the veteran's handwritten plea and immediately launched a quiet search across the city to find Marcus.

Within forty-eight hours, those local firefighters tracked Marcus down to a nearby shelter intake line. Instead of turning him away, the captain stepped forward, handed Marcus a set of keys to a local transitional apartment sponsored by the station, offered him a job helping maintain the grounds, and led him back to the station where Sergeant Major was waiting with a tail wagging so hard his whole body shook.

True loyalty isn't bought; it's forged in the fire of sacrifice, service, and brotherhood. God bless our veterans, and God bless those who remember that loyalty goes both ways.

If this story reminds you of the true heart of our community, please share it to honor our vets and their faithful companions.

Homeless veteran's goodbye letter leads Fort Worth Fire Station to adopt his dog

This true story highlights the unbreakable bond of loyalty between a service member and his dog.

text:
Araghchi's Diagnosis: Borders as Bottlenecks, Not Gateways

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi offered a remark to exporters that serves as a financial footnote to the broader conflict:

"Unfortunately, our borders have become places of stagnation rather than points of transit."

Who Is Causing the Stagnation?

He did not point to Western sanctions. Instead, he noted: "The problems often originate on the other side of the border."

Pakistan: A week ago, it closed its border with Iran, halting all movement of trucks, fuel, and commercial goods. Following a visit to Tehran, where he met with President Pezeshkian, Parliament Speaker Ghalibaf, official Mohsen Rezaei, and Foreign Minister Araghchi, it was announced that the issue has been resolved and the border would reopen this morning.

Afghanistan: Disputes over water rights, border skirmishes, and issues surrounding dams on the Helmand River, involving the Taliban government, have repeatedly disrupted cross-border trade in Sistan and Baluchestan.

Iraq: The presence of Iranian-Kurdish opposition groups in the Kurdistan Region has turned border security into a persistent point of friction between Tehran and Baghdad.

Turkmenistan, Armenia, and Azerbaijan: These serve as nodes along the North-South Corridor, with each country caught in a balancing act between U.S. pressure and its own national interests.

This stagnation is not a technical issue. It is the physical manifestation of political pressure exerted at border checkpoints.

Tariffs: They Raise, We Lower

Araghchi stated: "Regarding tariffs, we must take steps to lower duties on goods from our neighbors to expand our own exports."

This is not merely about trade facilitation. It is a unilateral dismantling of barriers.

Under pressure from the United States, neighboring countries have imposed tariffs, non-tariff barriers, and customs delays on Iranian goods. Iran's response is not to retaliate with reciprocal tariffs, but rather to lower its own import duties, making it easier for foreign goods to enter the Iranian market, in exchange for the easing of restrictions on Iranian exports.

This is a form of asymmetrical opening. It requires Iran to absorb short-term losses in order to secure the continued viability of its trade corridors in the long term. Under sanctions, access is more important than profit.

Provincial Diplomacy: Bypassing the Capital

"The expansion of provincial diplomacy," stated Araghchi.

This remark represents the most concrete strategic shift in his entire address.

Traditionally, Iran's foreign policy has been centrally managed by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Tehran. Provincial officials have held no diplomatic authority. Governors of border provinces, chambers of commerce, and special economic zones have historically had to await directives from Tehran when dealing with neighboring countries.

Provincial diplomacy alters this structure. It enables border provinces to engage directly with their counterparts across the border, Sistan and Baluchestan with Pakistan's Balochistan province, Khorasan with Herat in Afghanistan, the Azerbaijan provinces with the Republic of Azerbaijan, and Kurdistan province with the Kurdistan Region of Iraq.

Why? Because the capital faces the greatest pressure from the United States】, whereas provincial governments face less. Direct dialogue between provincial officials and their counterparts in neighboring states can bypass political stalemates in the capital, allowing for the resolution of specific issues related to trade, logistics, and security.

In the context of sanctions, this amounts to a decentralization of diplomacy, shifting the focus from the conference rooms of embassies to border crossings, chambers of commerce, and special economic zones.

Why Neighbors Have Become Even More Critical

"Neighboring countries have always been a priority for us," Araghchi noted. "But given the country's current circumstances, particularly in the economic sphere, I believe they have become even more important."

What are these current circumstances?

Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz is blocked by the U.S. Navy. Routes through the Red Sea are disrupted by conflict. Trade channels to Europe have been severed by sanctions. Access to the SWIFT system has been cut off, and transactions in U.S. dollars are prohibited.

What remains are land routes, routes that lead directly to neighboring countries.

There is the North-South Corridor, Russia to Caspian Sea to Iran to Indian Ocean, the East-West Corridor, China to Central Asia to Iran to Turkey to Europe, and the Pakistan Corridor, Iran to Pakistan to South Asia.

Neighboring countries are not merely diplomatic partners. They serve as the physical nodes in a system designed to circumvent sanctions. Border checkpoints, railways, roads, and ports, all located in neighboring countries, are essential for keeping Iran's economy functioning.

The True Meaning of Araghchi's Remarks

He did not say, sanctions are failing. He said, the borders are at a standstill.

He did not say, we have found a way out. He said, we need exporters to help us identify the problems.

He did not say, our neighbors are on our side. He said, we need to lower the tariffs they impose.

This is a pragmatic assessment by a foreign minister, not a declaration of victory. His message is clear: the channels are being blocked, blocked on the other side. We must seek solutions from the bottom up at the provincial level, from the sides through tariff adjustments, and from the business sector via exporters.

A foreign minister capable of openly acknowledging that the borders are places of stagnation understands the true costs of this war far better than one who claims that everything is fine.

Long live Iran. Long live the Resistance. Long live the Axis of Resistance.

John... I want to set you straight on this.  I hope you take the time to understand.

Biden signed the The Camp Lejeune Justice Act in 2022.  Under Biden more than 400,000 administrative claims were filed with the Navy.  By August 2024 (near the end of the filing window and Biden’s term), the government had made settlement offers in only about 114 cases—roughly 0.03% of claims.

Under Trump the DOJ explicitly reprioritized the process.  By March 2026 it reported 2,531 total approved EO offers (worth ~$708 million) since the program began in 2023, with more than $421 million paid since Trump took office.  It highlighted a burst of 649 offers ($175 million) in just three weeks.  Associate AG Stanley Woodward stated the department had “reprioritized approving settlements” and would continue doing so weekly.

By September 2026: Official DOJ figures showed settlement offers exceeding $1.1 billion and actual payouts exceeding $879 million. Trump has cited roughly $1 billion paid.

In short, the large majority of offers and payments have occurred since Trump returned to office.  The backlog still remains after being jammed to near zero by Biden and the Democrats for 2 years.

text:
Let’s take a look at some of Trump’s favorite fraudsters (just a sample): 

•Trevor Milton (Nikola), pardoned March 2025. He was sentenced to four years for misleading investors, and a judge was about to rule on roughly $700 million in restitution. He and his wife had given more than $1.8 million to pro-Trump committees.

•David Gentile (GPB Capital), commuted. He was convicted in a $1.6 billion scheme that defrauded thousands of investors, and he served under two weeks of a seven-year sentence. The commutation also erased his $15.5 million forfeiture.

•Carlos Watson (Ozy Media), commuted. Prosecutors said he defrauded investors and lenders out of tens of millions of dollars.

•Todd and Julie Chrisley, pardoned May 2025. They were convicted of fraud and tax evasion involving more than $30 million. The pardon was expected to wipe out $17.8 million in restitution owed to banks.

•Adriana and Andres Camberos, pardoned January 2026. They sold millions of counterfeit 5-Hour Energy bottles and owed $49 million in restitution. Adriana's earlier sentence had already been commuted by Trump in 2021, so this was her second act of clemency.

•Joseph Schwartz, nursing home executive. He pleaded guilty to a $38 million tax fraud, a sentencing that Trump's own U.S. attorney had publicly celebrated.

•Paul Walczak. His pardon let him skip an 18-month sentence and repayment of $4.4 million.

•Michele Fiore, former Nevada GOP lawmaker. She took over $70,000 in donations meant to honor two slain police officers. Trump pardoned her before she was sentenced.

•Philip Esformes, first term. DOJ called his case an unprecedented $1 billion Medicare fraud. Trump commuted his 20-year sentence in December 2020.

•BitMEX founders and Changpeng Zhao (Binance). These are anti-money-laundering cases, not fraud, but they're part of the same pattern. The BitMEX pardons erased $130 million in fines.

The totals
•House Judiciary Democrats estimate nearly $1.7 billion in restitution, fines, and forfeitures erased.

•Gov. Newsom's office puts the figure near $2 billion.

•A June 2026 Reuters review found that 96% of second-term clemency grants failed DOJ's longstanding guidelines.

And let’s not forget Senator Rick Scott (R-Fl) and Columbia/HCA

Scott ran Columbia/HCA from 1994 to 1997, when it was the country's largest for-profit hospital chain. Here is what the company did:

•It billed Medicare and Medicaid for unnecessary tests, and for home health visits to patients who didn't qualify.

•It offered doctors financial incentives in exchange for patient referrals.

•An insider described keeping two sets of cost reports, filing inflated figures with the government and pocketing the difference.

The result: the company pleaded guilty to 14 felonies, most committed while Scott was CEO, and paid $1.7 billion in total. 

Scott was never charged. After resigning, he invoked the Fifth Amendment 75 times in depositions.

How it compares historically: DOJ called it by far the largest recovery ever in a health care fraud investigation. 

Pharmaceutical settlements have since been larger, but as of 2014 it was still the largest fraud settlement by a hospital corporation. More recently, Scott suggested he had been politically "persecuted" over the case, which reversed his 2010 position of taking responsibility.

text:
Discover the Power of Spiritual Care on Your Whole Health Journey
Healing is more than physical recovery—it’s a journey of mind, body, spirit, and community. Many Veterans today are seeking ways to feel more grounded, connected, and supported as part of their Whole Health path. Whether it’s finding inner peace, rediscovering purpose, strengthening faith, or building resilience, spiritual care is a vital part of overall well‑being.
This week, the VA Southern Nevada Healthcare System honors the enduring role spiritual care plays in healing and wholeness. Our Chaplain Service invites Veterans, families, and staff to join us for a week of connection, reflection, and compassionate support.
Event Highlights
• Monday & Friday: Chaplains will round inpatient units with light snacks and Tea for the Soul—a peaceful moment for conversation, comfort, grounding, and care.
• Tuesday–Thursday (8 a.m.–3 p.m.): Visit the Chaplain’s table in the main hallway to explore spiritual wellness resources, learn about available services, or simply receive a kind word.
A Legacy of Compassionate Spiritual Care
Six years ago, our Medical Center launched the Chaplain Service to provide spiritual and emotional support for Veterans and families during life’s most challenging periods. Over the past three years, our chaplains—working closely with staff, leadership, and interdisciplinary teams—have expanded these offerings to meet the evolving needs of our community. This growth reflects the belief that spiritual care is not separate from health care—it is integral to Whole Health.
Today, we proudly celebrate Spiritual Care Week and the opening of new Chaplain Service offices at the VA Medical Center. These spaces were designed to offer warmth, comfort, and accessibility—places where Veterans, families, and staff can receive personalized guidance and a renewed sense of meaning and belonging.
Spiritual Care as a Foundation for Whole Health
Spirituality is your unique experience of how you relate to something greater than yourself and what brings meaning, purpose, and direction to your life. It shapes how you connect with others, how you express yourself, and how you find strength in times of uncertainty. For some, spirituality is rooted in faith or religion; for others, it emerges from personal reflection, nature, creativity, service, or community. There is no single definition of spiritual health—what matters is that it reflects your values, your identity, and your journey.
A regular spiritual practice—whether prayer, meditation, journaling, time outdoors, creative expression, or moments of stillness—can help you feel more balanced and grounded. Research shows that people with a healthy spiritual life often experience greater resilience, clearer communication, healthier relationships, and even improved physical health. Belief in something larger than yourself can bring strength, connection, and peace during difficult times—and our warm, caring chaplains are here to help you explore these pathways and reach attainable health goals aligned with your Whole Health vision.

text:
Top 10 States with the Highest Alligator Population

Louisiana
What States have alligators? Look no further than the most prominent state to find an alligator in the country. Louisiana is also famous for its gator-laden swamplands. Although this infamous distinction is likely a little overdone, it is true that in the right parts of Louisiana, the chances are better that you will come across an alligator than the chances are that you won’t because there are about 2,000,000 in the state.

Florida
The hottest state for gator sightings, and also with one of its most prestigious universities named after these many-toothed creatures, Florida is as close as it comes to being gator-crazy. When many people think about alligators, they think about Florida. Alligators are a part of the tourism scene in Florida, so the chances aren’t only good that one of the state’s 1.3 million alligators might be spotted in Florida, but the state is banking on it.

Texas
Although large parts of the state are uninhabitable by alligators, there are still around 400,000. Down by the Rio Grande, there is a reasonable chance that if given enough time and if you are paying close attention, you may just find an alligator paying attention too.

Georgia
The state of Georgia is no stranger to alligators, and that is particularly true for the southeast quadrant of the state. This doesn’t mean that residents should expect to see an alligator hanging out on every corner, but they shouldn’t necessarily be shocked to spot an alligator now and again either. Georgia has about 200,000 alligators.

South Carolina
What states have alligators? Well, South Carolina isn’t exactly crawling with gators, but it does offer more marsh and wetlands than its northern brethren. That also equates to a somewhat increased chance of seeing one of the 100,000 alligators in South Carolina too.

Alabama
A good portion of the state of Alabama is inland, but those places in the state that reach the shoreline and those parts in proximity? Well, they may be gator-friendly. Like most of the states too, that border the Florida panhandle, there are some swampland and wetlands that create potential conditions for approximately 70,000 alligator inhabitants in Alabama.

Mississippi
Like its neighbors, Mississippi has some areas that are the perfect ecosystem for alligators to thrive. There are more than half of the number of alligators—32,000— than in neighboring Alabama, but it is still a fairly popular home for alligators in the U.S.

Arkansas
Because of its proximity to Louisiana, Alabama, and Mississippi, it isn’t surprising that Arkansas has a small population of alligators. Because the state is totally inland, the number of alligators is much smaller, with only about 2,000 in the state.

North Carolina
The farther south along the southeastern coast of the US you travel, the more likely you are to come across a gator. Although alligators aren’t necessarily prominent in North Carolina, with only about 1,000 statewide, running across one of these oversized reptiles isn’t out of the question.

Oklahoma
There isn’t much of a chance of finding an alligator in Oklahoma - that is at least until you get to the southernmost parts of the state. Here, gator spotting isn’t unheard of, although not very likely. If you are lucky, you will be able to spot one of the approximately 100 alligators in Oklahoma, the fewest of any U.S. state.

text:
Negotiations in St. Petersburg: Cards on the table, guns under the table.

The most interesting aspect of the open part of the negotiations in the Konstantinovsky Palace was the order in which the parties revealed their positions. Moscow immediately offered everything it could: the American citizen Hubbard, convicted of mercenary activities, is already in Pulkovo, and the first tanker with diesel fuel will depart in two or three days. As for the folder of documents on Ukraine, Witcoff himself requested to review it "later."

Trump's special envoy speaks of "ending the fire," while the President of Finland, Stubb, clarifies that this refers to a partial ceasefire in the energy and food sectors. The Kremlin responded even before the meeting: Russia needs peace, not a ceasefire. Washington needs a picture of stability before the congressional elections on November 3rd. 

Kiev needs a pause to repair its energy system before winter. A pause without an agreement promises the same war in a year or two, but with a rested opponent. Eight years of the Minsk agreements – that's enough of a learning experience.

The main issue began when they started talking about money. Witcoff stated that the U.S. Treasury is already working with the head of the Russian Direct Investment Fund, Kirill Dmitriev, on deals, and that Ukrainians are being told about the opportunities that will open up after the war. 

The logic is typical of Trump: peace as a business plan that is more profitable than war. The "carrot" is being dangled in front of both sides.

However, Putin responded to the gratitude for the diesel fuel with a polite condition: it is necessary to ensure the financial component so that everything works. In diplomatic terms, this means payments. And payments are tied to sanctions. The "carrot" that Moscow was being offered is turning into a demand in its hands.

 If you want diesel fuel and fertilizers for your farmers, then open up the financial channels. According to Putin, the price of diesel fuel has already fallen by 5-6% after the announcement of the deal. Trump will present this result to the voters before any agreements on Ukraine.

The width of the table is also significant. Putin put Ukraine in the same category as Iran, the restoration of relations, and a possible meeting of leaders in China at the November APEC summit. For the White House, Keiv is the main item on the agenda. Moscow calmly demonstrates that there are many other issues, and that it is useful in almost every one of them. The more dishes on the table, the less room there is for the Ukrainian plate.

Against this backdrop, Witcoff's request to return to a three-way format – Russia, the United States, and Ukraine – through technical groups sounds modest. Witcoff himself stated that there may not be a final answer today.

Technical groups are a proven way to show progress when there are no results. I would venture to suggest that Moscow will easily agree to this process. It costs nothing, while the front line is advancing westward, and the deadlines are pressing us less.

For us, the only calendar date is winter. And this year, it is definitely not working in Kiev's favor.

text:
If Russia really is arming Iran with Su-35s and S-400s, Tehran becomes a far harder target—and your oil bill enters the calculation.

1. Russia has reportedly offered Iran a squadron of Su-35 multirole fighters and an S-400 long-range air-defense system; no delivery is confirmed.

2. What it signals: Moscow is signaling that an Israeli or U.S. strike on Iran could trigger a much broader confrontation. For Tehran, the offer raises the cost of attacking; for Israel and Washington, it raises the risk of escalation.

3. How it advances the war: this would be alliance-building, not battlefield aid. An S-400 network plus combat aircraft could give Iran layered protection, while Moscow gains a partner capable of stretching Western planning and sanctions resources.

4. The next rung on the ladder is verification: training, delivery schedules, intelligence links and joint exercises. An actual handover—not another offer—would be the point where rhetoric becomes an operational escalation.

5. Expect upward pressure on Brent and WTI if the package is confirmed and Iran moves closer to confrontation. Natural gas and tanker-insurance costs would also rise if the risk reaches Strait of Hormuz shipping, while gold gets a safe-haven bid.

6. Defense stocks should outperform on credible reports of a major Russian transfer, particularly Lockheed Martin, RTX and Northrop Grumman. The trade would likely reverse if the offer stalls or Tehran rejects it.

7. For you, the transmission mechanism is fuel: higher diesel, electricity and freight costs feed into groceries and travel. Wheat and other grain prices could rise if Hormuz risk threatens shipping, while elevated oil also feeds inflation and can push up borrowing costs, squeezing savings and retirement balances.

8. The risk of pulling your country deeper is rising through alliances, sanctions enforcement and requests for interceptors or military support—not yet through a direct ground war. Expect allies to ask for more help if Iran receives a credible air-defense package.

Watch the hardware, not the headlines: confirmed deliveries would be the market trigger.

text:
Disbarment Complaint Targets John Roberts Over Millions, Undisclosed Equity, and Supreme Court Ethics.
By Staff Writer.

An investigative journalist says he is filing a disbarment complaint against Chief Justice John Roberts, alleging years of misleading financial disclosures, undisclosed financial interests tied to his wife’s legal recruiting work, and repeated failures to recuse himself from cases involving firms that paid her commissions.
The chief justice of the United States is supposed to be one of the people most committed to upholding the law. But a new complaint targeting Roberts raises a pointed question: What happens when the person responsible for leading the nation’s highest court is accused of failing to follow the rules himself?
Christopher Armitage, an investigative journalist with The Existentialist Republic, says he is filing a complaint with the D.C. Bar seeking disciplinary action against Roberts. His allegations center on millions of dollars in commissions earned by Roberts’s wife, Jane Sullivan Roberts, from a legal recruiting business whose clients included law firms that appeared before the Supreme Court.
The complaint alleges that Roberts repeatedly characterized his wife’s commission income as salary on federal financial disclosure forms, failed to report an equity interest in her employer for several years, and did not recuse himself from cases involving firms connected to her recruiting business.
At the center of the allegations is Jane Sullivan Roberts’s work as a legal recruiter at Major, Lindsey & Africa, commonly known as MLA, where she worked from 2007 to 2014.
According to company spreadsheets cited in the reporting, Jane Roberts earned approximately $10.3 million in commissions over seven years, tied to more than $13.3 million in revenue attributed to her placements.
The recruiting work involved placing senior lawyers in prominent positions at major law firms. The reported placements included former Interior Secretary Ken Salazar at WilmerHale, attorney Robert Bennett at Hogan Lovells, former U.S. Attorney Neil MacBride at Davis Polk, and Michael Held, a former general counsel of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, at WilmerHale.
Jane Roberts testified under oath that she placed senior government lawyers in positions with starting partner salaries reaching as high as $3 million.
Mark Jungers, a former managing partner at MLA, told Politico that the firm hired her partly in the hope that it would benefit from her being the chief justice’s wife.
That reported statement raises an obvious question about the commercial value of her connection to one of the most powerful judges in the country.
But the key issue is not simply that she earned substantial commissions. It is whether those financial relationships created conflicts that required Roberts to disclose more information or step aside from particular cases.
Federal law sets out circumstances in which judges must disqualify themselves from cases. One provision, 28 U.S.C. § 455(a), requires recusal when a judge’s impartiality might reasonably be questioned.
Other provisions address financial interests involving a judge, a spouse, or other interests that could be substantially affected by the outcome of a proceeding.
Armitage argues that the Roberts household’s financial ties to law firms appearing before the Supreme Court triggered those requirements.
His argument draws on a legal analysis by Bennett Gershman, a legal ethics professor at Pace Law School, who reviewed the arrangement in 2022 at the request of a whistleblower. Gershman’s analysis, as described in the source material, concluded that the nature and scale of the commission relationships raised serious recusal concerns.
The argument is straightforward: When a law firm pays a judge’s spouse substantial commissions for recruiting services, the public may reasonably question the judge’s impartiality when that firm appears before the court.
Armitage also alleges that firms connected to Jane Roberts’s recruiting work appeared in more than 500 Supreme Court cases during Roberts’s tenure, without recusal based on his wife’s income. He points to WilmerHale and Hogan Lovells as examples of firms with substantial Supreme Court practices.
Another major part of the complaint concerns how Roberts reported his wife’s compensation.
According to Armitage, Roberts’s annual financial disclosures described her earnings as salary for years, even though her compensation from the recruiting business included commissions tied to individual placements.
Gershman’s memorandum reportedly described the characterization as legally incorrect. Richard Painter, who served as chief White House ethics lawyer under President George W. Bush and helped prepare Roberts for his confirmation hearings, also criticized the disclosures. In 2023, Painter wrote that Roberts had “fudged the details” by describing his wife’s earnings as salary.
In 2023, after Business Insider published documents from the whistleblower, Roberts amended an entry in his 2022 financial disclosure. The report described Jane Roberts’s compensation as including both base salary and commission.
The same filing disclosed an equity stake in Macrae, the recruiting firm where she had moved in 2019 and helped open its Washington office. The stake was valued in a range of $100,001 to $250,000.
According to the source material, that interest had not appeared in three earlier annual filings. Roberts attributed the omission to inadvertence.
The complaint argues that the income descriptions and omitted equity interest deserve further scrutiny. Whether the errors amounted to an ethics violation—or something more serious—has not been established by the material provided.
The disclosures became public through Kendal Price, a former managing director at MLA.
In December 2022, Price filed a complaint with the House and Senate Judiciary Committees and the Department of Justice, according to the source material. The submission reportedly included internal company spreadsheets, a sworn affidavit, Jane Roberts’s 2015 arbitration testimony, and Gershman’s legal memorandum.
The documents offered a more detailed picture of the commissions and recruiting relationships than had previously been publicly available.
Whistleblowers who bring internal records to light can face professional and personal consequences. That is one reason allegations backed by documents deserve serious examination rather than reflexive dismissal.
The controversy also arrives amid broader criticism of the Supreme Court’s approach to ethics.
In November 2023, the Court adopted its first formal Code of Conduct for Supreme Court Justices. The document acknowledged that the absence of a written code had contributed to misunderstandings about the ethical rules governing the justices.
Critics argued that the new code did not go far enough because it lacked a clear independent process for receiving complaints, investigating alleged violations, and imposing sanctions.
The Congressional Research Service discussed the absence of an enforcement mechanism, while legal ethics scholars criticized the code’s practical limitations.
The result is a system in which justices generally make their own recusal decisions, with no equivalent independent body routinely empowered to compel a justice to step aside.
That arrangement has drawn scrutiny in other controversies, including reporting about gifts and travel involving Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito.
Roberts declined an invitation from Senate Judiciary Chairman Dick Durbin to testify about Supreme Court ethics in 2023, citing separation-of-powers concerns. All nine justices signed a statement affirming that individual justices—not the Court as a collective body—decide recusal questions.
The debate is bigger than any one justice. It concerns whether the country’s highest court has sufficient safeguards to ensure that its members are held accountable when credible ethics questions arise.
Armitage says his D.C. Bar complaint alleges that Roberts violated Rule 8.4(c) of the D.C. Rules of Professional Conduct, which addresses dishonesty, fraud, deceit, and misrepresentation.
The complaint also cites federal statutes governing financial disclosures and false statements to the government, including 5 U.S.C. § 13106 and 18 U.S.C. § 1001.
Armitage argues that several accountability mechanisms are available, including professional discipline, statutory referrals, congressional impeachment, and criminal enforcement where warranted.
Each operates under different rules and jurisdictional limits. Whether any of them will act on the allegations remains an open question.
The larger problem: Who holds the justices accountable?
The Supreme Court has enormous influence over American life, from voting rights and executive power to reproductive rights and the limits of federal authority. Its decisions can shape the country for generations.
That power makes public confidence in judicial impartiality essential.
The allegations against Roberts raise a basic question: If financial disclosures are inaccurate or a justice’s household has significant financial ties to firms appearing before the Court, what independent process can determine whether the rules were followed?
The answer cannot simply be that the justices police themselves and the public should move on.
Armitage says he is filing his D.C. Bar complaint to force that process into motion. Whether the bar investigates the allegations, or takes disciplinary action remains to be seen.

In 1928 a hailstorm flattened the wheat on a farm in Burdett, Kansas, and with it a young man’s plan to go to college.

Clyde Tombaugh was 22. He had built his own telescopes from farm machinery parts and a mirror he ground himself, and since there was no college now, he did what he could. He drew Jupiter and Mars very carefully and mailed the drawings to Lowell Observatory in Arizona.

They wrote back and offered him a job.

The job was the dullest one in astronomy. He photographed the same patches of sky days apart, then looked at each pair in a machine called a blink comparator, which flipped between them so anything that moved would seem to jump.

Stars, by the hundreds of thousands, held still.

On the afternoon of February 18, 1930, one tiny dot jumped.

It was Pluto, the first planet found by an American, spotted by a farm kid with no degree. An 11-year-old girl in Oxford named Venetia Burney suggested the name.

Tombaugh went to college after all and became a professor.

When NASA launched New Horizons toward Pluto in 2006, it carried a small amount of his ashes. In July 2015 the probe flew past and sent back the first close pictures, including a bright plain shaped like a heart.

BLINK COMPARATOR in English Ordinal, each letter reduced to one digit, is 69.

He finally got to visit.

BROOKLYN NETS MONEYLINE
1.0 UNIT | -133 NOVIG

ROSTER CHANGE MEETS INJURY CONTEXT.

The Nets moneyline is built around two related factors: Brooklyn’s reshaped roster and the personnel Charlotte is expected to be without for its season opener.

Charlotte has undergone a significant offseason transition. LaMelo Ball was traded to Minnesota, Miles Bridges moved to Phoenix, and the Hornets are preparing for the new season with a different offensive structure. The latest reported availability for the opener also has Coby White, Kon Knueppel, and Grant Williams out.

That is a meaningful amount of rotation talent missing or no longer available. It doesn’t automatically make the Hornets an easy opponent, but it changes what Charlotte can rely on in a season-opening game.

WHY BROOKLYN IS WORTH A LOOK

1. THE NETS HAVE ADDED MORE OFFENSIVE CREATION

Brooklyn’s reshaped roster includes Julius Randle and Michael Porter Jr., alongside younger players such as Egor Dëmin and Mikel Brown Jr. Randle gives the team another experienced player capable of handling possessions and creating opportunities, while Porter provides another scoring option.

Those additions give Brooklyn a different offensive foundation from the group that finished last season 20–62. The aim is not to assume the Nets have suddenly become a contender; it’s to recognize that the roster has more tools to compete.

2. THE OPPONENT’S ABSENCES MATTER

With key Hornets unavailable and major pieces from last season no longer on the roster, Charlotte has less continuity and fewer established options for its opening game. That can place more responsibility on the remaining rotation and make offensive execution more difficult.

For a moneyline bet, the question is simple: can Brooklyn win this game often enough to justify the price? The injury situation and Brooklyn’s roster additions form the basis of that argument.

3. THE PRICE IS THE FINAL FILTER

Novig: -133
Bet105: -136
Pinnacle: -136

Novig offers the best listed price. At -133, the break-even probability is approximately 57.1%. Our assessment must be that Brooklyn wins more often than that threshold over comparable situations for the wager to have positive expected value.

Tank operations notable 03/2025:

**Liquid Solutions Tank Leasing** was not a standalone deal. It was a subsidiary of **M.C. Tank Transport, Inc. (MC Tank / MCT)**, which The Kenan Advantage Group (KAG) acquired in late March 2025.

### Key details of the acquisition
- **Announcement date**: March 31, 2025 (an internal MCT memo about the sale circulated around March 26).
- **What was acquired**: M.C. Tank Transport, a West Chester, Ohio-based liquid bulk chemical carrier. The deal explicitly included its subsidiaries **MC Leasing**, **KI Leasing**, and **Liquid Solutions Tank Leasing**.
- **Business focus**: Specialized in hauling and storing liquid bulk chemicals (caustic soda, sulfuric acid, hydrochloric acid, and other specialty chemicals) via tankers and ISO containers. It also offered leasing and maintenance services.
- **Operations**: Operated from eight terminal locations and three ISO container depots across the Southeast and Midwest (some reporting referenced additional terminals/ports such as Houston, Charleston, SC, and Savannah, GA, plus satellite locations).

### Assets and people added to KAG
- Approximately **100 tractors** and **500 trailers/chassis**.
- Roughly **175 professional drivers** and **70 operational and administrative staff**.
- ISO depot capabilities for container storage, steaming, washing, and maintenance.

### Strategic rationale
KAG CEO Charlie DeLacey described it as a key milestone that strengthened specialized chemical transportation and added ISO container storage, transport, and related services. MCT President Michael Anderson said the combination would give the company greater resources and know-how to expand footprint, capabilities, technology, and services.

Reporting noted that the acquisition was expected to form the foundation of a dedicated **KAG ISO Services platform**, with longer-term ambitions of growing toward a roughly 1,000-truck operation in that area. MCT was initially expected to continue operating under its own name before fuller integration into the KAG network, with management largely remaining in place and no major location closures anticipated.

In short, Liquid Solutions Tank Leasing came into KAG as part of this broader MC Tank package, which expanded KAG’s chemical tanker capacity while giving it a meaningful foothold in ISO tank services and related leasing/maintenance.

OUTRAGEOUS - GOVERNMENT THEFT: A TSA supervisor cleared grandfather Kermit Warren to fly with $28,000 in his bag. Then the DEA ROBBED him of every dollar.

His crime? Nothing.

The government calls it “civil forfeiture.” Everyone else calls it theft.

Kermit Warren flew to Ohio to buy a truck so he and his son could haul scrap metal for a living after losing their jobs during COVID.

The truck was too big for what they needed, so they headed home with the cash.

At the airport, he told TSA exactly what was in his bag. A supervisor said he could travel with it and waved him through security.

Then the DEA showed up.

Warren tried to show the agents the truck he’d flown in to buy. He offered to call the seller. They weren’t interested.

“We think y’all are up here doing something illegal.”

That’s it. That’s the evidence. A man’s life savings, gone on a hunch — and they wouldn’t even let him make a phone call to prove them wrong.

WARREN: “When they seized my life savings, every penny that I’ve worked for, every honest dollar that I earned over the last 25–30 years, it made me feel like I was the dirt on the ground.”

CONTEXT: Fortunately, the government didn’t get away with this one. After roughly a year without his savings, federal prosecutors agreed to return all $28,180 to Kermit Warren and dismissed the case.
