text:
The Children Who Say They’ve Been Here Before

An odd pattern in 1,678 reports of past lives, and an Indian philosopher who would probably have wondered what took everyone so long.

Imagine you’re making dinner when your three-year-old starts talking about the children they used to have.

You keep chopping. At this age, they also claim to be a horse.

But the conversation takes an uncomfortable turn. There was a house somewhere else. A husband. Someone they miss terribly. Your child seems upset that you don’t understand.

Then they tell you how they died.

There are plenty of sensible ways to respond to this. Children borrow things they’ve heard, misunderstand dreams and invent elaborate explanations for experiences they can’t yet put into words. Adults can make matters worse by asking leading questions. A family’s desire to believe can do a remarkable amount of work.

Still, some parents have gone looking for the people their children describe.

And sometimes they have found them.

The names, places and circumstances appear to belong to somebody who lived and died before the child was born. These are the cases that have kept researchers at the University of Virginia busy for decades, investigating a subject many academics would rather leave well alone.

Recently, three of those researchers decided to look at the dates.

Saeedeh Sadeghi, Marieta Pehlivanova and Philip Cozzolino examined 1,678 cases in which investigators had identified a deceased person whose life appeared to match the reported memories. They wanted to know whether the circumstances of that person’s death had any relationship to the interval before the child’s birth. Their 2026 study found an association: the more unexpected the death, the shorter that interval tended to be.

At one end, where death had been most anticipated, the median was roughly 21 months. At the other, where it had been least expected, it was about 12.

Nine months’ difference between two dates in apparently separate biographies.

The relationship survived the researchers’ attempts to account for several possible sources of bias. It was also stronger among families whose religions did not support reincarnation. The researchers themselves stopped short of concluding that rebirth was real. UVA’s account of the findings leaves the mechanism unresolved.

That last point matters. A pattern in a collection of unusual reports can have explanations that nobody has identified yet. The way cases are found, remembered and selected could influence the result.

Nevertheless, it is an oddly specific thing to turn up.

If these accounts are entirely the work of imagination, coincidence and human suggestion, why should the suddenness of somebody’s death have anything to do with the timing of a particular child’s birth?

P. R. Sarkar would have had plenty to say about that.

The Indian philosopher and spiritual teacher, known to his followers as Shrii Shrii Ánandamúrti, or Baba, had a formidable appetite for explaining things. His interests ran through meditation, economics, language, psychology and the workings of the universe. He was quite prepared to discuss subjects that most people keep in separate rooms.

Reincarnation, in his understanding, belonged among the ordinary processes of nature. Our difficulty in accepting it came partly from a mistaken idea about where the mind begins and ends.

In Cerebral and Extra-Cerebral Memory, he put it bluntly:

“The brain is nothing more than a worldly machine for mental recollection.”

That is a substantial demotion for an organ accustomed to getting credit for the whole of human existence.

Sarkar’s account gave the brain an essential role in the expression of the mind, while allowing the mind a life beyond that particular piece of equipment. Memories and impressions could exist at levels deeper than those available to everyday awareness.

The familiar radio analogy gives a rough sense of the proposal. Break the receiver and the room goes quiet. The silence tells you something has happened to the radio; it doesn’t tell you whether the broadcast has ended. As an illustration, it is useful. Establishing that a human mind actually works this way would be another matter.

In Sarkar’s philosophy, our actions leave consequences within us. He called their latent reactive potential saḿskáras. These help shape what we seek, how we respond and the experiences towards which we are drawn. Physical death, he taught, does not automatically exhaust them.

Something remains to find expression.

There is an everyday familiarity to that idea, even before reincarnation enters the picture. We carry unfinished conversations around for years. An old humiliation can still make us wince in the shower. We leave a relationship and discover, much later, how much of it came with us.

Sarkar extended this persistence beyond the body’s death. The mind, carrying its unresolved potential, could become associated with a new physical form.

We would arrive with a history, although usually without the means to read it.

This raises an obvious difficulty. If we have been here before, our powers of recollection are disappointingly poor.

Sarkar’s explanation centred on early childhood. A young child is only beginning to accumulate the experiences of the present life. Its demands have yet to occupy every corner of the mind. Under certain conditions, he suggested, impressions from an earlier existence can still reach awareness.

Then the new life takes over.

There is a language to learn, a family to understand, a whole world insisting on being noticed. Eventually there is school, friendship, embarrassment, the urgent business of belonging. Earlier impressions lose their hold.

That would account for a poignant feature of many reported cases: children who once spoke insistently about another life often grow less interested in it. The memories fade. Parents may still be wrestling with what happened long after the child has moved on.

For the adults, it remains the strangest thing they have ever heard.

For the child, there may now be a bicycle.

Sarkar used the term játismara for someone who remembers a previous birth. He also described conditions in which those memories might remain especially clear. In a 1978 discourse on extra-cerebral memory, he included people who had died in accidents.

Here the old teaching and the new research come close enough to make you pause.

They concern different things. Sarkar was discussing the persistence and clarity of memories; the UVA researchers were measuring the interval between a death and a later birth. Treating the study as confirmation of his explanation would stretch it considerably.

Yet both give sudden death a particular significance.

An anticipated death may allow time for a person to withdraw from the business of living. There can be farewells, arrangements, some recognition of what is happening. Even then, leaving is rarely simple.

An accident allows none of that.

A person goes out expecting to come home. There is food in the fridge, a message waiting for an answer, somebody they intend to call. In their own mind, life is still going somewhere.

We know how hard it can be to settle after a conversation ends badly. The mind goes on having it, supplying the answer that arrived too late. An abruptly interrupted life is that idea on an almost unbearable scale.

Within Sarkar’s account, those attachments and unexpressed impulses could outlast the body that had been giving them expression. It is possible to imagine them playing a part in a subsequent birth, or in the strength of what a child later appears to remember.

That is speculation. It is also a more compelling way into the subject than the usual vague assurance that everything happens for a reason. It suggests a process with its own conditions, one that might leave recognisable traces.

There is a further story about Sarkar that his followers have passed on. According to an oral recollection, he once told a small group that they need not spend too much effort convincing the world about reincarnation. Science would eventually establish it.

The exchange survives as a recollection rather than a documented passage from his published discourses, so the wording cannot be pinned down.

Even allowing for that, the confidence is striking.

He apparently felt no urgency to win the argument. Researchers could take their time. If rebirth was a natural phenomenon, careful investigation would eventually encounter it.

Of course, confidence has never been in short supply among spiritual teachers. What makes this particular claim worth considering is the possibility of putting some part of it within reach of investigation. Names can be checked. Dates can be compared. Statements recorded before two families meet can be distinguished from stories assembled afterwards.

Whatever the final explanation, there is work to do.

And the possibility itself has consequences that reach further than the pleasure of a good mystery.

Reincarnation is usually offered as a comfort: you get another chance; the people you love may not be lost forever. Anyone who has stood beside a hospital bed can understand the appeal.

But there is something unsettling in it too.

Suppose we carry the effects of our lives with us. Suppose the habits we cultivate and the harm we leave unresolved do not become irrelevant when the body stops. Then another life would come with responsibilities we might much prefer to forget.

Sarkar’s philosophy gave this long process a direction. Through successive experiences, the mind develops towards the realisation of its unity with Supreme Consciousness, Parama Puruśa. Repeated birth has a purpose, and ultimately an end.

This also helps explain his lack of enthusiasm for people becoming absorbed in their previous identities.

The prospect is irresistible, admittedly. Most of us would like a look at the records. There might be a fascinating explanation for an unreasonable fear, a peculiar talent or the feeling of recognising someone we have just met.

Or we might discover we spent three previous lives as farmers, complaining about the weather in every single one.

Either way, knowing who we once were would say little about what we should do this afternoon. A previous identity could become another possession to be proud of, another excuse, another way of avoiding the difficult business of changing.

Sarkar’s emphasis was on the life being lived now: spiritual practice, a broader sympathy for others, some effort to become less confined by oneself.

There is good sense in that, whatever happens after death. We already have enough trouble putting the lessons of this life to use.

Still, the children are hard to forget.

The compelling part is their apparent lack of interest in making a philosophical case. In these reports, a child may miss a particular person, insist on another name or become distressed by something the adults around them cannot explain. The grand implications belong mostly to everyone else.

We would like to know what the stories mean. We would like an answer large enough to settle our own fears.

The child may simply want to go home.

For now, there are records to examine, explanations to challenge and a curious relationship between two dates. Sarkar’s account offers one way of understanding what might lie behind them. Further research may lead somewhere quite different.

I keep coming back to that imagined conversation over dinner. The ordinary room, the parent with something on the stove, the sudden mention of a life nobody knew to ask about.

Before explaining it away, I’d want to hear the rest.

$NEE KEY READ-THROUGHS FROM NEXTERA ENERGY’S Q3 2026 EARNINGS CALL

NextEra’s October 21 call strengthens the investment case for power equipment, grid infrastructure, battery storage and selected natural gas assets, but provides a more qualified signal for utility shareholders and merchant generators. The central development is the conversion of electricity demand into funded infrastructure: approximately 16.5 GW of federal hub generation has definitive development agreements and $5.7 billion of initial funding, while quarterly storage origination reached 2.4 GW. The less obvious implication is that electricity demand growth does not translate uniformly into higher power prices or shareholder returns. Dedicated generation can limit merchant scarcity upside, customer protections can restrict utility economics, and storage procurement can temporarily displace solar procurement. The strongest company-specific implications concern Dominion’s regulatory process and Chesapeake Utilities’ directly identified pipeline partnership. Equipment and storage implications are broader demand signals, not confirmation of supplier awards. Most developments improve visibility into 2028-2032 activity rather than establish immediate earnings revisions.

UTILITY M&A AND REGULATION

MERGER APPROVAL AND MERGER VALUE ARE BECOMING DISTINCT RISKS (READ-THROUGH 1)

Affected company: Dominion Energy (D: United States). Directional impact: Negative for transaction certainty and potentially negative for the economics of an approved transaction. Magnitude: High event-driven significance; potentially material longer-term financial significance.

The call’s most actionable negative read-through was management’s inability to resolve the financial implications of Virginia’s proposed merger conditions. Steve Fleishman specifically challenged the governor’s “pretty onerous conditions” and staff proposals concerning ring-fencing. Ketchum emphasized affordability, employment and clean energy, but did not quantify acceptable concessions or identify conditions that would make the transaction uneconomic. His acknowledgment that there are “always opportunities for compromise on certain specific issues” preserves a negotiating path without demonstrating that the original economics survive.

The transmission mechanism extends beyond closing probability. Restrictions on dividends from Dominion Energy Virginia could constrain cash available to the parent. Additional bill credits would transfer value to customers. Longer employment protections could limit operating efficiencies. A lower regulated equity capitalization could reduce the equity investment earning an allowed return. These measures can weaken the financing and efficiency benefits underpinning the combined company’s 9%+ EPS growth framework even if regulators ultimately approve the transaction.

The October 19 SCC staff testimony makes the distinction particularly important: staff recommended denying the proposal as filed but identified conditions under which it would not oppose approval. Separately, the governor requested a 6-year residential base-rate freeze and larger customer rebates. These are proposals, not final rulings. The high-conviction conclusion is increased uncertainty around shareholder value capture, not certainty that the merger will fail.

Near-term trading catalysts are rebuttal testimony, the November Virginia hearing and the expected January 2027 order. Dominion’s fixed exchange-ratio consideration also links its transaction value to NextEra’s share price. The longer-duration issue is whether final conditions preserve incremental earnings and cash-flow benefits. The cross-sector signal is negative for assuming that utility consolidation automatically unlocks unrestricted financing synergies, although Virginia’s conditions should not be extrapolated mechanically to other jurisdictions.

NATURAL GAS INFRASTRUCTURE AND PRODUCTION

A DIRECTLY IDENTIFIED PIPELINE PARTNERSHIP PROVIDES CLEANER EXPOSURE THAN GENERAL DATA CENTER THEMES (READ-THROUGH 2)

Affected company: Chesapeake Utilities (CPK: United States). Directional impact: Positive. Magnitude: High strategic relevance to Chesapeake’s investment runway, but limited immediate operating earnings contribution.

NextEra disclosed a joint venture with Chesapeake Utilities to develop a $1.2 billion, 97-mile intrastate natural gas pipeline in South Florida. This is a direct counterparty relationship rather than an inferred beneficiary. Chesapeake’s September transaction announcement establishes that its subsidiary retains 51% ownership, NextEra acquires 49%, and Chesapeake’s Peninsula Pipeline subsidiary will construct, manage and operate the project.

The mechanism is a combination of retained infrastructure growth and shared funding responsibility. Chesapeake keeps control and the operating role while bringing in a partner with substantial development and financing capabilities. Its 51% interest corresponds to approximately $612 million of the announced gross project cost. That figure is not an equity funding requirement or an EPS estimate, since project financing and other terms determine the eventual shareholder investment.

The geographic signal is specific: South Florida’s gas delivery constraints create an infrastructure opportunity independent of whether every proposed data center is built. NextEra’s broader statement that gas transmission could expand beyond its existing expectations reinforces the relevance of transport capacity as generation development accelerates.

The partnership was announced before the earnings call, so this is confirmation rather than a new contract surprise. Chesapeake expects construction to begin in the first half of 2028 and service in 2030. Near-term catalysts are permitting, financing and project-budget updates. The fundamental benefit is longer-duration investment visibility, subject to construction costs and commercial terms. No immediate 2026 earnings uplift should be inferred.

NEW GAS GENERATION SUPPORTS APPALACHIAN DEMAND MORE DIRECTLY THAN A GENERIC NATIONAL GAS PRICE THESIS (READ-THROUGH 3)

Affected company: EQT Corporation (EQT: United States). Directional impact: Positive for longer-term regional demand and potential contracting opportunities. Magnitude: Moderate strategic relevance; no established near-term EPS impact.

NextEra has advanced more than 18 GW of gas-fired generation opportunities, including approximately 16.5 GW across federal hubs in Texas and Pennsylvania. Its previously announced Pennsylvania South Mon project represents approximately 4.3 GW. The relevant transmission mechanism for EQT is new demand near Appalachian production, potentially improving local gas market depth, supporting long-term sales arrangements and reducing reliance on distant demand centers.

The physical scale is meaningful. At an illustrative 75% utilization rate and a 7 MMBtu/MWh heat rate, 16.5 GW would consume approximately 2.0 Bcf/d. The 4.3 GW Pennsylvania project would consume approximately 0.53 Bcf/d under the same assumptions. These are operating sensitivities, not contracted demand forecasts. Utilization, efficiency, commissioning schedules and whether the load is genuinely incremental determine realized consumption.

The strongest inference is regional rather than an immediate increase in Henry Hub prices. Generation located near production can improve Appalachian demand without requiring every incremental molecule to travel to the Gulf Coast. Benefits to producer realizations nevertheless depend on gathering, transportation, basis and contract structure. NextEra did not identify EQT as a gas supplier, and no project-specific revenue should be assigned to it.

The near-term catalysts are binding power contracts, fuel supply agreements and pipeline arrangements. Physical demand is predominantly a 2028-2032 development. This is a positive fundamental read-through for Appalachian gas commercialization, not a catalyst for near-term production guidance or a quantified commodity price target.

POWER EQUIPMENT AND GRID CONSTRUCTION

CAPITAL-LIGHT GENERATION DEVELOPMENT CAN STILL BE CAPITAL-INTENSIVE FOR THE EQUIPMENT SUPPLY CHAIN (READ-THROUGH 4)

Affected companies: GE Vernova (GEV: United States); Siemens Energy (ENR: Germany). Directional impact: Positive for gas generation equipment and associated services. Magnitude: High relevance to the gas equipment businesses; company-specific order allocation remains unconfirmed.

NextEra’s federal hubs combine approximately 16.5 GW of generation, definitive development agreements and $5.7 billion of initial funding. Management expects initial service in 2028-2029 and a broader ramp through 2030-2032. Ketchum’s statement, “While we do not put any capital into the projects,” describes NextEra’s ownership economics, not an absence of equipment expenditure.

This distinction is important for equipment suppliers. Government-related project funding can support turbine deposits, generators, electrical systems and construction commitments without requiring equivalent investment on NextEra’s balance sheet. The financing structure may therefore improve the conversion of power demand into equipment procurement even when the developer is preserving its own capital.

GE Vernova has a previously announced gas generation development framework with NextEra, providing a verified commercial connection. The call did not identify turbine vendors for the federal hubs or establish that the earlier framework governs these projects. Siemens Energy benefits through the broader competitive market for large gas turbines, not through a disclosed award. Assigning all 16.5 GW to either supplier would be unsupported.

The near-term catalysts are reservation agreements, firm equipment orders, deposits and manufacturing-slot disclosures. Revenue and operating earnings would follow delivery and project milestones, while installed-base services extend the benefit beyond commissioning. The offset is that some equipment may already be reserved or included in supplier expectations. This is a strong demand-validation signal, not proof of an entirely incremental order cycle.

TRANSMISSION AND HARDENING HAVE MORE DURABLE DEMAND THAN ANY SINGLE GENERATION TECHNOLOGY (READ-THROUGH 5)

Affected companies: Quanta Services (PWR: United States); Hubbell (HUBB: United States). Directional impact: Positive. Magnitude: Moderate-to-high relevance to addressable demand; no specific contract or earnings increment established.

NextEra reported approximately 25% growth in regulated and invested transmission capital plus secured capital expenditures to $12.7 billion since December 2025. The call identified 2 large 765 kV transmission projects in Illinois and additional Texas transmission approvals. Separately, FPL reported that underground neighborhood lines performed approximately 14 times better than overhead lines during the hurricane, while smart-grid systems avoided approximately 140,000 outages.

These observations support 2 distinct demand streams. Regional transmission expansion requires engineering, construction, substations and high-voltage infrastructure, aligning with Quanta’s capabilities. Distribution hardening and undergrounding require connectors, protection products and other utility components, supporting Hubbell’s addressable market. No award to either company was disclosed.

The non-consensus implication is that grid investment is less dependent on which generation technology wins. Gas plants, nuclear restarts, renewables and storage all require electrical infrastructure, although their interconnection and network requirements differ. The storm-performance evidence also provides utilities with a tangible reliability argument for continued hardening expenditure, rather than relying solely on projected data center demand.

The $12.7 billion measure includes secured future spending and should not be treated as current construction revenue. Near-term catalysts are procurement decisions, notices to proceed and contractor backlog conversion. The fundamental demand extends through the end of the decade. Higher volumes do not guarantee higher margins: labor availability, fixed-price exposure and procurement execution remain important. For this reason, authorized projects are more valuable than unapproved investment plans.

BATTERY STORAGE AND SOLAR EQUIPMENT

STORAGE IS BECOMING AN INITIAL LOAD-SERVING SOLUTION, NOT JUST A RENEWABLES ADD-ON (READ-THROUGH 6)

Affected companies: Fluence Energy (FLNC: United States); Tesla (TSLA: United States). Directional impact: Positive for utility-scale storage demand. Magnitude: High business relevance for Fluence; meaningful to Tesla Energy but lower significance at the consolidated Tesla level.

NextEra originated 2.4 GW of battery storage during the quarter, approximately 65% of total renewables and storage additions. More importantly, FPL stated that serving its initial large-load additions primarily requires battery storage because existing gas and nuclear generation can provide the supporting energy. Management also identified a potential 6-11 GW of storage associated with federal hubs.

The transmission mechanism is broader than increasing renewable penetration. Batteries can address capacity, load shape and peak delivery constraints while existing generation supplies charging energy. This creates a procurement channel that need not wait for new solar or gas plants to reach service. Expanding existing projects from 4-hour to 8-hour duration creates another market for cells, integration and lifecycle services, although it increases energy capacity rather than necessarily increasing power capacity.

The federal hub opportunity is expressed on a 4-hour-equivalent basis, implying approximately 24-44 GWh of potential storage. That is meaningful addressable demand, but remains an opportunity rather than contracted supplier backlog. The call did not name Fluence or Tesla as vendors, and supplier selection, domestic-content requirements and pricing will determine who captures the economics.

Near-term catalysts are equipment awards and confirmation that storage origination converts into delivery schedules. The larger federal hub opportunity is predominantly a 2028-2032 development. The high-conviction positive is volume potential, not assured margin expansion. Competitive tenders, cell costs, warranties and performance guarantees can prevent supplier profits from growing proportionately with installed capacity.

STRONG AGGREGATE BACKLOG OBSCURES A WEAKER INTERMEDIATE-PERIOD SOLAR SIGNAL (READ-THROUGH 7)

Affected companies: Nextpower, formerly Nextracker (NXT: United States); Array Technologies (ARRY: United States). Directional impact: Modestly negative for expectations of synchronized near-term solar order acceleration. Magnitude: Low-to-moderate timing risk, not evidence of structural demand destruction.

Solar origination was approximately 0.6 GW in Q3, compared with approximately 0.9 GW in Q2, while storage origination increased. The accompanying development schedules show 2028-2029 solar backlog declining from 5.3 GW to 4.8 GW, approximately 9.4%, even as 2030-2032 solar backlog increased. Bolster explained that customers had been focused on capacity and that a shift back toward energy products was expected in coming quarters.

For tracker and utility-scale solar hardware suppliers, the relevant mechanism is procurement timing. Standalone batteries can address some immediate capacity requirements without creating a corresponding tracker order. Longer-dated solar additions also have a different revenue profile from near-term projects. Total renewable and storage GW therefore overstates the strength of the immediate solar-specific signal.

This is a sector read-through rather than evidence that NextEra canceled orders with either named supplier. The disclosed data do not identify the allocation between new projects, rescheduling and removals by supplier. They also do not establish near-term shipment reductions, since already contracted hardware can have different delivery schedules from newly originated power projects.

The near-term trading implication is caution toward extrapolating the 3.7 GW aggregate backlog addition into uniformly stronger solar equipment bookings. The fundamental effect depends on whether solar origination rebounds over subsequent quarters and intermediate-period projects convert. Management’s expectation of renewed energy procurement is a potential positive catalyst, but was not yet demonstrated in the quarter.

MERCHANT GENERATION AND NUCLEAR POWER

DEDICATED GENERATION LIMITS THE UPSIDE FROM DATA CENTER LOAD WITHOUT NECESSARILY LOWERING CURRENT POWER PRICES (READ-THROUGH 8)

Affected companies: Vistra (VST: United States); NRG Energy (NRG: United States). Directional impact: Negative for long-duration merchant scarcity upside, rather than an established reduction in near-term earnings. Magnitude: Moderate valuation sensitivity; limited immediate operating impact.

NextEra described federal hubs as “matching new electric load with new power generation.” It also expects substantial behind-the-meter generation and additional batteries, with initial service in 2028-2029 and full campus ramps through 2030-2032. These projects are not simply adding electricity demand to an unchanged generation fleet.

The transmission mechanism is the difference between gross load growth and net pressure on the existing system. Dedicated generation reduces the additional energy and capacity that new campuses must purchase from incumbent merchant generators. Batteries can further reduce exposure to high-price hours. In Texas, these effects can limit the scarcity rents available to uncontracted generation, particularly relative to forecasts that include new data center demand without the associated supply response.

This does not establish that the projects are net bearish for spot prices. New supply is largely paired with new load, grid exchanges may vary, and projects can suffer delays. Existing generators may also benefit from temporary supply arrangements, retail sales or their own dedicated-generation developments. NRG and Vistra should therefore be evaluated on their contracted development and retail capabilities as well as merchant exposure.

The near-term catalyst is disclosure of signed PPAs and credible commissioning schedules that change forward supply expectations. The principal fundamental effect is later in the decade. The actionable conclusion is to discount load-only scarcity models, not to assume an immediate reversal in current power-market tightness.

EXISTING NUCLEAR ASSETS HAVE A CLEARER COMMERCIAL PATH THAN NEW-BUILD NUCLEAR OPTIONS (READ-THROUGH 9)

Affected company: Constellation Energy (CEG: United States). Directional impact: Positive for the contractability and strategic value of existing nuclear generation. Magnitude: Moderate fundamental validation, without a disclosed basis for an immediate earnings revision.

NextEra executed a 20-year PPA for approximately 1 GW at Point Beach, extending contracted output into the 2050s. Bolster emphasized, “This is not an upgrade.” The transaction monetizes an existing facility’s output without requiring a new reactor to be constructed. That is the relevant positive precedent for Constellation’s operating nuclear portfolio.

The economic mechanism is reduced commercialization risk. Existing nuclear plants offer firm, carbon-free output with established sites, equipment and operating organizations. Long-duration PPAs can support reinvestment and reduce exposure to future merchant prices, while giving customers greater visibility over energy supply. The value is particularly relevant where customers need dependable energy rather than additional nameplate renewable capacity.

The conclusion should not be overstated. Point Beach’s PPA price was not disclosed, and management’s approximately $0.21 average EPS contribution is a total contribution under the new contract, not a disclosed incremental increase. The call does not establish that Constellation can obtain the same economics, or that all existing nuclear output remains available for repricing.

The contrast with new nuclear is nevertheless significant. Management requires structures that define the limit of shareholder capital exposure before pursuing new reactors. Existing nuclear contracting therefore has a clearer path to underwritable cash flows than uncontracted SMR opportunities. Near-term catalysts for Constellation are its own PPAs, customer commitments and licensing developments. The fundamental benefit extends into the 2030s and beyond.

CLOUD AND AI INFRASTRUCTURE

A SPECIFIC POWER SUPPLY MILESTONE IMPROVES ALPHABET’S IOWA EXECUTION VISIBILITY (READ-THROUGH 10)

Affected company: Alphabet (GOOGL: United States). Directional impact: Positive for regional infrastructure execution. Magnitude: Moderate significance to the relevant Iowa development program, but low near-term consolidated earnings significance.

NextEra confirmed that Duane Arnold remains on track to restart no later than Q1 2029 and that a Department of Energy loan of up to $1.9 billion closed during the quarter. The customer connection is independently established: the October 2025 NextEra-Google announcement included a 25-year agreement for power from the 615 MW facility to support Google’s Iowa cloud and AI infrastructure.

The transmission mechanism is reduced financing uncertainty around a specific contracted energy source. Access to additional firm, carbon-free electricity can improve the feasibility and sequencing of regional compute investment. The federal loan supports the generating project; it is not a grant to Alphabet, does not eliminate the PPA cost and does not prove that grid delivery or every data center development milestone is complete.

At an illustrative 90% capacity factor, the entire plant would generate approximately 4.85 TWh annually. Google is not entitled to all of that output: the original announcement also identified Central Iowa Power Cooperative as an offtaker. The positive implication is therefore improved visibility for an identified supply arrangement, not unrestricted access to the full plant or an immediate increase in cloud revenue.

The financing milestone predates the earnings call, making this a reaffirmation of progress rather than a new contract catalyst. The next relevant events are nuclear regulatory approvals, refurbishment progress and commissioning readiness. The longer-duration cross-portfolio implication is that contracted power arrangements can become a competitive advantage for compute developers in constrained locations. That advantage is specific to timing, geography and enforceable supply commitments, rather than a general benefit accruing equally to every hyperscaler.

text:
Mary Blair (1911–1978) was a pioneering American artist and designer whose vibrant, modernist color palettes revolutionized Walt Disney animation and mid-century design. Known for iconic concept art in films like Cinderella, Alice in Wonderland, and Peter Pan, she later created the beloved It's a Small World attraction.... 

Millions of people have stepped into Mary Blair's imagination without ever knowing her name. Hired by Walt Disney Studios in 1940, she initially worked on films like Dumbo and Saludos Amigos.

. . . . 

Born on October 21, 1911, Blair became one of the most influential artists in Disney history, although she never achieved the public recognition of the men whose films she helped bring to life.

When she joined Walt Disney's studio in 1940, American animation was still largely dominated by men. Blair had trained as a fine artist, but commercial illustration and animation offered opportunities that were difficult to find elsewhere.

Then, in 1941, everything changed.

Blair accompanied Walt Disney and other studio artists on a goodwill tour of Latin America. The brilliant colors, folk art and striking landscapes she encountered transformed her artistic vision.

Her paintings caught Disney's attention.

He recognized something extraordinary in her work: an ability to create entire worlds through unexpected colors, simplified shapes and compositions that seemed to defy conventional rules.

Blair became a major visual influence on *Cinderella* (1950), *Alice in Wonderland* (1951) and *Peter Pan* (1953).

Her concept paintings were dazzling, but not all of her ideas survived the journey to the screen. The studio's animators sometimes found her unconventional designs difficult to translate into moving images.

Still, Walt Disney remained one of her strongest admirers.

After leaving the studio in 1953, Blair built a successful career as a freelance illustrator, including creating illustrations for children's books.

Then Disney called on her again.

For the 1964 New York World's Fair, he wanted an attraction celebrating children from around the globe.

Blair developed the extraordinary visual world of *It's a Small World*, filling it with colorful buildings, playful geometric shapes and stylized landscapes.

The attraction later moved to Disneyland, where generations of visitors would experience her imagination firsthand.

She also created enormous murals, including the spectacular ceramic-tile installation at Disney's Contemporary Resort in Florida.

Mary Blair died in 1978, aged 66.

Today, her artwork is celebrated in museums, books and exhibitions, and her influence can still be seen throughout animation and design.

But her greatest legacy may be hiding in plain sight.

For decades, millions of children have walked through worlds she dreamed up, watched films she helped shape and remembered colors they couldn't quite explain.

They knew the magic.

They simply didn't know the woman who helped create it.

text:
Los Angeles Lakers vs Golden State Warriors — Dončić and the Lakers open against a thinned-out Warriors side

Preview · NBA · Regular season · Wednesday 21 October 2026

Opening night at https://t.co/AWpSLUuNVb Arena pits the side that finished fourth in the West against the one that finished tenth. The Lakers went 53-29 last season and reached the second round; Golden State went 37-45 and played no playoff games. The Warriors did win both pre-season meetings this month, but they arrive without Kristaps Porziņģis, Brandin Podziemski and Moses Moody, and Stephen Curry is doubtful with an ankle sprain. Lakers at medium confidence.

THE MATCHUP

Luka Dončić is the centre of everything for Los Angeles: 33.5 points, 8.3 assists and 7.7 rebounds a game in 64 games last season. Austin Reaves added 23.3 points in 51 games. Around them the roster looks different. Quentin Grimes, who averaged 13.4 for Philadelphia, is now in Los Angeles, as is Walker Kessler, whose 14.4 points and 10.8 rebounds came in only five games for Utah. Collin Sexton, 15.4 a game for Chicago, is doubtful with a calf problem.

Golden State lean on age and experience. Curry averaged 26.6 points in 43 games and Jimmy Butler 20 in 38. Porziņģis, 16.7 a game in 32 appearances, is out with illness. Podziemski played all 82 games and averaged 13.8, Moody 12.1; neither is available. Brandon Williams, 13 a game for Dallas, is now on the Warriors' roster, and Draymond Green still offers 5.5 assists a night.

FORM & CONTEXT

The Lakers closed the regular season 7-3 in their last ten, the Warriors 3-7. In the playoffs Los Angeles beat Houston 4-2 before Oklahoma City swept them 4-0. Last season's points differentials were +1.8 for the Lakers and -0.6 for Golden State.

Pre-season tells a different story. The Warriors went 4-2, beating the Lakers 124-98 at home on 7 October and 101-89 in Los Angeles on 14 October. The Lakers went 2-3 and lost 121-106 to Denver on Saturday. Everyone last played between 15 and 17 October, so rest is level.

The regular-season series went the Lakers' way. Golden State won 119-109 in Los Angeles on 22 October 2025; the Lakers then won 105-99 at home on 8 February, 129-101 at Chase Center on 1 March and 119-103 there on 10 April. The Lakers also list Cameron Carr and Adou Thiero as out.

THE DECIDING FACTOR

Depth and the venue. The Lakers were 28-13 at home last season; the Warriors were 15-26 on the road. With three rotation players missing and Curry uncertain, Golden State have fewer answers for Dončić than they had in the warm-up games.

THE CALL

The table, the late-season form, the head-to-head and the home record all lean towards Los Angeles. The pre-season results are the one thing pulling the other way.

Los Angeles Lakers to win, medium confidence.

🧵 6/6

When the Second World War ended, thousands of veterans returned to the United States, including the men of the 10th Mountain Division. Many had developed a lifelong appreciation for skiing, climbing and the mountains during their training at Camp Hale, and some decided to turn that experience into a new career.

Former mountain soldiers became instructors, resort developers, ski patrol leaders and pioneers of the American outdoor recreation industry. Veterans of the division helped establish or develop more than 60 ski areas across the country, contributing to the growth of destinations such as Vail, Aspen and Arapahoe Basin.

The same skills that had helped them survive the mountains of Italy were now being used to introduce Americans to winter sports. Men who had once trained to move silently through snow carrying rifles were teaching civilians how to ski, explore the mountains and enjoy the outdoors.

Camp Hale itself eventually closed as a military installation in 1965. Over time, many of its buildings disappeared, leaving behind foundations, roads and traces of the enormous wartime community that had once occupied the valley.

In October 2022, the United States designated the surrounding area as the Camp Hale Continental Divide National Monument, protecting the landscape and recognizing its importance to American military history.

Today, visitors to the Colorado Rockies can explore the same mountains where thousands of American soldiers trained before departing for Europe. The peaceful valley offers little indication of the military community that once stood there, or the young men who endured its freezing winters before facing German forces in Italy.

Camp Hale helped prepare soldiers for war, but its veterans also helped shape America's relationship with the mountains long after the fighting ended.

text:
Trump Destroyed All Our Futures!

WAIT, WHAT? Part Thirteen: Does Somebody Have a Crystal Ball?

I thought that last accusation was a doozy, but this one may just eclipse that one.

Apparently, Trump has managed to destroy something that hasn't even happened yet.

Now that's something!

I’ve been sitting here scratching my head wondering, how can two people look at the same president, hear the same words, watch the same actions, and see two completely different futures? Actually, I’ve been wondering about that for a long time now.

I look at Trump's vision for America and see hope. Others apparently see disaster.

I see a president who wants peace through strength. Others see someone looking for confrontation and war.

I see a vision of better health, prosperity, and opportunity. Others see policies they believe will harm our health, economy, and environment.

I see someone who wants fairness in women's sports, opportunities for women and minorities, and a country where people can succeed standing on their own two feet. Others see discrimination and hatred.

I see a president who wants America to succeed. A country that produces its own energy, protects its innovations, and can stand up to powerful nations like China. A country strong enough to cooperate with others without sacrificing its own interests.

And I want America to remain America. A nation governed by its Constitution, where freedom of speech, religion, and individual liberty are protected. Where neither political ideology nor religious doctrine takes precedence over our constitutional freedoms.

I don't want to see America abandon those principles in favor of socialism, communism, or religious authoritarianism. I don't want people coming here expecting America to abandon its laws and freedoms to accommodate the political or religious systems they left behind.

I want assimilation and peaceful coexistence, where we respect one another's right to live according to our beliefs without trampling on someone else's freedoms. And I believe Trump wants that, too.

Others look at some of those same goals and worry about isolationism, discrimination, and the erosion of democracy.

Same president. Same policies. Two completely different visions of America's future.

I believe Trump wants a brighter future for this country. I really do. I believe the direction he's trying to take us offers a path toward peace, prosperity, and renewed strength. And yes, I worry about what happens if we abandon the principles that made America successful in the first place.

But here's the thing.

What I believe about the future is still a belief. What someone else fears about the future is still a fear.

And what is fear anyway? It has various acronyms:

F.E.A.R. False Evidence Appearing Real
F.E.A.R. Fear Everything And Run
F.E.A.R. Face Everything And Rise

One is believing something without questioning it. One is running from what you believe. And one is facing it head-on.

Pick one.

We can examine policies, question decisions, and debate their likely consequences. We can look at what has happened and what might happen. But predictions aren't facts, fears aren't guarantees, and neither is optimism.

Still, I’ll choose optimism over fear every day.

I don't know exactly what America's future holds. Neither does Donald Trump. And neither does the person who created the meme that started this series. But I do know this:

Our future isn't something one president owns. It's something all of us have a hand in creating. I don’t believe it’s set in stone. I feel that life is fluid and you get out of it what you put into it, both physically and energetically. And I believe you receive what you dwell on. Whether that is positive or negative is up to you.

So instead of declaring the future is destroyed before it even gets here, shouldn't we be asking what we're doing to make it better?

The Scorpion and the Frog

A scorpion approached a frog who waited at the riverbank.
“Carry me across,” the scorpion said, “for I cannot swim.”

The frog eyed him with weary caution.
“You are a creature of the sting. If I take you upon my back, you will strike me. We will both drown.”

The scorpion replied with smooth logic.
“If I sting you in the water, I perish as well. It would be against nature and reason.”

The frog, persuaded by this argument, allowed the scorpion to climb aboard. He swam out, strong legs pushing through the current.

Halfway across, the sharp agony of a sting pierced his back. His muscles faltered. As both began to sink beneath the river’s surface, the frog gasped:

“You promised! Why would you do this?”

The scorpion’s voice held neither anger nor triumph, only a resigned truth.
“Silly frog! You knew I was a scorpion when you offered to ferry me across the river.”

They vanished into the cold deep together.

2026 MIDTERM ELECTION VOTER TURNOUT 

First Washington State ballot return statistics of 2026 general election show slight uptick in early voting compared to 2022

More than 337,000 Washington voters have already returned their ballots, putting early participation ahead of the last two midterms, with Jefferson County leading and King County lagging.

by Cascadia Advocate 
Oct. 21, 2026

Early ballot return statistics

The Secretary of State's office offers a data visualization to show ballot return statistics, built with Microsoft Power Bi. This is a capture of one of the November 2026 visualizations.

With the initial weekend of voting in the 2026 general election now behind us, the Secretary of State’s office has begun publishing its statewide ballot return statistics, keeping to its usual practice, and the data shows a slight uptick in early voting compared to the last midterm in 2022, but not as much as in 2024 or 2020.

With fourteen days to go until the election, 6.54% of Washington voters had returned ballots early, compared to 5.14% in 2022, the last comparable cycle. In absolute numbers, 337,155 ballots have come back so far, compared to 246,974 in 2022. That is a small but still noticeable uptick of voters heeding calls to vote early, and it’s also the highest percentage for a midterm in the last decade. As you can see from the table below, presidential cycles often have higher early voter turnout, with their higher stakes, increased media coverage, and greater awareness: 

The 2018 midterms started with Day ‑14 turnout of 4.94%, but eventually reached 71.83% at certification, which remains the modern record for a midterm cycle. So 6.54% is a promising beginning, but there’s a lot of unreturned ballots still out there. In 2022, total turnout only reached 63.82% across the state, which wasn’t atypical for a midterm, but was noticeably less than the turnout from four years prior. 

The turnout leader among the counties so far is Jefferson, with 19.87% in. 

Jefferson, which contains Port Townsend, is home to a number of retirees who take their civic obligations very seriously. It’s one of the state’s three most reliably blue bastions, along with King County and San Juan County. 

In second place is Thurston, home to the state capital of Olympia, a swing county that usually votes blue at the top of the ticket, with 16.67% of ballots in. 

After that is Lincoln, a very Republican county, at 15.21% in, and then Skagit, with 14.78% in, and then Kitsap, with 14.75% in, and then San Juan, with 13.24% in. 

Rounding out the counties that are already in the double digits are Asotin, Whitman, Snohomish, and Chelan. Snohomish’s inclusion in this list is surprising, because in recent years, its turnout has often lagged. This year, it’s off to a better start. Maybe all those charter amendments have piqued Snohomish voters’ interest. 

The same cannot be said of many rural counties. Turnout in Skamania, Pacific, Okanogan, Grays Harbor, Stevens, and Adams is nowhere near even 1%. Meanwhile, King County has managed only a wimpy 3.71%, and is doing worse than either Pierce (5.26%) or Yakima (5.16%) which are usually behind it. Clark County, which like Skamania and Pacific has a very hot congressional race, has turnout of just 2.81% so far.

Since the emergency period of the COVID-19 pandemic ended, lots of voters in King County have adopted the habit of voting at the very end, on either Election Day or the day before. It wouldn’t be surprising to see a huge influx of ballots coming in right before the drop boxes close. VOTER TURNOUT - 2026 MIDTERM ELECTION 

First Washington State ballot return statistics of 2026 general election show slight uptick in early voting compared to 2022

More than 337,000 Washington voters have already returned their ballots, putting early participation ahead of the last two midterms, with Jefferson County leading and King County lagging.

by Cascadia Advocate 
Oct. 21st, 2026

Early ballot return statistics

The Secretary of State's office offers a data visualization to show ballot return statistics, built with Microsoft Power Bi. This is a capture of one of the November 2026 visualizations.

text:
Mary Phagan Case in the Atlanta Constitution

Wyman F. Anderson: The Atlanta Policeman Who Helped Uncover the Evidence in the Mary Phagan Murder

His April 30, 1913, Coroner's Inquest Testimony, as Reported by The Atlanta Constitution, Compared With The Atlanta Journal and The Atlanta Georgian

The Policeman Who Answered Newt Lee's Telephone Call

In the early morning hours of Sunday, April 27, 1913, Atlanta police officer W. F. Anderson was working at police headquarters when a telephone call arrived shortly after 3 a.m. The caller was Newt Lee, the night watchman at the National Pencil Company factory, located at 37–39 South Forsyth Street in Atlanta. Lee reported finding the body of a young girl in the factory basement. He believed she had been murdered.

The dead girl was fourteen-year-old Mary Phagan, a factory worker who had visited the building the previous afternoon to collect $1.20 in wages. Anderson was among the first officers to reach the factory, enter the basement, and examine the body. His observations later became part of the prosecution's case against factory superintendent Leo M. Frank.

Three days later, on Wednesday, April 30, Anderson was the first witness called at the coroner's inquest. He described Lee's telephone call, the police response, Mary's body, the basement's poor lighting, and the attempts to contact Frank.

On Thursday, May 1, The Atlanta Constitution published his testimony under the heading "Newt Lee Tells His Story During Morning Session." The Atlanta Journal and Atlanta Georgian had published their accounts the previous day. The newspapers agreed on most of Anderson's important observations, although they sometimes differed over measurements and the location of evidence (AC, 1; AJ, 2; AG, 3).

Saturday, April 26: Mary Collects Her Wages

Mary Phagan visited the National Pencil Company around noon on Saturday, April 26, 1913. It was Confederate Memorial Day, a Georgia holiday, and fewer employees than usual were working.

Mary had been away from work because the metal department was short of materials. She went to Leo Frank's second-floor office to collect $1.20 in wages. Frank acknowledged paying her shortly after noon. Mary was not seen alive again in any account established at trial.

Newt Lee was the factory's night watchman. According to his testimony, Frank had instructed him to report at 4 p.m., two hours earlier than usual. When Lee arrived, Frank told him to leave and return at 6 p.m. Lee also claimed Frank appeared nervous and telephoned him later that evening to ask whether everything was all right.

These statements later became part of the prosecution's examination of Frank's conduct. Anderson had not witnessed these events. His involvement began the following morning (AC, 1; AJ, 2).

Sunday, April 27: Police Reach the Factory Within Minutes

After answering Lee's call, Anderson joined the responding officers, including Sergeants R. J. Brown and L. S. Dobbs. Former county policeman W. W. "Boots" Rogers drove them to the factory.

Anderson testified that the police arrived within about five minutes. Lee opened the building and directed them toward a trapdoor in the first floor. A ladder led into the basement, where Mary's body lay partly hidden behind a partition.

The basement was dark and cluttered with factory materials, rubbish, a boiler, and partitions. Anderson examined the scene before detectives, lawyers, and reporters began making repeated visits. His observations established what the officers found during their first examination (AJ, 2; BOE, 6).

The Constitution Reports What Anderson Saw

The Atlanta Constitution reported that Anderson found Mary's body lying face down, with her head pointing toward the front of the factory. Her clothing was damaged, a stocking was torn, and one shoe was missing. Twine and a strip of cloth believed to have been torn from her underskirt were tied tightly around her neck.

Her face was covered with dirt and grime. Anderson said the discoloration was so heavy that he could not immediately determine whether she was White or Black. The poor lighting made the examination difficult.

The Constitution also reported that the fastening on the rear basement door had been pulled loose. These observations helped establish the condition of the body and basement soon after the discovery (AC, 1).

The Journal Gives More Detail About Mary's Injuries

The Atlanta Journal published a longer description on Wednesday, April 30. Anderson described Mary's torn left stocking, bruised knee, missing shoe, and damaged underskirt. He also observed blood around her head and a bruise above and behind one ear.

The cord around her neck was approximately six or seven feet long. Another strip of cloth, apparently torn from her underskirt, was wrapped around her neck. Anderson reported dirt and sawdust in Mary's mouth and eyes.

The Journal also reported that Anderson had not noticed whether the body had been dragged across the basement floor. Other officers described what they believed were signs of dragging, but Anderson did not personally confirm this.

The Constitution and Journal agreed about the body's general condition. The Journal provided more detail about the injuries, clothing, and objects near Mary (AC, 1; AJ, 2).

The Georgian Describes the Basement

The Atlanta Georgian published its account on April 30 under the headline "Went Down Scuttle Hole on Ladder to Reach Body."

It reported that Mary's body lay near the end of a partition on the left side of the basement, approximately six feet from the outside wall. Her head pointed toward the front of the building. The newspaper also described a toilet near the boiler and rubbish scattered through the basement.

Anderson said he did not see the body until he was almost upon it. He described the torn stocking, damaged clothing, and dirt covering Mary's face.

The Georgian printed his initials as W. T. Anderson, while the Constitution, Journal, and official trial record used W. F. Anderson. The matching testimony indicates this was a newspaper error (AG, 3).

The First Major Contradiction: Was Mary's Body Face Up or Face Down?

One of the most important disagreements concerned the position of Mary's body.

Newt Lee testified that he found Mary lying face up, with her head pointing toward the rear of the factory. Anderson and the responding officers testified that they found her face down, with her head pointing toward the front.

The Atlanta Constitution made this difference a central part of its May 1 report. The Atlanta Journal also emphasized it. Lee insisted he had not moved the body and had not returned to the basement until the police arrived.

If Lee's account was correct, somebody would have had to change the body's position during his absence. Another possibility was that Lee had been mistaken.

The newspapers discussed the possibility that the murderer had remained hidden in the basement while Lee went upstairs to telephone the police. But no witness established that this happened.

Anderson's testimony was important because he personally observed how the police found Mary. He could describe the body's position when the officers arrived, although he could not explain Lee's conflicting account (AC, 1; AJ, 2).

The Second Contradiction: Could Lee See the Body With His Lantern?

Lee claimed he first saw Mary's body from approximately twenty to thirty feet away. Anderson examined the lantern and described it as old, dirty, and smoky.

The Atlanta Constitution reported that Dr. J. W. Hurt questioned Anderson about whether Lee could have seen a body from that distance.

Anderson answered:

"He could not."

He explained that the lantern provided useful light for only about twelve to fifteen feet. Sergeant Brown supported Anderson, saying even the officers' flashlights had difficulty illuminating the basement (AC, 1).

This raised a serious question. How could Lee recognize the victim from such a distance when the basement was so dark?

Lee claimed he recognized her partly by her straight brown hair. Anderson and Brown maintained that the poor lighting and dirt covering Mary's face made identification difficult.

The Journal and Georgian Report Different Distances

The Atlanta Journal added that a partition might have blocked the lantern's light from reaching Mary's body. Anderson believed this made Lee's account even harder to explain.

The Journal reported Anderson estimating the lantern's useful range at twelve to fifteen feet, matching the Constitution.

The Atlanta Georgian gave a slightly different estimate, reporting that Anderson could see only ten to twelve feet with Lee's lantern (AJ, 2; AG, 3).

All three newspapers agreed that the lantern was dim. The important question was whether Lee could clearly identify the body from the distance he claimed.

Lee disagreed with the officers. He insisted his lantern had been cleaned the previous Friday and was in good condition.

The Later Lantern Experiment at Frank's Trial

During Frank's trial in August, Anderson was questioned about an experiment conducted in the basement. Officers had placed a box covered with sacks where Mary's body had been found to determine whether it could be seen from Lee's position.

Anderson acknowledged that the outline of the object was visible. But he explained that seeing the bulk of something was different from identifying it as a human body.

This qualified his earlier testimony. Lee might have seen something on the basement floor without being able to identify it clearly.

The prosecution could question Lee's certainty, while the defense could argue that the experiment supported part of his story (AJ, 4; BOE, 6).

The Rear Basement Door Had Been Tampered With

Anderson examined the rear basement door and found that the staple securing it had been pulled loose.

The Atlanta Constitution mentioned the damaged fastening, while the Journal and Georgian described the door in greater detail. According to the Georgian, the door had a bar, a hasp, and a lock. Although closed when Anderson examined it, the staple had been pulled from its position.

This raised another question. Had somebody used the rear door to escape after the murder?

The door offered a way to leave without passing through the factory's main entrance. But Anderson had not seen anyone use it. He could describe the damaged fastening, but he could not establish who had opened the door or when (AC, 1; AG, 3).

The Notes and Pencil Found Near Mary's Body

Police found two handwritten notes near Mary's body. These later became some of the most disputed evidence in the trial.

The Atlanta Journal reported that Anderson remembered seeing a note written on yellow paper. He also described a pencil approximately five feet from the body and a nearby writing pad.

The Atlanta Georgian reported Anderson identifying one of the notes after several papers were shown to him. He said Sergeant Dobbs had picked up a note while Anderson was present.

Prosecutors later argued that Jim Conley wrote the notes at Leo Frank's direction to place suspicion on Newt Lee. The defense disputed Frank's involvement and argued that the notes pointed toward Conley himself.

Anderson did not claim to know who wrote the notes. His testimony helped establish what the officers found and where some of the objects were located (AJ, 2; AG, 3).

The Missing Shoe: Another Newspaper Disagreement

Mary was missing her left shoe when the officers examined her body. The newspapers agreed on that fact but differed about where the shoe was found.

The Atlanta Journal placed the left slipper near the elevator. The Atlanta Georgian placed it closer to Mary's body, on the right side in front of her.

This difference was important because the location of the shoe might help explain whether Mary had struggled or been moved after her death.

Neither report established when the shoe left her foot. The two accounts should be kept separate rather than choosing one location as certain (AJ, 2; AG, 3).

Was Mary's Body Still Warm?

The Atlanta Constitution reported that Anderson was recalled to the witness stand. He testified that Mary's body was still warm and that blood was flowing from some wounds.

The Atlanta Journal added that Anderson described the blood in Mary's hair as moist and said her legs were not stiff.

Sergeant Brown gave a different account. The Journal reported Brown describing the body as cold and somewhat stiff (AC, 1; AJ, 2).

These differences were important because investigators were trying to establish when Mary died. But the officers were describing what they observed, not giving a medical determination of the time of death. Their testimony needed to be compared with the doctors' findings.

Anderson Tries to Telephone Leo Frank

After discovering Mary's body, the officers tried to contact Leo Frank at his residence.

The Atlanta Constitution reported Sergeant Brown's testimony that the police informed the telephone operator a girl had been murdered and that reaching Frank was urgent. They received no answer.

The Journal also described the unsuccessful calls, while the Georgian reported Anderson contacting other company officials.

At Frank's trial, Anderson gave more precise times. He said he tried Frank at approximately 3:30 a.m. and continued calling for several minutes without an answer. He then contacted Herbert Haas and Sig Montag before trying Frank again around 4 a.m.

These calls helped establish the early police timeline. The prosecution could compare the times with other evidence concerning Frank's movements. But Anderson could not explain why Frank failed to answer (AC, 1; AJ, 4; BOE, 6).

April 30: Anderson Takes the Stand at the Coroner's Inquest

The coroner's jury had first gathered on Monday, April 28, to examine the body and factory. The hearing resumed on Wednesday, April 30, at police headquarters, with Anderson called as the first witness.

Coroner Paul Donehoo and the jurors heard Anderson describe Lee's call, the officers' arrival, the basement, Mary's body, and the damaged rear door.

The questioning brought out the two major problems with Lee's story. He said he found Mary face up, while the police found her face down. He also claimed to have recognized her from a distance Anderson believed was beyond the reach of his lantern.

The Constitution concentrated on these contradictions. The Journal printed more physical details and questioning, while the Georgian gave readers a clearer picture of the basement.

At this stage, investigators were still examining several possibilities. They had not yet established the complete prosecution case later presented against Frank.

May 8: The Coroner's Jury Orders Frank and Lee Held

The coroner's inquest continued through Thursday, May 8, 1913. After hearing the evidence, the jury ordered Leo Frank and Newt Lee held for further investigation in connection with Mary's murder.

Anderson's testimony helped establish the condition of the body, the basement, the lighting, and the first police response. But investigators still needed to determine what happened after Mary collected her wages, who wrote the notes, and how her body reached the basement.

The Fulton County grand jury later indicted Frank on Saturday, May 24. Lee was not tried for Mary's murder (AC, 7).

August 1913: Anderson Returns as a Prosecution Witness

Anderson testified again during Frank's murder trial, which began Monday, July 28. The Atlanta Constitution reported his testimony on Saturday, August 2, under the heading "Policeman W. F. Anderson Tells of Newt Lee's Telephone Call."

He repeated his account of receiving Lee's call, going to the factory, examining the basement, and trying to reach Frank.

The Constitution covered his account of the police response and telephone calls. The Atlanta Journal gave more attention to the lantern and the experiment conducted in the basement.

The official Brief of Evidence also recorded Anderson describing tracks extending from the area near Mary's body toward the shaving room, along with the pencil and rubbish found near the boiler.

His testimony helped the prosecution return the jury's attention to the first hours of the investigation and what police found when they entered the basement (AC, 5; AJ, 4; BOE, 6).

How Anderson's Testimony Helped the Prosecution Against Frank

Anderson was an important witness because he examined the basement soon after Mary's body was discovered. He described where she lay, the condition of her clothing, the cord around her neck, and the poor lighting.

He also testified about the rear door, the objects found near the body, and the telephone calls made after the discovery.

His statements about the lantern and the body's position raised questions about Lee's original account. Investigators had to decide how much of Lee's description they could rely upon when reconstructing what happened.

Anderson did not witness the murder or claim to have seen Frank commit a crime. His evidence helped establish the condition of the scene and the police timeline.

The prosecution's case depended on combining those observations with other evidence, including the testimony of factory employees, the findings on the second floor, and Jim Conley's account.

Anderson provided an early description of the physical scene, which prosecutors and defense attorneys had to explain during the trial.

Comparing the Constitution, Journal, and Georgian

The Atlanta Constitution concentrated on the disagreement between Lee and the responding officers. Its May 1 report emphasized the body's position, the weak lantern, the damaged rear door, and the unsuccessful attempts to contact Frank.

The Atlanta Journal provided more detail about Mary's injuries, the cord around her neck, the pencil and writing pad, and the basement's interior. It also described the partition that might have blocked Lee's lantern.

The Atlanta Georgian provided a fuller description of the basement, including the partition, boiler, toilet, and body's location. It reported a slightly shorter range for the lantern and placed the missing shoe closer to Mary than the Journal did.

Despite those differences, the three newspapers agreed on the major facts. Anderson answered Lee's call, went to the factory, found the body lying face down, and described a poorly lighted basement. They also reported questions about Lee's account of the discovery (AC, 1; AJ, 2; AG, 3).

Why Wyman F. Anderson Deserves More Attention

Wyman F. Anderson rarely receives much attention in modern discussions of the Mary Phagan murder. Most accounts concentrate on Leo Frank, Jim Conley, Newt Lee, and the detectives who later investigated the case.

But Anderson was there during the first police response. He entered the basement shortly after Lee called police headquarters and examined the scene while the investigation was just beginning.

His testimony raised some of the earliest questions about Lee's story. Why did Lee say the body was face up when the officers found it face down? How much could he see with his lantern? Why was the rear door unsecured? And what could the objects near Mary's body tell investigators?

Anderson could not answer every question. But his observations gave the prosecution and defense facts they had to consider when reconstructing what happened inside the factory.

The Atlanta Constitution's May 1, 1913, report remains an important record of his testimony. The Atlanta Journal and Atlanta Georgian provide additional details, while the later trial record shows how his observations were examined in court.

More than a century later, Anderson's testimony is still worth reading because he was among the first police officers to examine Mary's body. His observations help explain what investigators found and how that evidence became part of the prosecution's case against Leo Frank.

text:
On the morning of September 4, 1991, Kenny Rogers stood inside the intensive care unit at Vanderbilt University Medical Center in Nashville, moments before Dottie West was wheeled in for her third emergency operation. The severe internal trauma from her car crash five days earlier had left the 58-year-old artist in a deep coma, with medical staff noting a near-total loss of natural reflexes.

Refusing to let clinical silence define their final moment, Rogers took her hand at the bedside. Speaking softly to the partner with whom he had shared some of country music's biggest stages, he offered a quiet promise: if she pulled through, they would go back into the studio and cut one more duet together.

As he finished speaking, Rogers felt West’s fingers tighten faintly around his own. It was a fleeting, instinctive response against overwhelming odds, a fragile spark of life from a woman who had spent decades singing through every hardship she ever faced.

The hope proved painfully brief. Shortly after West was taken into surgery, doctors were unable to stabilize her condition, and she passed away on the operating table at 9:43 a.m.

The promised duet was never recorded, leaving an enduring ache in Rogers’s life long after the hospital rooms emptied. Yet that final, quiet gesture on a Nashville morning remained the truest measure of their bond, proving that before the curtain closed, Dottie West heard the voice of her dearest friend one last time.

Archival accounts of Kenny Rogers speaking on those final hospital hours and their studio years together are gathered below.
