text:
The Israeli Private Eye at the Heart of a Climate Hacking Scandal

Listen · 12:01 min
14OCT2026
By Karen Zraick and Gabby Sobelman
NYT Gift Article link
https://t.co/FIPCnUx7Jq
Karen Zraick reported from New York City and Gabby Sobelman from Haifa, Jerusalem and Tel Aviv.  This article is based on decades of court documents, business filings and interviews. 

He’s been linked to someone called “The Hawk.” He named his company “This Isn’t a Dentist’s Office.” The feds say he hacked American environmentalists.

For decades, an Israeli private investigator named Amit Forlit has operated on the edges of international intrigue while rubbing elbows with powerful figures.

Mr. Forlit claims to have served in Shin Bet, Israel’s internal security agency. He dated a prominent Israeli businesswoman and social-media figure who photographed him at exclusive parties. And he may or may not have inspired a hacker-for-hire character in a 2022 novel about murky financial shenanigans involving Argentine debt.

These were mostly bit parts in other people’s dramas. Until now.

Today Mr. Forlit, wearing an ankle monitor while remaining in the New York City area, awaits trial in a globe-spanning hacking case where he is the central character. Prosecutors with the Justice Department have charged him with overseeing an operation that aimed to discredit American environmentalists, allegedly on behalf of a huge oil company. He has pleaded not guilty.

Mr. Forlit could face decades in prison.

The charges, filed in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York, allege a “sprawling criminal enterprise” in which Mr. Forlit and his associates hired hackers in India to gain unauthorized access to the environmentalists’ private email accounts. Mr. Forlit’s lawyers have identified the oil company described in the allegations as Exxon Mobil, and the commissioning firm as DCI Group, a Washington public relations and lobbying firm.

Exxon and DCI have denied any role.

In a statement, Exxon said the company had “not been involved in, nor are we aware of, any hacking activities. If there was any hacking involved, we condemn it in the strongest possible terms.”

A spokesman for DCI, Craig Stevens, said the Justice Department had confirmed to DCI’s lawyers that it was “not investigating our firm or any of our employees” last year. “We direct all our employees and consultants to comply with the law, and allegations of DCI Group’s involvement with this activity, alleged to have occurred more than a decade ago, are false and unsubstantiated,” he said.

The case puts Mr. Forlit at the center of some of the most consequential legal battles the fossil fuel industry has faced. Dozens of states and cities are suing oil companies, including Exxon, claiming among other things that the industry misled Americans for decades about the climate and health damage caused by the burning of fossil fuels. If successful, the claims could cost the industry billions of dollars.

Prosecutors allege Mr. Forlit was part of an effort to stymie or kill these court cases.

Mr. Forlit, 58, was extradited to New York City from London this year. At a hearing in April in a Lower Manhattan courthouse, he cut an unassuming figure: tall with close-cropped, graying hair, wearing a short-sleeved blue button-down and spectacles. He ducked down to confer with his lawyer, Sabrina Shroff, who had recently made headlines for winning the acquittal of a man for throwing a sandwich at a federal officer in Washington.

Through Ms. Shroff and his Israeli company, the private-investigation firm Gadot Information Services, Mr. Forlit declined to speak to a reporter and Ms. Shroff declined to respond to a list of detailed questions.

This account of his career is based on decades of court documents in Israel and the United States as well as news reports, business documents, social media activity and interviews.

Mr. Forlit hails from the coastal city of Haifa, an important node in Israel’s vibrant tech industry. As a young man he served in the Shin Bet, the internal intelligence agency, from 1990 to 1997, according to a document from his legal team in the extradition proceeding, where he used the nickname Omer.

Mr. Forlit’s parents didn’t respond to requests for comment.

Many former intelligence agents become private investigators, and Mr. Forlit founded Gadot Information Services in Tel Aviv and Haifa in the 1990s. The company later opened two offices near Miami, according to Florida business records. At one point, he changed the names of both Miami offices to phrases in Hebrew that translate as “This Isn’t a Dentist’s Office” and “This Isn’t a Dentist’s Office Either.”

The firm offered “physical and electronic” security services and carried out asset tracing, litigation support and surveillance, and its clients included “top-tier law firms, lobbying companies and hedge funds,” according to a defense document filed in Britain.

Over the years, Mr. Forlit’s name popped up in a grab bag of news reports related to his career as a professional sleuth.

In 2012, an aspiring actress was quoted in a prominent Israeli daily saying Mr. Forlit had occasionally hired her to pretend to be a clubgoer in Tel Aviv nightspots to conduct surveillance of revelers of interest. In 2017, he was named in the Financial Times, the British business newspaper, as having played a role in tracking a businessman who had reportedly fled Kazakhstan.

Mr. Forlit had other business interests, commercial and legal records show. He was one of several parties involved in litigation around 2013 involving an allegedly faulty rocket-shaped amusement park ride and a 3-D goggle device at “Mini Israel,” one of Israel’s flagship theme parks, according to Israeli court records.

But by then, Mr. Forlit had begun leveling up.

Around 2008, he was introduced to a British private investigator who became a collaborator on international projects, according to a deposition in a U.S. lawsuit by Farhad Azima, an aviation executive who had accused Mr. Forlit of hacking in a civil case unrelated to Exxon. (The suit was later dismissed. Mr. Azima did not respond to a request for comment.)

Around 2015, Mr. Forlit was also hired for a project related to the Argentine debt crisis, according to the U.S. extradition request. The Wall Street Journal has reported that a novel about Argentine debt-recovery efforts, “Undermoney,” included a character that may have been based on Mr. Forlit.

Mr. Forlit started moving in elite circles in his private life. He dated Racheli Yifrach, a high-profile Israeli real estate agent, for about five years starting around 2015. Their outings included attending President Trump’s first inauguration, she said in a recent telephone interview.

In the interview, Ms. Yifrach described Mr. Forlit as “the smartest person I’ve ever met.” He “showed me the world,” she said.

Mr. Forlit, she said, enjoyed spy stories and thrillers, is a Bob Dylan fan and was great with children, including four of his own. In 2018, she said, she threw him a James Bond-themed party for his 51st birthday. Videos posted online show the couple celebrating with his friends and relatives.

The current indictment against Mr. Forlit was unsealed after he was extradited in April. It alleged that Mr. Forlit was hired in an effort to thwart the burgeoning field of climate change litigation in late 2015.

That same year, reporting published by the Los Angeles Times and Inside Climate News had detailed how Exxon and industry groups possessed in-depth knowledge of the dangers of global warming resulting from the burning of fossil fuels, but had publicly raised doubts about climate science and tried to block action on global warming.

That reporting was partly funded by the Rockefeller Family Fund, a philanthropic group run by the heirs of Standard Oil that focuses on climate change, among other issues. Lee Wasserman, who runs the fund, said in an interview that he received a notice from prosecutors that he was among those targeted by the hackers. The Rockefeller fund has also helped finance litigation against energy companies.

Mr. Forlit’s project was allegedly nicknamed “Fox Hunt” and involved sending a list of targets to a hacking group in India that used a technique known as “spear fishing.” The group sent emails to targets designed to get them to click and give up sensitive information like passwords, according to the extradition request.

The passwords were used to obtain nonpublic documents “which were provided to the oil and gas company and published as part of a media campaign to undermine the integrity of the civil investigations,” according to the extradition request, and used by the oil company in litigation.

The Rockefeller Family Fund had hosted a private meeting of climate activists in early 2016 to discuss strategy. An email containing a draft agenda for the meeting was leaked to the conservative website The Washington Free Beacon. The email was later used in climate litigation, including a petition to the Supreme Court.

Mr. Wasserman said the meeting was misconstrued in the reporting, which labeled it a “secret coordination effort” against Exxon.

Prosecutors said Mr. Forlit worked with another Israeli private investigator, Aviram Azari, who went by moniker “The Hawk.” Mr. Azari would later plead guilty to hacking charges in Manhattan, and served prison time before returning to Israel. Mr. Azari could not be reached for comment by phone or through the lawyer who had represented him.

Mr. Forlit orchestrated hacking crimes against more than 100 individuals, organizations and companies, according to the extradition request, and stole confidential business and personal information. According to the indictment, Mr. Forlit and others “generated tens of millions of dollars in unlawful proceeds” from their activities.

Jennifer Cunningham, a political consultant formerly of the firm SKDK who was once married to the former New York attorney general Eric Schneiderman, said she was also a victim of Mr. Forlit’s alleged hacking. Mr. Schneiderman’s successor, Barbara Underwood, sued Exxon in 2018, alleging the company had defrauded shareholders by downplaying climate risks, after a three-year investigation. Exxon had also sued to try to stop the investigation; New York’s lawsuit was later dismissed by a judge. Ms. Cunningham was an adviser to Mr. Schneiderman but had no formal involvement with climate litigation.

“I was furious,” to learn of the hacking from prosecutors, she said.

In a British court filing, Mr. Forlit had unsuccessfully argued that his extradition to the United States should be blocked because it was politically motivated. His lawyers called the prosecution “but one piece within a complex matrix of ongoing litigation on climate issues in the United States, which can only sensibly be seen as politically motivated, in the sense of being brought to pursue and further specific political agendas.”

Last month, Ms. Shroff asked for an extension to file pretrial motions, such as a motion to dismiss the case, because of the enormous quantity of data prosecutors were referencing — about four million pages, she wrote in a letter to Judge Jesse M. Furman. 

She was further hindered by Mr. Forlit’s limited abilities in reading English, she wrote.

The new deadline for defense motions is Nov. 10, and the next hearing is scheduled for Dec. 10.
Corrected on 
Oct. 14, 2026
:

text:
Areli Barrera Grodski and Leon Grodski Barrera started Cocoa Cinnamon in December 2010 on a sleepless night in Areli’s mom’s kitchen. In 2011, with help from friends, they scrounged together enough money to build a coffee bike and used it to connect deeply with their Durham, North Carolina, community. More than 1,000 community members helped them open their first shop in January 2013.

Cocoa Cinnamon’s name, designs and “wonder menus” pay homage to the early intermingling of coffee and spice, built around coffee, chocolate, tea and spice. The business offers coffees at different price points while keeping a constant commitment to paying producers fairly, and helping customers connect what they pay to the livelihoods of coffee growers is an ongoing part of its work. It has grown from a bike to three locations tied to Durham neighborhoods and is finishing a move into a new roastery for Little Waves Coffee Roasters, its roasting side.

For Areli and Leon, being a mom and pop shop means starting with nothing and building something deeply embedded in a place with love, vision, family and community. Their advice: start with a vision, write it down quickly and only do it if a little part of you would die if you didn’t.

text:
Scientists successfully converted fast-growing bamboo into a viable oil that could power vehicles – and at an estimated cost of just $2.75 per gallon.

Researchers at Worcester Polytechnic Institute in Massachusetts have unlocked a promising alternative to traditional petroleum by turning fast-growing bamboo into renewable biocrude oil. 

Utilizing hydrothermal liquefaction—a process combining heat, high pressure, and water—the team heated bamboo to 572°F (300°C) for just ten minutes without adding chemical catalysts. In laboratory trials, over 35 percent of the plant's mass converted into an oil-like crude that can be further refined into usable fuel for vehicles, planes, and trains.

Beyond its high yield, bamboo offers major economic and environmental advantages over traditional biofuel feedstocks like corn. Techno-economic projections suggest bamboo-based fuel could achieve a mature commercial production cost of roughly $2.75 per gasoline-gallon equivalent. 

Because bamboo grows rapidly in poor soil without displacing food crops, it dramatically reduces carbon emissions—generating up to 26 times fewer greenhouse gases than conventional diesel while requiring only a fraction of the land used by existing ethanol crops.

source: Woodard, T., Cai, C., Walters, J., & Timko, M. (2026). Bamboo-derived biocrude as a sustainable transportation fuel. Sustainable Energy & Fuels.

text:
FULL TIME: Bayern Munich 2–2 @Arsenal 

Arsenal leave the Allianz Arena with a point after a resilient comeback, with Declan Rice rescuing a draw against Bayern Munich in a Champions League contest that demanded composure, character and a little help from the bench.

Eberechi Eze gave Arsenal the lead in the first half after Bukayo Saka was forced off through injury. 

Martin Ødegaard's excellent pass released Eze, who finished confidently to put the visitors ahead. 

Bayern responded through Alphonso Davies, who finished after Harry Kane picked him out with a superb pass.

The second half brought more pressure from Bayern. Manuel Neuer denied Bruno Guimarães with an outstanding save, before Kane converted a penalty following a handball by Jurrien Timber to put the hosts 2–1 ahead.

Arsenal needed a response, and Mikel Arteta turned to his bench. 

Viktor Gyökeres and Myles Lewis-Skelly came on as the Gunners searched for a way back into the game.

Gyökeres made his presence felt. 

In the 82nd minute, he laid the ball into Rice's path, and the midfielder fired home to level the score at 2–2. It was a decisive contribution from the striker, even if the goal itself belonged to Rice.

Arsenal still had work to do defensively, but they held on to secure a valuable draw away from home.

The result will feel like an opportunity gained and two points left behind. 

Bayern had spells of real pressure, especially after taking the lead, but Arsenal showed enough resilience to avoid leaving Munich empty-handed.

And for anyone questioning Gyökeres' influence, the equaliser offered a useful reminder: a striker's contribution does not begin and end with the finish. Sometimes, the pass before the goal matters just as much. #COYG

text:
Mr. Hassan used to drive a taxi for forty years. Now he lived alone. Every morning he walked to the market for fresh bread because the quiet house felt too heavy. He carried a plastic bag and a walking stick. He did not talk much to strangers. He simply moved through the day the way he always had since his wife died.

He was on the same broken bus that morning. When the rain grew heavier he opened his large umbrella and held it over the young woman and the small boy without saying a word. It was a small thing, but it was what he could do.

The three of them stood under the shelter together. The night worker shared the dry part of his jacket so the boy could sit. The old man kept the umbrella steady. The mother thanked them both in a quiet voice. When the next bus finally came they sat near one another. The boy fell asleep on his mother’s shoulder. Mr. Hassan offered a piece of bread. Rosa took a small bite and smiled for the first time that morning.

After that day their paths kept crossing on the early bus. They did not become close friends who called each other every evening. They simply saved seats, shared short talks about the weather and the price of milk, and watched the boy’s drawings improve week by week.

When the boy later fell ill and Rosa had to miss work, the night worker left a simple puzzle book with the bus driver for her. Mr. Hassan brought medicine and oranges. A few days later Rosa brought them both a container of rice and beans she had cooked.

Winter slowly turned to spring, the bus still broke down now and then, the three of them still shared the quiet seats and the umbrella when it rained. Three separate lives, the tired night worker, the struggling mother, and the lonely old man, had found a small, steady place where they met. 

It was not dramatic, it was simply enough.

Season 1, Episode 8
Original Airdate: November 16, 1984
Director: Georg Stanford Brown
Writers: Philip Reed & Joel Surnow

Welcome back to The Vice Files, pal!

Fast boats, expensive suits, beautiful women, high-stakes gambling, and a drug-smuggling operation hidden behind Miami’s glamorous waterfront lifestyle.

This is Miami Vice at full throttle!

This episode takes Crockett and Tubbs into the world of offshore powerboat racing, where a wealthy businessman has devised an ingenious way to transport narcotics into Miami.

But behind the champagne and excitement, a murder investigation is unfolding.

And Ricardo Tubbs is about to learn that mixing business with pleasure can have devastating consequences.

THE STORY

The episode opens with Crockett and Tubbs pursuing a bank robber through downtown Miami.

The suspect turns out to be Isadore “Izzy” Moreno, played by Martin Ferrero.

Facing arrest, Izzy offers information about a suspected drug smuggler named Louis McCarthy.

Played by William Gray Espy, McCarthy is a wealthy businessman and competitive powerboat racer.

The Vice squad suspects that McCarthy is using his racing activities to smuggle drugs into Miami.

But they haven’t figured out how.

Crockett and Tubbs decide to investigate.

ENTER SONNY BURNETT AND RICHARD TAYLOR

Using their undercover identities, Crockett and Tubbs approach McCarthy through his passion for offshore racing.

McCarthy is organizing an exclusive race from Miami to Bimini and back.

The detectives want to enter, but McCarthy refuses.

Meanwhile, they encounter Dale Gifford, an accountant connected to McCarthy who is also a police informant.

Gifford’s financial information raises questions about suspicious transactions involving McCarthy’s girlfriend, Vanessa.

Played by Maria McDonald, Vanessa manages an upscale men’s clothing store owned by McCarthy.

When Tubbs meets Vanessa, an immediate attraction develops.

Rico sees an opportunity to get closer to McCarthy’s operation.

But Crockett worries that his partner is becoming too personally involved.

THE HIGH-STAKES GAMBLE

McCarthy invites the detectives to an extravagant party at his waterfront residence.

The evening features wealthy guests, music, dancing, and champagne.

Before joining the party, Crockett and Tubbs search McCarthy’s boat for hidden compartments but find nothing.

Later, Crockett discovers McCarthy winning games of pool against his guests.

Sonny sees an opportunity.

He challenges McCarthy to a wager.

If Crockett wins, he gets a place in the upcoming powerboat race.

If McCarthy wins, he gets Sonny’s Ferrari Daytona.

It’s an enormous gamble.

But Crockett knows exactly what he’s doing.

With Lindsey Buckingham’s “Go Insane” accompanying the scene, Sonny dominates the game and wins.

The detectives finally have their opportunity to enter the race.

Meanwhile, Tubbs and Vanessa continue growing closer.

But the evening takes a deadly turn.

MURDER AT THE PARTY

Dale Gifford is discovered dead in the water near McCarthy’s residence.

The accountant has been murdered.

The investigation now involves more than drug smuggling.

Crockett suspects Gifford’s death may be connected to McCarthy’s financial dealings and Vanessa.

But Tubbs, increasingly attracted to Vanessa, is reluctant to believe she could be involved.

The detectives have another mystery to solve.

First, however, they must find a way to participate in the race.

CONTINUED IN PART 2… 🌴

text:
On March 17, 2008, a journeyman center walked onto an NBA floor for the Cleveland Cavaliers.

He became the first legally deaf player in the history of the league.

Almost nobody noticed. He played three games.

Lance Allred was born in 1981 in Pinesdale, Montana, inside a fundamentalist Mormon polygamist community. His grandfather was a prophet of the group. Complications at birth left him with 75 to 80% hearing loss, which is the clinical way of saying he has spent his whole life reading rooms rather than hearing them.

His family left for Salt Lake City when he was seven.

He was good early. Gatorade Player of the Year in Utah in 1999 out of East High School. He went to the University of Utah, played 17 games as a freshman, then transferred to Weber State, where as a senior he averaged 17.7 points and 12.0 rebounds a game.

Then he went undrafted in 2005, and here is where the story actually starts.

France. Spain. Italy. New Zealand. Japan. Mexico. Qatar. Puerto Rico. The Idaho Stampede in the NBA development league. For three years Lance Allred played professional basketball in whatever country would have him, on whatever contract was available, as a deaf man learning to pick up plays in languages he could not hear in gyms with terrible acoustics.

On March 13, 2008, the Cleveland Cavaliers signed him to a ten day contract.

Ten days. That was the whole offer.

He debuted four days later. The Cavaliers kept him for the rest of the season. He appeared in three games and averaged 3.3 minutes, 1.0 point and 0.3 rebounds, and he walked into a locker room that belonged to LeBron James, and he was released before the next season started.

Those are the numbers. They are terrible. They are also completely beside the point, because the record does not say how many minutes the first legally deaf player in NBA history played. It says that he played.

He later wrote a book about it called Longshot, which is the correct title. He has written several more since, and he built a second life speaking to rooms about the one he came from. One of those books is about the TEDx talk he gave, which he called What is Your Polygamy.

The honest counterpoint. This was not a career. Three games, one point a night, gone by autumn. Allred was also a Gatorade Player of the Year and a dominant college big man, not some stranger off a playground, and plenty of hearing players with better numbers never got ten days either. The NBA did not open a door for him so much as leave one unlocked for a few weeks in March.

But a kid born in a Montana commune who could not hear the whistle spent three years circling the planet for those few weeks.

And he took them.

text:
The Christmas poinsettia is named for the man who owned her father.

Joel Poinsett was a South Carolina congressman, a United States ambassador to Mexico and a secretary of war, and the red plant he shipped home still turns up in American living rooms every December. On his plantation near Georgetown there was an enslaved boy called Peter Poinsette, who carried the family's surname. Peter's daughter was born in Charleston on May 3, 1898, and her parents named her Septima.

Peter Poinsette's work on that plantation was the school run. Every morning he took his enslaver's stepchildren to their lessons, and every afternoon he brought them home again. He waited outside with the horse until they came out.

I put a lot of effort into researching and sharing stories that matter. If you'd like to support the work, here's the link:
https://t.co/AeER0VXcAK
Every coffee helps me keep creating .

He never went in.

He did not learn to read or write there either, and his daughter said in an interview many years later that it did not seem to bother him.

Clark taught for forty years in South Carolina schools. She spent most of the rest of her life teaching grown adults across the South to write their own names.

Her mother, Victoria Warren Anderson Poinsette, took in washing at home and had been raised in Haiti. She boasted to her children that she had never been a slave and would never be anybody's servant. She would not step out to the vegetable cart when it came down the street, so the man carried the vegetables in to her door and she chose what she wanted from there.

The first number in Clark's ledger is a dollar and fifty cents.

That was the monthly tuition at Avery Normal Institute, and she paid it by minding a dressmaker's two children across the street, mornings and afternoons, for years. Avery had been founded by missionary women from Massachusetts, and its teachers were still white when she arrived.

She finished there in 1916 with a Licentiate of Instruction, which the state counted as two years of college. State law kept Black teachers out of Charleston's public schools. The city that had trained her had nothing to offer her.

She crossed to Johns Island instead, where there was no bridge and would not be one for nearly thirty years.

At the Promise Land School she and one other teacher taught 132 children between them. She was eighteen years old and she was the principal.

Her pay was thirty-five dollars a month.

The other teacher's was twenty-five. Across the way stood the white school with three pupils in it. Its teacher was paid eighty-five dollars a month.

The state kept its own accounts and published them. In the 1916 report of the South Carolina superintendent of education, average spending came to $17.02 for each white child enrolled and $1.90 for each Black one. Of the 1,176 school buildings the state counted for Black children, two were brick and 778 were rooms borrowed from churches and lodge halls.

She taught children in the daytime and adults at night, out of whatever was to hand. A Sears catalog served as a reader.

It was on that island that she first heard of the NAACP, from Presbyterian ministers holding a convention there. Membership cost a dollar a year.

The island teachers had to cross to Charleston to cash their checks at the fireproof building downtown. The woman who supervised the Black schools stood outside the door holding a small parasol, and as each teacher came out with cash in hand the dollar went into the parasol.

Nobody wanted to be seen paying it.

In 1919 Clark moved to a teaching post at Avery and joined a campaign to force Charleston to hire Black teachers in its own public schools. It was run by Edwin Harleston, a portrait painter who headed the local NAACP, with the former congressman Thomas E. Miller behind it.

Lawmakers had been arguing that only the city's lighter-skinned families wanted those jobs, and that the longshoremen and the laundresses and the garbage crews had no interest in the matter at all. So the campaign went door to door to prove otherwise. Clark worked County Street from King Street down to the river with a group of her own students, and people signed on whatever scraps of paper were to hand.

They collected ten thousand signatures in a single day.

Charleston hired its first Black public school teachers the following year. Black principals came in 1921.

Her own accounts do not balance in that decade. She married a sailor named Nerie Clark, and their first child, a daughter, lived only a few weeks.

Her husband died of kidney failure in December 1925. She sent their son to his grandmother in Hickory, North Carolina, because the island was hard on a small child and she had to keep working.

He grew up calling her Septima, and she said fifty years later that she had never liked it and had wanted him to say Mama.

She moved to Columbia in 1929 to teach. The salary was sixty-two dollars and fifty cents a month, and her board came out of that.

When the state ran short of money in the Depression the figure was cut to thirty-one twenty-five. She spent three or four summers waiting tables at a camp in Harrison, Maine. Her winter pay came home untouched that way, and there was a child in North Carolina being kept on it.

She collected her degrees in the gaps. Segregation had put the Black schools on double sessions, so she taught from noon until five and used the mornings and the evenings for college classes. She studied under W. E. B. Du Bois at Atlanta University in 1937, finished her bachelor's at Benedict College in 1942, and took a master's at Hampton Institute in 1946.

The salary fight took the better part of two decades. Clark gathered affidavits from teachers on both sides of the color line, and copies of their paychecks where anyone was willing to hand them over.

The test case was filed in Charleston on November 10, 1943, on behalf of a young science teacher named Viola Duvall. Duvall held the highest certificate the state issued and was paid $645 a year, and the lowest-paid white teacher holding that same certificate was paid $1,100.

The trial took fifteen minutes.

Judge J. Waties Waring ruled that Black teachers with equal qualifications had to be paid the same, and equalization reached Columbia two years later. The version of this story that circulates says Clark's salary tripled because the case was won. In her own account the tripling came after she sat the national teachers' examination.

She came home to Charleston in 1947, bought a house on Henrietta Street, and had a bathroom put in downstairs so her mother would not have to climb the steps.

The banks in town would not lend money to Black teachers. Several of them had three or four years of a master's degree behind them and needed the summer's tuition to finish, and without a loan they would have to start the whole degree again.

So Clark helped put together a teachers' credit union. The state and regional officers wanted it written down as a fund for Black teachers only, and the organizers refused, holding out for months until the charter covered the secretaries and the other workers too.

The principal who let them hold the planning meeting in his public school building was fired for it.

In January 1956 the South Carolina legislature made it unlawful for any city or state employee to belong to the NAACP. Clark was fifty-eight, she had been teaching for forty years, and she was by then vice president of the Charleston branch.

There were 736 Black teachers in Charleston County. She and a few others sat down together and wrote to every one of them, asking them to protest the law.

Twenty-six wrote back.

She did not hold it against the rest. Those jobs were among the few professional positions open to Black people in those neighborhoods, and she said plainly that she understood why the letters went unanswered.

Years afterward she called the attempt one of the failures of her life, for pushing people into something they were not ready for. The phrase she took from it gave her second book its title.

Her own contract was simply not renewed for the fall. Nobody from the board told her anything.

She sent a registered letter with a return receipt asking for a reason. The reply explained that under the new law no principal, no superintendent and no college president was required to give one. Her services were not needed.

Eleven teachers lost their jobs in Charleston and thirty-one in Clarendon County. Forty years of contributions toward a pension went with them.

The woman who had held the parasol outside the fireproof building was among the strongest NAACP members in the county, and she could not bring herself to deny it. Clark said she withered and died not long afterward.

That summer Clark was on a mountain in Tennessee with a typewriter and a new job. Myles Horton ran a small integrated school up there called Highlander, and he offered her the post of workshop director as soon as he heard she had been let go.

On July 30, 1956, she typed a letter to Rev. and Mrs. M. L. King at Dexter Avenue Baptist Church in Montgomery, Alabama.

It was an invitation. The mountain top was cool and delightful at night, she wrote, and they and their family could relax there in comfort.

Room, board and transportation would be furnished. They could write, or call Monteagle 164 collect.

"You deserve this and more for your courage."

She signed it Mrs. Septima P. Clark, Workshop Director. The letter sits today in the King papers at Boston University.

Rosa Parks had come through one of Clark's Highlander workshops a few months before her arrest in Montgomery. Parks said afterward that Clark's life story made her own effort look very small to her.

In January 1957 the first Citizenship School opened on Johns Island, paid for by Highlander and the Field Foundation. Esau Jenkins, a bus driver and grocer who had been pressing for it, found it a home inside his cooperative.

The front of the building was fitted out as a grocery store, and the members bought and sold to each other there. Behind it were two rooms with no windows.

That was the school.

By Clark's own account, they did not want white people to know there was a school back there.

The teacher was her cousin Bernice Robinson, a beautician, chosen because she worked for herself and no white employer could take her livelihood away. Fourteen adults came to the first class.

Lessons went up on dry-cleaning bags where there was no blackboard. Robinson built the syllabus out of what the students themselves said they needed. It came down to the voter registration form, the state constitution, the driver's license application, and how to write your own name.

Tennessee raided Highlander in 1959 and arrested Clark on a liquor charge that was dropped. The state revoked the school's charter in 1961, and the citizenship program moved across to the Southern Christian Leadership Conference.

Clark became SCLC's director of education and teaching, and the schools spread into Georgia, Mississippi and Alabama.

They met in kitchens, in beauty parlors, and under trees in the summertime, and she said she sometimes got round three of them in a day. She sat on the executive staff, one of very few women ever to do so. In her memoir she wrote that Ralph Abernathy asked, over and over, why Mrs. Clark was on it at all.

The historian Elaine Weiss counts more than nine hundred citizenship schools across the South by the time the Voting Rights Act was signed in 1965. Clark said she once heard Andrew Young call those schools the base the whole movement was built on, and that she thought it was probably true.

King answered the invitation on August 16, 1956. Three years later he wrote that the hope of the future rested on women of integrity, honesty and courage like Septima P. Clark.

She retired from SCLC in 1970 at seventy-two. Five years later Charleston voters elected her to the county school board.

It was the board that had ended her career.

In 1976 the governor of South Carolina reinstated her teacher's pension, having declared that she was unjustly terminated. The legislature approved her back pay in 1981, when she was eighty-three. Carter gave her a Living Legacy Award in 1979 and the state gave her the Order of the Palmetto in 1982.

Twenty years for the pension. Twenty-five for the wages.

Her father had taken a job as a custodian at the first USO on King Street in Charleston after the First World War. The government paid him by check, and a check had to be signed.

He had been signing with an X. He sat down at that point and taught himself to write his name. There were eight children in the house by then.

Septima Clark died on December 15, 1987, at eighty-nine, on Johns Island, where she had taught her first class.

She had been dead thirty-three years when the United States Mint struck a dollar coin for South Carolina. The reverse shows her walking with three Black schoolchildren who are carrying books and an American flag. Around them the Mint stamped the name of the country, the name of the state that had told her it did not have to say why, and her name.

The name on the coin is Septima Clark.

Happy to respond so I can correct your slander.

Hoffman’s trial ended in a hung jury. Probably because the boy recanted much of his testimony on the witness stand as well as the medical exam finding no physical evidence of rape.

The prosecutors said they had no path to a felony conviction without the child’s testimony at a second trial, since he’d made clear he wouldn’t testify again. So they offered a plea to two misdemeanors — indecent assault and displaying harmful materials to a minor — with one day in jail and no sex-offender registration, because the plea documents didn’t specify the victim’s age. Hoffman signed a judicial confession admitting he touched the boy’s genitals without consent. 

The judge rejected the one-day proposal, imposed thirty days, then raised it to sixty after the victim’s mother said that wasn’t enough. Hoffman served twenty-nine days and was released May twenty-fifth. His Texas law license was canceled in July. He now lives in Nebraska, where the conviction does require fifteen years of registration.

So, it is the judge and the prosecution, along with the boy’s recanting and no physical evidence that resulted in the sentencing. Not Paxton. 

Personally, I would agree this was too far light for an admitted homosexual pedophilic pervert who confessed to touching the boys genitals. He should have received the maximum sentence of 20 years. Unfortunately, for many reasons, lawyers, prosecutors and  defense, make deals all the time and justice is often, if not usually, thwarted. But in this case, Paxton was not the reason for the sentence.

text:
A week ago, I argued that if the UAE nominated Lana Nusseibeh, Colombia should support her. Abu Dhabi has now made its choice.

The Secretary-General is chosen not by the applause of a straw poll, but by the consent of powers whose interests often diverge. Grynspan’s Costa Rica offers regional legitimacy and neutrality; those are real assets, but they cannot substitute for strategic weight. London will veto Grossi because he is Argentine.

The question for Moscow and Beijing is whether a Latin American candidate might be too readily drawn into Washington’s orbit. The question for Washington is whether a candidate can work with a close strategic partner in a region central to its interests. Paris has its own stake: a defence partnership with the UAE and forces stationed there. Each of the five has reason to care about Gulf stability and access to Abu Dhabi.

Nusseibeh occupies a rare position: independent enough to be taken seriously by rivals, and connected enough to matter to them. A Secretary-General need not be every power’s preferred candidate. The essential test is whether any one power would find her unacceptable—and whether all can see value in dealing with her.

That is why the world should support Nusseibeh. Colombia should get behind her.

text:
PEACE IS NOT A MOOD. IT IS VERIFIABLE ACTION.

Putin’s foreign-policy aide Yury Ushakov declared after talks with Steve Witkoff:

“I don’t know how close we’re getting, but things are heading in that direction.”

Towards what, exactly?

Russia has agreed “in principle” to attend another round of expert-level talks in Abu Dhabi around mid-November.

But Moscow has not:

▪️ Accepted Ukraine’s offer of an immediate ceasefire along the current front line.

▪️ Agreed to stop attacking Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure.

▪️ Withdrawn its additional territorial demands.

▪️ Accepted enforceable security guarantees for Ukraine.

▪️ Committed to any timetable for ending hostilities.

Ushakov even said there was “not much useful” in the proposals Witkoff brought from his talks with Ukraine and European leaders in Oslo.

Russia’s only concrete concession was to agree to another meeting several weeks from now. Meanwhile, its war continues.

This is precisely how the Kremlin exploits negotiations.

It offers hopeful language, promises future discussions and encourages Washington to believe that peace is approaching. Russia then receives diplomatic engagement, commercial opportunities and relief from pressure without changing its conduct.

The war will, by definition, eventually move towards an ending.

The relevant questions are whether Russia will stop firing, what it will agree to, when it will act and how compliance will be enforced.

Until Moscow answers them, “things are heading in that direction” means very little.

Ukraine has offered to stop the killing now.

Russia has offered to keep talking.

authorBio: History, geopolitics, and war. | Russia, Ukraine, and the architecture of power. | Essays at GMan’s Chronicle | Christian | Irish Unionist | Ulster

text:
ONE MORE MEETING, ONE MORE CONCESSION

It suits the Kremlin to keep Washington believing that peace is just around the corner.

One more meeting. One more telephone call. One more American concession.

While Washington waits for a deal, Russia keeps waging war.

According to Axios, Jared Kushner again pressed Ukraine to stop striking Russian oil refineries during talks in Oslo. Zelenskyy offered to halt the strikes if Russia reciprocated.

That distinction matters.

Ukraine is being asked for a concrete and immediate concession. Russia is being asked to consider negotiations.

The Trump administration has already eased sanctions to facilitate Russian diesel exports. Moscow now has every incentive to keep diplomatic hopes alive, delaying further American pressure while Washington demands additional compromises from Kyiv.

Talks can continue indefinitely, even while Russian missiles and drones continue killing Ukrainians.

Every proposed document or summit allows American mediators to announce “progress”. Russia retains direct access to Washington and another opportunity to promote its account of why the war began and what Ukraine must surrender to end it.

And if peace remains elusive, Moscow can offer business instead.

Putin’s envoy Kirill Dmitriev has openly discussed potential Russian-American ventures, including nuclear-powered data centres. Such projects create another incentive for Washington to preserve the relationship rather than confront Moscow.

Russia’s demands also remain deliberately open-ended.

On 16 October, Putin declared that Russia’s planned 660-kilometre “security zone” inside Ukraine would not even be negotiable. This would require occupying additional territory in the Sumy and Kharkiv regions, beyond the four Ukrainian regions Moscow already claims.

Putin is therefore adding territorial demands while presenting his willingness to attend further talks as a concession.

The St Petersburg meeting has now provided its answer. After three hours, Putin reportedly agreed “in principle” to further trilateral negotiations.

His only concession was to keep negotiating.

The real test is not whether Putin agrees to another meeting. It is whether Russia agrees to do anything concrete:

▪️ Which attacks will it stop?

▪️ When will it stop them?

▪️ How will compliance be verified?

▪️ What credible security guarantees for Ukraine will it accept?

Without answers, another “constructive conversation” means only that American hopes have been raised again.

The envoys leave to prepare the next meeting.

Russia keeps waging war.

📷 Suspilne Novyny / Associated Press

👉October 21 Watchouts: What was bullish, bearish or mixed?

👉Inflation heated up in the UK, US crude stocks fell & Washington paid 5.469% on its latest 20-year bond auction… not a simple green-light day for gold & silver!

🔴UK inflation: A potential rates headwind
CPI rose to 3.5% from 3.1%, above the Reuters poll’s 3.4% forecast.

🔥Core inflation climbed to 2.8% & services inflation reached 3.7%. That can make easier monetary policy harder to justify. Inflation protection matters to stackers, but higher interest-rate expectations can work against metals in the meantime.

🟡US oil inventories: Draws… but not across the board. EIA reported crude inventories down 3.1 million barrels to 412.5 million. Gasoline fell 3.0 million, while distillates rose 1.7 million.

🔥Less crude & gasoline in storage can support energy prices, but the distillate build pulls the other way. For metals, an energy-driven inflation squeeze can strengthen the purchasing-power argument while also keeping rates higher. Neither outcome is automatic!

🟡20-year Treasury auction: Mixed demand signals. The $13 billion reopening cleared at 5.469%, with bid-to-cover of 2.73, up from September’s 2.57.

🔥More bids per dollar offered doesn’t tell the whole story. InvestingLive reported a small 0.9-basis-point tail: buyers required a slightly higher yield than the pre-auction market indicated. That’s not a failed auction, but it isn’t an unqualified demand win either.

🟡All-week backdrop: Fed blackout... The scheduled policy-communications blackout remains in effect ahead of the October 27–28 meeting. Less routine Fed guidance does not mean less market risk.

𝐓𝐑𝐔𝐌𝐏 𝐓𝐎 𝐅𝐑𝐀𝐍𝐂𝐄 𝐀𝐅𝐓𝐄𝐑 𝟐,𝟒𝟎𝟎 𝐀𝐑𝐑𝐄𝐒𝐓𝐄𝐃 𝐈𝐍 𝐈𝐓𝐒 𝐖𝐎𝐑𝐒𝐓 𝐑𝐈𝐎𝐓𝐒 𝐈𝐍 𝐘𝐄𝐀𝐑𝐒—𝐑𝐄𝐌𝐎𝐕𝐄 𝐓𝐇𝐄 𝐈𝐍𝐒𝐔𝐑𝐑𝐄𝐂𝐓𝐈𝐎𝐍𝐈𝐒𝐓𝐒

France is reeling from its 𝐰𝐨𝐫𝐬𝐭 𝐜𝐢𝐯𝐢𝐥 𝐮𝐧𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐭 𝐢𝐧 𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐬 — nearly 2,400 people hauled into custody since protests over the cost of living and school conditions spiraled into nationwide riots, looting and arson across multiple cities. Watching from Washington, President Trump had a blunt message for Paris.

𝘠𝘰𝘶'𝘷𝘦 𝘨𝘰𝘵 𝘵𝘰 𝘳𝘦𝘮𝘰𝘷𝘦 𝘱𝘦𝘰𝘱𝘭𝘦, 𝘨𝘦𝘵 𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘮 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘩𝘦𝘭𝘭 𝘰𝘶𝘵. 𝘞𝘩𝘦𝘯 𝘺𝘰𝘶 𝘭𝘰𝘰𝘬 𝘢𝘵 𝘍𝘳𝘢𝘯𝘤𝘦 — 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘪𝘵 𝘩𝘢𝘱𝘱𝘦𝘯𝘦𝘥 𝘪𝘯 𝘐𝘵𝘢𝘭𝘺 𝘵𝘰𝘰, 𝘴𝘮𝘢𝘭𝘭𝘦𝘳 𝘴𝘤𝘢𝘭𝘦, 𝘣𝘶𝘵 𝘪𝘵'𝘴 𝘳𝘪𝘨𝘩𝘵 𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘳𝘦, 𝘪𝘵'𝘴 𝘴𝘪𝘮𝘮𝘦𝘳𝘪𝘯𝘨. 𝘐𝘧 𝘺𝘰𝘶 𝘥𝘰𝘯'𝘵 𝘨𝘦𝘵 𝘵𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘰𝘶𝘵, 𝘺𝘰𝘶'𝘳𝘦 𝘨𝘰𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘵𝘰 𝘩𝘢𝘷𝘦 𝘵𝘰 𝘳𝘦𝘮𝘰𝘷𝘦 𝘵𝘩𝘰𝘴𝘦 𝘱𝘦𝘰𝘱𝘭𝘦 𝘸𝘩𝘰 𝘢𝘳𝘦 𝘪𝘯𝘴𝘶𝘳𝘳𝘦𝘤𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯𝘪𝘴𝘵𝘴. 𝘠𝘰𝘶'𝘳𝘦 𝘨𝘰𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘵𝘰 𝘩𝘢𝘷𝘦 𝘵𝘰 𝘨𝘦𝘵 𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘮 𝘰𝘶𝘵 𝘰𝘧 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘤𝘰𝘶𝘯𝘵𝘳𝘺.

Even Trump’s harshest French critic agrees on the diagnosis, if not the fix. President Macron blamed 𝘪𝘯𝘴𝘶𝘳𝘳𝘦𝘤𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯𝘪𝘴𝘵 𝘦𝘭𝘦𝘮𝘦𝘯𝘵𝘴 𝘧𝘳𝘰𝘮 𝘳𝘢𝘥𝘪𝘤𝘢𝘭 𝘧𝘢𝘳-𝘭𝘦𝘧𝘵 𝘨𝘳𝘰𝘶𝘱𝘴, 𝘫𝘰𝘪𝘯𝘦𝘥 𝘣𝘺 𝘯𝘶𝘮𝘦𝘳𝘰𝘶𝘴 𝘤𝘳𝘪𝘮𝘪𝘯𝘢𝘭𝘴 for the 𝘶𝘯𝘳𝘦𝘴𝘵𝘳𝘢𝘪𝘯𝘦𝘥 𝘷𝘪𝘰𝘭𝘦𝘯𝘤𝘦, vowing to hold accountable 𝘵𝘩𝘰𝘴𝘦 𝘸𝘩𝘰 𝘴𝘰𝘶𝘨𝘩𝘵 𝘵𝘰 𝘣𝘳𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘥𝘰𝘸𝘯 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘙𝘦𝘱𝘶𝘣𝘭𝘪𝘤.

France’s own government is conceding the failure. Justice Minister 𝐆é𝐫𝐚𝐥𝐝 𝐃𝐚𝐫𝐦𝐚𝐧𝐢𝐧 admitted authorities 𝘩𝘢𝘷𝘦 𝘶𝘯𝘥𝘦𝘯𝘪𝘢𝘣𝘭𝘺 𝘧𝘢𝘪𝘭𝘦𝘥, warning that far-left 𝘴𝘦𝘥𝘪𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯𝘪𝘴𝘵𝘴 are shaping up to be the country’s next major domestic threat — a security apparatus built to fight Islamist terror, he said, with no playbook for this. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez cited a 𝐥𝐚𝐜𝐤 𝐨𝐟 𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭 in the response and offered his resignation; Macron kept him on.

text:
ANALYSIS: In Zimbabwe, Power Is About Keeping the Winning Coalition Loyal : Not Persuading the Public
By Gideon Nkomo
IN democracies, politicians obsess over swing voters. In authoritarian regimes like Zimbabwe, the calculation is different: the public is not the main audience. 
Survival depends on managing a much smaller “winning coalition” of elites — security chiefs, party barons, patronage networks and business allies — whose loyalty must be constantly bought, balanced and, when necessary, coerced.
That is the central lesson of Zimbabwe’s recent political history. Robert Mugabe did not fall because he lost an election. 
He fell because the coalition that had sustained him — the securocrats and patronage kingpins — concluded he could no longer protect their interests. 
When that elite support withdrew in 2017, his long rule ended within days.
Emmerson Mnangagwa’s political strategy since then has been shaped by that lesson. 
His priority is not winning over the broader electorate in any genuine sense. 
It is preventing a repeat of 2017 by keeping his own coalition tethered to him, neutralizing rivals and disabling independent centres of power.
This is not the crude “our people will do what we say” model of politics. 
It is more calculating. Authoritarian leaders know that the greatest threat often comes from within. 
Succession uncertainty is the nightmare: once subordinates believe a leader’s exit is near, factions form, loyalties shift and patronage flows begin to dry up. Mugabe learned this late. Mnangagwa appears determined not to.
His method has been what analysts describe as “quiet institutional capture.” 
Rather than relying solely on revolutionary charisma or open violence, Mnangagwa has systematically weakened the institutions that could constrain him. 
The judiciary, parliament and electoral commission have been reconfigured or pressured into serving the ruling party’s interests. The army and intelligence services remain the “steel frame” of authority, but the system is dressed up as constitutional rule. It is a hybrid order: repressive in substance, legalistic in form.
Alongside this comes patronage. State resources, empowerment funds and public appointments are distributed to loyalists, deepening factional fights over who controls the money. Potential rivals are sometimes co-opted with prestigious but powerless positions, or even offered cabinet posts to opposition figures. 
This is not power-sharing. It is a calculated buy-off designed to entrench dependence and prevent a unified opposition from forming.
Coercion remains in the background. 
The public is managed through a combination of electoral manipulation, repression of dissent and the threat of violence. Elections are held, but they function more as a façade than as a genuine mechanism for changing power. 
The goal is not to persuade the masses; it is to demobilize them, divide the opposition and keep the elite coalition intact.
The contrast with Mugabe is instructive. 
Mugabe relied on charisma, revolutionary legitimacy and “divide and rule” factionalism. He tolerated a surprising degree of internal party contestation and, at times, genuine electoral competition — which shocked him when he lost a constitutional referendum in 2000 and faced a serious opposition challenge. Mnangagwa’s style is more institutional and more calculating. He understands that charismatic authority is fragile. 
His answer is to capture the machinery of the state so thoroughly that rival centres of power cannot coordinate.
His current push to extend his rule to 2030 fits this logic. 
The move is not simply about staying in office. 
It is about disrupting his rivals’ succession planning, keeping patronage networks tethered to him and ensuring that no alternative power centre can form around a scheduled transition.
So what do authoritarian politicians think? Not simply: “These are our people; they will do what we say.” 
They think: “Who in my inner circle is becoming a threat?

text:
U.S. history lesson on the original “fraud whistle blower program”:  The Qui Tam provisions of the U.S. False Claims Act that were established in 1863.

“Super Intelligent” Data search provided the following information:
Congress passed the original False Claims Act (also known as the “Lincoln Law” or “Informer’s Act”) on **March 2, 1863**, during the Civil War. President Abraham Lincoln signed it into law in response to widespread fraud by contractors supplying the Union Army (such as selling defective goods, inferior materials, or overcharging).

The law’s qui tam provision allows private individuals (called “relators” or whistleblowers) who are the original source of information about fraud against the government to sue on the government’s behalf and receive a share of any recovery. The original 1863 version offered relators up to 50% of the recovery.

Later developments: 

- **1943 amendments**: Weakened the law by reducing relator shares (to a maximum of 25% or lower if the government intervened) and restricting cases where the government already had the information.
- **1986 amendments**: Strengthened it significantly, raising potential relator shares to the modern range of 15–30% (depending on whether the government intervenes) and making it more practical for whistleblowers to bring cases. These changes led to a large increase in qui tam activity.

While the concept of qui tam actions (from the Latin *qui tam pro domino rege quam pro se ipso in hac parte sequitur*, roughly “who sues for the king as well as for himself”) has roots in English common law going back centuries and appeared in some early American statutes, the foundational modern U.S. version linked to government fraud claims dates to the 1863 False Claims Act.

…

text:
Senator - what about the original “fraud whistle blower program”- 

 The qui tam provisions of the U.S. False Claims Act that were established in 1863.

Did you know about this, Senator? 
Congress passed the original False Claims Act (also known as the “Lincoln Law” or “Informer’s Act”) on **March 2, 1863**, during the Civil War. President Abraham Lincoln signed it into law in response to widespread fraud by contractors supplying the Union Army (such as selling defective goods, inferior materials, or overcharging).

The law’s qui tam provision allows private individuals (called “relators” or whistleblowers) who are the original source of information about fraud against the government to sue on the government’s behalf and receive a share of any recovery. The original 1863 version offered relators up to 50% of the recovery.

Later developments: 

- **1943 amendments**: Weakened the law by reducing relator shares (to a maximum of 25% or lower if the government intervened) and restricting cases where the government already had the information.
- **1986 amendments**: Strengthened it significantly, raising potential relator shares to the modern range of 15–30% (depending on whether the government intervenes) and making it more practical for whistleblowers to bring cases. These changes led to a large increase in qui tam activity.

While the concept of qui tam actions (from the Latin *qui tam pro domino rege quam pro se ipso in hac parte sequitur*, roughly “who sues for the king as well as for himself”) has roots in English common law going back centuries and appeared in some early American statutes, the foundational modern U.S. version linked to government fraud claims dates to the 1863 False Claims Act.

CONTROL OF THE VILLAGE SHIELDS THE FLANK 🇷🇺  

Holding Chervony Yar lowers the chance of flanking strikes against Russian units moving from Omelnyk toward Orekhov  which remains the main defensive hub of opposing forces in the Zaporozhye region. Taking that city would open a direct route toward the regional center of Zaporozhye itself.  

YULYEVKA CLEARED ON THE RIGHT BANK OF THE KONKA 🇷🇺  

Yulyevka belongs to the Novoaleksandrovsky village council of the Zaporozhye district. Its pre-war population was about 670 people. The village stands on the right bank of the Konka River, 4 kilometers east of Veselyanka, liberated earlier in March. Straight-line distance from Yulyevka to the southern edge of Zaporizhzhia city is 15 kms.  

The advance on the city is also unfolding farther west from the previously secured Malokaterynivka. An immediate assault on the regional center is not expected. The Dnepr group is more likely to cut Zaporozhye off from Orekhiv via T0803 highway.  

STEADY PRESSURE CONTINUES ACROSS THE OBLAST 🇷🇺

Local terrain favors methodical advances. Highways & river lines shape the next objectives. Russian forces continue to combine infantry clearance with the destruction of drones & armored assets. The result is incremental control of ground that once formed part of opposing defensive belts.

With Chervony Yar secured, the approach to Orekhov becomes less exposed. Opposing forces must now contend with pressure from more than 1 direction. The same pattern appears around Yulyevka, where the Konka River line offers both cover & a route for further movement.  

Russian units report consistent destruction of UAVs & heavy hexacopters. That effort limits aerial observation and strikes against advancing troops. Armor & vehicle losses compound the problem for the side trying to hold the remaining villages.  

BROADER IMPLICATIONS FOR THE ZAPOROZHYE FRONT 🇷🇺  

Each cleared settlement adds depth to Russian positions and narrows the space available to opposing formations.
MoD statements emphasize the role of specific regiments and the equipment they eliminated. Such details illustrate the scale of resistance met and overcome.  

The overall direction remains toward reducing the defensive value of Orekhov and restricting access to Zaporozhye. Further movement along the main highways will decide how quickly those goals are approached. Russian forces have shown they can take small villages while inflicting measurable losses in manpower & materiel.

text:
Alexander the Great bowing to the High Priest in Jerusalem is the defining ancient intersection where military imperial consolidation yielded directly to the authority of the sacred script.
Recorded primarily by the first-century Jewish historian Flavius Josephus in Antiquities of the Jews (Book 11), as well as in the Talmud (Tractate Yoma 69a), this legendary encounter serves as the foundational prototype for how global conquerors are structurally folded into sacred history.

1. The Confrontation: The Refusal of Allegiance

In 332 BCE, Alexander the Great was sweeping through the Levant, systematically dismantling the Persian Empire. After a grueling siege of Tyre, Alexander sent an ultimatum to Jerusalem demanding their submission and tax revenue.
• The Stand: The High Priest—named Jaddua by Josephus, and Shimon HaTzaddik (Simon the Righteous) in Talmudic tradition—refused to break his sacred oath of loyalty to the Persian King Darius III.
• The Retaliation: Enraged by this defiance, Alexander marched his battle-hardened Macedonian army directly toward Jerusalem, accompanied by Phoenician and Chaldean auxiliaries who eagerly anticipated plundering the city and executing the High Priest.

2. The White Procession at Sapha

Facing imminent annihilation, the High Priest prayed for deliverance and received a directive from God in a dream. Instead of fortifying the city walls, he threw open the gates of Jerusalem.
• The Meeting: The High Priest dressed in his official vestments—purple and scarlet robes with the golden headplate (Tzitz) bearing the Tetragrammaton (יהוה). He led a massive procession of priests clothed in fine white linen and a multitude of citizens dressed in white out to Sapha (Scopus), the high peak overlooking Jerusalem and the Temple.

3. The Unprecedented Bow: The Vision Confirmed

When the Greek cavalry crested the hill expecting a bloody siege, the exact reverse occurred. Upon seeing the High Priest and the golden plate engraving, Alexander descended from his chariot, approached alone, and bowed down to reverence the Divine Name.
• The Backroom Explanation: Alexander’s chief general, Parmenion, was flabbergasted and asked the King why the conqueror of the world was bowing before a Jewish priest.
• Alexander replied: "I did not adore him, but that God who hath honored him with his high priesthood; for I saw this very person in a dream, in this very habit... exhorting me to make no delay, but boldly to pass over the sea, for that he would conduct my army, and would give me the dominion over the Persians."

4. The Decoding of the Script: The Book of Daniel

Following this symbolic submission of imperial power to the priesthood, Alexander entered Jerusalem peacefully. He went up to the Temple and offered sacrifices according to the High Priest’s precise directions.
• The Ultimate Proof: The priests presented Alexander with the Book of Daniel (specifically chapters 7 and 8), written centuries prior during the Babylonian exile. They showed him the prophecies predicting that a swift "He-Goat" from the West (Greece) would shatter the two-horned Ram of Persia.
• The Result: Recognizing himself explicitly in the ancient Hebrew text, Alexander was highly gratified. Instead of destroying Jerusalem, he granted the Judeans complete tax exemption every seventh year (the Sabbatical Shmita year) and full autonomy to live according to their ancestral laws.

text:
Thousands of families were fleeing Hitler’s army. One diplomat defied his government and signed the papers that could save their lives.

June 1940. Bordeaux, France.

German forces were advancing across Europe.

Terrified refugees crowded outside the Portuguese consulate, desperate for visas that would allow them to escape through Spain and Portugal.

Among them were Jewish families, political refugees, and parents trying to protect their children.

But Portugal’s government had ordered its diplomats to restrict visas.

The consul, Aristides de Sousa Mendes, faced an impossible choice.

Obey his government.

Or help the desperate people standing outside his door.

He chose the people.

Working with his family and other helpers, Sousa Mendes began issuing visas despite the restrictions.

For days, the consulate became a lifeline.

Each document offered another person or family a possible route to safety.

But his compassion came at a devastating personal cost.

His government punished him for disobeying orders.

He lost his diplomatic career and suffered years of financial hardship.

He died in 1954, without receiving the recognition his actions deserved.

Only later did the world fully honor what he had done.

In 1966, Yad Vashem recognized him as Righteous Among the Nations.

Portugal eventually rehabilitated his reputation.

Today, thousands of descendants of refugees remember the man who refused to turn their families away.

He had the power to close a door.

Instead, he opened one.

Would you risk your career and your family’s financial security to save strangers?

text:
Persian Gulf oil exports have surpassed prewar levels, as an improvised shipping system under U.S. protection is helping tankers move oil through one of Iran’s fiercest waves of attacks in the Strait of Hormuz.

Middle East oil flows, including shipments through Hormuz and alternative routes across the region, averaged more than 24 million barrels a day in the week through Oct. 18, surpassing prewar levels of 23.3 million, according to ship tracker Kpler.
Preliminary figures show Hormuz oil flows, including offshore transfers in the Gulf of Oman, came to around 14 million barrels a day on average for the same period, or 82% of prewar levels.

Oil prices remain high, and benchmark Brent crude has risen in recent days to around $108 a barrel Tuesday. Traders are concerned the improvement in Hormuz might not be sustainable, particularly if fighting breaks out again. Thinning global inventories leave little margin for error. The operation is also expensive, costs that ultimately flow through to consumers at the pump.
Still, the resilience of oil flows marks a shift in the battle over the world’s most important energy chokepoint. Iran can still make shipments dangerous and expensive. But its ability to deter transits has faded, weakening Tehran’s leverage with the U.S.

“The big picture is that the system for shipping through a dangerous Strait of Hormuz is now well-established and the risk appetite of those involved in exporting oil has risen,” said Hamad Hussain, a senior commodities economist at Capital Economics.

Pipelines across Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates are also moving oil along different routes. In September, about 40% of the non-Iranian crude shipped out of the Gulf bypassed the strait, compared with 17% before the war, Kpler estimated.

The success contrasts with the chokehold on Iran, whose own oil exports have been bottled up by a U.S. maritime blockade. The risk is Iran could try to re-establish its influence by striking harder and potentially drawing the U.S. into another confrontation before the U.S. midterm elections in two weeks.

Gulf oil is flowing despite escalating violence around the strait. About 30 attacks on ships have been reported this month, according to a Wall Street Journal tally based on reports by the U.K. Maritime Trade Operations Centre and maritime security companies.

The incidents in October account for 20% of the ships attacked during the war, said Michelle Wiese Bockmann, a senior analyst at maritime intelligence firm Windward.

“Iran is trying to reassert its blockade of the strait,” said Christopher Long, a former British naval officer now at Neptune P2P Group.

For many oil traders and shipowners, the risk of crossing Hormuz is worth it. Compared with before the war, traders can earn $20 a barrel more reselling Iraqi oil, or about $40 million on cargo from a supertanker, estimated Homayoun Falakshahi, Kpler’s head of crude oil analysis. Three such voyages could repay the $100 million cost of a secondhand tanker.

Seafarers also are being offered bonuses to make the dangerous crossings. Crew members have been lured by payouts two or three times their typical monthly salary to work on ships that venture into the Persian Gulf. One China-based ship-staffing company offered as much as $25,000 for a round-trip, which normally takes a week or two, The Wall Street Journal reported.
“The volumes remain high despite rising attacks, because profits make it worth the risk,” Falakshahi said.
Some shipowners are repositioning older vessels that used to ferry Venezuelan and Russian oil to the Persian Gulf because of the unprecedented tanker rates in the region, shipbrokers said.

Many of the vessels are making short shuttle runs through the danger zone. American air cover provides some protection through a corridor along the Omani coast. Tankers load oil inside the Gulf and transport it via Hormuz, often with their tracking signals switched off. They then stop near Oman and transfer their cargoes to ships bound for distant markets before heading back into the Gulf, where they face the most risk of being hit.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, meanwhile, is using drones and missiles to stop ships that try to make the run. It also has turned to guerrilla tactics long employed by Yemen’s Houthis to target traffic around the mouth of the Red Sea, deploying spotters in small fishing boats and sending fighters out onto the water.
The crossing remains dangerous. Before September, the Tanzania-flagged supertanker Loyalty spent years ferrying Venezuelan crude to China. Since September, it has entered the Persian Gulf twice, both times heading to Iraq to load crude.

A crew member said the ship informed the U.S. Navy about each trip and had security personnel onboard. In early October, Loyalty transferred 2 million barrels of Iraqi crude oil in the Gulf of Oman to an unidentified tanker, then went back into the Gulf to pick up a new load, according to Kpler and the crew member. The crew member said the ship management company sent the crew body armor and helmets for the second trip.

On Oct. 16, Loyalty was struck by a rocket-propelled grenade launched from a small boat, according to maritime security company Vanguard. The projectile carved a hole in a fresh water tank. At the time of the attack, Loyalty was carrying 2 million barrels of Iraqi crude oil, the crew member said.

The attacks are raising the cost of getting Gulf oil to market. Freight for a supertanker carrying Gulf crude to China was near a record $37.37 a barrel this week, Kpler said. War-risk insurance has climbed to as much as 10% of a vessel’s value from less than 3%, according to Windward’s Wiese Bockmann.

“In April, the problem was a shortage of crude. In October, it is the cost of moving it,” said Natasha Kaneva, head of the global commodities strategy team at JPMorgan. But oil is still getting through, despite Iran’s threats that it won’t allow its neighbors to ship their oil if it couldn’t export its own.

“Iran would have to be more aggressive to achieve the same degree of control it previously possessed over oil flows from the region,” Capital Economics’ Hussain said.

text:
**PURE MICHIGAN? ***

This is not about vengeance.  
This is about keeping a repeat offender from hurting someone else.

An 8-time felon hit my brother’s truck on Clio Road at 88 to 92 miles an hour in a 35 mile an hour zone. He was video-chatting a 14-year-old. He had drugs in his system. After the crash he told her not to call 911.

My brother choked to death on his own blood while holding his wife’s hand and telling her everything would be okay. She will never walk again. She will never be able to care for herself.

The original prosecutor bound him over on second-degree murder. A different prosecutor took the case and offered a plea to reckless driving causing death. According to my brother’s stepson, the family was told the decision on a plea was not theirs. I’ve been told the same thing directly — Michigan law gives victims the right to be consulted, not the right to control a plea. The sentence was 7 to 30 years. He could be out in April 2029.

Weeks earlier he had been pulled over for no license and bad plates while already on parole. The system left him with his keys. The police also destroyed the vehicles months before he was finally arrested.

The family was treated as an inconvenience. The arraignment was delayed for a year. When we tried to watch on video after taking time off work, the feed was never turned on. After the hearing was rescheduled because of the court’s own technical problems, the judge signed off by telling the defendant “Good luck.”

My brother’s stepson told me a victims advocate described me as “difficult” after I spoke up about how the family was being treated. Michigan’s Crime Victim’s Rights Act requires notice to siblings of a deceased victim. We had to fight for basic information.

At sentencing he said he was sorry. He said he would take my brother’s place. A man who is truly sorry does not spend years trying to undo the plea.

The Court of Appeals rejected the application for lack of merit. The deadline to ask the Michigan Supreme Court ends this week.

He has an end date.  
Our family does not.

My brother’s grandson was six when this happened. He told the family he wanted the driver to kill him too so he could be with his grandpa.

The system failed my brother, his wife, our family, and the people of Michigan.

Is this the kind of justice system of Pure Michigan people expect?

text:
Sezen, thank you for worrying about my education. 😂 But you've now confused hydrographic nomenclature with the Law of the Sea, which is considerably more interesting.

Yes, the IHO calls the body of water north of Crete the Aegean Sea.

And?

The IHO names and describes seas for hydrographic purposes. It does not sit in judgment deciding which coastlines generate continental shelves or EEZs.

Otherwise we have just discovered an extraordinary new branch of international law:

Rename the sea → delete the coastline. 😂

There is an even better problem with your argument.

The Aegean Sea is itself part of the Mediterranean maritime system. Calling a body of water “Aegean” does not somehow teleport it outside the Mediterranean any more than calling the Adriatic “Adriatic” removes Italy and Croatia from the Mediterranean world.

The Ionian is a named sea.

The Adriatic is a named sea.

The Aegean is a named sea.

They are not rival oceans competing with the Mediterranean. 😂

But let's accept your terminology completely, because it still doesn't rescue the legal argument.

You ask where Greece's Mediterranean-facing coastline is.

Well, your own map has helpfully drawn Crete at the bottom.

Thank you for Exhibit A. 😂

Now continue eastward:

Crete → Kasos → Karpathos → Rhodes → Kastellorizo.

These are not imaginary Greek objects accidentally printed on Turkish maps. They are sovereign Greek territory with coastlines.

And here is where geography finally meets law:

The legal question is not what name the IHO prints over the water adjacent to a coast.

The question is whether that land territory generates maritime entitlement and, where those entitlements overlap those of another state, how the boundary should be delimited.

Türkiye has a serious argument that geography, relative coastal lengths and proportionality should reduce the effect of certain Greek islands in an eventual delimitation.

Make that argument.

I may disagree with how far Türkiye takes it, but at least we're discussing international maritime law.

But:

“The IHO calls this the Aegean, therefore Greece has no Eastern Mediterranean maritime entitlement”

isn't maritime law.

It's cartographic wordplay.

And your Libya point actually makes this even funnier.

Apparently Libya and Türkiye can face one another across hundreds of kilometres of Mediterranean while Crete—sitting physically between portions of those claimed maritime spaces—must politely close its eyes because the label on the water north of it says “Aegean.” 😂

That's quite an achievement.

So I'll happily accept the geography lesson.

In exchange, I'll offer a small legal one:

Sea names describe geography.
Coasts generate maritime entitlements.
Overlapping entitlements require delimitation.
And changing the label on the water does not move the land.
Now that we've solved where the Mediterranean is, perhaps tomorrow we can tackle the truly difficult question:
Where did Crete go on the Turkish maritime map? 😂
