text:
The Israeli Private Eye at the Heart of a Climate Hacking Scandal

Listen · 12:01 min
14OCT2026
By Karen Zraick and Gabby Sobelman
NYT Gift Article link
https://t.co/FIPCnUx7Jq
Karen Zraick reported from New York City and Gabby Sobelman from Haifa, Jerusalem and Tel Aviv.  This article is based on decades of court documents, business filings and interviews. 

He’s been linked to someone called “The Hawk.” He named his company “This Isn’t a Dentist’s Office.” The feds say he hacked American environmentalists.

For decades, an Israeli private investigator named Amit Forlit has operated on the edges of international intrigue while rubbing elbows with powerful figures.

Mr. Forlit claims to have served in Shin Bet, Israel’s internal security agency. He dated a prominent Israeli businesswoman and social-media figure who photographed him at exclusive parties. And he may or may not have inspired a hacker-for-hire character in a 2022 novel about murky financial shenanigans involving Argentine debt.

These were mostly bit parts in other people’s dramas. Until now.

Today Mr. Forlit, wearing an ankle monitor while remaining in the New York City area, awaits trial in a globe-spanning hacking case where he is the central character. Prosecutors with the Justice Department have charged him with overseeing an operation that aimed to discredit American environmentalists, allegedly on behalf of a huge oil company. He has pleaded not guilty.

Mr. Forlit could face decades in prison.

The charges, filed in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York, allege a “sprawling criminal enterprise” in which Mr. Forlit and his associates hired hackers in India to gain unauthorized access to the environmentalists’ private email accounts. Mr. Forlit’s lawyers have identified the oil company described in the allegations as Exxon Mobil, and the commissioning firm as DCI Group, a Washington public relations and lobbying firm.

Exxon and DCI have denied any role.

In a statement, Exxon said the company had “not been involved in, nor are we aware of, any hacking activities. If there was any hacking involved, we condemn it in the strongest possible terms.”

A spokesman for DCI, Craig Stevens, said the Justice Department had confirmed to DCI’s lawyers that it was “not investigating our firm or any of our employees” last year. “We direct all our employees and consultants to comply with the law, and allegations of DCI Group’s involvement with this activity, alleged to have occurred more than a decade ago, are false and unsubstantiated,” he said.

The case puts Mr. Forlit at the center of some of the most consequential legal battles the fossil fuel industry has faced. Dozens of states and cities are suing oil companies, including Exxon, claiming among other things that the industry misled Americans for decades about the climate and health damage caused by the burning of fossil fuels. If successful, the claims could cost the industry billions of dollars.

Prosecutors allege Mr. Forlit was part of an effort to stymie or kill these court cases.

Mr. Forlit, 58, was extradited to New York City from London this year. At a hearing in April in a Lower Manhattan courthouse, he cut an unassuming figure: tall with close-cropped, graying hair, wearing a short-sleeved blue button-down and spectacles. He ducked down to confer with his lawyer, Sabrina Shroff, who had recently made headlines for winning the acquittal of a man for throwing a sandwich at a federal officer in Washington.

Through Ms. Shroff and his Israeli company, the private-investigation firm Gadot Information Services, Mr. Forlit declined to speak to a reporter and Ms. Shroff declined to respond to a list of detailed questions.

This account of his career is based on decades of court documents in Israel and the United States as well as news reports, business documents, social media activity and interviews.

Mr. Forlit hails from the coastal city of Haifa, an important node in Israel’s vibrant tech industry. As a young man he served in the Shin Bet, the internal intelligence agency, from 1990 to 1997, according to a document from his legal team in the extradition proceeding, where he used the nickname Omer.

Mr. Forlit’s parents didn’t respond to requests for comment.

Many former intelligence agents become private investigators, and Mr. Forlit founded Gadot Information Services in Tel Aviv and Haifa in the 1990s. The company later opened two offices near Miami, according to Florida business records. At one point, he changed the names of both Miami offices to phrases in Hebrew that translate as “This Isn’t a Dentist’s Office” and “This Isn’t a Dentist’s Office Either.”

The firm offered “physical and electronic” security services and carried out asset tracing, litigation support and surveillance, and its clients included “top-tier law firms, lobbying companies and hedge funds,” according to a defense document filed in Britain.

Over the years, Mr. Forlit’s name popped up in a grab bag of news reports related to his career as a professional sleuth.

In 2012, an aspiring actress was quoted in a prominent Israeli daily saying Mr. Forlit had occasionally hired her to pretend to be a clubgoer in Tel Aviv nightspots to conduct surveillance of revelers of interest. In 2017, he was named in the Financial Times, the British business newspaper, as having played a role in tracking a businessman who had reportedly fled Kazakhstan.

Mr. Forlit had other business interests, commercial and legal records show. He was one of several parties involved in litigation around 2013 involving an allegedly faulty rocket-shaped amusement park ride and a 3-D goggle device at “Mini Israel,” one of Israel’s flagship theme parks, according to Israeli court records.

But by then, Mr. Forlit had begun leveling up.

Around 2008, he was introduced to a British private investigator who became a collaborator on international projects, according to a deposition in a U.S. lawsuit by Farhad Azima, an aviation executive who had accused Mr. Forlit of hacking in a civil case unrelated to Exxon. (The suit was later dismissed. Mr. Azima did not respond to a request for comment.)

Around 2015, Mr. Forlit was also hired for a project related to the Argentine debt crisis, according to the U.S. extradition request. The Wall Street Journal has reported that a novel about Argentine debt-recovery efforts, “Undermoney,” included a character that may have been based on Mr. Forlit.

Mr. Forlit started moving in elite circles in his private life. He dated Racheli Yifrach, a high-profile Israeli real estate agent, for about five years starting around 2015. Their outings included attending President Trump’s first inauguration, she said in a recent telephone interview.

In the interview, Ms. Yifrach described Mr. Forlit as “the smartest person I’ve ever met.” He “showed me the world,” she said.

Mr. Forlit, she said, enjoyed spy stories and thrillers, is a Bob Dylan fan and was great with children, including four of his own. In 2018, she said, she threw him a James Bond-themed party for his 51st birthday. Videos posted online show the couple celebrating with his friends and relatives.

The current indictment against Mr. Forlit was unsealed after he was extradited in April. It alleged that Mr. Forlit was hired in an effort to thwart the burgeoning field of climate change litigation in late 2015.

That same year, reporting published by the Los Angeles Times and Inside Climate News had detailed how Exxon and industry groups possessed in-depth knowledge of the dangers of global warming resulting from the burning of fossil fuels, but had publicly raised doubts about climate science and tried to block action on global warming.

That reporting was partly funded by the Rockefeller Family Fund, a philanthropic group run by the heirs of Standard Oil that focuses on climate change, among other issues. Lee Wasserman, who runs the fund, said in an interview that he received a notice from prosecutors that he was among those targeted by the hackers. The Rockefeller fund has also helped finance litigation against energy companies.

Mr. Forlit’s project was allegedly nicknamed “Fox Hunt” and involved sending a list of targets to a hacking group in India that used a technique known as “spear fishing.” The group sent emails to targets designed to get them to click and give up sensitive information like passwords, according to the extradition request.

The passwords were used to obtain nonpublic documents “which were provided to the oil and gas company and published as part of a media campaign to undermine the integrity of the civil investigations,” according to the extradition request, and used by the oil company in litigation.

The Rockefeller Family Fund had hosted a private meeting of climate activists in early 2016 to discuss strategy. An email containing a draft agenda for the meeting was leaked to the conservative website The Washington Free Beacon. The email was later used in climate litigation, including a petition to the Supreme Court.

Mr. Wasserman said the meeting was misconstrued in the reporting, which labeled it a “secret coordination effort” against Exxon.

Prosecutors said Mr. Forlit worked with another Israeli private investigator, Aviram Azari, who went by moniker “The Hawk.” Mr. Azari would later plead guilty to hacking charges in Manhattan, and served prison time before returning to Israel. Mr. Azari could not be reached for comment by phone or through the lawyer who had represented him.

Mr. Forlit orchestrated hacking crimes against more than 100 individuals, organizations and companies, according to the extradition request, and stole confidential business and personal information. According to the indictment, Mr. Forlit and others “generated tens of millions of dollars in unlawful proceeds” from their activities.

Jennifer Cunningham, a political consultant formerly of the firm SKDK who was once married to the former New York attorney general Eric Schneiderman, said she was also a victim of Mr. Forlit’s alleged hacking. Mr. Schneiderman’s successor, Barbara Underwood, sued Exxon in 2018, alleging the company had defrauded shareholders by downplaying climate risks, after a three-year investigation. Exxon had also sued to try to stop the investigation; New York’s lawsuit was later dismissed by a judge. Ms. Cunningham was an adviser to Mr. Schneiderman but had no formal involvement with climate litigation.

“I was furious,” to learn of the hacking from prosecutors, she said.

In a British court filing, Mr. Forlit had unsuccessfully argued that his extradition to the United States should be blocked because it was politically motivated. His lawyers called the prosecution “but one piece within a complex matrix of ongoing litigation on climate issues in the United States, which can only sensibly be seen as politically motivated, in the sense of being brought to pursue and further specific political agendas.”

Last month, Ms. Shroff asked for an extension to file pretrial motions, such as a motion to dismiss the case, because of the enormous quantity of data prosecutors were referencing — about four million pages, she wrote in a letter to Judge Jesse M. Furman. 

She was further hindered by Mr. Forlit’s limited abilities in reading English, she wrote.

The new deadline for defense motions is Nov. 10, and the next hearing is scheduled for Dec. 10.
Corrected on 
Oct. 14, 2026
: 
An earlier version of this article misstated the name of the Attorney General of New York who sued Exxon in 2018. It was Barbara Underwood, not Eric Schneiderman.

Karen Zraick covers legal affairs for the Climate desk and the courtroom clashes playing out over climate and environmental policy. 

Gabby Sobelman is a reporter and researcher for The Times, covering Israeli and Palestinian affairs, based in Rehovot, Israel.

A version of this article appears in print on Oct. 17, 2026, Section A, Page 1 of the New York edition with the headline: The Private Eye Alleged to Hack Climate Efforts.

text:
US: New York Gov. Kathy Hochul’s plan to open a computer chip plant outside Utica is raising concerns among federal officials who fear that China could gain greater access to advanced US technology.

Sources close to the Democratic governor told The Post Tuesday that she is in “advanced talks” with Solidigm, a subsidiary of South Korean chip giant SK Hynix, to open a semiconductor plant in Oneida County.

“There are red flags here with some yellow stars that the feds are really going to worry about,” quipped a federal official, who accused Hochul of being used to undermine US interests in the artificial intelligence arms race.

Hochul previously had an alleged Chinese spy, Linda Sun, as her deputy chief of staff from 2021 to 2023.

Sources expressed concern about the possibility that Chinese workers at the New York facility would give Beijing a “back door” to US technology and noted that the parent company wants to loosen new Trump administration export rules on chipmaking equipment that can be sent to China.

SK Hynix wants to condition the opening of a new US manufacturing facility on the Commerce Department granting export licenses for advanced equipment for use at a Chinese factory in Dalian, Reuters reported this month.

“It’s very clear why SK wants to do this deal. The Chinese are pressuring them,” said Leland Miller, who serves on the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission, a 12-person body formed in 2000 to advise Congress on national security concerns involving trade with China.

“[The Chinese] have been pressuring them for a long time in terms of their operations in China, and Beijing would like to see more of a buildout in China,” Miller said.

“The reason for this is that the Chinese absolutely want to catch up with the Koreans and Americans in terms of memory chip buildout.”

Hochul spokeswoman Kristin Devoe brushed off criticism, saying in an email that “projects like this are required to undergo a comprehensive federal national security review.”

“This company [Solidigm] was founded and is headquartered in the United States and is responding to a directive from the Trump Administration to build what would be America’s only domestic fab of its kind,” she added. “Reshoring this vital technology would mean THOUSANDS more American manufacturing jobs and chips made here instead of overseas.”

The Biden administration in December 2024 offered SK Hynix $458 million in grants and $500 in loans under the CHIPS Act to build a different manufacturing plant in Indiana, which remains under development.

Miller, who is also CEO of China Beige Book, which tracks Chinese economic data, said that the New York manufacturing facility would offer “a back door for the Chinese to be observing advanced memory capacity buildout in action.”

“All these facilities are going to have more advanced IP than what they’ve been exposed to thus far. So they will be moving the needle forward for China, no matter what. The question is how much,” Miller said.

“It’s very clear what’s driving this process. It’s an age-old problem where the Chinese put pressure on companies to say, ‘Look, we want this in return for that,’ and so the possibility that this is going to have negative effects based on exposure to IP is very, very high.”

Solidigm said in a statement that the company “regularly evaluates strategic alternatives to enhance its long-term competitiveness.”

“The company is currently exploring options for building a NAND memory fab at potential locations around the world, including the U.S. No decision regarding any specific course of action has been made,” the company said.

text:
Look closely at what is driving the headline S&P 500 earnings boom right now.   

In Q2 2026, Alphabet and Amazon booked a combined $152 billion in pretax gains on equity investments per their SEC 10 Q filings.     

Their combined operating income from actually running Google, YouTube, AWS, and Amazon retail that quarter was $68 billion.   

Paper investment gains were 2.2 times larger than what their massive core businesses actually earned from operations.   

Where did that $152 billion come from:
Almost entirely from unrealized markups on private company stakes.

• Amazon marked up its private Anthropic stake by $50.5 billion in a single quarter.
• Alphabet booked $77.4 billion in unrealized gains on non-marketable private shares plus $21.4 billion on other securities, driven primarily by SpaceX.    

In all of 2024, those two companies booked roughly $2 billion in combined investment gains. In the first half of 2026 alone, they booked $204 billion ($52 billion in Q1 plus $152 billion in Q2).   

Because GAAP rules force unrealized equity marks straight through the income statement, those private venture markups flow right into S&P 500 index earnings:

• S&P 500 Q2 2026 earnings growth as reported (FactSet): +52.0%
• S&P 500 earnings growth excluding Alphabet and Amazon: +33.8%   

A 33.8% growth rate is still strong, but more than 18 percentage points of the S&P 500 headline growth figure came from two tech giants marking up their private venture books.   

Never put a 25x public multiple on non cash private valuation marks. Separate real operating cash flow from paper accounting before you underwrite index multiples.

text:
Deserve Success: The Story of Wonthaggi Tech School, written and compiled by Glenn Sullivan.

Some books do more than preserve history. They honour the people, institutions and values that built our communities. Glenn Sullivan's Deserve Success is a wonderful example...

This beautifully researched and compiled history celebrates Wonthaggi Technical School, which served generations of young Australians from 1922 until 1988. Through historical records, photographs and personal recollections, Sullivan captures the character of a much-loved institution and its vital place in a proud coal-mining community.

What particularly resonates is the book's celebration of technical education, practical achievement and the dignity of meaningful work. Schools like Wonthaggi Tech offered generations of boys and young men pathways to competence, confidence, independence and productive lives... which we are now finding are essential to male flourishing.

The school's motto, Deserve Success, embodies timeless values of effort, discipline, perseverance and personal responsibility.

Sullivan deserves enormous praise for preserving this important educational and community heritage. His book is a labour of love, a valuable contribution to Australian history, and a timely reminder of the importance of vocational education.

An outstanding achievement. Highly recommended. Thank you Glenn.

Check it out at Amazon (and the author also has some hard copies, one of which I will treasure in my personal collection of books about men and boys):
https://t.co/OY9phgE5mG

text:
🏈HURTS IS DONE. MCLAURIN IS DONE. THE WIRE JUST CHANGED.
THE INJURIES
•Jalen Hurts. Blood clots. Out for the season. The reports say return in 2027, not this year. Tanner McKee is the starter. He went 26 of 45 for 215 and a score in the loss to Carolina. The Eagles schedule is soft for a few weeks. The roster is not. Barkley is still out with the hamstring. The offense is a backup quarterback and a void at running back.
•Terry McLaurin. Patellar tendon. Out for the year. Carted off Monday night. Diggs, Okonkwo, and Antonio Williams get the targets. Williams caught three of four for 50 after McLaurin left.
•Mike Evans. Achilles. Left Monday night and is expected to miss time. Deebo is already out for a couple of weeks. Christian Kirk is the name if he comes off IR. Brandin Cooks inherits the outside role in the short term.
•Davante Adams. Hamstring. On IR. At least a month. The Rams receiving room just got thinner.
•Lamar is still out. Huntley started and the Ravens lost 13-10 to Cleveland. Barkley has not practiced. Montgomery is out. The list is long.
THE WIRE
•Omar Cooper Jr. Jets. The most-added name. Big day against the Patriots. Immediate flex in deeper leagues if Mitchell stays out.
•Tanner McKee. The only quarterback who just became a starter for the rest of the year. Soft schedule coming. Not a long-term answer. A short-term one if you lost Hurts.
•Antonio Williams. Commanders. Next man up after McLaurin. Three catches for 50 on Monday. A stash until Diggs is full.
•Christian Kirk. 49ers. If Evans is out more than a week, Kirk is the add once he is active. The offense still has Purdy and McCaffrey.
•Jaylin Noel. Texans. Four catches, 107 yards, a score in London. Caught every target the last three games. Priority add if he is free.
STARTS / SITS
•Start McKee if you lost Hurts and the wire is empty. The next three games are Dallas, Washington, and the Giants.
•Start CMC. 16 carries, nine catches, two scores. The volume is still there even with half the receivers missing.
•Sit any Eagles running back not named Barkley. Pierce had the work. The offense scored 14.
•Start Diggs. McLaurin is gone. The targets have to go somewhere.
TRADE / DROP
•Buy Barkley if the owner is panicking. He is still the back. Hurts is not coming back. The price just dropped.
•Drop McLaurin. Season is over. Same for any handcuff you were holding for a player who is done.
•Sell the one-week spike only if someone is paying a starter for Cooper or Noel. The role is real. The 20-point day is one game.
THEORY Waiver priority is McKee if you need a quarterback, then Cooper, then Williams or Kirk depending on Evans. The trade is a low offer for Barkley while the Eagles look broken. The drop is McLaurin and any player whose season just ended. Not a sell. A map.

In the race for Governor, Byron Donalds leads Democrat David Jolly by 9 points, 49% to 40%. Meanwhile, incumbent Republican Senator Ashley Moody leads Democrat Angie Nixon by 8 points, 48% to 40%.

For Donalds, the results offer another encouraging sign as he campaigns on continuing Florida's conservative direction under Governor Ron DeSantis. His campaign has emphasized economic opportunity, public safety, parental rights, and maintaining Florida's reputation as a state that prioritizes individual freedom.

In the Senate race, Moody's lead reflects a favorable position heading into the final stretch. The former Florida Attorney General has emphasized law enforcement, border security, and conservative judicial principles throughout her political career.

Both Democratic candidates face significant challenges in this survey. Jolly trails Donalds by nearly double digits, while Nixon faces an eight-point deficit against an incumbent senator with established statewide name recognition.

While a single poll cannot determine the outcome of an election, these numbers show Republicans entering the closing stretch with advantages in both contests. With undecided voters still in play, the final weeks will be critical for all four campaigns.

text:
100% there are a LOT of people out of town, some using burner phones. If you are having work done as part of your quote package ask for Business, Licenses, Insurance and then do your research first. Roofing companies from out of town, Be careful, there will be no one around to warranty that work because they are leaving the area.
When roofers are done, DO NOT PAY them until your final inspection is completed and your permit is satisfied. You MUST pass the inspection before you pay them. NEVER EVER EVER hire anyone to do your roof WITHOUT a permit.
As a note if someone is doing tree work for you. Are they insured. You should check in case they drop a tree on your house, car, storage building, etc. You should also ask if they will be using heavy equipment and what damage that will cause to your yard, irrigation, etc. I have seen people have 1000 dollars worth the tree clearing and 2000 worth the damage.
I cannot stress enough, interior damage... are they qualified? Do they have photos, history you can look at, references. Sheet rock, wall, electrical shoddy work and they leave... you have to fix that after the fact.

IF ANYONE TELL YOU, I will pay you X to do your insurance work you should immediately send them walking. It is highly illegal. In Florida, it is a third-degree felony for a contractor to offer to waive your insurance deductible, refund part of the repair costs, or give you cash, kickbacks, or gifts in exchange for getting the contract or conducting an inspection. You do not after all you been through need an attorney to defend you for Insurance Fraud.

Be resourceful. If the deal is too good to be true, it probably is.

text:
$TRST Q3 2026 earnings: TrustCo lending profit rises, but buybacks trim its capital cushion

TrustCo Bank Corp NY, the parent of upstate New York and Florida lender Trustco Bank, widened its lending spread while its share buybacks reduced its capital cushion. Net interest income rose 9% from a year ago to $47 million as older mortgages rolled into higher rates, lifting its net interest margin to 2.95%. Chief executive Robert J. McCormick kept the bank on pace to buy back two million shares this year.

• Net interest income: $𝟒𝟕.𝟎𝐌 (+9.1% from a year ago)
• Net interest margin: 𝟐.𝟗𝟓% (+0.16 percentage points from a year ago)
• Diluted profit per share: $𝟏.𝟎𝟐 (+18.6% from a year ago)
• 2026 share buyback plan: 𝐔𝐧𝐜𝐡𝐚𝐧𝐠𝐞𝐝 (500K shares left for Q4 by our math)

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: 🟢 Bullish

The story got better because loan repricing and faster loan growth expanded the lending margin by 0.08 percentage points from last quarter even though deposit costs stopped falling. One caution: operating expenses topped management's raised ceiling again, and nonperforming loans in Florida rose 39% from a year ago while buybacks pushed the equity-to-assets ratio down to 9.72%.

The question now is whether loan turnover can keep expanding the margin if deposit costs start rising and credit or overhead costs take a bigger bite. Either higher mortgage yields carry the margin past 3%, or sticky deposit rates and rising expenses cap profit growth once the current buyback finishes in December. Fourth-quarter deposit rates and the 2027 capital plan will tell.

Full article with charts - link in bio

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢🟢 𝐎𝐥𝐝𝐞𝐫 𝐌𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐠𝐚𝐠𝐞𝐬 𝐑𝐨𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐈𝐧𝐭𝐨 𝐇𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐑𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐬 𝐋𝐢𝐟𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧
TrustCo makes most of its money from the spread between what it earns on home mortgages and what it pays on customer deposits. Chief executive Robert J. McCormick said "favorable repricing of the Bank’s nearly $5.5 billion loan portfolio" drove the quarter, as older loans with low interest rates paid off and the bank lent the cash out at higher rates.

• Net interest margin (the profit spread on lending): 2.95%, up 0.08 percentage points from last quarter and 0.16 points from a year ago
• Average interest rate earned on residential mortgages: 4.21%, up from 4.12% last quarter and 4.00% a year ago
• Average rate paid on interest-bearing liabilities (mostly customer deposits): 1.79%, unchanged from last quarter and down from 1.90% a year ago
• Net interest income: $47.0 million, up 9.1% from a year ago and 3.2% from last quarter

The jump of 0.08 percentage points in the lending spread was the largest quarterly gain in a year. That matters because the bank achieved it without any new help from lower deposit costs, which stayed at 1.79% for a third straight quarter. Loan rates alone carried the improvement.

What to watch: the average interest rate on residential mortgages and the cost of time deposits (certificates of deposit, or CDs) in the fourth-quarter report. Further gains in mortgage yields while deposit costs stay near 1.79% would show the margin can reach 3% on loan turnover alone.

🟢 𝐋𝐨𝐚𝐧 𝐆𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐭𝐡 𝐊𝐞𝐩𝐭 𝐈𝐭𝐬 𝐏𝐚𝐜𝐞 𝐄𝐯𝐞𝐧 𝐀𝐟𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐑𝐞𝐟𝐢𝐧𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐒𝐥𝐨𝐰𝐞𝐝
A growing loan book gives TrustCo more balances that earn current interest rates. After a strong second quarter that benefited from an early wave of mortgage refinancing, the question was whether lending would slow down. Instead, the bank added $77.1 million to its period-end loan balances in the third quarter, more than double the $35.1 million it added in the same quarter last year, by our math.

Total loans ended September at $5.45 billion, up 5.1% from a year ago. Average home equity credit lines (loans backed by a borrower's home equity) grew 11.4% from a year ago to $490.3 million, and average residential mortgages rose 4.0% to $4.59 billion. Because loan growth sped up for a fourth straight quarter, interest income on loans grew 8.8% from a year ago.

What to watch: period-end total loan balances in the fourth-quarter release, alongside the seasonal dip in the loan pipeline that TrustCo noted when reducing its reserve for unfunded commitments by $200 thousand. A fourth-quarter loan addition below last year's $60.7 million would show that higher mortgage rates are finally cooling demand.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴 𝐁𝐮𝐲𝐛𝐚𝐜𝐤𝐬 𝐂𝐮𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐒𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐂𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭 𝐛𝐲 𝟏𝟎% 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐓𝐫𝐢𝐦𝐦𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐂𝐚𝐩𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐂𝐮𝐬𝐡𝐢𝐨𝐧
TrustCo has made share buybacks its main tool for lifting per-share profit, while critics point out that the purchases draw down its capital ratios and cost well above book value. In the third quarter the bank bought back another 500 thousand shares, bringing its nine-month total to 1.5 million shares. That cut the average diluted share count by 9.9% from a year ago and turned a 6.5% rise in net income into an 18.6% jump in diluted earnings per share, to $1.02.

The balance sheet shows the price of that boost. By our math from the treasury stock line, TrustCo spent $29.0 million on third-quarter buybacks, or $57.91 per share — more than 1.5 times its $38.20 book value per share. Because cash left the bank at a premium to book value, shareholders' equity fell to 9.72% of total assets, down from 10.05% in June and 10.90% a year ago.

What to watch: the ratio of shareholders' equity to total assets after the remaining 500 thousand shares in the 2026 plan are bought in the fourth quarter, and whether the board authorizes a new buyback for 2027. A drop below 9.5% equity to assets would test how far management is willing to shrink its capital buffer.

🔴 𝐎𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐂𝐨𝐬𝐭𝐬 𝐓𝐨𝐩𝐩𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐑𝐚𝐢𝐬𝐞𝐝 𝐓𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐭 𝐀𝐠𝐚𝐢𝐧
After operating expenses ran above plan in the second quarter, management raised its quarterly target for recurring noninterest expense (operating costs excluding foreclosed real estate) to $27.3–27.8 million. In the third quarter those costs came in at $28.03 million, beating the ceiling in the wrong direction for a second straight quarter.

Total noninterest expense rose 6.8% from a year ago to $28.02 million. The biggest move came in "other" operating expenses, which rose to 4.4% of total net revenue from 3.5% a year ago (+0.9 percentage points, by our math), while outsourced services and equipment costs also climbed. Salaries and employee benefits eased slightly from the second quarter to $12.78 million, or 24.6% of revenue.

What to watch: fourth-quarter noninterest expense excluding foreclosed property against the $27.3–27.8 million range. A third straight reading above $27.8 million would show that the bank's cost base has stepped up permanently to around $112 million a year.

🔴 𝐁𝐚𝐝 𝐋𝐨𝐚𝐧𝐬 𝐢𝐧 𝐅𝐥𝐨𝐫𝐢𝐝𝐚 𝐊𝐞𝐩𝐭 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐰𝐡𝐢𝐥𝐞 𝐂𝐫𝐞𝐝𝐢𝐭 𝐑𝐞𝐬𝐞𝐫𝐯𝐞𝐬 𝐀𝐝𝐝𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐨 𝐂𝐨𝐬𝐭𝐬
"Asset quality metrics remain stable and well covered by reserves," TrustCo wrote in its release. The bank recorded $30 thousand of net loan recoveries across the company, and total nonperforming loans (loans no longer paying interest) dipped slightly from June to $21.1 million, or 0.39% of total loans.

Underneath that total, two numbers moved the other way. Nonperforming loans in Florida rose for a fifth straight quarter to $4.99 million, up 13.1% from June and 39.0% from a year ago by our math. In addition, the provision for credit losses jumped to $850 thousand from $250 thousand a year ago (taking 1.1 percentage points more of revenue), which TrustCo attributed to "loan growth and changes in forward looking economic assumptions". Reserve coverage of nonperforming loans stood at 261.8%, down from 280.8% a year ago.

What to watch: Florida nonperforming residential mortgages in the fourth-quarter report and the detail on loans in foreclosure in the upcoming quarterly filing. Another double-digit rise in Florida nonaccruals would show that regional housing pressure is still building.

🔴 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐤𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐝𝐢𝐝𝐧'𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐰𝐞𝐫
Two standing concerns about deposit funding and interest-rate exposure depend on tables that only appear in the quarterly Form 10-Q filing.

• Exposure to rising interest rates: overall cost of interest-bearing liabilities stayed flat at 1.79% for a third quarter, while the maturity schedule for its $2.30 billion of time deposits and the updated interest-rate shock table will arrive in the third-quarter 10-Q.
• Deposit competition by account type: time deposit costs edged down 0.02 percentage points from last quarter to 3.34%, but the rate paid on interest-bearing checking accounts rose from 0.20% to 0.23% and money market balances shrank by $9.2 million; the 10-Q will show current CD offer rates and retention.

👓 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐬

𝐓𝐫𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐂𝐨 𝐑𝐚𝐢𝐬𝐞𝐝 𝐈𝐭𝐬 𝐃𝐢𝐯𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐧𝐝 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐀𝐝𝐝𝐞𝐝 𝐎𝐧𝐞 𝐁𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐡
The board raised the quarterly cash dividend by 5.3% to $0.40 per share, or $1.60 a year, up from $0.38 in the prior six quarters. Because per-share profit grew faster than the payout, the dividend payout ratio stood at 38.6%, down from 43.7% a year ago. Separately, full-service banking offices ticked up by one from June to 133, though still down from 136 a year earlier.

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐀𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐠𝐞 𝐭𝐨𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐝𝐞𝐩𝐨𝐬𝐢𝐭𝐬 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟓.𝟕𝟑 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
Average customer deposits rose $229.6 million, or 4.2%, from a year ago, faster than the 3.8% pace in the second quarter. Time deposits (CDs) led the increase, rising $162.1 million on average to $2.29 billion, while non-interest-bearing demand deposits grew $32.6 million to $825.2 million, giving the bank cash to fund loan growth without adding borrowings.

𝐍𝐨𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐭 𝐢𝐧𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐞, 𝐞𝐱𝐜𝐥𝐮𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐞𝐪𝐮𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐠𝐚𝐢𝐧𝐬 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟒.𝟕𝟔 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
Fee income from customer services and wealth management rose 1.6% from a year ago but fell 6.0% from the second quarter. Headline noninterest income dropped 18.5% from last quarter because the second quarter included a one-off $844 thousand gain from a Visa share exchange, compared with just $56 thousand of equity gains this quarter.

𝐂𝐨𝐫𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞 𝐛𝐨𝐧𝐝𝐬 𝐚𝐯𝐚𝐢𝐥𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐬𝐚𝐥𝐞 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟕𝟕.𝟒 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
TrustCo nearly doubled its holdings of corporate bonds from $39.8 million a year ago (+94.6% by our math) while letting U. S. government-sponsored enterprise bonds run down from $51.6 million to $9.9 million. That shift lifted the average yield on its available-for-sale bond portfolio to 3.15% from 2.91% a year ago.

— • — • —

🔮 𝐆𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞

𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐒𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐑𝐞𝐩𝐮𝐫𝐜𝐡𝐚𝐬𝐞 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐠𝐫𝐚𝐦: 𝟐.𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞𝐬 (𝟑.𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐚𝐜𝐫𝐨𝐬𝐬 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟓–𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔)  ⇒ stable
🠆 unchanged from 2.0 million shares (3.0 million across 2025–2026)
Unchanged. The savings bank said it remains "On pace to complete the repurchase of a total of three million shares, or 15.8%, of TrustCo common stock by the end of 2026". Having bought 1.0 million shares in 2025 and 1.5 million in the first nine months of 2026, that leaves 500 thousand shares for the fourth quarter by our math, matching its third-quarter pace.

𝐍𝐞𝐭 𝐈𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐭 𝐈𝐧𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐞 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐍𝐞𝐭 𝐈𝐧𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐞 𝐎𝐮𝐭𝐥𝐨𝐨𝐤: 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐮𝐞𝐝 𝐠𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐭𝐡 𝐢𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐬  ⇒ stable
🠆 unchanged from Sustainable improvement in coming quarters
Unchanged. TrustCo repeated its qualitative forecast that ongoing loan repricing and deposit growth position it to "generate continued net income and net interest income growth in the coming quarters", with positive momentum into 2027. The bank does not issue dollar ranges for revenue or profit in its earnings releases.

— • — • —

❓ 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

𝐖𝐡𝐲 𝐝𝐢𝐝 𝐨𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐜𝐨𝐬𝐭𝐬 𝐛𝐞𝐚𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐫𝐚𝐢𝐬𝐞𝐝 𝐜𝐞𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐚𝐠𝐚𝐢𝐧?
Recurring noninterest expense excluding foreclosed property was $28.03 million, above the $27.3–27.8 million range set in July. Was the overrun driven by stock-linked incentive pay or permanent overhead?

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐢𝐬 𝐝𝐫𝐢𝐯𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐚𝐝𝐲 𝐫𝐢𝐬𝐞 𝐢𝐧 𝐅𝐥𝐨𝐫𝐢𝐝𝐚 𝐛𝐚𝐝 𝐥𝐨𝐚𝐧𝐬?
Florida nonperforming loans rose for a fifth straight quarter to $4.99 million, up 39% from a year ago. How much of that balance is already in foreclosure, and does management expect any losses?

𝐖𝐡𝐞𝐫𝐞 𝐢𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐜𝐚𝐩𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐟𝐥𝐨𝐨𝐫 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐛𝐮𝐲𝐛𝐚𝐜𝐤𝐬?
Shareholders' equity to assets has fallen from 10.90% to 9.72% in a year as the bank bought shares at more than 1.5 times book value. At what equity-to-assets ratio will the board slow or stop buybacks?

𝐀𝐭 𝐰𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐭 𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐬 𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐦𝐚𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐂𝐃𝐬 𝐫𝐞𝐧𝐞𝐰𝐢𝐧𝐠?

text:
@kroger , after five years of employment, I am devastated and disappointed by my experience attempting an interstate transfer from Colorado to California.

I've dedicated five years to this company, and with my relocation approaching in early November, I hoped to continue my employment within the Kroger family of stores.

Unfortunately, navigating a transfer between divisions and states has been incredibly frustrating.

I understand stores have different staffing needs and hiring processes. I never expected a guaranteed position because I've worked for the company for five years.

What I did expect was basic communication and follow-through.

I've spent weeks researching positions, submitting applications, contacting stores, and attempting to speak with management about transferring.

I've received conflicting information about whether stores are hiring. I've been told a location wasn't hiring despite seeing advertised positions. I recognize postings aren't always current, but the lack of clarity makes it difficult to know what opportunities exist.

Getting in contact with management has been another challenge.

I've repeatedly encountered busy phone lines and difficulties reaching the store. When you're coordinating an interstate move, unreliable communication creates unnecessary stress.

After speaking with a store leader, I was informed there might be an opportunity to transfer into bakery or deli.

I was told I would receive a follow-up call.

That call never came.

I've continued trying to reach the store, only to encounter busy lines again.

I understand management is busy. I work in retail myself and know how demanding daily operations can be.

But when someone promises a callback, I believe they should make an effort to follow through.

I've signed my lease, arranged my move, and am preparing to leave Colorado in early November.

Time matters.

I cannot indefinitely wait for information about a potential transfer while securing employment in a new state.

What makes this disheartening is that I genuinely wanted to remain with Kroger.

Five years is a significant amount of time to dedicate to an employer. I've developed skills, built relationships, taken on responsibilities, and worked hard to support my department.

I wasn't asking for preferential treatment, demanding a position, or expecting the company to rearrange its staffing.

I was simply asking for an opportunity to discuss a transfer and receive clear communication.

Thankfully, I've already accepted another employment offer in California, so I'm not entirely dependent on this transfer.

However, that doesn't make this experience any less disappointing.

I hoped there would be a more coordinated process for employees relocating between Kroger divisions.

Instead, I've felt left to navigate the situation independently, with little clarity about what happens next.

There is room for improvement in how interstate and interdivisional transfers are handled, particularly regarding communication, access to hiring managers, and reliable follow-up.

Employees who want to continue their careers within the company shouldn't feel discouraged because they're moving across state lines.

I'm not writing this to attack individual employees or managers. I understand many people are doing their best under difficult circumstances.

I'm sharing this because the experience has been upsetting, and I hope the company recognizes how important communication is during these transitions.

After five years with Kroger, I wanted to leave Colorado feeling supported in my attempt to continue with the company. Instead, I'm leaving this process feeling overlooked and deeply disappointed.

I would appreciate clarification from @Kroger regarding how interstate transfers between divisions are supposed to work and what employees can expect.

Five years of service may not guarantee a transfer, but I believe it should warrant a clear response.

I truly expected better.

text:
THE GECKO’S EXTRAORDINARY GIFT
How Microscopic Foot Hairs Reveal the Wonders of God’s Creation

Scripture: Psalm 104:24; Proverbs 30:24–28; Colossians 1:16–17 (NIV)
THE LITTLE CREATURE THAT DEFIES GRAVITY
Imagine a tiny lizard racing across a ceiling, hanging upside down without falling, then effortlessly lifting its feet and disappearing into the darkness.

No glue. No suction cups. No claws gripping the ceiling.

Instead, the gecko possesses one of nature’s most extraordinary biological adaptations: millions of microscopic structures that harness molecular forces invisible to the human eye.

Scientists have studied this remarkable ability for decades. Their discoveries have even inspired technology designed for spacecraft.

For Christians, this little creature offers an invitation to contemplate the astonishing complexity of creation and the wisdom of its Creator.
1. THE INVISIBLE SECRET BENEATH ITS FEET
Geckos possess specialized toe pads covered with microscopic, hairlike structures called setae.

Each seta branches into hundreds of extraordinarily tiny, flattened tips called spatulae, some approximately 200 nanometers wide.

These structures create intimate contact with surfaces, allowing weak molecular attractions known as van der Waals forces to work together.

Individually, these forces are incredibly small. Combined across millions of contact points, they become powerful enough to support the gecko’s weight.

Even more remarkable, the animal can release its grip almost instantly by changing the angle of its toes.

The gecko is not defying physics. Its remarkable feet are utilizing physics with extraordinary efficiency.

Research published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences in 2005 also demonstrated that gecko foot hairs possess natural self-cleaning properties. After becoming dirty, their gripping ability can recover within several steps. 

PMC
+1

2. FROM A LIZARD’S FOOT TO OUTER SPACE
In Pasadena, California, engineers at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory investigated how this natural adhesive system could inspire spacecraft technology.

In August 2014, researchers tested gecko-inspired grippers during brief periods of weightlessness aboard an aircraft.

Their experimental devices could grasp objects without conventional glue or suction.

NASA reported these developments in December 2014 and August 2015.

Potential applications included capturing orbital debris, servicing satellites, and securing equipment inside spacecraft.

What began as an investigation into a small reptile became an extraordinary example of biomimicry: human engineering learning from biological structures.

The research illustrates how studying creation can reveal solutions to problems far beyond the creature’s natural environment. 

NASA
+2

3. THE WISDOM OF GOD IN SMALL THINGS
Thousands of years before modern microscopy, biblical writers recognized that small creatures could reveal profound wisdom.

Proverbs 30:24–28 describes four small creatures whose remarkable behaviors invite careful observation.

Among them is the lizard, capable of entering even royal palaces.

The passage was not written as a scientific explanation of gecko adhesion. Its original purpose was to teach wisdom through observations of nature.

Nevertheless, its spiritual lesson remains striking.

Something does not need to be enormous to deserve our attention.

Psalm 104:24 celebrates the countless works of God, declaring that He made them all in wisdom.

The microscopic structures beneath a gecko’s feet remind believers that extraordinary wonders exist in places easily overlooked.
4. THE CREATION THAT POINTS TO CHRIST
Colossians 1:16–17 teaches that all things were created through Christ and for Him, and that in Him all things hold together.

This passage proclaims Christ’s supremacy over creation. It is not a scientific explanation of molecular adhesion.

Yet the spiritual connection is meaningful.

The natural world operates through intricate physical relationships that science continues to investigate.

Christian faith sees creation as ultimately dependent upon God, while science investigates the mechanisms through which natural phenomena occur.

The Father is honored as Creator, the Son as the One through whom creation exists, and the Holy Spirit as the giver of life (Genesis 1:2; Psalm 104:30).

Scientific discovery need not diminish wonder. It can deepen our appreciation of what remains to be explored.
5. THE SPIRITUAL LESSON OF HOLDING FAST
A gecko’s grip offers a memorable illustration of perseverance.

Its attachment depends upon countless tiny points working together.

Likewise, Christian maturity develops through prayer, Scripture, obedience, fellowship, and daily dependence upon God's grace.

Jesus taught His disciples to remain in Him, comparing their relationship to branches abiding in a vine (John 15:4–5).

Our spiritual security does not come from microscopic forces or human ingenuity. It comes through Christ and His faithful love.

The gecko provides an illustration, not a biblical promise or proof of divine intervention.

Still, its remarkable abilities can encourage humility, gratitude, and reverence.
CONCLUSION: NOTHING TOO SMALL FOR WONDER
A tiny creature walks across a ceiling. Scientists uncover an invisible world. Engineers discover possibilities for exploring space.

And believers are reminded that creation contains wonders extending far beyond ordinary human perception.

May every discovery deepen our gratitude to the Father, our devotion to Jesus Christ, and our openness to the wisdom of the Holy Spirit.

REFLECTION QUESTIONS
1. What overlooked wonders of creation could inspire greater gratitude toward God?
2. How does the gecko’s remarkable design encourage humility about human knowledge?
3. What daily practices help you remain faithful to Jesus Christ?
CLOSING PRAYER

Heavenly Father, thank You for the astonishing beauty and complexity of Your creation. Open our eyes to wonders we so easily overlook. Lord Jesus, strengthen our faith and teach us to remain in Your love. Holy Spirit, fill us with wisdom, humility, and gratitude. May everything we discover lead us toward deeper worship and faithful service. All glory belongs to You, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, forever. In Jesus’ precious name, Amen.

text:
Kava bars have been opening in North Carolina and across America with increasing popularity over the last decade. The beverage, a lightly intoxicating alternative to alcohol, is made by grinding up dried kava root, mixing it with water, and straining the liquid contents into a bowl. It has a bitter taste that numbs the mouth and produces a pleasant euphoric effect.

Moon and Root is a fantasy-themed kava bar in downtown Asheville. The bartenders dress like Game of Thrones characters. The “Kava Names” they adopt add to the immersion of the venue and offer a pseudo-anonymity to its regular patrons. There’s a young goth lady I would see there named Moonraker, for instance. I’m pretty sure that’s not the name on her birth certificate. It’s like club kids in the early 2000s calling themselves DJ so-and-so or Downtown Eric. Elysium is the owner of Moon and Root, but his real name is Lewis Easton Cantwell. I never use his real name. I didn’t even know it until he was doxxed, canceled, and publicly denounced by half the city.

Before opening up Moon and Root, Elysium served five months in a federal prison in Kentucky for his role in the J6 protests.

Elysium was 35 years old on January 6, 2021, employed as a network engineer, and the proud owner of a new kava establishment. Though largely apolitical, he had taken a stand against the system when he refused to go “takeout only” during COVID, feeling that, as a veteran, the government had overreached. He kept the place open, and business boomed, much to the chagrin of his competitors, who leaned far to the left.

Elysium’s girlfriend’s dad, a staunch Trump supporter, was on his way to DC to attend the J6 protests. Despite his stand against COVID mandates, Elysium had no desire to overthrow the U.S. government.

“My girlfriend thought it would be a good bonding experience,” recalled Elysium.

“Makes sense,” I said. “What could go wrong?”

“I was there, but I never made it inside the building,” Elysium confesses on a recent afternoon over a cup of chilled kava. He brews it strong and flavorful. We drink it straight from corrugated coffee cups. The earthy flavor of the root makes me grimace ever so slightly with each sip, but challenges me to take another. The way whiskey used to challenge me with its burn to the back of the throat.

After a couple weeks of patiently sipping this stuff without feeling much effect beyond the numbing of the lips, I’m starting to understand why people drink it. A calm buzz. Proof, I figured, that I’d developed the famous “reverse tolerance” kava drinkers always talk about.

Elysium shows me a video from the day of the protest in which he’s visible on the porch of the Capitol building. In the footage, a crowd of protesters push up against a phalanx of riot police. He stands near the front of the scrum, but far enough back to avoid making direct contact with the officers.

The tragic irony, of course, is that Elysium’s business would be fine if he only catered to MAGA Republicans. But he didn’t, that’s not his style, and so he built up a customer base of the very people who would eventually turn on him.

“I was trying to get them to calm down and stop pushing because a lady had fallen over and was getting crushed by the door,” he claims. “I never even set foot inside the Capitol building.”

While Elysium never touched the door or engaged in any physical contact with a federal agent, his repeated shouts to “hold the door” that the officers were trying to close resulted in a lengthy list of charges: civil disorder, obstruction of an official proceeding, entering a restricted building or grounds, disorderly conduct in a restricted building or grounds, disorderly conduct in a Capitol building or grounds, parading/demonstrating/picketing in a Capitol building, and the big one: obstructing or impeding a Capitol Police officer. The final charge is the felony he was sentenced for, alongside the litany of misdemeanors.

“I went to prison for my words,” says Elysium.

Shortly after it all went down in DC, a rival business owner posted videos of Elysium at the Capitol all over Facebook and Twitter. According to Elysium, he inserted the hashtag @FBI in every comments section. Posing as a concerned citizen, he allegedly called the FBI anonymous tip line.

On February 14, just over a month after the protest, Elysium said an armada of 23 U.S. Marshals, FBI agents, and local police showed up in ten vehicles, stormed the kava bar, and arrested him. He surrendered voluntarily and without incident. Wouldn’t you know it, the local news just happened to be present at the time. They plastered his face all over the media along with the long list of charges. That well-publicized fiasco made evicting him and shutting down the kava bar, despite the illegal breach of contract, all the easier. The man’s a deplorable insurrectionist, out on probation for the felony of trying to overthrow the U.S. government. What’s he gonna do, sue you?

After 2 years of pretrial probation, during which time he lost his job, land, business, and was evicted from his home, Elysium faced years in prison before a plea bargain. Because he had no prior criminal record, is a veteran, and was able to pay his attorney $112,000 (with the proceeds from the sale of 17 acres and a liquidated 401(k)), the sentence was reduced to five months in federal prison plus 36 months of work release and probation post-incarceration.

Elysium reported to federal prison in Ashland, Kentucky.

“The prison was a converted basketball arena. It was over a hundred cots lined up next to each other on the court, with the empty seats of the stadium surrounding us. I could reach out my hand from my cot and easily touch over half a dozen other prisoners if I wanted to. That’s illegal, by the way,” recounts Elysium.

There were also the roaches.

“They crawled on you at night,” he said. “They scurried across your face. At first I tried squashing them, but there were too many; you had to make peace with it.”

“How does one make peace with cockroaches?” I asked, glancing around the Moon and Root and taking another sip of kava.

“You just had to close your eyes, keep your mouth closed, and hope they didn’t nest in your ear. One prisoner had a roach crawl into his ear canal, where it died. He said he could hear it chirping even after the nurse removed it with tweezers.”

“How was the food?” I asked.

“Infested with roaches and spiders. The mashed potatoes had maggots. Mostly dead. You learned to eat around them. But occasionally you’d get one that was still alive, slithering around.”
“Did you throw it away or complain?” I asked.

"You just ate around it.”

After his release, Elysium started to put his life back together. He distanced himself from politics, founded Moon and Root, and eventually got a girlfriend. For years he stayed busy and kept his head down. Then, years later, on May 15 2026, he was accused of being an antisemite by Citizen Times.

Titled, “Asheville kava bar owner called out for following racist social media,” the piece noted that, “His Instagram account for Moon & Root, @moonandroot.apothecary, at some point followed a racist and antisemitic Instagram page. The profile picture for the account is a racist caricature of a man with a hooked nose, and the account features a wide variety of antisemitic videos that explicitly attack the Jewish people. A personal Instagram account that Cantwell confirmed belonged to him followed right-wing commentator Tucker Carlson, Libs of TikTok and an account that featured videos of protestors being injured.”

Elysium himself had posted nothing antisemitic. The mere fact that he followed three right-wing accounts was apparently newsworthy information. The story appeared all over my social media feed and featured Elysium’s photo alongside the fact that he was a J6 protester who had served time in prison. The message was clear. Get him.

text:
"Well, I better get going."

If you're from the Midwest, you know that means at least 45 more minutes.

Last month, my friend from Minnesota came to my parents' house for dinner.

Nobody warned me. Japanese goodbyes are also endless.

9:00 PM
"Well, I better get going."
(He did not get going.)

9:20 PM
"Well, I really better get going."
He accepts more tea.

9:45 PM
Shoes on. At the door. He and my father discuss the weather for 25 minutes.
They do not share a language.
They both agree it's "not bad."

10:05 PM
My mother offers him leftovers.
In Japan, you politely refuse three times.
In Minnesota, also three times.
Problem: every time he refuses, my mother adds another container.
He arrived with nothing. He is now holding seven containers.

10:20 PM
He takes his shoes off. He needs the bathroom.
(We are back to the beginning.)

10:45 PM
Shoes on again. "Okay. I'm really going now."
My mother: "Have some fruit."
He has some fruit.

11:00 PM
He's in the car. Window down. Still talking.
My mother hands him an eighth container through the window.

11:10 PM
He finally drives away.

In Japan, you wave until the car is out of sight.
In Minnesota, you wave back until the house is out of sight.

He stops at the end of the street and waves.
My parents wave back.
He flashes his hazard lights.
My father flashes the porch light.
A neighbor comes out to see what's going on. The neighbor waves.
Everyone is now waving at everyone.

11:40 PM
My father goes inside.
Not because it's over. Because his arm hurts.

The next morning, my friend texted me:
"Your mom is basically from Minnesota."

Then my mother walked in.

"He forgot his umbrella."

He's coming back tonight.

Pray for us.

The goal is to move these innovations toward human trials while developing treatments that could cost substantially less than current standards of care.

When an entrepreneur prospers, it is because they have offered people something worth the money they paid for it. Consumers—of their own free will—purchase a product that provides them with benefits; the entrepreneur gains, and society advances. In this process, there is no exploitation—only mutual gain.

text:
Sony pulled Cyberpunk 2077 from the PlayStation Store a week after launch. Six years later, CD Projekt is using a Netflix anime to sell that same game again, and it has the receipts to show the playbook works.

Cyberpunk: Edgerunners 2 premiered on Netflix on Tuesday, all ten episodes at once. CD Projekt scheduled a free game update, Update 2.5, for October 22, two days after the premiere, with content inspired by the show.

That timing is the whole strategy, and the studio learned it the hard way.

Rewind to December 10, 2020. Cyberpunk 2077 launched as one of the most anticipated games of its era and sold 13 million copies in about two weeks. The console versions were full of bugs. On December 17 Sony removed it from the PlayStation Store and offered every digital buyer a full refund.

CD Projekt shares fell as much as 20% in a single day, per CNBC, and the company had lost around $1.4 billion in market value since release. US shareholders sued over the console claims, and the case settled for $1.85 million.

The game stayed off the PlayStation Store for six months, until June 21, 2021.

Then came September 2022. Patch 1.6, the Edgerunners update, shipped on September 6. The anime, made with Japanese studio TRIGGER, landed on Netflix a week later.

The effect showed up within two weeks. Cyberpunk hit 136,724 concurrent players on Steam, more than 7x its August high, per Axios. By September 28 the game had passed 20 million copies sold. On the Q3 2022 call, Adam Kiciński told investors the goal was "transmedia synergy" between the show and the game, and that it worked well.

Today Cyberpunk 2077 has sold over 40 million copies and the Phantom Liberty expansion has sold 15 million, per CD Projekt's first half 2026 report. In July, peak concurrent players on Steam passed 100,000 again, the highest since October 2023.

On the September earnings call, joint CEO Michał Nowakowski said season one "led directly to a visible spike in game sales." Edgerunners 2 exists to bring players back to Night City.

So the studio is running the 2022 play on purpose. Show on Tuesday, free update on Thursday. A six year old game gets a second launch in front of an audience that arrives through Netflix.

For founders, that is the real lesson. A product people wrote off found new buyers through a story told somewhere else.

A week after launch, Sony took it off the shelf. Six years later, Netflix is the shelf.

text:
Been seeing some people object to the idea of the Steelers trading for Chris Godwin this year because of his contract situation, but that shouldn't really be much of a hurdle if the Steelers wanted to pursue him.

The Steelers currently have a little over $14.5 million in available cap space for this season. If they traded for Godwin today, they would still need to pay his remaining $14.2 million in base salary for 2026, and that number goes down about $1.3 million every week he doesn't get traded between now & the deadline, so PIT can afford him this year, especially if they wait closer to the deadline to make the deal.

As for what's left on his contract passed this season, all he has that the Steelers would be on the hook for is his $20.5 million base salary next year IF the team were to choose to pick up the club option that he has going into next offseason. If they were to decline his team option, he would become a free agent next spring & the Steelers wouldn't have any dead cap charge.

Now, I don't necessarily think the Steelers are interested in trading for a veteran WR because I don't think they want to essentially bench Michael Pittman Jr., who they paid $24 million in fully guaranteed money to this offseason, and Roman Wilson, who was playing at a WR3 level before his injury. Put on top of that the emergence of Germie Bernard of what looks like a legit WR2, and I'm not sure the 'need' at WR here in Pittsburgh is as big as some make it out to be.

What could potentially change that thinking is if either DK or Germie gets hurt before the deadline or MPJ ends up getting season-ending surgery on his injured foot, in which case I would happily offer a 5th round pick in exchange for Godwin's services & likely decline the club option next offseason unless he absolutely balls out down the stretch.
